papers.title: Cautious Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient Methods
papers.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are indispensable tools for modeling complex phenomena in physics and engineering. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional numerical solvers by directly incorporating physical constraints into neural network loss functions. Despite their advantages, PINN training requires multi-objective optimization, which often leads to significant gradient conflicts among boundary, initial, and residual loss terms. The Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient (ConFIG) method addresses these conflicts; however, integrating ConFIG with adaptive optimizers such as Adam introduces a critical vulnerability: the conflict-free direction generated by ConFIG is further processed by the optimizer, and the resulting weight update may no longer be conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. To address this issue, Cautious ConFIG is proposed as a concise three-line extension to the ConFIG algorithm that empirically restores the conflict-freeness guarantee prior to the weight update. The method is evaluated on three PINN benchmarks: the 1D Viscous Burgers' equation, the 1D Nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements over the standard ConFIG baseline. Additionally, the stabilizing effect of cautious masking and its reaction to conflict severity, task number, and optimizer lag are investigated using a simple toy system.

papers.intro:
Partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely applied in physics Sommerfeld (1949), chemistry Jamwal et al. (2025), engineering Ames (1965), and finance Duffy (2013) to model complex phenomena that evolve over space and time. These equations implicitly define a function of several variables, and solving a PDE with given initial and boundary conditions involves determining this function. Traditionally, PDEs and their initial boundary value (IBV) problems are solved using numerical methods that discretize the domain into a finite set of subregions. The solution function is then represented as a set of values corresponding to these subregions. For example, the PDE can be reformulated as a time-stepping rule by approximating partial derivatives with finite differences. Discretization may introduce artifacts, particularly for complex geometries, and the number of subregions can increase exponentially with the number of dimensions, a phenomenon known as the curse of dimensionality Bellman (2015). Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) Raissi et al. (2019) have gained significant attention in recent years by directly parameterizing the solution function with a neural network. This approach mitigates discretization errors and alleviates the curse of dimensionality. As a mesh-free method, it is well-suited for complex geometries. Furthermore, formulating IBV problems as neural network training enables the utilization of recent advances in deep learning architectures and optimization techniques. However, PINNs also present limitations, as deep learning methods are less well-understood regarding error analysis and generalization compared to classical numerical approaches. While numerical methods reliably yield solutions when conditions such as the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy criterion Courant et al. (1952) are satisfied, training a neural network in a high-dimensional loss landscape can be unpredictable. One notable challenge in PINN training is gradient interference. Each IBV condition is formulated as a separate loss function, and the resulting gradients can interact adversely, severely hindering convergence. The ConFIG method Liu et al. (2025) was developed to address the gradient interference problem by computing an update direction that is conflict-free with respect to all task gradients. However, the ConFIG direction typically serves as an input to another optimizer, such as Adam Kingma and Ba (2014), and the resulting update direction may not remain conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. Consequently, the conflict-freeness property is often lost before the weight update is applied. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce Cautious ConFIG, a simple three-line extension compatible with any ConFIG-optimizer combination. It incurs negligible computational overhead, is easily parallelizable on the GPU, and effectively restores ConFIG’s mathematical properties. • We evaluate Cautious ConFIG on three challenging PINN benchmarks: the 1D viscous Burgers equation, the 1D nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow, observing substantial performance improvements over the baseline (19% to 28% relative improvement). • We analyze the effectiveness of Cautious ConFIG by monitoring key metrics during PINN training and present a computational model demonstrating that Cautious ConFIG produces update directions that align more closely with task gradients under conditions of severe conflict, numerous tasks, and significant optimizer lag.

papers.title: Concentrated Causal Influence, Distributed Diagnostic Information: Cognitive Impairment Decisions in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.

papers.title: Triplon dynamics from partial Kondo screening in frustrated heavy-fermion systems
papers.abstract: The partially disordered (PD) phase, in which magnetically ordered and Kondo-screened sites coexist, has been proposed as a possible ground state of geometrically frustrated heavy-fermion systems. We investigate its dynamical properties in the half-filled periodic Anderson model on a triangular lattice by calculating the dynamical spin susceptibility within the random-phase approximation built on a self-consistent Hartree-Fock solution. We show that successive quantum phase transitions from the Kondo-insulating phase to the PD phase and to a magnetically ordered phase are driven by the condensation of triplon modes originating predominantly from the Kondo-screened sites. In the PD phase, magnons and triplons coexist and hybridize, leading to characteristic level repulsion in the excitation spectrum. These results reveal how triplet excitations evolve into collective magnetic modes across the successive phase transitions and highlight the dynamical interplay between magnetic order and Kondo screening in frustrated heavy-fermion systems.

papers.intro:
Rare-earth compounds exhibit a rich variety of correlated-electron phenomena arising from the interplay between conduction electrons and localized magnetic moments. Two competing mechanisms emerge from this interplay. One is the Kondo effect, in which conduction electrons screen localized magnetic moments through the formation of Kondo singlets [27, 54]. The other is the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction, whereby conduction electrons mediate effective exchange interactions between localized moments and promote magnetic ordering [41, 22, 53]. The competition between Kondo screening and the RKKY interaction lies at the heart of heavy-fermion physics [7] and has long served as a paradigmatic framework for understanding emergent quantum phases and quantum criticality, including unconventional superconductivity and non-Fermi-liquid behavior [30, 12].

Geometrical frustration can further enrich the competition between Kondo screening and magnetic ordering. While frustration in localized-spin systems is often relieved through the formation of noncollinear magnetic orders [3] or exotic quantum states such as valence-bond solids [2], resonating-valence-bond states [5], and quantum spin liquids [51, 46], heavy-fermion systems, in contrast, possess an additional mechanism for relieving frustration through on-site Kondo screening. This extra degree of freedom may stabilize a partially disordered (PD) state schematically shown in Fig. 1(a), in which a subset of local moments is quenched by Kondo screening while the remaining moments participate in magnetic order [28]. Indeed, such states have been experimentally observed in geometrically frustrated heavy-fermion compounds, including CePdAl, which hosts a distorted kagome lattice of Ce ions [1, 29, 37, 32, 9], and UNi4B, which contains a triangular-lattice arrangement of U ions [31, 35, 13, 14, 42, 36, 52, 47, 50, 19, 17, 40]. However, the microscopic origin and stability of the PD state remain subjects of active debate.

To address this issue, extensive theoretical studies have been carried out using microscopic models for heavy-fermion systems. Among them, the periodic Anderson model (PAM) [4], which incorporates both the hybridization between conduction and localized electrons and the on-site Coulomb repulsion of localized electrons, has served as a minimal framework for describing the competition between Kondo screening and magnetic ordering. In the limit of strongly localized ff electrons, the PAM reduces to the Kondo-lattice model (KLM) [45], which has also been widely employed to investigate the PD state. Various theoretical studies have reported the stabilization of the PD state as a ground state in frustrated heavy-fermion models [33, 15, 16, 34, 6, 23]. A variational Monte Carlo study has provided evidence for a PD ground state in the KLM [33], whereas the PD state has been obtained within self-consistent Hartree-Fock calculations and cluster dynamical mean-field theory in the PAM [6].

Since the PD state is characterized by the coexistence of magnetically ordered and Kondo-screened sites, its theoretical description requires both an appropriate treatment of quantum fluctuations associated with Kondo screening and sufficient spatial resolution to capture the underlying site-dependent order. Simultaneously satisfying these requirements remains a challenging task, and consequently the stability of the PD state can depend sensitively on the theoretical approach employed. Furthermore, understanding the dynamical properties of the PD state is equally important. While previous studies have primarily focused on its ground-state properties, collective excitations provide complementary insights into the nature and stability of the underlying order. Specifically, two of the three sublattices develop collinear Néel order, whereas the remaining sublattice remains Kondo-screened. We further elucidate the evolution of the collective excitation spectrum in the PD phase and identify a previously unexplored instability toward a nine-sublattice magnetic order. Furthermore, we find hybridization and level repulsion between triplon and magnon modes in the PD phase, revealing a nontrivial coupling between magnetically ordered and Kondo-screened sites. papers.title: Search-Based Testing of Modality Sensitivity in Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process images and text jointly, yet robustness evaluations often perturb these inputs separately or assess only predefined corruption levels. Such evaluations provide limited evidence of which modality is more susceptible to perturbations and whether smaller changes across both modalities can jointly expose failures. We present MoST, a black-box testing framework that characterizes modality sensitivity by comparing image-only, text-only, and joint perturbations. MoST uses multi-objective search to select and combine perturbations and adjust their severity, seeking prediction degradation while limiting changes to images and prompts. We evaluate MoST on four VLMs performing object localization on ImageNet and driving images. The models exhibit distinct sensitivities: textual perturbations dominate for some, whereas others are susceptible across both modalities. In several configurations, joint perturbations match or exceed the effectiveness of single-modality perturbations with smaller modifications to each input. In a human study, 60-76% of assessments across models judge the perturbed inputs sufficiently understandable to perform the task, and human localization is more accurate than that of the corresponding VLMs. These results show that evaluating modalities separately can overlook failure-inducing combinations and that modality sensitivity provides a more detailed account of VLM robustness than aggregate failure rates alone.

papers.intro:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) combine visual observations and natural language to perform tasks such as object localization, visual question answering, and scene understanding (Zhang et al., 2024). Their application to autonomous driving and other safety-critical settings requires systematic evaluation of their behavior under degraded inputs (Zhou et al., 2024; Orjuela et al., 2026). Prediction quality depends on both the information available in each modality and the model’s ability to interpret the two inputs jointly.

Their application to autonomous driving and other safety-critical settings requires systematic evaluation of their behavior under degraded inputs (Zhou et al., 2024; Orjuela et al., 2026). Prediction quality depends on both the information available in each modality and the model’s ability to interpret the two inputs jointly.

Visual and textual inputs can deteriorate independently or simultaneously. Images may be affected by adverse weather, sensor noise, motion blur, or compression artifacts (Lambertenghi et al., 2025). Textual instructions may contain transcription errors introduced by speech recognition (Ahlawat et al., 2025), as well as spelling errors, ambiguity, or changes in meaning introduced by users or upstream components. Evaluating these conditions requires distinguishing susceptibility to visual perturbations, textual perturbations, and their combination. This distinction can help developers identify which input conditions require additional testing and mitigation.

Evaluating these conditions requires distinguishing susceptibility to visual perturbations, textual perturbations, and their combination. Existing robustness evaluations commonly measure performance under predefined corruption levels or assess perturbations to individual modalities (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019; Sui et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2024). Although these evaluations quantify performance degradation, aggregate scores can conceal differences in the perturbations required to expose failures. Two models with similar failure rates may differ substantially in their susceptibility to image and text modifications. Moreover, perturbing both modalities may expose failures with smaller changes to each input than perturbing either modality alone.

papers.title: From Freehand Demonstrations to Autonomous Robotic Ultrasound: An Anatomy-Anchored Learning Framework
papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.

papers.intro:
Ultrasound is one of the most widely used medical imaging modalities owing to its real-time imaging capability, non-invasive nature, portability, and relatively low cost [1]. It plays an important role in a broad range of diagnostic and interventional procedures. However, conventional ultrasound scanning remains highly operator-dependent. This dependence on individual skill can lead to considerable variability in image quality and examination outcomes, limiting the standardization and accessibility of ultrasound imaging [2]. Robotic ultrasound offers a promising solution to these challenges by enabling precise, repeatable, and consistent probe manipulation [3]. Nevertheless, autonomous ultrasound scanning is difficult to achieve using manually designed control strategies alone. Many scanning skills rely on subtle adjustments learned through extensive clinical experience. Such expert behaviors are often difficult to formulate explicitly as predefined trajectories or control laws [4]. Robot learning, and imitation learning in particular, therefore provides a promising framework for acquiring ultrasound scanning skills directly from expert demonstrations and transferring them to autonomous robotic systems.

Imitation learning enables robots to acquire control policies directly from expert demonstrations by learning a mapping from sensory observations to robot actions [5]. Early approaches commonly formulated this problem as behavior cloning [6], in which a policy is trained to reproduce the actions demonstrated under corresponding observations. More recently, generative visuomotor policies have substantially improved the ability to model complex and multimodal robot behaviors, such as Diffusion Policy [7] or Flow-based policies [8, 9]. In parallel, vision-language-action models have incorporated pretrained vision-language representations and large-scale robot datasets to improve semantic reasoning and generalization across manipulation tasks [10, 11].

Their observations commonly include one or more third-person or wrist-mounted camera views together with robot states, such as joint configurations or end-effector poses [12], while force or tactile measurements may additionally be used for contact-rich tasks [13]. Such observations are well suited to manipulation, where the identities, positions, and spatial arrangements of objects can vary substantially across demonstrations and deployment environments. External vision provides the global scene context required to interpret these variations, while robot states are often represented in a global or robot-base coordinate frame to relate the end effector to the surrounding workspace [14].

Unlike general manipulation, robotic ultrasound is an anatomy-conditioned and locally constrained interaction once the probe has been initialized at the target anatomical region. At this stage, continuous third-person observations may provide limited additional information for probe navigation. They also introduce dependence on the workspace configuration. These setup-specific dependencies complicate demonstration collection and can limit generalization across environments and robotic platforms. We therefore argue that external vision is better used for anatomical localization and initial probe placement, rather than as a continuous observation during scanning.

However, removing third-person vision does not imply that ultrasound images alone provide a sufficient representation of the scanning process. Unlike conventional RGB videos, ultrasound images do not directly depict the motion of the probe relative to the patient. Each frame represents a two-dimensional cross-section of three-dimensional anatomy, and out-of-plane probe motion cannot be reliably tracked based only on ultrasound images. Ultrasound feedback alone therefore provides an incomplete and potentially ambiguous representation of probe motion and spatial context.

We decompose autonomous ultrasound scanning into two phases: an anatomy-guided, rule-based probe initialization phase and a learned probe navigation phase. During initialization, anatomical feature detection is used to place the probe at a scan-specific starting pose. Once stable contact has been established, the learned policy takes over and performs local probe navigation using four complementary modalities: ultrasound images, a probe-mounted wrist-camera view, contact force, and probe pose relative to an anatomical anchor. The ultrasound image provides direct information about the internal anatomy, while the wrist camera captures the local interaction between the probe and the scanning region, including probe motion relative to the patient surface. Force measurements characterize the contact condition, which strongly affects both image quality and tissue deformation.

papers.title: Automated Fetal Magnetocardiography Reconstruction Using a Biophysical Forward Model
papers.abstract: Objective: Fetal magnetocardiography (fMCG) enables early detection of cardiac disease by non-invasively measuring fetal electrophysiological activity. However, current signal estimation methods for fMCG require complex, labor-intensive human processing because they rely on blind source separation or template-based projection techniques. Methods: We propose an automated signal reconstruction approach that recovers fetal and maternal cardiac activity from fMCG measurements without manual annotation. Our approach leverages the relationship between measurements and cardiac signals via a biophysically grounded forward model that represents cardiac sources as time-varying magnetic dipoles. This enables reconstruction of physiologically interpretable three-dimensional vectorcardiographic signals along with their spatial position. Results: Validation on synthetic data with known ground truth confirms accurate recovery of cardiac source parameters. On real fMCG recordings, the reconstruction shows strong agreement with established reference methods. Conclusion: The proposed forward-model approach automatically reconstructs fetal and maternal cardiac activity from fMCG recordings and produces signals in an interpretable vectorcardiographic source domain. Significance: Automated, interpretable fMCG reconstruction could make fetal cardiac assessment more reliable and support potential translation into prenatal care.

Prior work on fetal signal extraction used blind source separation approaches, such as Independent Component Analysis (ICA), to decompose the measured field into source components [Esc+25, Wur+23, WSW22a, Str+20, Str+20a, Mur+15, YW11, Ara+05]. These approaches assume statistical independence between fetal and maternal signals. This drives the decomposition into statistically rather than physically determined components and typically fragments each cardiac source across multiple components (see Supplement 2 for illustration). As a result, the morphology of the extracted signals lacks a consistent physical interpretation and varies between recordings. This necessitates manual processing during reconstruction, annotating the extracted components as maternal, fetal, or noise, which is time-consuming and prone to error. Applying ICA across all spatial axes (x,y,z)(x,y,z) also ignores the explicit vectorial field information that could guide a biophysically grounded separation. Other work applied spatial filtering methods [Esc+18, WH17, CVW06] to suppress or enhance signal components based on their alignment with spatial target structures. To construct signal and interference subspaces from noisy data, these approaches typically rely on manual template selection or on averaging spatial structures from hundreds to thousands of heartbeats, which neglects variation within and between beats. However, neither approach explicitly models the relationship between the measured magnetic field and the underlying cardiac sources.

papers.title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions.

papers.intro:
Post-training is a primary driver of capability gains in large language models (Ouyang et al., 2022), and its paradigms differ along two axes: whether training trajectories come from the model itself, and how dense the learning signal is. Supervised finetuning (SFT) imitates curated demonstrations, providing dense token-level targets on teacher-forced trajectories the model never visits at inference, which induces exposure bias (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024) and erodes existing capabilities (Shenfeld et al., 2026b). Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on the model’s own rollouts (Guo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024), avoiding this mismatch but compressing supervision into a single scalar per trajectory. On-policy distillation (OPD) combines the two: the student samples its own trajectories, and a teacher supplies dense next-token targets at the states it visits (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for a stronger teacher by constructing teacher and student from the same parameters under asymmetric conditioning (Zhao et al., 2026a; Shenfeld et al., 2026a). Across this progression, external supervision is relocated rather than removed: SFT requires reference solutions, RLVR gold answers, OPD a stronger teacher, and OPSD a privileged context, typically the ground-truth solution.

In language models, self-training is an established approach to self-improvement (Zelikman et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024; Zuo et al., 2025). The model solves problems, filters its solutions by agreement with a reference answer or its own majority vote, and is finetuned on those it retains. These methods, however, still train on a curated problem set, which must be collected anew for every task (Singh et al., 2024). Yet a language model can pose problems, not only solve the ones it is given (Zhao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). Therefore, we investigate whether a language model can self-train without labels or a curated problem set, requiring only topic descriptors from which it generates its own training problems.

In this work, we propose On-Policy Self-Training (OPST), an approach to self-train a language model with dense supervision derived from self-generated privileged information (Figure 1). We remove both ground-truth answers and the curated problem set: conditioned only on a coarse topic descriptor, the model synthesizes both a query and the privileged information (PI) used to train on it. Since the generated question-answer pairs are no longer human-curated, the quality of this data can be noisy. Hence, we filter the generated data along two axes: Pseudo-verification ensures that a problem is well-formed, requiring the model to reproduce its answer in a fresh context and under a paraphrase. Further, we apply a consensus gate to ensure that the problem is informative, discarding problems whose answer the student already consistently reproduces across on-policy rollouts. Because the gate is evaluated against the current student, the difficulty of the retained curriculum implicitly evolves as the student model improves. On the quality-filtered samples, we train the model with on-policy self-distillation (Figure 2), where the teacher provides high-quality token-level supervision to the student, limiting catastrophic forgetting of existing capabilities acquired from supervised data (Shenfeld et al., 2026b; Shenfeld et al., 2026a). In this work, we propose On-Policy Self-Training (OPST), an approach to self-train a language model with dense supervision derived from self-generated privileged information (Figure 1). We remove both ground-truth answers and the curated problem set: conditioned only on a coarse topic descriptor, the model synthesizes both a query and the privileged information (PI) used to train on it. Since the generated question-answer pairs are no longer human-curated, the quality of this data can be noisy. Hence, we filter the generated data along two axes: Pseudo-verification ensures that a problem is well-formed, requiring the model to reproduce its answer in a fresh context and under a paraphrase. Further, we apply a consensus gate to ensure that the problem is informative, discarding problems whose answer the student already consistently reproduces across on-policy rollouts. Because the gate is evaluated against the current student, the difficulty of the retained curriculum implicitly evolves as the student model improves. On the quality-filtered samples, we train the model with on-policy self-distillation (Figure 2), where the teacher provides high-quality token-level supervision to the student, limiting catastrophic forgetting of existing capabilities acquired from supervised data (Shenfeld et al., 2026b; Shenfeld et al., 2026a). This asymmetry is crucial in a purely synthetic setting. The student’s supervision is therefore extended by what the teacher can infer from the privileged, generated context, exceeding what the generated answer alone provides. Iterating this loop improves the model over successive rounds, while an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher stabilizes against self-induced distribution drift.

papers.title: Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.

papers.intro:
Quantitative measurements are essential components of clinical image interpretation. Anatomical dimensions, lesion diameters, and ventricular volumes provide objective information for diagnosis, disease characterization, and longitudinal follow-up [1, 2]. In ultrasound (US), obtaining these measurements often requires identifying anatomical landmarks and manually positioning calipers or tracing anatomical boundaries. These procedures increase examination workload and are subject to intra- and inter-observer variability [3, 4]. Deep learning has therefore been widely investigated to automate US measurement, with promising results in anatomical segmentation, landmark localization, and quantitative cardiac assessment [5, 6, 2]. Nevertheless, many existing systems operate on predefined anatomical targets and output schemas [7, 8, 9].

Advances in biomedical visual question answering and radiology report generation demonstrate the potential of a shared vision-language backbone to support diverse image interpretation tasks [10, 11, 12]. Realizing this capability, however, requires accurate numerical prediction alongside language generation.

A central challenge lies in the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based output modeling, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Clinically relevant quantities, such as distances and diameters, are continuous variables, whereas autoregressive VLMs typically represent numerical values as token sequences and optimize their likelihood through categorical next-token prediction. Although language models can learn numerical relationships, this objective does not explicitly account for the magnitude of numerical errors [13, 14]. For example, depending on the tokenizer, the value ’10.1’ may be decomposed into ’10’, ’.’, and ’1’, each generated sequentially. Such a representation does not explicitly preserve numerical proximity: similar values may have different tokenizations, and token-level prediction errors do not directly reflect distances between the corresponding values. For caliper-based measurements, small perturbations in endpoint coordinates should produce correspondingly small changes in the measured length; however, conventional token-based prediction does not explicitly enforce this geometric relationship. Errors in individual digits or decimal placement can also substantially alter the predicted value, potentially compromising measurement precision. Furthermore, token-by-token generation for inferring numerical values can introduce cumulative errors, hindering precise diagnostic measurements.

Our objective is to support multiple quantitative measurement tasks through a common language-conditioned interface while retaining the numerical precision required for meaningful image assessment. The shared architecture enables task conditioning through text prompts and joint learning across measurement targets. The main contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce HAD-VLM, a unified framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous diffusion-based prediction for prompt-conditioned US measurement. • We develop a five-tuple measurement representation and a coordinate-length consistency mechanism to couple anatomical localization with numerical estimation. • We evaluate the framework across multiple US measurement tasks and analyze the effects of cross-task learning, continuous prediction, and the hybrid architecture on measurement accuracy and language performance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to introduce a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion formulation for quantitative US measurement, targeting precise numerical prediction while preserving the flexible language capabilities of VLMs within a single unified model. Specifically, we evaluate the framework in both ultrasound and X-ray imaging to examine its applicability across modalities. These findings support the potential of HAD-VLM for accurate, language-guided quantitative medical image assessment.

papers.title: Image Morphology of Misaligned Magnetically Arrested Disks
papers.abstract: Horizon scale images probe the plasma dynamics and spacetime in the vicinity of accreting black holes. Interpreting these images requires models that connect image morphology to the structure of the underlying accretion flow. Disk misalignment is expected in many systems, yet most horizon scale image analyses assume that the emitting flow is aligned with the black hole spin. We investigate whether tilted accretion flows produce image features distinguishable from axisymmetric flows and whether their effects can be absorbed by changes in aligned model parameters. Using general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of tilted magnetically arrested disks spanning black hole spins $a^*=-0.9375$ to $0.9375$ and initial disk tilts $0^\circ$ to $30^\circ$, we generate synthetic images and quantify their morphology through fits to an aligned, semi-analytic emission model. Using this approach, we show that high spin prograde models show little sensitivity to disk tilt, as the inner emitting flow aligns with the black hole spin. In contrast, retrograde tilted disks develop warped, non-axisymmetric inner structure that distorts the inner shadow and strongly alters image morphology. While the aligned semi-analytic model reproduces most prograde images well, retrograde tilted disk images are fit less accurately and yield biased inferred parameters, especially for spin. The image morphologies indicate that tilt affects horizon scale images only when misalignment survives into the near horizon emitting region, motivating image models that include disk tilt as an explicit degree of freedom when alignment is uncertain.

papers.intro:
Accretion disks around black holes are often modeled under the assumption that the disk angular momentum is aligned with the black hole spin axis. Such alignment, however, may not be generic. In the context of supermassive black holes (SMBHs), misalignment could be a natural outcome of their evolution. Tidal disruption events can supply material to the SMBH at random orientations relative to the spin axis, while SMBH mergers can reorient the spin of the remnant relative to gas supplied on larger scales by the host galaxy [16]. Although tidal interactions eventually tend to align a tilted disk [39], for TDEs these alignment timescales can be comparable to the system’s observational lifetime [41, 17], and for SMBHs, repeated merger events can generate recurrent tilted disk configurations [26].

Observations of both X-ray binaries and active galactic nuclei support the possibility of disk misalignment. In both systems, observations suggest that the large scale accretion disk may not always be aligned with the black hole spin axis, assuming that the misaligned jet traces the spin direction [37, 27]. In some AGN, reflection spectroscopy further reveals warped disk geometries consistent with misaligned accretion flows [31]. Additionally, some quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) have been interpreted with models that invoke disk spin misalignment [23].

Misaligned accretion disks exhibit a broad range of phenomena not present in their aligned counterparts. Misalignment induces nodal precession of particle orbits through the Lense-Thirring effect [28], with a characteristic rate that scales steeply with radius and linearly with spin, Ω∝a∗/r3\Omega\propto a^{*}/r^{3}. As a result, a tilted disk composed of noninteracting rings would undergo differential precession, twisting and warping the flow [36].

Real disks, however, couple neighboring annuli through internal stresses. This response depends on disk thickness, where thin disks can undergo Bardeen-Petterson alignment, in which the innermost disk aligns with the black hole spin while the outer disk remains misaligned [1]. Thick disks, in contrast, can support standing bending wave patterns in which the misalignment varies with radius [24]. GRMHD simulations of thick tilted disks also show high density plunging streams and standing shocks near the black hole [15]. The associated shock heating can raise the inflow temperature and dominate the resulting emission signatures [7].

Magnetic field structure can significantly alter the dynamics of tilted disks. In magnetically arrested disks (MADs) [22, 34], magnetic flux accumulation can power jets that torque the inner accretion flow and align to the black hole spin axis, especially for rapidly spinning black holes [29, 42]. Additionally, some MAD simulations exhibit little or no disk precession, as the disk is dominated by magnetic stresses [5]. The MAD alignment behavior contrasts with tilted standard and normal evolution (SANE) disks [35, 40], which generally show global precession and do not show strong alignment near the black hole [45, 42].

They find a warped and non-axisymmetric disk and jet due to Lense-Thirring precession alongside increased variability and an increase in the 2.2 μ\mum flux density with tilt. These trends are consistent with the findings of [46], which study a similar a∗=0.9a^{*}=0.9 SANE tilted disk. papers.title: The Galactic Center Reference Frame: A 30-Year Solution
papers.abstract: Stellar orbits probe the metric of and mass around the Sgr A* massive black hole. To enable study of the black hole, the surrounding mass, and tests of gravity, a precise reference frame must be established and maintained. We present an updated stellar maser-based reference frame for the inner parsec of the Galactic Center, referenced to the radio continuum of Sgr A*. This work synthesizes 30 years of astrometric observations of 15 SiO stellar masers and the Sgr A* continuum at 43 GHz. The uncertainty in the mean offset of the maser ensemble from Sgr A* is 0.08 mas in the current epoch and will decay to 0.10 mas by 2030. At a distance of 8.2 kpc, these correspond to position uncertainties of 0.6 AU and 0.8 AU, respectively, which is similar to or smaller than the stellar SiO-emitting region. The mean maser proper motion uncertainties are 0.05 mas yr$^{-1}$ in RA and 0.08 mas yr$^{-1}$ in Dec, corresponding to 1.8 km s$^{-1}$ and 3.2 km s$^{-1}$. The reference frame stability between IR and maser astrometry is 10~$μ$as yr$^{-1}$ (0.40 km s$^{-1}$) in RA and 15 $μ$as yr$^{-1}$ (0.57 km s$^{-1}$) in Dec. The masers show substantial variability in flux density and velocity structure, most notably IRS~7, which shows a 30-fold brightening in a blueshifted component since 2022. This variability may set a floor on future astrometry improvements and especially measurements of radial acceleration.

papers.intro:
Near-infrared observations of the orbits of stars close to Sgr A* conclusively demonstrated the presence of a massive black hole in the center of the Galaxy [20, 19]. This work relied on an astrometric reference frame enabled by simultaneous radio observations of stellar masers and the Sgr A* radio continuum [36, 45, 46]. Since the black hole was not historically visible in the near-IR imaging, measuring the offsets between IR-bright stars and Sgr A* required an intermediate step, relying on the simultaneous radio detection of Sgr A* and masers associated with a subset of the IR-detected stars. The angular offsets of IR-bright SiO maser-emitting stars from the ∼\sim1 Jy Sgr A* continuum, along with the masers’ proper motions, provide an astrometric reference frame for the orbital solutions of stars much closer to the massive black hole than the maser-emitting stars [36, 45, 46, 53, 41, 47, 11, 27]. This reference frame places Sgr A* at rest and at the coordinate origin, which is also the phase center for the radio interferometry.

This reference frame places Sgr A* at rest and at the coordinate origin, which is also the phase center for the radio interferometry.

While the GRAVITY interferometer operating at ESO’s VLTI can now detect Sgr A* in the near-IR continuum [22], it is still important to be able to refer IR positions to Sgr A* via the maser astrometry. The GRAVITY science fiber FWHM is ∼\sim74 mas in K-band [23]; stars at larger separations from Sgr A* thus continue to rely on imaging data obtained at the adaptive optics resolution and referencing positions via the maser stars. It is now also possible to address how well the positions of the mass (as measured by orbits), the near-IR emission of Sgr A*, and the radio emission of Sgr A* coincide. The Event Horizon Telescope map of Sgr A* shows an asymmetry, and one assumes that the mass is located near the center (and not the centroid) of the luminous ring [16]. Further, it is not obvious that the near-IR emission – either in the quiescent state or during flares – is centered on the mass. It is also likely that the unresolved 43 GHz radio continuum does not coincide at some level with the IR emission or the mass; the question is at what scale the standard assumptions break down.

The stars close to Sgr A* probe the black hole metric. So far, only effects of order β2\beta^{2} (β=v/c\beta=v/c), such as Schwarzschild precession [22], have been detected. These effects rely solely on the black hole mass, but in the next order in β\beta, the equations of motion contain a term that is sensitive to black hole spin, commonly referred to as Lense-Thirring precession. Measuring this effect requires stars on orbits with very small pericenter distances. The recent discovery of such a star, S-301, whose pericenter distance of 1.4 mas is roughly an order of magnitude smaller than that of S-02, could enable spin measurements of Sgr A* in the coming decades [1, 40, 48]. It is therefore important to be able to pinpoint the black hole mass location for such close flybys. At the fourth order, β4\beta^{4}, a quadrupole term enters the equations of motion. In general relativity, this term is fully determined by the black hole spin (assuming no charge), a consequence of the no-hair theorem [51, e.g.,]. Hence, measuring both spin and quadrupole moment constitutes a test of fundamental physics, but it requires proper motion measurements below 10 μ\muas yr-1 [51]. Applying analytical estimates from Will [51] to the orbit of S-301, we estimate Lense-Thirring precession rates of roughly 6 μ\muas yr-1 and quadrupolar precession rates of 0.2 μ\muas yr-1 assuming a black hole spin parameter χ=0.9\chi=0.9 [10].

Astrometric SiO maser observations have been ongoing for nearly three decades. While proper motions and the reference frame stability improve over time as t−3/2t^{-3/2}, assuming regular sampling, the flip side of this benefit is that astrometric solutions that are not updated will decay as time passes because the uncertainty cone grows over time. In this work, we update the reference frame and estimate its future decay. Section II describes the data sources, observations, and reduction used to form a 30-year astrometric solution for 15 SiO stellar masers. Section III outlines the astrometric methods that are described in detail in Darling et al. [11]. Section IV presents the improved astrometry and highlights the substantial variability in the maser spectra. We discuss the implications of the new reference frame and its decay over time in Section V, and we compare the maser-based reference frame to the Hosek et al. [27] HST-Gaia reference frame in Section VI. Section VII summarizes this work and discusses the future outlook for precise astrometry in the Galactic Center.

papers.title: Overview of Enhanced D-alpha and Quasi Continuous Exhaust H-modes at DIII-D
papers.abstract: We review the Enhanced D-alpha (EDA) and Quasi-continuous Exhaust (QCE) H-modes that have recently been achieved in the DIII-D tokamak. These scenarios are free of large type-I edge-localized modes (ELMs) and achieved at high fueling compatible with divertor detachment. This makes them promising operational regimes as ELMs are a major risk for fusion pilot plants (FPPs). Access to EDA H-mode and the associated quasi-coherent mode (QCM) was observed at low heating power barely above the L-H power threshold, and increased density enabled access to EDA H-mode even at higher heating powers. The QCE H-mode was achieved at simultaneously high density and heating power, characterized also by a QCM and small ELMs with transient peaks of the total power into the divertor below about 3MW, in line with observations at ASDEX Upgrade. During the QCE H-mode, the turbulence parameter alpha_t at the separatrix is about 1 and does not separate ELMy or EDA from QCE H-modes well. Peeling ballooning stability calculations suggest that the EDA H-mode pedestal is limited by transport far away from ideal magnetohydrodynamic instability, and the QCE H-mode pedestal operates close to the ballooning branch of the stability boundary. BOUT++ simulations qualitatively reproduce the pressure collapse characteristics of the different regimes and suggest an important role of n ~ 50 resistive ballooning modes localized near the separatrix at the X-point during EDA and QCE H-modes. This work provides a foundation and guidance for further research on the access conditions and physics mechanisms of EDA and QCE H-modes necessary for the extrapolation of these regimes towards an FPP.

papers.title: DRAMA-Eval: A Benchmark for Context-Aware, Multi-Turn, Multi-Speaker Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in speech generation are shifting toward context-aware, multi-turn, and multi-speaker synthesis. While these capabilities are in high demand for applications such as audiobook and audio drama production, evaluation has not kept pace with these advances. Beyond traditional zero-shot Text-to-Speech (TTS), modern systems in this domain primarily fall into three categories: instruction-controllable generation models, multi-turn dialogue models, and the audio branches of audio-visual generation models. However, existing benchmarks evaluate these paradigms in isolation, failing to provide a unified assessment of context modeling, instruction following, and multi-speaker generation. Meanwhile, recent progress in audio understanding models has made it feasible to evaluate such complex scenarios using LLM-as-a-Judge approaches. To bridge this gap, we introduce DRAMA-Eval, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating such systems. DRAMA-Eval utilizes structured script contexts and offers a holistic evaluation framework covering objective, local, and global aspects of generation quality, enabling the assessment of acoustic fidelity, sentence-level execution, and long-range coherence. We benchmark leading open-source and commercial models on a human?verified dataset. The results reveal critical weaknesses in long-range speaker consistency and implicit instruction following that require deep contextual understanding. To facilitate reproducible research, we release a 12-hour bilingual (Chinese-English) test set of manually corrected real-world scripts, accompanied by ground-truth audio, evaluation code, and benchmark results.

papers.title: Machine-Readable Operator Manuals over the ISO 11783 Network for Offline, Multilingual LLM Assistance
papers.abstract: If agricultural machinery is to support intelligent, offline assistance, then the system must access technical documentation dynamically. In this paper, the Semantic Synchronization of operator manuals over ISO 11783-based CAN buses is analyzed, defined as the process that brings the local knowledge base of a tractor-side assistant into agreement with the operator manual of the connected implement. Data transfer performance was benchmarked using Markdown, JSON, and XML; various open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) were also evaluated in cross-lingual query tasks. The automatic evaluation of the answers was validated against four human raters. A complete manual was transferred over a physical ISO 11783 network in 31 to 89 s, depending on format and transport settings, which is comparable to the object pool upload that operators already wait for at the first coupling of an implement. Markdown produced the smallest files, while the question-answering performance was comparable across the three formats for most models. With retrieval-augmented generation, locally run models answered most questions on the English manual correctly, with no advantage of the largest model over 7B and 8B models, but performed worse on the five other language editions. Keyword retrieval failed across languages, whereas semantic retrieval provided the cross-lingual capability. The exchange requires only a new parameter group that uses the existing request and transport mechanisms of ISO 11783, which makes it a candidate for standardization. The study is a proof of concept with inference on PC-grade hardware; deployment on embedded agricultural hardware remains future work.

papers.intro:
Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into agricultural machinery requires a robust solution for offline data access. Printed operator manuals cannot provide in-situ support in the tractor cabin because they are difficult to navigate during operations. Although researchers have investigated these LLMs for office and mobile support, applications now extend to embedded systems. To integrate these systems into agriculture, however, we must navigate the specific constraints of the standardized vehicle network.

Agricultural machinery in Europe features multi-brand systems where farmers connect implements to the tractor in a plug-and-play manner using ISO 11783 (, 2017). Farmers supplement the connected system with retrofit electronics, such as GNSS receivers and user terminals. ISO 11783 (ISOBUS) is the standard that interconnects the tractor, implement, user interface, farm management system, and precision farming task controller. This interconnected environment provides the necessary infrastructure for advanced data exchange.

In this paper, we explain how a local LLM-based assistant in an ISO 11783 system accesses textual data from other subsystems in an open network. Specifically, we examine machine-readable digital operator manuals stored in an implement’s Electronic Control Unit (ECU) and accessed by a tractor terminal in the tractor cabin. Access to these data is crucial in rural areas where internet connections are unreliable. Storing the manual in the implement ECU keeps it with the machine throughout its lifecycle. This study is a proof of concept: we evaluate the transfer on a physical ISO 11783 network and the question answering with locally run open-weight LLMs on PC-grade hardware, as a step toward deployment on resource-constrained ECUs. Unlike autonomous driving, where AI actuates the vehicle, the proposed system operates strictly as an information retrieval layer (Level 0 autonomy), which places the human operator as the sole decision maker.

The ISO 11783 series standardizes the user interface (Virtual Terminal, 2018), task data exchange (Task Controller, 2015) and diagnostics limited to version information, capabilities and I/O errors (, 2019), but it provides no mechanism by which an implement can supply its technical documentation to a local assistant on the tractor side, and existing retrieval-augmented systems rely on centrally maintained document collections (Ateş et al., 2025; Koopman et al., 2022). A standardized exchange is needed, which would allow tractor manufacturers to build their own assistants and implement manufacturers to provide their own serialization of the manual. Following the layered ISO/OSI architecture of ISO 11783, such an exchange should be added at the application layer as a new parameter group that uses the existing network management, request and extended transport mechanisms unchanged, rather than as a proprietary extension. We define Semantic Synchronization as the process that brings the local knowledge base of the tractor-side assistant into agreement with the manual of the connected implement, as in data synchronization: its input is the versioned manual stored in the implement ECU, its output a complete local copy together with the retrieval index built from it; it succeeds when the manual is received completely, its version matches the one announced by the implement and the index is built from it. In this study, the transfer and the indexing were implemented and evaluated, whereas the version check, the first-coupling protocol, the background image transfer and the source-verification interface are proposed design elements. Building on our preliminary study (Gun and Oksanen, 2025), we reuse its manual, question-answer dataset, prompts and retrieval configuration; the transfer over ISO 11783, the format comparison, the six language editions and the current models are new. This ManualSync project aims for standardized exchange of machine-readable operator manuals over ISO 11783 for offline, multilingual LLM assistance. We address three research questions: 1. Can a complete operator manual be transferred over ISO 11783 with the existing request and extended transport mechanisms within a practical time at the first coupling of an implement? 2. How do Markdown, JSON and XML compare in size, transfer time, token count and question-answering performance? 3. Can locally run open-weight LLMs answer operator questions from the transferred manual, and also across languages? What does each retrieval component contribute?

papers.title: Kolibri: A Sovereign European Model on the Pareto Frontier
papers.abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation. We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German. Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.

papers.title: Dipole chains of Bloch point singularities revealed by X-ray magnetic tomography
papers.abstract: Bloch point singularities play an important role in magnetic systems, mediating changes in topology in three dimensional configurations. However, until now they have only been observed as isolated objects or as part of individual topological textures. Here we present the experimental observation of a 1D dipole chain of Bloch points in an anisotropic chiral magnet using soft X-ray magnetic vector tomography. We identify that the chain of Bloch point singularities lies along a boundary between regions of opposite chirality and that neighbouring Bloch and anti-Bloch points are stable at separations down to 60 nm. The stability of the Bloch points is determined to be closely related to the surrounding topology of the magnetisation configuration and a threshold separation for the spontaneous annihilation of Bloch point-anti-Bloch point pairs within chiral domain walls is identified to be approximately 90 nm in distance. This observation of a chain of Bloch points and the insight into their stability, offers a route to explore the correlative behaviour of such topological point defects. The behaviour and control of such point defects is of relevance for the control of 3D magnetisation configurations, and provides a new route towards the creation of correlated configurations of singularities in a magnetic system.

papers.title: A Model-Agnostic Correction Framework for Short-Term Building Load Forecasting
papers.abstract: Short-term building load forecasting remains challenging because load patterns can change rapidly with weather and operating conditions. Data-driven forecasting models may become less reliable when the current operating regime is rare or poorly represented during training, even when similar situations exist elsewhere in the historical record. Recent advances in retrieval-augmented time series forecasting offer a promising way to adapt predictions to changing conditions by directly reusing relevant historical cases at inference time. Motivated by this idea, we propose WeL-RAC, a model-agnostic Weather-Load Retrieval-Augmented Correction framework that explicitly retrieves such evidence at prediction time. WeL-RAC retrieves historical cases that are similar to the current condition based on both recent load states and horizon-aligned weather forecasts. Their observed future load trajectories are then aggregated and used to correct the initial prediction, without retraining or modifying the base forecaster. We evaluate WeL-RAC on 31 building cases across three datasets, eight forecasting backbones, and four horizons from 1 to 18 hours. The framework improves the corresponding base forecasters in 90 of 96 dataset-level comparisons. Beyond accuracy, success and failure case studies further illustrate the framework's interpretability by tracing how retrieved historical evidence improves or degrades forecasts. These findings support explicit historical retrieval as an effective and interpretable complement to the building load forecasting.

papers.intro:
Buildings are a major source of energy demand and carbon emissions, making efficient building operation essential for the energy transition and climate-change mitigation [26]. In particular, short-term building energy forecasting supports operational decision-making by anticipating energy demand over the coming hours or days, thereby informing demand response, HVAC scheduling, peak-load management, model predictive control, and the optimisation of building energy efficiency and occupant comfort [3, 12, 37, 35]. Unlike long-term forecasts that primarily support planning and design, short-term forecasts must capture rapidly changing operating conditions and near-term external influences. This remains challenging because building loads are jointly affected by weather conditions, occupancy behaviour, HVAC operation, building thermal characteristics, and temporal usage patterns [51, 41, 18]. Their complex and time-varying interactions can induce nonlinear load dynamics and shifts in operating regimes, particularly under changing weather or abnormal building operation [33].

Their complex and time-varying interactions can induce nonlinear load dynamics and shifts in operating regimes, particularly under changing weather or abnormal building operation [33].

Existing studies have developed a wide range of building load forecasting models, including statistical, machine learning, deep learning, and hybrid approaches [12, 54]. These methods learn nonlinear temporal dependencies from historical loads and exogenous variables during training. Nevertheless, this training paradigm has a limitation in short-term load forecasting, where load patterns can change rapidly with weather and building operating conditions. Once trained, most parametric forecasters encode historical observations primarily in fixed model parameters and do not explicitly revisit individual past cases during inference [23]. Consequently, their predictions may become less reliable when the current operating regime is rare or underrepresented in the training distribution, even when comparable segments exist somewhere in the historical record. Although continual or online adaptation can update forecasting models as operating conditions evolve [33], a complementary approach is to access relevant historical experience directly at inference time without modifying the forecaster’s parameters. When the recent load state and weather resemble those of a previously observed segment, its subsequent load trajectory can provide a useful historical reference for the current forecast [28, 21].

The value of such historical analogues has been recognized in similar-day and nearest-neighbor-based forecasting methods, which typically select historical days with similar calendar or weather conditions and use their load profiles to construct forecasts. Existing methods span different strategies for similar-day selection, forecasting, and their integration [2, 38, 55, 28, 21]. However, similarity in building loads is inherently context dependent. Historical periods with similar recent load patterns may evolve differently under different future weather conditions, while weather-similar periods may correspond to different building operating states. Consequently, retrieval based on a single similarity criterion may select historical profiles whose future trajectories are not fully compatible with the current forecasting context. Moreover, because retrieved analogues represent only approximate matches to the current condition, using them as standalone forecasts may not be sufficiently reliable to replace an existing parametric forecaster.

Retrieval-augmented forecasting provides a natural way to complement a trained parametric forecaster with explicitly accessible historical information. Inspired by retrieval-augmented generation in natural language processing [31], recent time-series studies retrieve relevant historical segments and exploit their associated future trajectories or representations to improve forecasting [50, 23, 58, 8]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a key idea is to reuse the observed futures of similar historical segments and combine them with the prediction of the forecasting model. This paradigm is particularly attractive for short-term building load forecasting, where predictions must respond rapidly to changing operating and weather conditions. However, many existing retrieval methods primarily determine relevance from the observed input sequence itself [50, 23]. In usual, short-term building load forecasting not only consider the past load but also uses an additional source of information that can be exploited at retrieval time: weather forecasts over the prediction horizon are often available before the future load is observed. In particular, jointly considering the recent load state and weather conditions can help identify historical trajectories that are more compatible with the current forecasting context. Their observed future loads can then serve as a complementary reference for correcting the initial building load prediction. Such a retrieve-and-correct formulation enables fast adaptation to the current input while preserving the architecture and parameters of the forecaster.

Motivated by these considerations, this study proposes WeL-RAC, a Weather–Load Retrieval-Augmented Correction framework for short-term building load forecasting. The forecasting branch first generates an initial prediction using a base forecaster. The retrieval branch compares the current load state with historical load states in a numerical feature space, while comparing a textual summary of the upcoming weather forecast with horizon-aligned historical weather summaries in a semantic embedding space. The two similarity signals are then fused to retrieve the top-KK historical cases, whose observed future load trajectories are aggregated into a retrieved future trajectory. Finally, the correction module performs weighted fusion between the initial forecast and the retrieved future trajectory to produce the final prediction.

papers.title: Nanoscale origin of thermal anisotropy in monoclinic \texorpdfstring{$β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$}{beta-Ga2O3}
papers.abstract: Monoclinic $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ is a promising ultra-wide-bandgap semiconductor for power electronics, but its low and anisotropic thermal conductivity limits heat removal, making it a compelling model system for nanoscale thermal transport studies. Here, we demonstrate a pronounced nanoscale enhancement of thermal anisotropy and uncover the underlying phonon mechanism by combining complementary thermal and acoustic spectroscopy techniques with first-principles calculations. Anisotropic thermoreflectance thermometry determines the full thermal-conductivity tensor from angular measurements within the (100), (010), and (001) crystallographic planes. Angle-resolved Brillouin light scattering reveals that low-frequency acoustic phonons exhibit only weak velocity anisotropy, insufficient to account for the measured thermal anisotropy. Frequency-resolved ab initio Green--Kubo calculations show that the bulk anisotropy pattern emerges only when the accumulated conductivity includes phonon modes above 4 THz, whereas the sub 3 THz acoustic contributions are nearly isotropic. Extreme-ultraviolet transient thermal grating spectroscopy reveals that reducing the grating period to 28 nm strongly enhances the in-plane thermal anisotropy, most markedly in the (001) plane, where it reaches nearly twice its macroscopic value. Reconstructed and calculated mean-free-path (MFP) accumulation functions link this enhancement to the stronger directional contrast of short-MFP phonons. Together, these results identify high-frequency, short-MFP phonons as the dominant origin of thermal anisotropy in $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$, while low-frequency phonons attenuate the directional contrast at macroscopic scales.

papers.title: Beyond Data Schedule: Fast LLM Pretraining on Data Mixtures by Loss-Reweighting
papers.abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.

papers.title: Quadrotor Guidance for Tasks along Elliptical Boundary
papers.abstract: This paper presents a guidance method that enables a quadrotor uncrewed aerial vehicle to perform inspection tasks along an elliptical boundary enclosing a structure of interest. The proposed guidance approach leverages a bifurcation theory-based framework that supports multiple inspection tasks, including convergence to a desired viewpoint, switching between viewpoints along the boundary, constant-speed elliptical circumnavigation, and circumnavigation with sectorial dwell-time constraint. Stability analysis of the proposed guidance dynamics establishes convergence of the generated reference trajectories to the desired behavior. The control parameters in the proposed method further allow the settling time of the reference trajectory to be specified for each task. The resulting reference velocity expressions are closed-form and algebraically simple, facilitating practical implementation. A qualitative comparison with existing guidance methods highlights the flexibility of the proposed approach in achieving different inspection tasks through a unified framework, while relying on simpler guidance computations. The proposed guidance method is validated through numerical simulations using a six-degree-of-freedom quadrotor model with model uncertainties, and a cascaded sliding-mode controller that tracks the generated reference trajectories under bounded disturbances.

papers.intro:
Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), particularly quadrotors, are increasingly utilized for surveillance tasks because of their ability to access difficult-to-reach areas, reduce human error, enhance safety, and offer compact and cost-effective operation [20], [11]. Elliptical paths are widely adopted for perimeter patrolling [22], convoy monitoring [4], and target enclosure [34] due to their flexibility in shape, smoothness, and ability to efficiently circumscribe asymmetric regions. These properties make elliptical boundaries a preferable choice for standoff surveillance and inspection missions. Within such a framework, the quadrotor may be required to reach, hover and switch between designated viewpoints along the elliptical boundary or to perform circumnavigation along the boundary for continuous inspection.

Within such a framework, the quadrotor may be required to reach, hover and switch between designated viewpoints along the elliptical boundary or to perform circumnavigation along the boundary for continuous inspection.

A wide range of path-planning strategies are proposed for UAV-based inspection tasks. Several of these strategies formulate the inspection mission as an optimization problem, where the UAV is required to traverse a set of predefined viewpoints. For instance, Ref. [32] applies an ant colony optimization technique to obtain a trajectory of minimal length around a large structure. In Ref. [10], the inspection route is determined using a Zermelo traveling salesman framework to compute a time-optimal sequence connecting all target points. The work in Ref. [23] introduces a random inspection tree algorithm that yields the shortest trajectory covering all the viewpoints. Similarly, Ref. [3] proposes a hybrid approach that combines genetic algorithm with the A-star method to plan paths for inspecting inaccessible bridge surface cracks. It is noteworthy that optimization-based methods require relatively high computational effort for deducing the planning solution. An alternative approach is presented in Ref. [25], wherein an artificial potential field guides the UAV through successive viewpoints for indoor structure inspection. The methods reported in Refs. [32, 10, 23, 3, 25] primarily undertake a generic distribution of viewpoints and do not consider cases where viewpoints may follow a specific geometric locus or other spatial constraints. For example, when they are arranged along an elliptical path, a more sophisticated guidance framework is desired.

Elliptical circumnavigation provides a strategy in which a UAV follows an elliptical path which can facilitate continuous inspection. Various approaches are proposed to generate elliptical circumnavigation trajectories, including vector field methods [4, 16, 8, 12, 27, 5], geometry-based methods [9, 26], limit cycle based method [6], and sliding mode control [17, 31]. A notable limitation of elliptical circumnavigation is that it does not inherently accommodate scenarios in which the UAV is required to hover at specific viewpoints. The methods in Refs. [4, 16, 8, 12, 27, 5, 9, 26, 6, 17, 31] are also not applicable to scenarios in which the UAV is required to switch between designated viewpoints. Furthermore, in situations where closer observation is necessary through specific regions of the boundary, constant speed elliptical circumnavigation may be inadequate, thereby motivating an advanced sectorial dwell time constrained circumnavigation along the elliptical boundary.
