Furthermore, in situations where closer observation is necessary through specific regions of the boundary, constant speed elliptical circumnavigation may be inadequate, thereby motivating an advanced sectorial dwell time constrained circumnavigation along the elliptical boundary.

Existing UAV path planning methods generally address viewpoint-based planning, switching between viewpoints, and elliptical circumnavigation as independent problems, each involving different computational and information requirements. Such isolated treatment limits the flexibility and autonomy of UAV operations. Therefore, a unified framework integrating these trajectory generation strategies is desirable. Motivated by this requirement, we adopt a bifurcation theory–based approach. Bifurcation refers to the changes in a system’s dynamics that occur when its parameters vary and cross a critical threshold [15]. This phenomenon leads to alterations in the qualitative characteristics of the system’s fixed points, including modifications in their number and stability properties [30]. Consequently, bifurcation can be employed to design guidance laws that generate a variety of desired UAV trajectories. For instance, Ref. [1] utilizes a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation in the look-angle dynamics of a UAV relative to a stationary target, enabling stand-off tracking, spiral search, and target prosecution. In Ref. [2], pitchfork bifurcation is applied to artificial potential field-inspired velocity dynamics, allowing UAVs to form single-ring, double-ring, and cluster formations. Reference [7] employs Hopf bifurcation to achieve circumnavigation around a target using multiple UAVs. In another work Ref. [28], a two-parameter transcritical bifurcation is introduced for the line-of-sight distance kinematics in UAV engagement with a stationary target, which facilitates circumnavigation while achieving a prescribed settling time. The authors in Ref. [14] leverage infinite-period bifurcation in the line-of-sight kinematics to guide a quadrotor to a desired viewpoint, switching between viewpoints, and circumnavigation on a standoff circle. The methods presented in Refs. [1, 2, 7, 28, 14] are, however, restricted to circular paths.

papers.title: Supervised Source Separation of Electric Vehicle Interior Noise Using a Hybrid Transformer Architecture
papers.abstract: The interior sound of an electric vehicle is a superposition of several distinct noise contributions - wind noise, tire noise, powertrain (electric drive unit and inverter) noise, and auxiliary-drive noise - whose relative balance governs both the overall loudness and the perceived sound quality in the vehicle interior. Decomposing a recorded vehicle interior signal into these source contributions is a prerequisite for targeted acoustic engineering, but requires effortful measurement campaigns as well as expertise in the field of transfer path analysis. This work formulates the decomposition as a supervised, binaural source-separation problem with four target source contributions and adapts a hybrid time-spectrogram transformer architecture, originally developed for music demixing, to the domain of sound source separation for technical systems. To disambiguate source contributions, conditioning is introduced in the form of operating-state information, including electric drive speed, electric drive load, vehicle speed, and auxiliary-drive speed. Since isolated real-world reference stems are costly to obtain, the model is trained on a physics-based parametric data generator that synthesizes labeled component sounds from randomized virtual-vehicle hardware configurations and driving scenarios, so that the ground-truth contribution of each source is known by construction. Validation on both synthetic and measured vehicle interior sounds probes the achieved separation performance and underscores the feasibility of applying the proposed method for acoustic contribution analysis in technical systems.

papers.intro:
In vehicles with an internal combustion engine, the broadband and low-frequency engine noise acts as a masking noise that conceals many secondary sources. In battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs), this masking noise is absent, so that the remaining contributions – wind noise, tire noise, noise of the electric drive unit and its inverter, and noise of auxiliary components – determine the vehicle interior sound. The engineering of the interior sound of an EV is therefore concerned with the balance of these individual noise contributions. Thus, separation of the measured interior noise into its individual contributions is a useful tool for the acoustic development process, as it allows the perceived annoyance to be attributed to specific sources, the acoustic masking relations to be quantified, and the effect of design changes on the individual contributions to be assessed. This work investigates whether such a separation can be performed automatically by means of a learned separation model and reports the attainable separation quality in the given setup.

This work investigates whether such a separation can be performed automatically by means of a learned separation model and reports the attainable separation quality in the given setup.

Beyond this, we ask whether a model trained exclusively on physics-based synthetic data can be applied to measured vehicle interior noise, that is, whether the simulation-to-reality gap can be bridged by domain randomization of the virtual vehicle hardware. Both questions are posed with a practical decision in mind: whether the acquisition of measured training data with known source contributions – which requires transfer path analysis campaigns and is therefore costly – is justified by the separation quality that a learned model can be expected to reach.

Answering these questions requires bringing together two bodies of work that are usually treated separately: the acoustics of electric vehicle interior noise and its established, test-based contribution analysis on one side, and data-based audio source separation, developed mainly for music demixing and speech separation, on the other. The sources considered here are technical noise contributions with distinct physical excitation mechanisms that are permanently active, differ by orders of magnitude in level, and for which isolated reference recordings are not readily available. The following sections review both fields in turn and derive the resulting design choices.

Noise generation due to the tire-road contact during driving is a complex phenomenon that has garnered high interest in the scientific community [25]. Tire noise is transmitted to the vehicle cabin both via structural vibration and airborne noise transfer, exhibiting a broadband character that dominates in the low- and mid-frequency range [40, 24]. Apart from the broadband noise characteristic, the vibration due to the oscillation of air in the tire, referred to as tire cavity mode, is a tonal noise generation mechanism [2]. In a recent study on electrified vehicle interior noise, this cavity mode was found to be the only perceptible tonal component of tire noise in the vehicle interior [13]. The second noise source that exhibits broadband noise character is wind noise. Wind noise depends heavily on the driving speed and becomes a prominent contributor to the overall noise at high vehicle speeds [5, 39]. In [63], the main sources of wind noise are considered to be leakage noise, cavity noise and the noise generated by separated flows at the outer surface. Concerning the aeroacoustic sources on the vehicle outer surface, authors distinguish between monopole sources due to unsteady volumetric flow, dipole sources characterized by fluctuating surface pressures at solid boundaries and quadrupole sources caused by unsteady shear stresses [3, 39].

Noise generation due to the tire-road contact during driving is a complex phenomenon that has garnered high interest in the scientific community [25]. Tire noise is transmitted to the vehicle cabin both via structural vibration and airborne noise transfer, exhibiting a broadband character that dominates in the low- and mid-frequency range [40, 24]. Apart from the broadband noise characteristic, the vibration due to the oscillation of air in the tire, referred to as tire cavity mode, is a tonal noise generation mechanism [2]. In a recent study on electrified vehicle interior noise, this cavity mode was found to be the only perceptible tonal component of tire noise in the vehicle interior [13]. The second noise source that exhibits broadband noise character is wind noise. Wind noise depends heavily on the driving speed and becomes a prominent contributor to the overall noise at high vehicle speeds [5, 39]. In [63], the main sources of wind noise are considered to be leakage noise, cavity noise and the noise generated by separated flows at the outer surface. Concerning the aeroacoustic sources on the vehicle outer surface, authors distinguish between monopole sources due to unsteady volumetric flow, dipole sources characterized by fluctuating surface pressures at solid boundaries and quadrupole sources caused by unsteady shear stresses [3, 39].

Apart from the aforementioned broadband sources, order-harmonic tonal noise from the electric drive unit and auxiliary components is audible in the vehicle interior as well as high-frequency inverter noise. In [59], the authors review noise in electric machines and distinguish between magnetic, mechanical (load induced, auxiliaries, vibration modes), aerodynamic (air/ liquid /water cooling phenomena) and electronic (switching harmonics) noise sources. With a focus on the interior noise share of electric drive systems, high-frequency whining noise generated by electromagnetic forces and gear meshing of reducers as well as high-frequency inverter noise are particularly relevant [21, 32, 13].

Beyond the electric drive unit, auxiliary components often contribute tonal, order-harmonic noise, particularly audible at low vehicle speeds [41, 54]. Such auxiliary components include, but are not limited to, the electric refrigerant compressor, or media-supplying components of fuel cell systems, namely the air compressor and the hydrogen recirculation blower.

Transfer path analysis (TPA) is an established family of test-based methods for identifying potentials for acoustic improvements in complex mechanical systems and is frequently applied for vehicle interior noise engineering. Distinguishing between source strength and corresponding transfer function, it allows engineers to target both – sources and critical transmission paths. However, TPA methods like classical TPA and component-based TPA entail considerable effort: They require all relevant transfer paths from the noise sources to the receiver position to be instrumented with indicator sensors, typically microphones and tri-axial accelerometers [58]. Operational measurements are then performed and complemented by additional explicit transfer path measurements, where the vehicle is in standstill condition. Operational Transfer Path Analysis (OTPA), first introduced in [37], is frequently adopted as a lower-effort alternative in which the explicit quantification of source strengths and transfer functions is not the primary objective. Instead, OTPA delivers the contribution of each transmission path to the total interior noise from operational measurements only. While TPA can be described as a forward method that characterizes source strengths and transfer paths functions first, and then synthesizes the resulting interior noise contributions of the sources, OTPA can be seen as an inverse method. The measured receiver signal in the vehicle interior is an input to the algorithm, effectively being the quantity to be reconstructed by a linear time-invariant model, formed by multiplying the component-mounted indicator sensor signals with a transmissibility matrix that is fitted in the frequency domain in a least-squares sense. However, this approach has typical problems as analyzed in [14], such as errors in estimation of transmissibility, errors occurring due to missing paths and errors occurring when indicator signals are strongly correlated.

papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.

Many everyday manipulation tasks cannot be solved from the current camera image alone. A robot asked to place a cube on a target five times must know how many placements it has already made. A robot asked to lift the container that hides the green cube must have followed the containers while they were shuffled, and one asked to move a cube “in the same manner as before” must have noticed whether the demonstrator pushed or carried it. RoboMME [1] collects sixteen such tasks, and its evaluation shows that memory is the bottleneck for today’s robot policies: the best learned memory reaches about half the success of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} [2] executor driven by oracle subgoals.

papers.title: Electron Wavefronts Capture Nanoscale Movies of Hypersound at Surfaces
papers.abstract: Acoustic waves transport mechanical energy and elastic strain through solids, with material composition and shape governing their propagation. In the gigahertz hypersound regime, acoustic wavelengths reach tens to hundreds of nanometres, comparable to nanoscale device dimensions. Harnessing these waves underpins high-frequency signal processing, sensing, electromagnetic coupling and quantum control. Acoustic metrology probes elastic modes and internal interfaces. Yet directly imaging how nanoscale acoustic waves interact with local structure remains challenging, requiring picometre displacement sensitivity combined with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here we demonstrate full-field imaging of laser-induced hypersound at surfaces using reflected electron wavefronts. We introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy (ULEEM), exploiting the intrinsic surface sensitivity of few-electronvolt electrons. Coherent electron pulses down to femtosecond durations reflect from the topmost atomic layers, imprinting the evolving surface profile onto their wavefronts. Defocus converts phase variations into image contrast. In a thin van der Waals material, we image the thermoelastic generation and propagation of picometre-amplitude acoustic waves. Measured dispersion relations, interpreted through elastodynamic modelling, distinguish substrate-supported and locally detached regions, revealing how interfacial contact shapes propagation. Delayed wave emission reveals scattering at buried mechanical defects. Our results establish electron-wavefront imaging of nanoscale surface dynamics, enabling the exploration of ultrafast energy transport, structural transformations and coupled mechanical, electronic and magnetic phenomena.

papers.intro:
Surface-sensitive detection of acoustic waves provides access to structure and dynamics across an extraordinary range of length scales. Seismic waves reveal subsurface structures in geophysical exploration[12], while medical ultrasound forms images with submillimetre resolution from echoes generated at internal interfaces[13]. In solids, elastic waves transport mechanical energy and strain and increasingly serve as tools for probing and controlling materials properties[1]. At micro- and nanoscale dimensions, surface acoustic waves (SAWs) enable radio-frequency filtering[2], sensing[4], and couple mechanical motion to electronic[5], optical[3, 14], magnetic[6] and quantum systems[7, 8]. Advances in both fundamental studies and applications depend on understanding acoustic-wave generation, propagation, scattering and dissipation in heterogeneous media[10, 15].

Resolving hypersound requires the combination of subatomic displacement sensitivity, nanometre spatial resolution and ultrafast timing[16, 9]. Ultrafast scanning-probe and near-field microscopies have reached atomic to nanometre length scales and femtosecond time resolution[17], including direct imaging of coherent molecular motion[18]. Scanning-probe techniques map stationary nanoscale acoustic fields[19, 9, 20], while coherent X-ray and extreme-ultraviolet diffraction imaging reconstruct transient lattice and surface deformations[21, 22]. With even shorter wavelengths, electron microscopy offers complementary access through diffraction[23, 24, 25, 26] and secondary-electron contrast[27]. Photoemission contrast has been used to map the piezoelectric potentials of standing SAWs[28, 29]. Direct full-field imaging of propagating nanoscale surface waves remains challenging.

papers.title: Local Analogs of Little Red Dots: Clues to the X-ray Weakness
papers.abstract: A major question about JWST's little red dots (LRDs) at $z\sim4-8$ is the origin of their apparent X-ray weakness. Even deep Chandra stacks yield only tentative detections or broad-band limits and cannot distinguish among super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick (CT) obscuration. Local analogs offer a powerful complementary route. At $z\sim0.3$, similarly luminous sources require $\sim10^{3-4}$ less exposure for comparable signal-to-noise, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe the diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. Here we present a pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six "local little red dots" (LLRDs), V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies selected as low-redshift counterparts of LRDs. These sources show X-ray diversity: "X-normal" LLRDs resemble type 1 AGNs in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, whereas the "X-weak" stack lies $\sim0.5-0.7$ dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations while remaining compatible with the representative LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. The X-weak LLRDs also lack detected optical variability and have redder optical continua than X-normal LLRDs, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to those of high-redshift LRDs. The detection of the X-weak stack at $\sim3.3σ$ with the soft-X-ray-sensitive EP-FXT provides rest-frame $\sim2-3$ keV constraints difficult to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like CT geometry examined here, although modified variants remain possible. The simplest alternative is a mildly X-ray-weak corona ($Δα_{\mathrm{ox}}\sim-0.1$ to $-0.2$) with Compton-thin absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H}}\sim10^{22-23}$ cm$^{-2}$), consistent with the independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, our results offer a practical path for testing the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

papers.title: Side-Chain Engineering Controls Molecular Packing and Vertical Electron Transport in Discrete n-Type NDI-T2 Oligomers
papers.abstract: High-efficiency vertical charge transport in multilayer organic optoelectronic devices highly depends on molecular structure and arrangement. Using two T2-(NDI-T2)2 conjugated oligomers with ethylhexyl (EH) and octyldodecyl (OD) side chains as a model system, their effects on electron transport are investigated using, among other techniques, atomic force microscopy (AFM), conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM), grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), steady-state optical spectroscopy, and time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations. The oligomers of both materials exhibit relatively disordered structures in the as-cast state, whereas annealing enhances structural order and leads to side-chain-dependent changes in molecular stacking. EH-based films show a smaller annealing-induced photoluminescence shift than OD-based films, suggesting less pronounced stacking and conformational rearrangements, consistent with TDDFT-supported exciton analysis. The current-voltage characteristics are analyzed using the space-charge-limited current (SCLC) model. After annealing, both materials exhibit improved vertical electron mobility. The EH-based films reach a maximum mobility of 1.2 x 10^-4 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1. The combined results suggest that the shorter EH side chains modify the out-of-plane packing environment and facilitate vertical electron transport. These results establish a structure-property relationship between side-chain structure, molecular order, exciton coupling and vertical mobility, providing a molecular design basis for optimising organic semiconductors through side-chain engineering.

papers.intro:
Organic semiconductors have attracted significant attention as active materials in flexible electronic devices because their optoelectronic properties can be tuned through molecular design and they are suitable for solution processing [56, 52, 72, 69, 37, 79, 7]. In multilayer devices such as organic solar cells, organic light-emitting diodes, and organic spin valves, charge carriers must cross the electrode/organic layer interface to be injected and travel through the organic layer in a direction perpendicular to the substrate [7, 78, 20, 33, 71]. Therefore, device performance depends not only on interfacial energy level matching but also on vertical charge transport within the organic layers, the latter of which is closely related to molecular packing and structural order [36, 2, 19, 29]. However, existing research has primarily focused on in-plane charge transport in organic field-effect transistors, and there remains a lack of systematic understanding of how molecular structure and processing conditions jointly regulate out-of-plane transport [23, 14]. This issue is particularly important for n-type organic semiconductors, as molecular structure and processing conditions jointly influence film formation and molecular packing, thereby modulating intermolecular electron coupling and vertical electron transport pathways [23, 75]. Therefore, investigating the relationship among molecular structure, film packing, and vertical electron transport in n-type organic semiconductors is critical for optimizing the performance of vertical organic electronic devices.

Among n-type organic semiconductors, donor–acceptor conjugated systems based on naphthalene diimide (NDI) and bithiophene (T2) exhibit great potential because the electron-deficient NDI unit provides high electron affinity, while the NDI–T2 backbone enables efficient electron transport and good thermal stability [18, 59]. Charge transport in organic semiconductors is governed by the interplay between electronic coupling, molecular packing, energetic disorder, and molecular vibrations and may range from localized hopping or polaronic motion to transiently delocalized or more band-like regimes [12, 47]. In conjugated materials, the backbone provides efficient intramolecular transport pathways, whereas long-range transport additionally requires intermolecular electronic coupling. Molecular packing therefore determines both the magnitude and directionality of charge transport [64, 68]. Therefore, the microcrystalline molecular packing in the film strongly influences in-plane/out-of-plane charge mobilities and the anisotropic transport behavior. Although the benchmark polymer P(NDI2OD-T2) has been widely studied [73, 24, 58, 42, 4, 3], the batch-to-batch and molecular weight variation make studying the intrinsic structure-property relationship rather challenging [45, 41]. In contrast, discrete conjugated oligomers offer an intermediate molecular scale between monomers and polymers. Compared with monomers, they provide a longer and well-defined conjugated backbone over which charge transport can be examined across several covalently connected units, while still retaining a precisely defined molecular structure. At the same time, unlike conventional polymers, their fixed chain length avoids complications arising from molecular-weight distribution and dispersity. These characteristics make conjugated oligomers particularly suitable for establishing clear correlations between molecular structure, packing, orientation, and charge transport [25, 10]. Previously, we demonstrated synthetic access to discrete oligomers of the type T2-(NDI-T2) with chain lengths up to the heptamer [40], which are ideal for studying transport. Most existing research on side-chain engineering has focused on either in-plane carrier transport in field-effect transistors or active-layer morphology and charge generation in bulk-heterojunction solar cells [35, 9, 38, 76]. However, there remains a lack of quantitative studies on out-of-plane carrier transport in n-type oligomers that integrate vertical electrical measurements, fine-structure characterization, and modeling of transport mechanisms.

Most existing research on side-chain engineering has focused on either in-plane carrier transport in field-effect transistors or active-layer morphology and charge generation in bulk-heterojunction solar cells [35, 9, 38, 76]. However, there remains a lack of quantitative studies on out-of-plane carrier transport in n-type oligomers that integrate vertical electrical measurements, fine-structure characterization, and modeling of transport mechanisms.

In this work, two T2–(NDI–T2)2 oligomers containing the same conjugated backbone but different branched side chains, octyldodecyl (OD) and 2-ethylhexyl (EH), were investigated. Thermal annealing near TcT_{\mathrm{c}} was used to tune molecular packing and test its relation to the optical response and vertical charge transport. The resulting structural changes were examined using grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), X-ray reflectivity (XRR), and in-plane X-ray diffraction (IP-XRD), while film thickness and surface morphology were characterized by spectroscopic ellipsometry and atomic force microscopy (AFM). Changes in the optical response were evaluated using ultraviolet–visible (UV-vis) absorption and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, supported by time-dependent density functional (TDDFT) theory calculations. Vertical electron transport was investigated at both the nanoscale and device level using conductive AFM and vertical electron-only diodes. By combining these measurements, correlations among side-chain structure, annealing-induced molecular packing, optical response, and out-of-plane electron transport were established, providing insights into the optimization of n-type organic semiconductor films for vertical electronic devices.

papers.title: CoCarry: Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting for Dual-Humanoid Cooperative Carrying
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large-scale human motion data, motion retargeting, and motion imitation have enabled increasingly capable whole-body control for individual humanoids. Cooperative carrying is more challenging because successful coordination requires not only plausible individual motions, but also consistent cross-agent and agent-object relations, including shared grasp, relative configuration, and whole-body support. We introduce CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset containing 220 synchronized two-person sequences across 21 task schemes, five shared-object geometries, four terrain types, and approximately 61 minutes of motion. We further propose Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting, which starts from nominal individual motions and jointly refines both humanoids around the same prescribed object trajectory. Cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors preserve compatible four-hand grasp relations, while complementary upper object-interaction and lower support structures retain object-relative geometry and coordinated support. Across all 220 CoCarry sequences retargeted to two A3 humanoids, our method achieves 0.9995 contact preservation, reduces penetration duration by 67.0% and 71.0% relative to GMR and OmniRetarget, respectively, and maintains a 100% retargeting success rate. On CORE4D with Unitree G1 humanoids, it achieves 0.9906 contact preservation with zero measured sliding. We further validate the generated references through physics simulation and multiple real-world cooperative carrying experiments on two physical A3 humanoids, demonstrating their usability for downstream dual-humanoid control.

papers.title: OPTARI: An open-source software framework for clinical translation of optoacoustic imaging
papers.abstract: Combined optoacoustic (OptA) and ultrasound imaging is a promising modality across a wide range of pathologies. Its use in clinical research, however, is limited by a lack of analysis software accessible to users without programming expertise. Existing tools are either script-based engineering frameworks or proprietary vendor applications. We present OPTARI, an open-source graphical software application to facilitate large-scale clinical optoacoustic-ultrasound (OPUS) studies. OPTARI builds on the napari image viewer and the PATATO toolkit for OptA data processing. It supports native vendor and open HDF5 data formats, aligns with the IPASC standard, and is distributed as a standalone executable. Features include region-of-interest annotation, reconstruction, chromophore unmixing, deep-learning-based tissue segmentation, and temporal and spectral analysis modules. OPTARI offers a combination of features for clinical study analysis that none of the compared tools provide. The automated tissue segmentation produced results comparable to expert labeling for muscle tissue, and batch processing reduced analysis time from minutes to under one second per scan. The tool is used in ongoing clinical OPUS studies. OPTARI connects engineering frameworks with medical research and provides an open-source basis for reproducible and standardized analysis in clinical OptA imaging studies.

papers.title: National-Scale Multimodal Accessibility Fields from Open Geospatial Data
papers.abstract: Large-area accessibility analysis remains difficult to reproduce because multimodal routing, heterogeneous opportunity data, and reusable spatial outputs are rarely integrated in a single transparent workflow. We present MAPPER (Multimodal Accessibility and Place Profiling Engine for Arbitrary Regions), an open-data pipeline for multimodal accessibility analytics. The workflow builds walk, bike, car, and public transport travel-time graphs from OpenStreetMap and GTFS data, harmonizes mapped POI- and proxy layers representing the land-use side of the accessibility relation, and computes continuous accessibility fields using network kernel density estimation. A low-overhead native compute core (contraction-hierarchy routing, C++/OpenMP accessibility accumulation, DAG-style orchestration eliminating redundant computation) is the enabler that makes many graphs, large extents, and a broad layer set jointly tractable on commodity hardware. Outputs are sampled to a uniform H3 grid for downstream urban and regional analysis. A Germany-wide production run yields an H3-indexed accessibility dataset with nearly 40 million cells and 972 mode-layer fields across nine network and intermodal modes. Routing comparisons against an empirical mobility panel show low mean bias for walking, cycling, and car, while public transport results are interpreted more cautiously as schedule-based supply estimates sensitive to waiting and transfer assumptions. A Bavaria case study operationalizes the travel-time targets of the state's central-place planning system on the resulting fields and reveals strong modal differences in accessibility to basic services. The contribution is a reproducible framework for large-area multimodal accessibility analysis, with an aligned output structure designed for reuse in urban and regional analysis, planning support, and scenario modeling.

papers.intro:
Accessibility measures represent how transport networks and the spatial distribution of opportunities jointly shape the potential for interaction across urban and regional systems (Hansen, 1959a; Geurs & Van, 2004a). Yet large-area accessibility analysis remains difficult to implement in practice due to large combinatorial complexity. Many studies rely on bespoke preprocessing, single-mode routing, coarse zonal summaries, or locally tailored data assemblies, which makes results harder to compare, transfer, and reuse in downstream urban analytics (Marwal & Silva, 2022a; Mazzulla & Pirrone, 2024a).

Accessibility measures represent how transport networks and the spatial distribution of opportunities jointly shape the potential for interaction across urban and regional systems (Hansen, 1959a; Geurs & Van, 2004a). Yet large-area accessibility analysis remains difficult to implement in practice due to large combinatorial complexity. Many studies rely on bespoke preprocessing, single-mode routing, coarse zonal summaries, or locally tailored data assemblies, which makes results harder to compare, transfer, and reuse in downstream urban analytics (Marwal & Silva, 2022a; Mazzulla & Pirrone, 2024a).

These limitations matter for transport and land-use analysis in particular, because accessibility is the standard quantity through which the interaction of the two systems is measured: the transport side enters through multimodal travel-time impedance, and the land-use side enters through the spatial distribution of opportunities: services, workplaces, and other activity locations. Comparative questions about this interaction, such as whether land-use plans presume levels of access that the transport system actually delivers, require accessibility measures that are consistent across modes, regions, and opportunity types. National and supraregional analysis therefore requires workflows that can integrate multiple travel modes, heterogeneous opportunity representations, and a common output structure while remaining computationally tractable. The computational burden also grows quickly with the product of transport modes, opportunity classes, spatial granularity, and study extent. Continuous network-based fields are attractive in this setting because they reduce dependence on administrative units, preserve local spatial gradients, and produce smoothly varying surfaces that can be reused in planning analysis, scenario studies, and downstream statistical modeling. But they also require explicit choices about impedance modeling, source harmonization, and scalable computation.

papers.title: GLP Networking API Specification
papers.abstract: Multiagent deterministic GLP (madGLP) runs Grassroots Logic Programs (GLP) as agents that communicate solely by asynchronous message passing, and assumes fair delivery: every message sent is eventually delivered. Each agent runs on a person's smartphone, named by the person's public key. A grassroots platform depends on no global resource but the network, so agents must reach one another over Bluetooth Low Energy, on a local network, and across the Internet from behind NAT, via rendezvous servers anyone can run. What madGLP requires of such a network, and what the network requires of the platform, has not been specified. We specify the networking layer beneath madGLP. Anything that can be done in GLP is done in GLP: the layer provides only what GLP cannot reach - the network stack, the location service, application attestation, and cryptographic primitives. Three transport underlays share one interface. Over PAN and LAN, an agent advertises a rotating recognition token derived from its key and time slot, so a peer who knows the key recognises it before contact and nobody else can track it; whether it answers unrecognised contacts is a per-underlay trust level set by GLP. Over WAN, a rendezvous server is a static-address host running the headless layer and a GLP rendezvous agent that coordinates hole punching, relays no payload, and belongs to no social graph. On every underlay, peers establish a mutually authenticated Noise session from Ed25519 keys, then attest, bound to the handshake hash, that each runs the application published under its developer's key, verified against Apple's and Google's roots with no third party contacted. One message protocol, over UDP datagrams and GATT writes, provides the fair, unordered, atomic and authenticated delivery madGLP assumes.

Multiagent deterministic GLP (madGLP) [7] is a distributed runtime for Grassroots Logic Programs (GLP) [5] in which autonomous agents communicate solely by message passing, each agent on a person’s smartphone and named by the person’s public key. This document specifies the networking layer beneath madGLP: the interface that enables madGLP agents to run on separate devices communicating peer-to-peer, and the layer functions behind the system predicates by which GLP programs reach it. madGLP and the runtime’s side of the seam are specified in the implementation paper [7]; the seam predicates are in the language paper’s catalogue [5]; the operating system above the runtime, the Grassroots Super-App with its social graph (in preparation), is what decides whom to befriend and what an attested or unattested peer may be used for.

papers.title: Trajectory Matching: Discrete Flow Matching with Structured Actions
papers.abstract: The natural units of structured discrete generation are often not independent single-component edits but richer actions: attaching a fragment to a molecule, inserting a node together with an incident edge, or growing a hierarchy by adding a child. Yet most existing discrete flow matching methods (DFM) are restricted to independent component-wise edits over fixed-size states. This restriction stems from endpoint conditioning: endpoints fix the source and target during training but not the action sequence between them, making tractable conditional rates hard to define for complex actions that cannot be factorized component-wise. We propose trajectory matching, which conditions the flow on a full sequence of actions connecting the endpoints. This yields principled, simulation-free training targets for user-defined action spaces, including actions that change state size, modify multiple components, or depend on earlier actions. We prove that the resulting objective recovers the marginal flow and that trajectory matching strictly subsumes factorized DFM, while additionally capturing actions with prerequisite structure such as hierarchy growth or fragment-based molecule generation. Empirically, on tree and molecular graph generation, trajectory matching with domain-aligned actions matches or surpasses factorized DFM baselines (lifting MOSES validity from 92.8% to 99.2%) and transfers without retraining to substructure extension and linking. Trajectory matching enlarges the design space of discrete flow matching by turning the action vocabulary into a modeling choice. An interactive explanation of trajectory matching is available at https://niklaskemper.com/blog/trajectory-matching/.

papers.intro:
Many structured generation problems are most naturally expressed in terms of actions that reflect the structure of the domain rather than the structure of the representation. In molecular graph generation, for example, the natural actions are not single-component edits but operations like attaching a fragment to a partial structure or inserting an atom together with a bond. Such actions can change the size of the state, modify several components at once, and depend on one another—an atom can only be attached to atoms that have already been inserted. The value of such structured actions is well established in autoregressive models: fragment-based molecule generation (Jin et al., 2019), grammar-based code generation (Yin & Neubig, 2017), and insertion-based graph models (You et al., 2018) all exploit domain-aligned actions to achieve strong empirical performance.

However, existing discrete flow matching (DFM) (Campbell et al., 2024; Gat et al., 2024) and related non-autoregressive methods such as discrete diffusion (Austin et al., 2021) cannot easily express such actions. The reason is structural: DFM prescribes a conditional flow between sampled endpoints, and the corresponding rate must be tractable for training. To achieve this over combinatorially large state spaces, existing methods factorize the rate across components. This commits the model to fixed-size states, single-component edits, and independence between actions. Recent extensions (Havasi et al., 2025; Deutschmann et al., 2026; Lüdke et al., 2026) lift the fixed-size constraint by supporting insertions and deletions in specific domains, but they do so by mapping these operations into augmented state spaces where they again reduce to factorized single-component edits. Actions that modify multiple components or depend on one another therefore remain out of reach.

We address this gap with trajectory matching: rather than conditioning on endpoints alone, we condition on a full trajectory of actions connecting them. A trajectory specifies which actions are applied and in what order, leaving the conditional flow to determine only when each action is taken. This makes the conditional rate straightforward to define for general action spaces, including actions that change state size, modify multiple components, or depend on one another. The resulting training objective is still simulation-free and provably recovers the marginal data-generating flow. To make training efficient, we require an efficiently sampleable distribution over trajectories connecting the endpoints. We give explicit constructions for several settings, including actions with hierarchical dependencies. Our framework also recovers standard factorized DFM as the special case of independent component-wise actions with uniformly sampled orderings, placing factorized updates and actions with prerequisites within a common framework.

papers.title: Developing Security Metrics for Automated Compliance Checking
papers.abstract: To automatically check for compliance with security-related standards, prose requirements must be translated to technical properties to make them measurable. A multitude of metrics have been proposed in past literature, but they are lacking a systematic methodology for their elicitation. Without such a methodology, metrics remain inconsistent in their data models and abstraction levels, they exhibit considerable overlaps and are difficult to combine to comprehensively cover a standard's requirement. In this paper, we develop a data model for security metrics based on a systematization of compliance requirements, and we propose a methodology for their elicitation. The method is based on an ontology that enables a systematic development of metrics with a comparable degree of abstraction. We also present our initial work on an open-source effort that demonstrates that our approach also supports a collaborative development of metrics.

papers.intro:
Regulatory standards as well as internal security policies require a technical representation of security requirements to make them checkable in an automatic way. Today, systems and their security state can change rapidly—a continuous, automated conformance checking is therefore necessary and, in turn, requires metrics for their technical representation. More and more regulatory standards and certification schemes, for example the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), European Cloud Security Scheme (EUCS), C5, etc., are being created to increase the security standard in different areas, but a common basis for their systematic representation on a technical level is missing. Moreover, these standards often have considerable overlaps, so compliance engineering could benefit from such a common basis, i.e. technical metrics.

On the one hand, compliance standards are supposed to be generally applicable and long-lived—and thus cannot prescribe specific technologies and system-specific requirements which would be outdated soon. On the other hand, users of these standards, i.e., auditors and auditees, require a systematic way of making these requirements actionable and measurable.

papers.title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting solar flares is a challenging space-weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active-region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no-flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active-region-based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LuisBauer22/ARENA.

papers.intro:
Solar flares are transient releases of magnetic energy in the solar atmosphere that produce intense electromagnetic radiation. These events are associated with active regions (ARs), localized concentrations of strong and complex magnetic fields on the solar surface [9]. Radiation from the most energetic flares can perturb Earth’s ionosphere and affect radio communication and space-based technologies, making reliable flare forecasting an important problem in space-weather research. A central challenge in solar flare forecasting is the spatial scale at which the problem is formulated: A flare is observed as a global event, but its magnetic origin is localized to an AR. Consequently, two related questions arise: Will a flare occur within 24 h24\text{\,}\mathrm{h}, and which AR is responsible for it? The first question can be addressed using event-level flare catalogs, whereas the second requires associating individual flares with their source regions. Most existing data-driven forecasting approaches focus on the former, using either full-disk observations [22, 24, 29] or individual ARs [19, 27, 28, 14] as input. In contrast, combining ARs present in an observation provides a natural representation of the solar disk as a variable-sized set of physically meaningful regions.

Representations combining ARs introduce a mismatch between the available data and the desired labels. For each observation, it is straightforward to obtain a global label indicating whether a flare occurs within the subsequent 24 h24\text{\,}\mathrm{h}. Determining which of the ARs present at the observation time produces the subsequent flare, however, requires additional event-to-region association based on expert knowledge. Such origin annotations are consequently substantially more difficult to obtain and are available only for limited datasets [1, 5]. We therefore seek to learn from the readily available global flare labels while retaining the ability to identify the AR driving the prediction. This setting corresponds naturally to multiple-instance learning (MIL [6]). In MIL, a bag contains multiple instances but is associated only with a bag-level label. This paradigm has been particularly successful in computational pathology, where a high-resolution whole-slide image may be labeled according to the presence of a disease, such as cancer, while identifying the diagnostically relevant tissue regions requires costly expert annotation [16, 26, 7, 31]. We formulate solar flare forecasting analogously: An observation constitutes a bag, its associated AR cutouts are the instances, and the flare/no-flare label is assigned to the bag. The number of ARs can vary between observations, requiring an aggregation mechanism that is invariant to the number and ordering of instances. Importantly, information about the AR associated with a flare is not available during training.

papers.title: Out-of-sample prediction in SEM: A simulation-based comparison of maximum likelihood and (consistent) partial least squares
papers.abstract: Structural equation modeling (SEM) is widely used to study relationships among unobserved constructs. Over recent years, the interest in computing predictions with SEM has grown. Different prediction procedures have been proposed for this purpose, including MLpredict, which is based on maximum likelihood (ML) estimation, and PLS(c)predict, which is based on partial least squares (PLS). The out-of-sample predictive performances of these procedures have not yet been compared. In our work, we conduct a comprehensive Monte Carlo study to compare out-of-sample predictions of MLpredict and PLS(c)predict for indicators associated with endogenous constructs, so-called operative predictions. Here, we vary key design factors regarding, for instance, the strengths of structural relations, the training sample size, and the construct types in the data generating processes, which determine the presence or absence of construct misspecification. Across the investigated conditions, MLpredict and PLS(c)predict exhibit similar predictive performance according to two assessment criteria, indicating that neither procedure is uniformly superior for operative prediction. Out-of-sample predictive performance is driven mainly by the strength of the relations between the variables, whereas training sample size and construct misspecification have comparatively little influence on it. An exception is the occasionally inflated prediction error of PLScpredict, which is in line with previous findings for ordinal indicators. Overall, our results suggest that, in the studied setting, fine-grained methodological differences between traditional SEM and PLS-based procedures matter less for out-of-sample predictive performance than properties of the data generating process, such as the coefficient of determination of endogenous constructs.

papers.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search
papers.abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.7 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 19%. Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io

papers.intro:
The rapid scaling of LLMs (Yang et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023) has enabled previously unattainable capabilities, but introduced substantial computational and memory requirements that limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. To address these limitations, low-rank approximation using SVD has emerged as a principled and effective compression strategy (Qinsi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025d; Wang et al., 2025c; Chekalina et al., 2025). By decomposing dense weight matrices into smaller factors, SVD substantially reduces parameter counts and computational complexity while retaining easy-to-accelerate dense tensor computations. This ensures immediate compatibility with standard inference engines, avoiding the specialized hardware or sparse kernels that are often required by semi-structured or unstructured pruning approaches. Prior work has demonstrated that SVD-based methods yield significant inference acceleration, particularly in memory-bound regimes, while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art pruning techniques (Qinsi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025d). They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency.

This ensures immediate compatibility with standard inference engines, avoiding the specialized hardware or sparse kernels that are often required by semi-structured or unstructured pruning approaches. Prior work has demonstrated that SVD-based methods yield significant inference acceleration, particularly in memory-bound regimes, while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art pruning techniques (Qinsi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025d). They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency.

However, the full potential of SVD in modern LLMs is limited by two fundamental challenges: global rank allocation and decomposition quality. The primary bottleneck is the global allocation problem, which requires determining the optimal rank for each layer under a fixed parameter budget. Existing strategies fail to solve this optimization effectively, as they rely on uncalibrated local sensitivity proxies (Azizi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b) or expensive measurements (Thoma et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024) to determine layer importance. These methods typically neglect the non-linear error explosion inherent in deep networks (Huang et al., 2025), creating a critical misalignment between error proxy and actual degradation. Consequently, their ability to identify high-performance rank allocations remains limited. Further, high decomposition quality requires distinguishing and preserving the weight directions that are most critical for the downstream task. While Fisher-weighted SVD theoretically addresses this by aligning reconstruction error with the loss landscape (curvature), existing work (Chekalina et al., 2025) suffers from rank deficiencies under reasonable sample counts, limiting its effectiveness.

Existing strategies fail to solve this optimization effectively, as they rely on uncalibrated local sensitivity proxies (Azizi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b) or expensive measurements (Thoma et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024) to determine layer importance. These methods typically neglect the non-linear error explosion inherent in deep networks (Huang et al., 2025), creating a critical misalignment between error proxy and actual degradation. Consequently, their ability to identify high-performance rank allocations remains limited. Further, high decomposition quality requires distinguishing and preserving the weight directions that are most critical for the downstream task. While Fisher-weighted SVD theoretically addresses this by aligning reconstruction error with the loss landscape (curvature), existing work (Chekalina et al., 2025) suffers from rank deficiencies under reasonable sample counts, limiting its effectiveness.

In this work, we address both challenges by introducing LEMS for global rank allocation and KFAC-SVD for robust decomposition. LEMS introduces a layer-wise error model that integrates local sensitivity, empirical calibration, and a bias correcting error propagation. By explicitly modeling layer-wise error accumulation, we can formulate the search as an ILP and solve it efficiently. KFAC-SVD mitigates the rank deficiency that limits the decomposition quality of prior Fisher-based SVD by transitioning from sequence-based to token-wise statistics for the Fisher approximation. By accumulating token-level loss curvature information, we effectively prevent rank collapse, yielding a decomposition of significantly higher fidelity. Our contributions are threefold: 1. LEMS. We propose a layer-wise error model for rank allocation in SVD that captures both local sensitivity and global error propagation modeling error propagation via a bias. To obtain global rank allocations we search the error model with an ILP formulation. 2. Robust Fisher Decomposition (KFAC-SVD). We leverage a token-wise Kronecker-factor estimation in SVD to mitigate the rank bottleneck of prior Fisher-based SVD and improve its decomposition quality. 3. Empirical Validation. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3, KFAC-SVD improves WikiText2 perplexity by an average of 19% over baselines. LEMS further drives substantial accuracy gains of 2.1-4.7 p.p. compared to the best existing rank allocation methods. Crucially, it also generalizes to activation-based SVD and scales to the 70B parameter regime, achieving a 4.0 p.p. improvement over uniform rank allocation.

papers.title: Sobolev inequalities for sections and projections of log-concave functions
papers.abstract: Higher order sharp Sobolev and local Sobolev type inequalities for log-concave functions are established. The new inequalities directly imply the isoperimetric inequalities by Bollobás and Thomason in 1995, by Liakopoulos in 2019, and the recently discovered local isoperimetric inequalities from [1]. In order to do so, we make use of three ingredients. First, sets of functional inequalities proven by Alonso-Gutiérrez, Bernués, Brazitikos and Carbery in 2021. Second, a multidimensional polynomial optimization result that originated in [1] and was initiated by Bollobás and Thomason. Third, a new integral formula for the projection of a log-concave function that links the geometric part with the more functional versions via some dependence on the Hessian matrix restricted to subspaces.

papers.title: The ALMA Survey of Gas Evolution of PROtoplanetary disks (AGE-PRO): Evolution of dust properties from multi-wavelength observations
papers.abstract: Understanding the evolution of solids in protoplanetary discs is important to comprehend the formation of giant planets cores and terrestrial planets. The ALMA Large Program AGE-PRO studied key disc properties in a survey of 30 protoplanetary discs across three evolutionary stages: the embedded phase (0.5-1 Myr), the middle-age phase (1-3 Myr), and the end of the disc lifetime (2-6 Myr). Preliminary dust properties were estimated using 1.3 mm observations, but a multi-wavelength analysis provides a better constraint of important properties such as the dust disc mass, the dust temperature, and the maximum grain size. We present new ALMA 3.1 mm and 1.5 mm (Bands 3 and 5) continuum observations of the complete survey of 30 AGE-PRO discs. We fitted the observed visibilities and derived radial brightness profiles, spatially resolving 20 discs from the AGE-PRO sample at the two studied wavelengths. A multi-wavelength modelling was performed including also the radial profiles from the 1.3 mm observations. Our results replicate trends obtained from the single wavelength analysis: the dust disc size seems to be constant over age and the dust disc mass decreases with time, with a factor $\sim$10-40 uncertainty from opacity assumptions. This result implies much lower gas-to-dust mass ratios for the discs in our sample than previously reported. In addition, the derived spectral indices are consistent with optically thick emission in a large fraction of the AGE-PRO discs, in particular for the Ophiuchus and Lupus discs.

papers.intro:
Planet formation takes place in discs of dust and gas that orbit a young protostar, as a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum after the collapse of a molecular cloud. Although these discs are mainly composed of gas, with only a few percent of the total mass coming from dust, the solid component is crucial in the formation of planetary bodies: dust grains serve as the building blocks for pebbles and planetesimals, influencing the efficiency of core accretion and the composition of forming planets (Testi et al., 2014; Williams and Cieza, 2011; Drazkowska et al., 2023).

Planet formation takes place in discs of dust and gas that orbit a young protostar, as a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum after the collapse of a molecular cloud. Although these discs are mainly composed of gas, with only a few percent of the total mass coming from dust, the solid component is crucial in the formation of planetary bodies: dust grains serve as the building blocks for pebbles and planetesimals, influencing the efficiency of core accretion and the composition of forming planets (Testi et al., 2014; Williams and Cieza, 2011; Drazkowska et al., 2023).

A detailed understanding of these physical processes not only allows us to reconstruct the early stages of planet formation, but also provides essential clues to explain the large diversity observed among exoplanet systems. More than 6000 exoplanets have been discovered in past years, showing that planetary systems differ widely from what we observe in the Solar system (Winn and Fabrycky, 2015). Variations in the structure and evolution of protoplanetary discs can lead to different outcomes of the properties of planets (Andrews, 2020, e.g.,). Therefore, studying the physics of discs and the processes governing the assembly of pebbles, planetesimals, and planetary cores is crucial for linking the initial conditions and evolution in planet-forming discs.

Within these pressure bumps, radial drift is halted, collision velocities decrease, and particle growth can proceed further.

More recently, the ALMA Large Program AGE-PRO (“ALMA survey of Gas Evolution in PROtoplanetary discs”) observed 30 protoplanetary discs of different ages, ranging from 0.1 to 6 Myr, to explore how the gas emission evolves through the lifetime of the discs (Zhang et al., 2025). The sample is composed by 10 young class I/ Flat Spectrum discs from the Ophiuchus region (Ruiz-Rodriguez et al., 2025), 10 middle-aged class II discs from the Lupus region (Deng et al., 2025), and 10 class II discs from the old Upper Scorpius (UpperSco) region (Agurto-Gangas et al., 2025). In this programme, the gas disc mass was found to decrease rapidly over time (Trapman et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, the radius of the gas discs was constrained only for the Lupus and UpperSco discs (Trapman et al., 2025a), with older discs exhibiting larger radii (Zhang et al., 2025). papers.title: Investigating the trackability of landmarks in NBI and WLI
papers.abstract: Reliable visual tracking of anatomical landmarks in endoscopic video is a key prerequisite for computer-assisted interventions in laryngeal surgery. While Narrow Band Imaging (NBI) is clinically established for enhancing vascular contrast, its effect on automated tracking relative to conventional White Light Imaging (WLI) remains unexplored. We present a quantitative comparison of landmark trackability in NBI and WLI using a forward-backward error framework applied to 61 endoscopic videos from 39 patients. Two regions of interest are evaluated: the vocal folds (VF) and mucosa with a prominent vascular pattern (MPVP). We compare a classical feature-based tracker (CSRT) against learning-based point trackers (CoTracker3-Online and TrackOnR) across both modalities. NBI consistently reduced the forward-backward error in both regions, reaching statistical significance for the vocal folds, while failure rates stayed low. These findings indicate that NBI can improve tracking robustness in laryngeal endoscopy, with implications for motion analysis, navigation, and robotic assistance.

papers.intro:
Reliable markerless tracking of natural landmarks in endoscopic videos is an important prerequisite for many computer-assisted interventions and analysis tasks, including motion compensation [7] and navigation [5]. In laryngeal endoscopy, robust tracking of anatomical landmarks is particularly challenging due to frequent camera motion, tissue deformation, illumination changes, and partial occlusions. Accurate temporal tracking of structures such as the vocal folds could nonetheless support downstream applications such as automated screening workflows and robotic assistance systems.

Accurate temporal tracking of structures such as the vocal folds could nonetheless support downstream applications such as automated screening workflows and robotic assistance systems.

Besides conventional White Light Imaging (WLI), Narrow Band Imaging (NBI) is widely used in clinical practice to enhance the visualization of vascular structures and mucosal patterns. Soft tissue tracking in surgical scenes has been studied extensively for WLI [3], but the performance of modern trackers on NBI remains unexplored. From a computer vision perspective, the enhanced vascular texture in NBI could improve the temporal stability of visual features and thereby tracking robustness, while the altered image appearance and stronger local contrast may instead degrade certain methods. It thus remains unclear whether NBI generally improves trackability over WLI, and whether any benefit depends on the tracked anatomical region or the tracking algorithm.

papers.title: Inference-Time Prior Adaptation for Imbalanced Data Streams under Concept Drift
papers.abstract: Data stream classification under concept drift and class imbalance requires models to adapt continuously while maintaining strong minority-class performance. Many existing approaches rely on active memory management, in- cluding instance removal, memory restructuring, resampling, and synthetic data generation. We present PAI-KNN, a k-nearest neighbor classifier that adapts via inference-time prior adjustment rather than memory modification. PAI-KNN main- tains a simple sliding-window buffer and dynamically adjusts its decision rule using class prior estimates derived from recent observations. Evaluated on a mul- titude of synthetic data streams covering various imbalance and drift scenarios, PAI-KNN achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, per- forming particularly well under scenarios involving dynamic class imbalance and concept drift. These findings highlight the potential of inference-time adaptation in challenging non-stationary environments and suggest that adaptation in memory- based stream classifiers need not rely exclusively on memory modification.

papers.intro:
Data stream classification [18] often requires models to operate under two simultaneous challenges: concept drift and class imbalance. As data distributions evolve over time, classifiers must continuously adapt to changing data while maintaining reliable performance on underrepresented classes. This problem arises in numerous real-world applications, including fraud detection, network monitoring, and predictive maintenance. Existing approaches address concept drift and class imbalance in different ways. Many stream classifiers are model-based, maintaining either a single evolving model [10], [20] or a pool of models that are continuously updated, reweighted, or replaced over time [5], [13], [8], [21], often combined with drift detectors like ADWIN [4]. KK-nearest neighbor (KNN) classifiers, in contrast, are instance-based or lazy learners that maintain explicit memories of previously observed instances and perform prediction directly from stored observations. Several KNN-based stream classifiers have been proposed that address concept drift and class imbalance through increasingly sophisticated active memory management mechanisms [14, 1]. Adaptation is typically achieved through instance removal, restructuring, compression, or balancing operations. While effective, active buffer-management strategies increase algorithmic complexity and may prematurely alter or discard useful information. In this paper, we investigate whether adaptation in KNN-based stream classifiers must occur through memory modification. We propose PAI-KNN, a kk-nearest neighbor classifier that maintains a simple sliding-window memory and adapts through inference-time prior adjustment. By shifting adaptation from memory management to inference, PAI-KNN responds to changing class distributions without the need for expensive memory management mechanisms. We evaluate PAI-KNN on a benchmark of synthetic data streams [2] covering diverse imbalance and drift scenarios. Despite its simplicity, PAI-KNN achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods and performs particularly well under scenarios involving high class imbalance and concept drift. These findings suggest that inference-time prior adaptation can provide a simple and effective alternative to complex memory management by avoiding structural assumptions. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the preliminaries and basic concepts. Related work is discussed in Section 3. In Section 4, we present our proposed method PAI-KNN. The experimental evaluation is detailed in Section 5. Conclusions and outlook are provided in Section 6.

papers.title: AI-Augmented Research: Free to Write, Costly to Read
papers.abstract: We study a model in which artificial intelligence lowers the cost of writing faster than the cost of reading. Authors differ in reputation, and time-constrained readers, such as referees, choose between ignoring, verifying, and trusting papers. As writing costs fall, the band of verified papers shrinks: outsiders are no longer read, and established authors are no longer checked. In the ``costless writing limit,'' the share of verified papers vanishes, and a paper's impact depends on its author's reputation alone. Readers can escape the flood by asking AI to summarize the literature. These summaries aggregate papers reliably only if their errors are sufficiently independent. Once the share of papers written with the same AI exceeds a threshold, summaries inherit the AI's errors, and AI review filters out the original research that could correct them.

At the same time, understanding and verifying a proof, a data set, or a calibration still takes time. This paper asks what happens to the market for research when the cost of writing falls faster than the cost of verification.

papers.title: Reducing 6G Energy Consumption: TDD-Aligned Drain Voltage Modulation for Power Amplifiers
papers.abstract: The Power Amplifier (PA) of a base station operates inefficiently at partial load, where back-off from the peak output power wastes supply headroom. Adapting the PA drain voltage to the instantaneous signal recovers this loss but requires frequent switching, increasing hardware cost. We propose TDD-Aligned Drain Voltage Modulation (TDD-DVM), a drain voltage modulation scheme that instead selects the drain voltage level once per Time-Division Duplex (TDD) period based on the downlink resource load and switches the voltage during the uplink window. This is enabled by the authors' previous work on POLITE link adaptation, which spreads the transmit power over resources left unused at partial load and moves the PA into a regime where a lower drain voltage suffices. In a 3GPP Urban Macro system-level simulation across traffic loads, we compare TDD-DVM against baseline approaches under conventional and POLITE link adaptation. At equal delivered throughput, TDD-DVM with POLITE keeps the packet failure ratio of the full drain voltage while consuming up to 35% less power than it under conventional link adaptation and up to 7% less than it under POLITE, capturing most of the gain of an idealized reference at moderate loads and roughly half at the highest load.

Envelope Tracking (ET) follows the instantaneous signal envelope, recovering efficiency under the high Peak-to-Average Power Ratio (PAPR) of Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM)-based waveforms at the cost of a fast, wideband supply path and linearization to contain tracking-induced distortion[4]. Average Power Tracking (APT) instead follows the average transmit power over a tracking interval[6], which adapts more coarsely but requires only a slow supply path. In both cases, the supply is modulated at the Radio Frequency (RF) transmitter level and driven by the transmitted signal itself.

A complementary line of work reduces BS energy by exploiting traffic variation at the network level. In the time and frequency domains, widely studied approaches include BS sleep modes[7], symbol- or slot-level power shutdown[8], and carrier shutdown in 5G New Radio (NR) [9]. In the power domain, energy saving is addressed through transmit-power adaptation, as in Power Optimization for Low Interference and Throughput Enhancement (POLITE) [10, 11], which spreads a transmission over more resources at lower power whenever the cell is not fully loaded.

Adapting the drain voltage to the instantaneous signal requires expensive hardware, since the supply must follow the signal almost instantaneously. We instead update it on a slow time scale, once per Time-Division Duplex (TDD) period, and place the update in the Uplink (UL) period, which carries no Downlink (DL) transmission and allows a slow ramp without signal distortion, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The supply thus has the whole UL period to settle, orders of magnitude longer than the signal-driven timescales of ET and APT, so a far slower and cheaper supply path suffices. We address the problem of minimizing the time-averaged consumed PA power by selecting the drain voltage level once per TDD period, while still serving the offered DL traffic. In this paper, we propose the load-based TDD-Aligned Drain Voltage Modulation (TDD-DVM) algorithm, which selects the PA drain voltage based on the current resource load before the next DL transmission opportunity. Our main contributions are: • We align the drain voltage adaptation with the TDD frame, ramping up/down the PA supply once per TDD period during the UL, lowering the hardware cost of drain voltage switching. • We incorporate POLITE Link Adaptation (LA) into TDD-DVM. By lowering the transmit power whenever the cell is not fully loaded, POLITE moves the PA into a region where a lower drain voltage suffices, which TDD-DVM exploits to reduce the consumed power. • We evaluate our proposal against other baselines with extensive system-level simulations, analyzing consumed power, delivered throughput, and packet failure ratio.

papers.title: Cluster connectivity in DES Y3 data: impact on galaxy properties
papers.abstract: Connectivity, namely the number of cosmic filaments reaching out of groups or clusters, has recently emerged as an informative way to quantify environment. With the advent of wide-area photometric surveys, it becomes possible to measure connectivity on a statistically significant sample of clusters. In this work, we extract the cosmic web from the DES Y3 photometric data and measure the connectivity around clusters from several public catalogs up to $z < 1$. Cosmic filaments are extracted in 2D with DisPerSE (the parametrization of which is calibrated on simulations) in tomographic slices of fixed comoving thickness of 220 Mpc, with a constant sampling across the redshift range ($\sim 0.1$ galaxies Mpc$^{-2}$). We first recover the well-established trend that cluster connectivity increases with cluster mass at all redshifts. We then investigate the properties of cluster member galaxies and find that, at fixed mass, clusters with a higher fraction of red (elliptical) galaxies are more strongly connected to the cosmic web. Furthermore, by examining the radial profiles of the red and elliptical galaxy fractions, we obtain hints that galaxy populations may undergo pre-processing within filamentary structures before being accreted into clusters. Overall, we demonstrate that despite photometric redshift uncertainties and projection effects, our method allows for the quantification of the cosmic web environment around clusters in broad-band photometric surveys. This work is consistent with results based on the Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1). We plan to publicly release the cluster connectivity catalog as well as the cosmic filament catalog.

papers.intro:
The anisotropic large-scale distribution of matter in the Universe forms a complex web-like structure on multiple spatial scales, known as the cosmic web (de Lapparent et al., 1986; Bond et al., 1996). Galaxy clusters and super-clusters are connected to cosmic filaments, which are themselves found at the intersection of walls surrounding voids. The formation of the cosmic-web is well understood in the context of the hierarchical growth of structure (Zeldovich et al., 1982). Anisotropic matter fluctuations in the early universe are amplified by gravity and result in the complex distribution we see today. It has been shown in numerical simulations that almost 50%50\% of dark matter and 80%80\% of galaxies are in filaments (Cen & Ostriker, 2006; Aragón-Calvo et al., 2010; Cautun et al., 2014; Ganeshaiah Veena et al., 2018). Cosmic filaments are therefore the primary environment in which galaxies grow and evolve. Theoretically, it is expected that the properties of cosmic web filaments shape masses, star-formation rates (Song et al., 2021; Winkel et al., 2021; Galárraga-Espinosa et al., 2023; Bulichi et al., 2024, e.g.), morphologies and alignments of galaxies (Codis et al., 2012; Ganeshaiah Veena et al., 2019; Malavasi et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023, e.g.) growing within them, not only through their local density (e.g. Dressler, 1980; Lewis et al., 2002; Ball et al., 2008; Pandey & Sarkar, 2017; Kuutma et al., 2020; O’Kane et al., 2024, amongst others), but also because the anisotropic geometry of the matter distribution generates tides which in turn impact the accretion onto galaxies (Musso et al., 2018; Montero-Dorta & Rodriguez, 2024, e.g.). We have now observational evidence which corroborates these expectations, where galaxy properties vary depending on their location in cosmic filaments (Malavasi et al., 2017; Laigle et al., 2018; Castignani et al., 2022; Hoosain et al., 2024; Santiago-Bautista et al., 2020; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2026d, e.g.).
