In addition to its impact on galaxies in filaments, the geometry of the large-scale cosmic web environment is also expected to shape groups and clusters. Groups and clusters correspond to peaks of the density fields on which cosmic filaments intersect. Connectivity is the number of filaments to which a given cluster is connected. Recently, connectivity has emerged as a new metric to quantify the structure of the cosmic web environment around peaks (Einasto et al., 2020; Gouin et al., 2020a; Cornwell et al., 2022, e.g.). In particular, several studies have highlighted the correlation between connectivity and the state of relaxation of the clusters, suggesting that more connected clusters are less relaxed, since they are more likely to have undergone recent mergers (Darragh Ford et al., 2019; Kraljic et al., 2020; Gouin et al., 2021). Observational evidence also suggests that overall more connected clusters contain more passive and elliptical galaxies (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2026b). Beyond its interest for understanding galaxy populations, connectivity has also been proposed as a cosmological probe that complements classical statistics (Codis et al., 2018; Dome et al., 2023; Shim et al., 2023; Boldrini & Laigle, 2024, e.g.).

Galaxies are discrete and biased tracers of the underlying dark-matter (DM) distribution, but observationally, they represent an easy way to trace cosmic filaments. Ideally, we would rely on spectroscopic surveys because in principle they enable a full 3D reconstruction of the cosmic web (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2026c, e.g.). However, they are inevitably limited in volume and sampling. When it comes to measuring the connectivity of galaxy clusters, it is pivotal to work on a large volume of data to recover a statistically significant number of clusters. In addition, these catalogues are generally biased towards certain populations of galaxies (e.g. Hα\alpha-emitters, red galaxies, Lyman-break galaxies, etc.), which hampers the completeness and purity of the cluster identification. In this case, an alternative method is to work in projection with photometric redshifts and to perform a 2D identification of filaments. This approach was taken, for example, by Laigle et al. (2018) and Sarron et al. (2019a).

papers.title: The SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM): Technical Overview
papers.abstract: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V (SDSS-V) Local Volume Mapper (LVM) is an ultra-wide integral field spectroscopic survey of the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds, and a sample of galaxies in the local volume. The LVM spatially resolved spectroscopy covers the bulk of the optical range (3600-9800 A) at medium spectral-resolution (R = 2200-5500), and maps the disks of these galaxies at high physical spatial resolution (< 1 pc in the MW and ~10 pc in the Magellanic Clouds). Observations are carried out with the LVM Instrument (LVM-I), a custom-built robotic telescope, instrument, and facility located at Las Campanas Observatory (LCO) in Chile. In this article we present a technical overview of the LVM project. We describe the hardware, the survey observing strategy, and the details of how science and calibration observations are carried out. We provide a high-level overview of the survey data flow, including the reduction and calibration of the LVM spectra, and the production of the main data products that are released by the project. We also present an assessment of the LVM data quality and instrumental stability based on science observations. The main goal of this article is to serve as a primer for LVM users, providing the technical information required for the adequate analysis, modeling, and interpretation of the LVM data.

papers.intro:
The Local Volume Mapper [10, LVM,] is one of the three programs that comprise the fifth realization of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey [34, SDSS-V,]. The main goal of the LVM project is to study the physical processes that act at the interface between the gas and stellar components of galaxies. These include: the formation of new stars out of the inter-stellar medium (ISM); the injection and propagation of energy and momentum that feeds back from these stars to the ISM, setting its kinematic, ionization, and thermodynamic state; and the chemical enrichment of interstellar gas from the dispersal of heavy elements produced in stars.

The Local Volume Mapper [10, LVM,] is one of the three programs that comprise the fifth realization of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey [34, SDSS-V,]. The main goal of the LVM project is to study the physical processes that act at the interface between the gas and stellar components of galaxies. These include: the formation of new stars out of the inter-stellar medium (ISM); the injection and propagation of energy and momentum that feeds back from these stars to the ISM, setting its kinematic, ionization, and thermodynamic state; and the chemical enrichment of interstellar gas from the dispersal of heavy elements produced in stars.

To achieve this goal, the LVM maps the optical stellar continuum and line emission from the ionized ISM, including dense nebulae (e.g. H II regions, supernova remnants, and planetary nebulae) and the warm interstellar medium (WIM), across the complete disks of galaxies at very high physical spatial resolution. The LVM data provides access to key diagnostics of the physical conditions of stars and ionized gas from the small sub-pc “energy injection scales” in which individual ionizing sources act on the surrounding gas, up to the kpc “galactic scales” on which the integrated effect of these processes establishes the global thermodynamic, chemical, and kinematic structure of star forming galaxies.

The LVM survey obtains deep, ultra-wide area, high physical spatial resolution, optical integral-field spectroscopy across the southern Milky Way (MW) plane, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), and the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). The survey also contains two secondary programs: one covering a sparse grid of WIM-dominated high Galactic latitude pointings, and another covering a sample of nearby galaxies in the Local Group and beyond. A complete overview of the LVM, including the project’s scientific motivation and experimental design, is presented in [10].

papers.title: Embedding Large PQC KEMs in IKEv2
papers.abstract: Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms carry public keys far larger than the established VPN handshake protocol IKEv2 was designed for. At the same time, its initial exchange comprising the public keys cannot be fragmented. In response, the IETF discusses a range of protocol adjustments, yet these proposals have never been compared in terms of their performance and stability under identical conditions. We systematically screened the IETF document corpus for such proposals, added three of our own (one using forward error correction and two using IKEv2 with QUIC, namely QUIKE and QUIKE with a composite key exchange), identified two specification gaps in existing acknowledgment drafts, and implemented all eight on the same open-source codebase. Measurements across different bandwidths, latencies, and packet loss rates, and with ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, and Classic McEliece, total 126 500 handshakes in 1296 different configurations and show that no mechanism fully compensates for the effect of the key size on performance. For Classic McEliece, no approach handles challenging conditions acceptably. The approaches either congest the link or take up to nearly two minutes per handshake on average. For ML-KEM and FrodoKEM, there are two ways forward: building on already standardized extensions or delegating the transport. The former requires the larger implementation change and needs further optimization, such as acknowledgment mechanisms or error-correcting codes, but grants continuity and compatibility. The latter can use a composite key exchange to avoid these drawbacks and achieve a faster, more resilient handshake and leaner implementation, with QUIKE-composite offering the best overall performance.

VPN securely interconnect IT infrastructure over public networks like the Internet, representing a backbone for modern distributed systems. However, the prospect of a large QC (QC) threatens the asymmetric cryptography building blocks vital for establishing secure VPN connections. VPN securely interconnect IT infrastructure over public networks like the Internet, representing a backbone for modern distributed systems. However, the prospect of a large QC (QC) threatens the asymmetric cryptography building blocks vital for establishing secure VPN connections. Even more urgently, an attacker can perform store-now, decrypt-later attacks, recording VPN connections today and using a QC to break the key agreement and decrypt the data in the future.

New PQC (PQC) key agreement mechanisms also protect against the QC threat. They typically consist of KEM [1]. Compared to classical DH (DH) constructs, they use a new syntax and both their public keys and ciphertexts are drastically larger. This complicates integrating them into the prevalent VPN protocols designed and optimized for classical cryptography. One example is IPsec’s handshaking protocol IKEv2 [2], first published in 2005. Its IETF working group acknowledged the need for adaptation, publishing the first PQC key agreement RFC [3] in 2023 and discussing further optimizations and alternatives since. Yet, these approaches are complex and face reliability issues, especially considering large PQC KEM and difficult network environments [4, 5].

Such a fundamental change to a VPN protocol needs to balance requirements in terms of, but not limited to, performance, resilience, backwards compatibility, complexity, and implementation intrusiveness. The resulting situation is complex, exacerbated by a lack of comprehensive data even regarding the well-quantifiable dimensions of performance and network resilience. In response, we conducted a systematic search for all relevant proposals for PQC KEM protocol adjustments for IKEv2 discussed at the IETF. Additionally, we propose three novel approaches: one using FEC (FEC) and two versions of QUIKE, where we combine IKEv2 and QUIC. We evaluate all proposals in terms of performance and network resilience in one stable test environment. This yields clear and reproducible data for a fair comparison and discussion of the qualitative advantages and drawbacks of both the drafts already in discussion as well as our novel ones. It shows that for the largest KEM, no approach offers acceptably stable performance. For smaller and medium-sized KEM, two pathways arise: One follows the already standardized way, adhering to design decisions and keeping continuity, but requires more complex adjustments and optimizations to provide performance and stability. The other moves away from existing design decisions and breaks compatibility, but offers the highest and most stable performance with an overall simpler design, especially QUIKE with a composite key exchange. The results act as guidance and clarification for the standardization working group, the academic community, and implementers making trade-offs within their software. We enable this with the following contributions: • A systematic literature review across the IETF document corpus, identifying proposals for PQC KEM in IKEv2. • An approach to stabilize the transmission of fragmented large KEM keys in IKEv2 using FEC. • Two approaches which fuse IKEv2 and QUIC [6] into QUIKE, a fast and reliable VPN key exchange protocol for IPsec; one using the previous “one-ke-per-round” semantics and one using a composite key agreement. • The identification of two specification gaps, concerning key retention and retransmission limits, in drafts adding acknowledgments to IKEv2 fragmentation, and a defect in the QUIC library we build on. • A reproducible evaluation of the handshake time of all approaches under varying latency, bandwidth, and packet loss as well as with three different KEM. • A qualitative discussion of the approaches’ overall complexity, implementation intrusiveness, and practicability.

papers.title: A comprehensive reanalysis of HD 99458. Not a magnetic Ap star but an oscillating Algol with ongoing mass transfer
papers.abstract: Context. Since 2019, HD 99458 has been known as a unique example of a $δ$ Sct variable with chemical peculiarities of Ap type in an eclipsing binary. Aims. We aim to review the peculiar status of the star with new observational materials. Methods. The current study is the result of meticulous analysis of space-based photometry from Kepler K2 and TESS, multi-site spectroscopic and spectropolarimetric observations, as well as speckle-interferometric data. Asteroseismic modelling of stellar pulsation is an essential part of the research. Results. We find HD 99458 to be an eclipsing Algol-type system with active mass transfer from the cool companion filling its Roche lobe to the pulsating primary. We identified signatures of a disc and accretion with varying rates in spectra and light curves. The system's orbital period increases with the rate $\dot{P}_\mathrm{orb}$ of 5.045 s yr$^{-1}$, indicating potential multiplicity. We failed to detect traces of the primary's magnetic field or excessive abundances, both of which are necessary to classify HD 99458 as an Ap star. We have constrained the fundamental parameters of the pulsating primary and analysed its pulsation using asteroseismology. In space-based photometry, we identified pulsation modes with angular degree $\ell\leq3$. Two-dimensional Fourier analysis of spectroscopic time series reveals pulsations in the form of standing waves with the azimuthal orders $|m|=5\pm1$. Combined analysis of photometry and spectroscopy confirms the status of HD 99458 as a triaxial gravitationally distorted pulsator. Conclusions. Our comprehensive study affirms the new classification for HD 99458.

papers.intro:
Amid the surge of interest in the search for new exoplanets in space-based photometry obtained by the Kepler K2 mission (Borucki et al. 2010; Howell et al. 2014), Barros et al. (2016) identified HD 99458 as a candidate exoplanetary system after recognising periodic eclipses with a depth of 1.494%. In the follow-up study, 2019MNRAS.487.4230S identified the secondary as a low-mass red dwarf star rather than an exoplanet. The primary component was found to be an A-type pulsating δ\delta Scuti (hereafter, δ\delta Sct) star with extensive spots and anomalous chemical composition. The reported excesses of Fe, Si, and Ti exceeded 1 dex compared to the Sun, allowing the authors to classify the primary component of HD 99458 as an Ap star.

The Ap stars form a subgroup of the family of chemically peculiar (CP) stars, mostly main-sequence objects with abnormal spectra indicating a peculiar chemical composition. The fraction of CP stars among objects of a similar effective temperature is approximately 10%. 1974ARA&A..12..257P subdivided CP stars into four subgroups, where A stars with peculiar spectra occur in the groups CP1 and CP2. The populations of these groups differ in the character of variability, chemical composition, magnetism, and binarity. Strong, globally organised magnetic fields are the hallmark of Ap variables of the α2\alpha^{2} Canum Venaticorum (Hümmerich et al. 2018, ACV; ) type, or CP2 stars. Hereafter, we use Ap and CP2 interchangeably to refer to this class. According to the information presented in the Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) catalogue, HD 99458 is classified as a variable of ACV|CP|MCP|ROAM|ROAP|SXARI type with a score of 0.27 (Eyer et al. 2023; Gavras et al. 2023; 2023A&A...674A..14R).

In contrast to their non-magnetic siblings, the CP2 stars seem to avoid close binary systems. The fraction of the known systems harbouring magnetic components shrinks rapidly with a decreasing orbital period (Carrier et al. 2002; 2017A&A...601A..14M, e.g.). To the best of our knowledge, only three such systems with periods shorter than 3 days are known: HD 15144 (Bonsack 1981; Cowley & Hubrig 2008), HD 200405 (Carrier et al. 2002), and HD 99458. Of the three, only the object of this study undoubtedly has a companion, as its radial velocity varies with a high amplitude and photometry shows eclipses.

The δ\delta Sct variables are common among A-type stars. Many of them appear to be members of close binary systems. The δ\delta Sct variables are multi-periodic pulsators of luminosity classes V to III with masses between approximately 1.5M☉M_{\sun} and 2.5M☉M_{\sun} (Handler 2009). The observed light changes are caused by multiple radial and non-radial low-order pressure (pp) modes, which are excited through the κ\kappa mechanism (Handler 2009). In evolved δ\delta Sct stars, so-called mixed modes are often observed. These pulsation modes exhibit gravity (gg) mode characteristics in the interior and pp-mode characteristics near the stellar surface (Bowman et al. 2016).

The coexistence of the δ\delta Sct-type pulsation with the strong magnetic fields typical of Ap stars is an important observational effect with a wide potential application (Buysschaert et al. 2017; 2024bss..confE..74N, e.g.). On the one hand, asteroseismology is the only reliable method for probing the internal structure of stars. On the other hand, incorporating magnetic effects into the theory of stellar oscillations is challenging (2018CoSka..48...73W). Observationally, identifying δ\delta Sct pulsations in magnetic CP2 stars is also challenging. Spectral lines are simultaneously distorted by pulsation, Zeeman splitting, and chemical spots, complicating spectroscopic analyses (Gutteridge et al. 2026, see, e.g.). Consequently, only a small number of CP2 stars are currently reported to exhibit δ\delta Sct pulsations, most of which have been identified from photometry alone. As an example, 2025A&A...704A.134T reported only 13 stars. Many of these pulsators fall outside the classical instability strip, suggesting either inaccuracies in physical parameters or incorrect identification of pulsators as CP2 due to hidden binarity. Stellar pulsation with eclipses, as observed in HD 99458, provides a unique opportunity for a precise characterisation of the pulsator and its companion.

2019MNRAS.487.4230S considered the presence of a cool inflated companion with an accretion disc as an alternative interpretation of the out-of-eclipse variation of HD 99458. However, this scenario was rejected in favour of a fully detached binary with the CP2 primary due to weak observational support. The δ\delta Sct pulsators in eclipsing Algol-type semi-detached systems (oEA stars) exhibit characteristics similar to those of classical δ\delta Sct stars, yet their evolutionary status differs markedly due to mass transfer between components (2002ASPC..259...96M). In systems with large orbital inclinations and no eclipses, these pulsators can be difficult to distinguish from classical δ\delta Sct stars photometrically. They may instead be classified by the radial velocities and the pronounced variations in their spectral line profiles, which arise from the non-stationary nature of mass transfer and the presence of hot regions that formed by the interaction of the gas stream with the stellar atmosphere. The ongoing mass transfer, regulated by magnetic activity cycles of the Roche-lobe–filling late-type component, exerts a significant influence on the pulsational spectrum (Lehmann et al. 2020; 2022Galax..10...97M).

papers.title: The space of equators has infinite Hofer's diameter
papers.abstract: We settle several questions about Hofer's geometry of the two-sphere. We prove that the space of equators has infinite Hofer diameter, construct simple commutators of arbitrarily large Hofer norm, and exhibit a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism whose iterates escape to infinity in Hofer distance from the set of autonomous diffeomorphisms. Finally, we construct a bi-Lipschitz group monomorphism from the free group of rank two, equipped with its conjugation-invariant generator norm, into the Hamiltonian group equipped with Hofer's metric. The proof rests on an interplay between Lagrangian Floer theory in the fourth symmetric product of the sphere and combinatorial group theory. This paper was written with substantial assistance from AI.

papers.title: AutoMIL: Automated Multiple Instance Learning for Whole-Slide Image Classification
papers.abstract: Developing multiple instance learning pipelines for the classification of whole-slide images involves many interdependent design decisions and expertise in both pathology and machine learning. We present AutoMIL, an open-source framework that applies principles from the field of automated machine learning to tackle this task by automating integral pipeline steps, such as preprocessing, training and evaluation. In a benchmark evaluation with default settings, AutoMIL reached ROC-AUC scores of 0.94 on UBC-OCEAN, 0.99 on PCam and 0.93-0.96 on a TCGA-NSCLC subset, comparable to specialised pipelines in related work. Ensembling mainly improved performance on imbalanced data, showing that an automated pipeline must adapt to dataset characteristics. AutoMIL thus provides an accessible baseline for whole-slide image classification without manual pipeline configuration.

papers.title: Finite-Temperature Transconductance of Multiterminal Josephson Junctions with Topological Andreev Spectra
papers.abstract: Multiterminal Josephson junctions (MTJJs) provide a controllable platform for engineering topological Andreev spectra. At zero temperature, Andreev bound states (ABSs) with nonzero Chern numbers give rise to quantized transconductance between superconducting terminals. We derive the finite-temperature transconductance of MTJJs using linear-response theory. We first demonstrate the destructive role of temperature: changes in the thermal occupations of the ABSs destroy exact transconductance quantization. We then show that finite temperature can also play a constructive role by making the transconductance sensitive to finite-energy topological crossings hidden from the zero-temperature response. Our results establish the thermal limitations of transconductance quantization and identify finite-temperature transport as a probe of otherwise inaccessible topology in Andreev spectra.

papers.title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.

papers.intro:
Recent studies indicate that developers routinely integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) into their daily coding workflows [1, 2]. Beyond code generation, LLMs are used to iteratively refine code to reduce execution time and memory usage, tasks that previously required expert manual effort [3]. This growing practice implicitly assumes that performance improvements also translate into environmental benefits: that faster code is greener code. However, each optimization interaction carries two distinct energy costs: the inference energy consumed when the model produces code [4, 5], and the execution energy consumed when that code is later run [6]. Both costs are largely invisible to the developer, yet together determine whether an optimization yields a net energy benefit. However, it remains unclear whether the execution-time savings can offset the energy required to generate the optimization, or whether LLM-optimized code is more energy-efficient than code written by human developers [7, 8].

papers.title: DriveOSS: Dataset and Benchmark for 3D Anomaly Segmentation and Open-set Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed-set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real-world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed-set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real-world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open-set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround-view RGB cameras, a 128-beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real-world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in-distribution) and OOD (out-of-distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.
papers.intro:
Robust 3D scene understanding is essential for autonomous driving. Although recent semantic segmentation methods achieve strong performance on established benchmarks, they typically operate under a closed-set assumption, assigning every point to a predefined class. This assumption is violated when vehicles encounter unknown obstacles, such as construction materials or fallen cargo. Misclassifying such objects as known classes may lead to unreliable downstream decisions. Open-set semantic segmentation therefore requires jointly recognizing in-distribution (ID) classes and detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects.

Open-set semantic segmentation therefore requires jointly recognizing in-distribution (ID) classes and detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects.

While open-set segmentation has received increasing attention in 2D vision [29, 16, 14, 10], progress in 3D remains limited. Existing studies generally evaluate closed-set semantic segmentation and anomaly detection separately, although real-world systems require both capabilities. Moreover, standardized 3D open-set benchmarks remain scarce, particularly under adverse weather and illumination [25, 31]. Most driving datasets emphasize favorable daytime conditions and insufficiently represent nighttime, rain, snow, and reduced visibility [2, 25], which complicate both known-class recognition and unknown-object detection.

It provides synchronized LiDAR point clouds, surround-view RGB images, and point-wise annotations for known classes and unknown objects across diverse locations, weather, and illumination conditions. papers.title: On the Algebraic Structure of Lewis Carroll's Logic -- Behind the Looking Glass: A Mathematical Perspective
papers.abstract: Charles Ludwidge Dodgeson, better known by his literary pen name `Lewis Carroll', has a number of well known and cherished literary works to his credit, for example "Alice in Wonderland" and "Through the Looking Glass". Apart from this he is known to have a strong professional interest in mathematics and logic with an inclination towards an educational and recreational perspective. In this work we consider the algebraic structure behind Lewis Carroll's approach to classical logic and his logical puzzles. Starting with the arithmetic of $0$ and $1$, we develop the connections between Boolean-valued functions, sets and predicates, which we refer to as the "entangled trinity". This provides a common setting in which Carroll's approach and Boole's perspective can be understood. Particular attention is given to what is meant by "the conclusion" of a logical problem. We suggest a precise interpretation of a complete conclusion in terms of largest lower bounds involving only the predicates to be retained, thereby sharpening Carroll's approach. The role of natural language in choosing a suitable universe and identifying these predicates is discussed through a variety of examples. Finally, we present computerised solution methods, including the use of Boolean satisfiability solvers for larger puzzles.

Approaching logical issues with arithmetic means is really at the core of Lewis Carroll’s approach to classical logic, which in turn is close to Boole’s perspective, [1]. His criticism of Boolean logic is more from a didactical and intuitive perspective. Our discussion actually consoles Dodgson’s with Boole’s approach showing that in essence they are indeed the same, although looking quite different in interpretation and usage. As for the methods Lewis Carroll suggested to solve his puzzles, we have to say that they do give a conclusion, but only in simple cases they yield the sharpest conclusion, which is indeed what we shall be focusing on, since weaker conclusions can then derived trivially. Also, we have restricted our references merely to those actually used in the work presented here.

papers.title: AMICO galaxy clusters in KiDS-1000: Cosmological constraints from the two-point correlation function
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the clustering properties of an optically identified photometric galaxy cluster catalogue from KiDS-1000. The sample was identified by the AMICO algorithm and consists of 9049 clusters with $S/N\geq3.5$, in the redshift range $0.1\leq z<0.8$, spread over an effective area of 838.78 deg$^2$. Clusters are selected according to their observed intrinsic richness, with thresholds of $λ^*{obs}\geq 20,25,30$ within $0.10\leq z<0.30$, $0.30\leq z<0.45$ and $0.45\leq z<0.80$, respectively. We measure the multipoles of the two-point correlation function over different ranges of scales from 5 $h^{-1}$ Mpc to 150 $h^{-1}$ Mpc. We model the clustering signal in the context of the $Λ$CDM cosmology, accounting for the main observational effects, such RSDs and photo-$z$ uncertainties. The effective bias of the cluster sample is estimated via a mass-richness scaling relation. For the MCMC analysis, we adopt Gaussian priors on the parameters of the mass-richness scaling relation, and broad, uniform priors to derive cosmological constraints on the cold matter density parameter, the power spectrum amplitude and the structure growth parameter, $S_8\equivσ_8 \sqrt{Ω{m}/0.3}$. Specifically, we find $Ω_{m}=0.24^{+0.02}{-0.02}$ and $σ_8=0.86^{+0.13}{-0.10}$ representing an improvement in precision over both the 2D and 3D AMICO clustering analyses performed on the previous KiDS data release. Moreover, we obtain $S_8=0.77^{+0.10}_{-0.08}$ in $1σ$ agreement with the AMICO KiDS-1000 number counts constraints estimated from the same catalogue, as well as with some results from external early- and late-Universe data sets. Our work strengthens the potential of cluster clustering as a complementary and competitive probe, to be included and further developed with the final KiDS-Legacy data release, and in other future Stage-IV photometric redshift surveys.

papers.intro:
In the hierarchical cosmological framework, galaxy clusters are the latest gravitationally bound systems ever formed (Kaiser 1984), emerging from the nodes of the filamentary cosmic web and tracing the peaks of the large-scale matter density field (Bardeen et al. 1986; Tormen 1998). As multi-component systems, made up of dark and baryonic matter in different phases, they provide valuable insights about the structure formation process along cosmic time. Their assembly history reveals information about the dynamical environment in which they grow, contributing to shed light on some of the major open questions in cosmology. These include the nature of dark matter (Meneghetti et al. 2020; Eckert et al. 2022; Natarajan et al. 2026) and dark energy (Allen et al. 2011; Ghirardini et al. 2024). Recently, numerous theoretical and observational studies have shown that the abundance and the spatial distribution of galaxy clusters are powerful tools for constraining fundamental parameters of the Λ\Lambda-cold dark matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) model, such as Ωm\Omega_{m}, the total matter density parameter, and σ8\sigma_{8}, the square root of the mass variance on scales of 8 h−1h^{-1} Mpc (Costanzi et al. 2019; Lesci et al. 2022a; Lesci et al. 2022b; Chiu et al. 2023; Bocquet et al. 2024; Fumagalli et al. 2024; Ghirardini et al. 2024; Romanello et al. 2024; Sunayama et al. 2024; Abbott et al. 2025; Lesci et al. 2025, see, for instance,). In particular, the two-point correlation function of galaxy clusters offers several significant advantages in cosmological inference. Firstly, compared to galaxies, they are highly biased tracers, so their clustering signal is higher. They are also less affected by nonlinearities, enabling us to simplify theoretical modelling within the same range of scales under investigation. In addition, the ‘fingers-of-God’ (FoG) effect — the small-scale redshift-space distortions (RSDs) caused by the motions of tracers within virialised structures — is reduced (Veropalumbo et al. 2014; Sereno et al. 2015; Marulli et al. 2017, see, for example,). Finally, galaxy clusters are identifiable in optical and near-infrared wavebands due to their luminous starlight (Rykoff et al. 2014; Rykoff et al. 2016; Maturi et al. 2019; Maturi et al. 2025); in X-rays by exploiting the emission from their diffuse intracluster medium (Pacaud et al. 2016; Bulbul et al. 2024, ICM,); and in the millimetric band through the Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect (Sunyaev and Zeldovich 1970; Sunyaev and Zeldovich 1972), which is produced by the inverse Compton scattering between the hot ICM electrons and the cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons (Planck Collaboration et al. 2011; Hilton et al. 2021). This gives us the opportunity to calibrate scaling relations that link spectroscopic or photometric observables, accessible with telescopes, to the derived mass of the galaxy clusters (Okabe et al. 2010; Allen et al. 2011; Giodini et al. 2013; Sereno and Ettori 2015; Bellagamba et al. 2019; Lesci et al. 2022a; Seppi et al. 2024; Lesci et al. 2025). Although the galaxy bias remains difficult to model properly, and it is often treated as a nuisance parameter, measuring cluster masses enables us to estimate the effective bias of the cluster sample, beffb_{\mathrm{eff}}, as a function of the cosmological model (Paech et al. 2017; Lesci et al. 2022b; Romanello et al. 2024, see, for instance,), and therefore to break its degeneracy with σ8\sigma_{8}. Current Stage-III photometric surveys, such as the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) Subaru Strategic Program (Aihara et al. 2018, HSC-SSP; see), the Dark Energy Survey (Dark Energy Survey Collaboration et al. 2016; Bechtol et al. 2026, DES; see) and the Kilo Degree Survey (de Jong et al. 2017; Kuijken et al. 2019; Wright et al. 2024, KiDS; see), provide deep and multi-band imaging over thousands of square degrees, and a large number of galaxies that can be used successfully for clustering, weak-lensing and, in general, cosmological analyses. These surveys also represent a valuable testing ground for models and methods that aim to maximise the amount of cosmological signal that can be extracted from ongoing Stage-IV surveys, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (The LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration et al. 2018; Ivezić et al. 2019, LSST; see) and the Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Blanchard et al. 2020; Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). In this paper, we conduct a two-point correlation function analysis based on the fourth data release of the Kilo Degree Survey (hereafter referred to as KiDS-1000). The catalogue of galaxy clusters, identified by the Adaptive Matched Identifier of Clustered Objects (Bellagamba et al. 2018, AMICO; see) algorithm, has been described in Maturi et al. (2025), while the first cosmological results, derived from cluster abundance, as well as the weak-lensing calibration of the scaling relation, are presented in Lesci et al. (2025). In order to measure the appropriate statistical quantities and to run a full Bayesian inference, we make use of CosmoBolognaLib (Marulli et al. 2016)11 1 https://gitlab.com/federicomarulli/CosmoBolognaLib, a set of free software C++ and Python libraries. This work is part of a series of papers that employ AMICO KiDS-1000 clusters for both astrophysical and cosmological outcomes (Maturi et al. 2025; Lesci et al. 2025; Lesci et al. 2026, see, for example,). It is organised as follows: in Sect. 2 we present the AMICO KiDS-1000 cluster catalogue. In Sect. 3 we describe the methodology adopted to measure and model the cluster two-point correlation function and its multipoles. In Sect. 4 we discuss the results of the Bayesian inference, comparing them with publications from galaxy clusters cosmology available in the literature and with previous studies based on the KiDS survey. Finally, in Sect. 5 we draw our conclusions.

papers.title: Peaking self-similar solutions and continuation after blow-up for a quasilinear Hardy-Hénon equation
papers.abstract: We consider the quasilinear Hardy-Hénon equation $$ u_t=Δu^m+|x|^σu^p, \quad (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^N\times(0,T), $$ in the range of exponents and dimension $$ N\geq3, \quad σ\in(-2,\infty), \quad m>1, \quad p>p_S(σ)=\frac{m(N+2σ+2)}{N-2}. $$ We establish sharp ranges of exponents $(m,p,σ)$ guaranteeing existence of \emph{peaking solutions} in backward self-similar form $$ u(x,t)=(T-t)^{-α}f(|x|(T-t)^{-β}). $$ By peaking solutions we understand solutions blowing up at a finite time $T\in(0,\infty)$ but allowing for a continuation after the blow-up time. As a remarkable outcome, a number of ranges of exponents $σ$ and $m$ for which peaking solutions exist for any $p>p_S(σ)$ are deduced, contrasting to the previously considered exponent $σ=0$, where a Lepin-type critical exponent $p_L$ provides an upper bound for $p$.

papers.title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
papers.abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.

papers.intro:
Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide, necessitating scalable solutions for accurate and reliable diagnostics [8, 21, 7]. Echocardiography is central to this clinical challenge, providing a non-invasive, real-time window into cardiac structure and function. However, the life-saving potential of this technology is severely constrained by a global shortage of experienced interpreters [2, 29]. Achieving proficiency in echocardiography requires years of intensive training, creating a bottleneck that restricts access to timely diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings [24, 30, 45]. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising solution, current approaches remain fragmented. Existing tools are either task-specific models limited to predicting individual diseases [20, 13, 14, 27, 34], or general-purpose foundation models that perform isolated measurements and diagnosis without clinical context [10, 43]. Crucially, these systems operate as “black boxes,” failing to replicate the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning process of a cardiologist. Consequently, a critical gap remains: the absence of an AI system capable of comprehensive, trustworthy, and explainable echocardiographic analysis assistive to the echocardiographer.

However, the life-saving potential of this technology is severely constrained by a global shortage of experienced interpreters [2, 29]. Achieving proficiency in echocardiography requires years of intensive training, creating a bottleneck that restricts access to timely diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings [24, 30, 45]. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising solution, current approaches remain fragmented. Existing tools are either task-specific models limited to predicting individual diseases [20, 13, 14, 27, 34], or general-purpose foundation models that perform isolated measurements and diagnosis without clinical context [10, 43]. Crucially, these systems operate as “black boxes,” failing to replicate the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning process of a cardiologist. Consequently, a critical gap remains: the absence of an AI system capable of comprehensive, trustworthy, and explainable echocardiographic analysis assistive to the echocardiographer.

Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal large vision-language model that bridges this gap, functioning as an AI assistant designed to help echocardiographers interpret echocardiography, estimate cardiac measurements and draft reports. EchoChat represents a paradigm shift from narrow, task-specific algorithms to a system capable of executing complete clinical diagnostic analysis. It performs a comprehensive analysis covering an unprecedented range of 33 cardiac conditions and 22 cardiac measurements. Unlike previous iterations of medical AI, EchoChat generates complete, narrative diagnostic reports from raw echocardiography data and engages in evidence-based question-answering regarding its findings (Fig. 1a). We achieved this by developing a framework that emulates human expert learning and reasoning, integrating two core innovations as illustrated in Fig. 1c: an Echocardiography Knowledge Library (EKL), which grounds the model in a vast database of established cardiological science; and a Cardiologist-Like Reasoning (CLR) module, a bespoke Chain-of-Thought mechanism that enforces adherence to clinical guidelines and explicitly links conclusions to visual evidence.

Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal large vision-language model that bridges this gap, functioning as an AI assistant designed to help echocardiographers interpret echocardiography, estimate cardiac measurements and draft reports. EchoChat represents a paradigm shift from narrow, task-specific algorithms to a system capable of executing complete clinical diagnostic analysis. It performs a comprehensive analysis covering an unprecedented range of 33 cardiac conditions and 22 cardiac measurements. Unlike previous iterations of medical AI, EchoChat generates complete, narrative diagnostic reports from raw echocardiography data and engages in evidence-based question-answering regarding its findings (Fig. 1a). We achieved this by developing a framework that emulates human expert learning and reasoning, integrating two core innovations as illustrated in Fig. 1c: an Echocardiography Knowledge Library (EKL), which grounds the model in a vast database of established cardiological science; and a Cardiologist-Like Reasoning (CLR) module, a bespoke Chain-of-Thought mechanism that enforces adherence to clinical guidelines and explicitly links conclusions to visual evidence.

Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs derived from 46,358 echocardiographic examinations (Fig. 1b), EchoChat establishes a new state-of-the-art. In evaluations involving over 5,000 echocardiography studies across five external hospitals in the Netherlands, Austria, Spain, and China, EchoChat demonstrates enhanced diagnostic scope and performance, as well as generalization across diverse populations and acquisition protocols. Beyond the coverage of existing foundation models (18 conditions at most [10]), EchoChat extends diagnostic scope to a broad set of 33 conditions with 15 newly available challenging conditions achieving an average accuracy of 83.0% across four external test sets. Furthermore, EchoChat surpasses leading foundation models [10, 43] in both cardiac condition recognition (average recall improvement of 28.00% and 13.54% over EchoPrime [43] and PanEcho [10], respectively) and quantification (average R2R^{2} score increase of 0.294 and 0.275 over EchoPrime [43] and PanEcho [10], respectively). Notably, EchoChat achieved a mean absolute error in left ventricular ejection fraction estimation that was 1.79% lower than that of PanEcho [10], averaged equally across the five external clinical cohorts. In the EchoChat-routine echocardiographer collaboration study, EchoChat-routine echocardiographer collaborative reports improve average primary-diagnosis F1 scores from 72.78% to 82.75% compared with the unassisted echocardiographer group. Two senior echocardiographers blinded to report source also rated collaborative reports higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness, with mean scores 15.84% and 20.74% higher than those of unassisted routine reports, respectively. By democratizing access to high-level cardiac expertise and augmenting clinician performance, EchoChat offers a transformative path toward a new standard of global cardiovascular care.

papers.title: A frame-indifferent rank-one convex function in three dimensions which is not quasiconvex
papers.abstract: We construct a function $W:\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\to\mathbb{R}$ which is frame-indifferent, $W(QF)=W(F)$ for all $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, rank-one convex, but not quasiconvex. In a neighbourhood of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ the function is an explicit polynomial of degree four in the strain $F^TF-\mathrm{Id}$; the failure of quasiconvexity occurs at $F=\mathrm{Id}$ through a third-order mechanism of Šverák type, with test functions whose gradients are arbitrarily close to $\mathrm{Id}$. The polynomial is obtained from a geometrically linear example, a rank-one convex, non-quasiconvex quartic polynomial of the symmetric part of the gradient, by evaluating it at the strain $\frac12(F^TF-\mathrm{Id})$, adding a uniaxial prestress and a cubic correction, and enlarging the quartic term. The local function is extended to all of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ by adding a frame-indifferent polyconvex function which vanishes near $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. This work was carried out with the assistance of the AI model Claude Opus 5.5; the proofs of the main results have been formally verified in Lean 4.

Quasiconvexity is the natural condition for the existence of minimizers [3, 5], while rank-one convexity (ellipticity) is the condition that can be checked in practice. It is natural to ask whether the two notions are distinct also for frame-indifferent stored energy densities. Šverák’s construction does not respect (1.2), and we are not aware of a frame-indifferent example in the literature. Versions of Morrey’s question with the invariance requirements of elasticity are listed as open in [27], mainly in the planar case, where it is also observed that even for n≥3n\geq 3 no isotropic example seems to be known. We show that this is the case.

papers.title: An energy-stable parametric finite element framework for surface diffusion with moving contact lines on curved substrates
papers.abstract: We develop energy-stable parametric finite element methods for surface diffusion of solid films with moving contact lines on curved substrates. Discretizing both the film surface and the substrate patches allows the introduction of linear schemes that are unconditionally energy stable. A nonlinear variant of the schemes ensures that, in addition, the vertices of the substrate approximations remain attached to the true substrate throughout. Moreover, our framework can incorporate anisotropic surface energy densities, for both the film surface and the substrate, as well as different tangential motions. Numerical experiments in two and three space dimensions illustrate the practicality of the introduced methods.

papers.intro:
In solid-state dewetting, a thin solid film on a substrate changes its shape when it is annealed below its melting temperature. Mass moves along surfaces and interfaces rather than through the bulk, and the film may break up into islands. The process can damage microelectronic interconnects, and it can also be used to make ordered nanoparticles for catalysis, sensing, and nanowire growth; see the reviews of Thompson [42] and Leroy et al. [34].

Early finite element schemes for surface diffusion and related fourth-order flows were developed for graphs and parametric surfaces by Bänsch, Morin, and Nochetto [2, 3]. The parametric approach of Barrett, Garcke, and Nürnberg [15, 17, 21], commonly referred to as the BGN method, leaves the tangential mesh velocity free. This freedom accommodates moving junctions [20, 5] and usually gives well-distributed meshes without remeshing. Continuous-in-time, spatially discrete variants of the BGN approach are structure-preserving, in the sense that they decrease the surface energy while conserving the enclosed volume. The fully discrete BGN scheme also dissipates surface energy; however, it does not preserve the enclosed volume. A structure-preserving fully discrete BGN discretization for closed curves and surfaces was introduced by Bao and Zhao [12]. Extensions to curve networks and surface clusters were developed in [5], and an axisymmetric formulation was presented in [4]. Structure-preserving schemes based on Lagrange multipliers were proposed in [26, 28].

BGN methods also handle triple junctions of curve networks and surface clusters, interfaces that meet a fixed external boundary, and thermal grooving [14, 16, 20, 19]. A curved substrate adds a geometric difficulty. When the contact line moves, the areas of Γin\Gamma_{\rm in} and Γout\Gamma_{\rm out} change, and on a curved substrate this change depends on where the contact line lies. The curvature of the substrate also changes the dynamics: a small solid island migrates along the curvature gradient of the substrate [48]. For general prescribed Young angles, existing parametric methods for curved substrates treat curves: a curve attached to a prescribed substrate curve [11], or the generating curve of an axisymmetric surface [24]. For surfaces in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} with non-right Young angles on general curved substrates, we are not aware of a parametric method with a proved fully discrete energy law.

We consider substrates given as the zero level set of a function ϕ\phi. The main idea of this paper is to mesh the substrate as well as the film surface, so that the energies of all interfaces enter the discrete energy. The substrate vertices move with the contact line, and at each of them the discrete velocity is tangent to the substrate. This gives two kinds of schemes. The single-patch scheme glues the film surface to one substrate patch, Γin\Gamma_{\rm in} if γin≥γout\gamma_{\rm in}\geq\gamma_{\rm out} and Γout\Gamma_{\rm out} if γin≤γout\gamma_{\rm in}\leq\gamma_{\rm out}, and works with this single surface, which is closed in the first case. The full-substrate scheme, on the other hand, meshes both patches, so the contact line becomes a triple junction of three meshed surfaces. All these schemes are linear and uniquely solvable, and applying the area inequality of [15, 17] (see also [1]) on every meshed surface shows that they are unconditionally energy stable. Since the attachment constraint only makes the velocity of each substrate vertex tangent to the substrate, the vertices may leave a curved substrate. Upon utilizing a degree of freedom in the choice of discrete substrate normals, we are able to extend these linear schemes to a mildly nonlinear variant, which retains all the desirable properties and, in addition, guarantees that the substrate vertices stay exactly on the substrate. Extending the full-substrate scheme to anisotropic film and substrate energies is straightforward. To our knowledge, anisotropic substrate energies have not been treated by parametric methods for curved substrates.

papers.title: Low-Temperature Hybrid Monte Carlo for Perylene and Corannulene: Stabilizing Determinant and Force
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a real world physics study of the molecules perylene and corannulene at different doping levels, and calculating selected one-, two- (exciton) and three-body (trion) correlators. This has been done by performing Hubbard-model simulations near room temperature. We find, between charge neutral and doubly charged plateaus of perylene, an interaction-induced $ΔQ = 1$ plateau whose width grows with interaction strength and in which the ground state is a spin doublet rather than a singlet. The algorithmic advancement enabling this study simultaneously stabilizes the determinant and force calculations to machine precision at room temperature, while scaling as well as standard determinant Quantum Monte Carlo simulations of these systems. Furthermore, our formalism retains the full time-displaced (2-point) Green's function, allowing us to construct any $n$-body correlator, including those that contain disconnected diagrams.

Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) studies of the Hubbard model carried out at large β\beta (inverse temperature) keep the finite temperature effects like the zero-temperature extrapolation and excited state decay in correlator analysis under control. Large β\beta also reaches near room temperature or below, at which experiments are performed, so results are easier to compare with measurements.

papers.title: PARIS: Parallel Arithmetic Reduction and Integrated Selection for MSDF Inner Products
papers.abstract: Existing most-significant-digit-first (MSDF) accelerators serialize input-term processing, causing inner-product latency to increase with fan-in. This paper presents PARIS, an MSDF architecture that eliminates input-term serialization through parallel bit-plane reduction and shared carry-save residual selection. For $B$-bit operands, PARIS processes $B^2$ bit-position pairs, independent of fan-in within the supported tile, while generating exact MSDF outputs. Synthesized in 45\,nm at 100\,MHz, the 784-lane INT8 core occupies 0.008701\,mm$^2$ and completes an inner product in 88 cycles. Evaluation on two MNIST multilayer perceptrons demonstrates arithmetic-workload speedups of 240.44$\times$ and 180.47$\times$ over a matched reused-MSDF implementation, reducing arithmetic energy by 98.89\% and 98.58\%, respectively. A synthesized 16-engine accelerator occupies 0.90273\,mm$^2$ and meets the 100\,MHz timing constraint. Assuming immediate weight availability, it delivers a projected throughput of 24.33\,GOPS and an estimated energy efficiency of 1,581.14\,GOPS/W at unchanged mapped power. Bias-aware ReLU detection further reduces modeled arithmetic cycles by 5.52\% and 4.86\%. A separate 256-engine RTL implementation completes Model A in 259 cycles, demonstrating output-parallel scalability.

Fully connected layers require inner products over many input terms, contributing significantly to inference latency and energy consumption. Bit-parallel arithmetic provides high throughput but requires more hardware resources, whereas bit-serial arithmetic reduces hardware complexity at the cost of longer execution time. Consequently, reducing datapath width does not necessarily improve energy efficiency.

Most-significant-digit-first (MSDF) arithmetic generates the most significant result digits first, allowing successive operations to overlap after an initial delay δ\delta [1]. Recent MSDF accelerators reuse multiply–accumulate (MAC) units across the input terms of each neuron [2, 3, 4]. Although neurons can operate in parallel, their input terms are processed sequentially, causing inner-product latency to increase with fan-in. Other bit-serial accelerators improve throughput through reduced operand precision [5, 6, 7]. These approaches motivate an MSDF architecture that processes input terms concurrently while retaining digit-serial computation.

papers.title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes
papers.abstract: Symmetric polyconvexity provides a sufficient condition for weak lower semicontinuity in small-strain elasticity and a tractable lower bound for the relaxation of non-(quasi)convex energies. Since classical algorithms for computing such functions can be computationally expensive, neural network approximations have recently emerged as an alternative. A central difficulty with establishing such neural network based approaches for symmetric polyconvexity is the additional monotonicity property. As we show, the corresponding weight restrictions on ReLU-based input-convex networks do not yield universal approximation of the lifted representers. Here, we introduce symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) for constitutive modeling and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes. The deep architecture combines convexity with the monotonicity required of a representer in the space of minors. We prove a universal approximation theorem for symmetric polyconvex energies, without requiring isotropy, and quantify the number of affine pieces attainable by the lifted network and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies. Numerical examples illustrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential. Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed by construction, while the accuracy of the fitted energies and envelopes is assessed numerically.

papers.title: Homogenization of the Stokes equations in a domain perforated by a thin truss
papers.abstract: We consider the homogenization problem of the stationary Stokes equations in a periodically perforated domain whose solid structure consists of a thin truss. That is, the width $a_ε$ of the truss tends to zero faster than the period size $ε$. We identify the different scaling regimes and derive the corresponding effective equations. In the critical regime, we obtain the Brinkman equations, while in the subcritical regime, we recover the unchanged Stokes equations. In a subrange of the supercritical regime, we derive Darcy's law as the effective equation. Furthermore, we explicitly compute the effective coefficients in the Darcy and Brinkman limits. Moreover, as a tool in the analysis, we establish the analogous homogenization result for a periodic forest of cylinders. Finally, we also consider the homogenization result for a fence of cylinders.

papers.intro:
Flow through porous media occurs in many natural and designed situations, for instance sandstone, lungs and manufactured filters (see [BFOMTVW19]). In many situations the Reynolds number of the flow is very low such that the fluid can be modeled by the incompressible Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions at the interface of the fluid and the solid phase. The complex microsctructure of a porous medium renders the analytic and numerical treatment of this problem very complicated. Thus, in applications, one usually works with effective models that do not require to resolve the interaction between the fluid and the microsctructure through boundary conditions. The most classical of these models is Darcy´s law (see [Dar56]). Darcy´s law has been extended to the Forchheimer equations to incorporate nonlinear (inertial) effects and to the Brinkman equations which formally interpolate between the Stokes equations and Darcy´s law. Despite decades of very active research in mathematics, physics and engineering, the regime of validity of these equations is still under a lot of debate. While Darcy´s law is originally an empirical model and there is vast experimental evidence for its validity (see [KV03], [TB11], [BFOMTVW19], [BEFN22] and the references therein), there seems to be little experimental data that match the Brinkman equations. Consequently, there is a very active discussion in the physics and engineering literature about the validity of the different models depending on the microstructure of the porous medium (see [LA00], [Aur09], [NB17], [BFOMTVW19], [Ehl22]). This has even led to a discussion in the literature whether the effective viscosity in the Brinkman equations should be chosen different from the viscosity of the fluid in order to fit experimental data (see [GA94], [NB17, Section 1.5.3], [Aur09]). However, it is also be argued that the solid volume fraction needs to be very small in the Brinkman regime and that this implies that the viscosity remains unchanged (see [NB17], [Aur09]). Yet, the Brinkman equations are used in many applications, in particular, when flow between clear fluid and porous media is considered (see [NN74]) or when interaction with boundaries is important (see [KV03]). Darcy´s law has been rigorously derived as the homogenization limit of the Stokes equations in perforated domains both for disconnected and connected solid phases (see [Tar80], [Pol87], [All89]). For vanishing solid volume fraction, Darcy´s law and the Brinkman equations have been rigorously derived only for disconnected solid phases (see [All90], [All91]). However, it has been formally argued (see [Aur09], [How74]) that the Brinkman equations are valid for fibrous media where the fiber diameter is much smaller than their characteristic length. Fibrous media appear in many applications and the computation of the effective permeability, which decides whether the Brinkman regime is valid, has received considerable attention (see [TB11]). In the present paper, we give the first rigorous derivation of the Brinkman equations and Darcy´s law in the connected case for vanishing solid volume fraction in the homogenization limit. We consider three types of geometries: forests of cylinders (which are only connected through the boundary of the domain), trusses and fences (see Figure 1).

papers.title: Bose-Einstein condensate in a shell: nonlinear modes and symmetry breaking
papers.abstract: The state of a quantum particle confined to a spherical surface is commonly described using spherical harmonics, which play a crucial role in solving many scientific problems featuring spherical symmetry. A mean-field description of a system of many interacting quantum particles confined to a spherical shell naturally leads to nonlinear generalizations of spherical harmonics. In this study, we analyze the emergence of such nonlinear modes in a shell-shaped Bose-Einstein condensate with both repulsive and attractive two-particle interactions. We find several classes of nonlinear modes. The first kind is an analytical continuation of a single spherical harmonic or their superposition for nonvanishing atom-atom interaction. Some of these solutions have planar counterparts in the form of Townes solitons and Townes vortices, which either appear stable even in the case of attractive interactions or can be stabilized by three-particle interactions. The second kind originate from symmetry-breaking bifurcations in the case of a repulsive interaction, and therefore have no linear counterparts. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of a breathing dynamics that oscillates primarily between an unstable soliton and a stable vortex necklace state. Our findings show that the physics of nonlinear matter waves on curved geometries differs substantially from that in planar systems, suggesting the feasibility of observing these unconventional wave patterns experimentally.

papers.intro:
Many phenomena in nature are determined by underlying geometry, in particular, by the number of dimensions and space topology. Here, the term ”space” may refer to configuration (coordinate) space, momentum space, or more generally to an abstract parameter space. For example, in the random walk [1], which is a fundamental process in physics, chemistry, biology, engineering, economics, sociology, etc., the probability to return to the origin is unity in one and two dimensions but smaller than 0.35 for dimensions larger than three. In addition, Bose-Einstein condensation [2] occurs only in three spatial dimensions and does not exist in one and two. Moreover, the Huygens-Fresnel principle [3] describing the wavefront dynamics of electromagnetic waves is only valid in odd spatial dimensions. The topology of space brings constants of motion into play and results in concepts such as geometrical phases [4, 5], as well as topologically- and symmetry-protected states [6, 7, 8].

papers.title: PULSES: multi-agent AI for autonomous excited-state model building and dynamics
papers.abstract: Simulating molecular excited-state processes requires resolving electronic and nuclear dynamics, but the cost of direct quantum-chemical calculations limits accessible system sizes and timescales. Machine-learning models can extend these simulations, yet they often need to be tailored to specific molecular systems and scientific objectives. Building and deploying such models requires coordinated decisions across conformational sampling, quantum-chemical labelling, model training, validation and dynamics. Here we introduce Paired agents for Unified Learning and Simulation of Excited States (PULSES), a multi-agent system that automates this workflow within expert-approved boundaries. A human expert and planner define the scientific objective, methods and decision boundaries, while an orchestrator coordinates domain agents and artifact-specific scientific assurance during execution. We evaluate PULSES on 15 computational chemistry tasks and demonstrate end-to-end applications to perylene exciton Hamiltonians, solvent-dependent biphenyl relaxation, and excited-state proton transfer in 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline. These results demonstrate traceable, expert-bounded construction and deployment of specialized excited-state models, while retaining scientific validation as a requirement rather than assuming that successful execution establishes correctness.

papers.title: Optimal collective investment under regulatory uncertainty
papers.abstract: We study optimal collective investment subject to a Value-at-Risk (VaR)-type constraint that accounts for uncertainty about future regulatory requirements. The constraint incorporates several possible wealth thresholds and imposes a minimum weighted average probability of meeting them. We characterize the optimal terminal wealth, which combines regions of constant wealth at regulatory thresholds with Merton-type investment regions. Unlike a classical VaR constraint with only one threshold, our formulation generates protection against several thresholds. For two possible thresholds, we identify when both are protected and when protection concentrates on the larger one. Numerical results show that the regulatory constraint can substantially reshape the optimal payoff and generate large welfare losses relative to unconstrained investment when the required compliance probability is high, even the smaller wealth threshold is high, or initial capital is limited. In heterogeneous investor pools, welfare losses depend strongly on the composition of the risk aversions and the Pareto weights governing risk sharing. Losses are particularly pronounced when highly risk-averse investors dominate the pool. Moreover, investors with smaller capital contributions can bear disproportionately large shares of the total welfare loss, while larger contributors may bear less than their capital-proportional share. Thus, regulatory uncertainty not only reduces aggregate welfare but can also create substantial disparities in how its costs are distributed among investors.

papers.intro:
Insurance companies, pension funds, and other delegated investment institutions manage wealth on behalf of beneficiaries with heterogeneous preferences, different contract histories, and long-dated liabilities. Their investment decisions must account for financial-market risk as well as regulatory requirements that may change before these liabilities are settled. Uncertainty about the applicable solvency benchmark can affect how much wealth an institution seeks to protect and in which market states it provides that protection. This raises a central question: how do optimal investment and investor welfare change when the regulatory wealth requirement is not known in advance?

Insurance companies, pension funds, and other delegated investment institutions manage wealth on behalf of beneficiaries with heterogeneous preferences, different contract histories, and long-dated liabilities. Their investment decisions must account for financial-market risk as well as regulatory requirements that may change before these liabilities are settled. Uncertainty about the applicable solvency benchmark can affect how much wealth an institution seeks to protect and in which market states it provides that protection. This raises a central question: how do optimal investment and investor welfare change when the regulatory wealth requirement is not known in advance?

For institutions managing a common investment pool, this question also has a distributional dimension. Investors differ in their risk aversions and capital contributions, while a single investment policy serves the collective as a whole. The consequences of that policy depend both on the aggregate investment outcome and on the rule used to distribute wealth among investors. A regulatory constraint imposed on the pool can therefore affect its members very differently. Even when the aggregate welfare cost is moderate, particular investors may experience substantial losses or bear a disproportionate share of the total cost. Understanding investment under regulatory uncertainty consequently requires examining both the optimal investment policy and the allocation of its welfare costs within the collective.

A second aspect is that Solvency regulations constrain investment decisions by imposing requirements on the distribution of future assets relative to liabilities. Such requirements affect admissible portfolios, capital needs, and the allocation of risk among beneficiaries. Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) constraints are prominent examples of downside-risk restrictions studied in this context. However, the effective regulatory benchmark need not be known with certainty at the time of investment. Its future application may depend on revisions of regulatory rules, supervisory interpretation, internal model approval, the classification of liabilities, or the treatment of different business lines. Institutions with legacy guarantees and heterogeneous groups of policyholders may therefore face several future requirements. Investment decisions made today must account for the possibility that different wealth thresholds will become relevant at the end of the investment horizon.

We address the aforementioned issues by studying optimal collective investment subject to a VaR-type constraint that incorporates several possible wealth thresholds. The constraint requires the weighted average probability of meeting these thresholds to exceed a prescribed compliance level. Collective welfare is evaluated through a Pareto aggregator of individual utilities, which accommodates heterogeneous risk preferences and determines how terminal wealth is shared among investors. Our analysis focuses on two questions. First, how do the possible thresholds and the required compliance level shape optimal terminal wealth and its welfare cost? Second, how does the combination of this constraint and collective risk sharing distribute that cost among investors, and which investors bear a disproportionate burden?

Our study connects several strands of the literature. Classical continuous-time portfolio choice begins with Merton, (1969); Merton, (1971) and is further developed through martingale and duality methods, for example in Cox and Huang, (1989). Within the literature on downside-average compliance constraints, Basak and Shapiro, (2001) analyze optimal trading strategies under VaR-based risk management and show that such constraints can generate nonstandard risk-taking incentives. Related contributions study shortfall, VaR, ES, and more general downside-risk restrictions; see, among others, Gabih et al., (2005), Chen et al., 2018a (), Chen et al., 2018b (), Wei, (2021), Redeker and Wunderlich, (2018), Bäuerle and Chen, (2023), Chen and Nguyen, (2024), Chen et al., (2024), and Bäuerle and Göll, (2026). These studies examine how risk constraints affect optimal terminal wealth and how probability-based restrictions introduce non-concavities into the investment problem. For the axiomatic foundations of risk measures, we refer to Artzner et al., (1999) and Föllmer and Schied, (2011).

Uncertainty and ambiguity have long been recognized as relevant to investment decisions; see Ellsberg, (1961) and Klibanoff et al., (2005). Uncertainty about public policy and regulation affects asset prices and risk premia, see Pastor and Veronesi, (2012); Pastor and Veronesi, (2013). In optimal portfolio selection, parameter uncertainty, partial information, and ambiguity have been examined in various dynamic settings; see, among others, Cvitanic et al., (2006), Björk et al., (2010), Balter et al., (2021), Bäuerle and Mahayni, (2024), and Chen et al., (2025). Our focus differs from these approaches in that the uncertainty concerns the regulatory wealth requirement rather than the drift, volatility, or probability model of the financial market. We incorporate this uncertainty directly into the admissible set through a weighted compliance requirement across possible thresholds. The classical VaR constraint with a single fixed threshold is recovered as a special case.

papers.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
papers.abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.

papers.title: SWE-Clar: Can Coding Agents Clarify Incomplete Client Requirements and Deliver Greenfield Software?
papers.abstract: Greenfield software development in freelance settings requires coding agents to turn incomplete client requests into working software. This makes requirement clarification essential, yet clients may be unable to provide continuous feedback over long development cycles, and receiving their answers does not guarantee correct understanding of complex requirements. These challenges motivate two benchmark design choices: clarification precedes code implementation, and its effectiveness is assessed through explicit tests of requirement understanding. Guided by these choices, we introduce SWE-Clar, a benchmark grounded in real, high-value client commissions to evaluate requirement clarification and code implementation in this setting. It comprises 100 tasks based on real software development jobs on Upwork, each with at least US\$4,000 in total payments. Each task begins with multi-round interaction between a coding agent and a client agent, followed by separate runs for code implementation with acceptance testing and clarification assessment. For the latter, we construct 512 questions paired with reference answers from real client-freelancer interactions, covering both explicitly stated requirements and those inferred from the conversational context. Both runs begin from the same clarification context but remain isolated, preventing assessment questions from guiding code implementation. Experiments with nine frontier models show that even GPT-6 Astra, which has the highest observed implementation score, achieves a task pass rate of only 67%, underscoring the challenge of independent software delivery in this setting. The dataset and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/upwork/SWE-Clar.
