As large language models (LLMs) improve at coding and reasoning, coding agents are expanding from generating simple code snippets (Chen et al., 2021) to tackling complex software engineering tasks (Yang et al., 2024). These advances create opportunities to automate software development services and deliver business value (Peng et al., 2023; Miserendino et al., 2025; Yi et al., 2025; Mazeika et al., 2025), particularly in greenfield software development, which involves building new software from scratch rather than modifying existing codebases (Ding et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026). On freelance platforms such as Upwork11 1 https://www.upwork.com/, agents could act as freelancers to undertake high-value client commissions (Figure 1). However, these commissions typically begin with requests that leave critical functional and interface requirements unspecified (Nuseibeh & Easterbrook, 2000), so coding agents must proactively seek clarification through client interaction (Mu et al., 2024). Evaluating coding agents for greenfield software development in freelance settings therefore requires assessing both code implementation and requirement clarification.

Recent work has extended coding-agent evaluation beyond code implementation to include requirement clarification, enabling coding agents to interact with client agents to recover missing requirements (Wu & Fard, 2025; Fang et al., 2026; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Raghavendra et al., 2026; King & Flanigan, 2026). However, these benchmarks primarily focus on tasks derived from programming datasets and software repositories, leaving the demands of greenfield software development in freelance settings insufficiently represented. Our observations of real commissions for such greenfield software development projects highlight two characteristics, illustrated in Figure 1. First, building complete software projects from scratch often entails a prolonged development process, making continuous client feedback during code implementation difficult to sustain. Second, these projects involve multiple complex requirements that freelancers may not fully understand even after receiving answers to their questions. Consequently, benchmarks that assume continuous client feedback (Wu et al., 2026; Raghavendra et al., 2026) and assess clarification primarily through information acquisition (Fang et al., 2026; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026; Trinh et al., 2026) may not adequately assess coding agents’ ability to fulfill these commissions independently.

GPT-6 Astra has the highest observed implementation score, with a task pass rate of only 67%, underscoring SWE-Clar’s value as a challenging testbed for identifying limitations in coding agents’ ability to fulfill real client commissions.

papers.title: System One models Are Not Better Rerankers
papers.abstract: System One models, or decision models, answer a question about an input with a calibrated probability instead of generated text. Within weeks of the first release, in September 2026, they were used as rerankers. We test whether the decision fine-tuning behind them makes a better reranker than plain reranker fine-tuning of the same model. For six Qwen backbones from 0.6B to 27B parameters and ten TREC DL and BEIR collections, we compare the untuned model, asked zero-shot, with its decision fine-tunes and its reranker fine-tunes, two of which we train ourselves. In our work, we draw the conclusion that decision fine-tuning never makes the better reranker. From 0.6B to 9B, reranker fine-tuning wins on every backbone by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10, also on zero-shot collections, and at 27B the two tie. Up to 9B, decision fine-tuning adds nothing over simply asking the untuned model. Moreover, we find that the calibration advantage of decision models depends on the question. Asked whether a passage answers the query, they are better calibrated than the published reranker fine-tunes from 4B on. Asked a slightly different question from prior work, they lose this advantage. Lastly, calibration does not make up for a worse ranking: up to 9B, a reranker fine-tune keeps the better passages at a fixed threshold. If you need a reranker, fine-tune a reranker.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Loss Exploration for Vision-Based Perception under Non-IID Data
papers.abstract: Vision-based image classification models benefit from Federated Learning (FL) across vehicles, however learning accurate models from distributed vehicular cameras is challenging due to data heterogeneity and privacy concerns. To improve performance on non-IID data, advanced FL optimization approaches have emerged that share auxiliary insights, such as client gradient behaviors. While these gradient-guided optimized FL methods improve the model accuracy, their reliance on sharing additional gradient information introduces a previously unexplored privacy vulnerability. In our empirical privacy-leakage experiment, we show that a malicious server can infer clients' label sets from shared guidance matrices under heterogeneous client label distributions (simulated via Dirichlet-based label partitions), between 50% and 84% accuracy. To address this privacy leakage, we propose PPFLex that replaces the central server with three Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) servers to securely compute the global guidance matrix and perform federated averaging under semi-honest and malicious MPC server assumptions. We evaluate PPFLex on widely used traffic-sign classification datasets (e.g., GTSRB and BTSC) as representative autonomous vehicle perception benchmarks, comparing against baselines. Our results show that PPFLex achieves accuracy comparable to the plain-text FedLEx pipeline while preventing privacy leakage, incurring acceptable MPC overhead.

papers.intro:
Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) increasingly rely on machine learning to enable vision-based perception in intelligent transportation systems. In real-world deployments, perception models are broadly employed to support training of image-based tasks within diverse automotive scenarios. These models are typically trained on large datasets, allowing them to predict class labels for provided images [1]. Applications such as cooperative perception, driver monitoring, object detection and tracking, and traffic sign recognition contribute to Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), and depend on large-scale visual data collected from distributed vehicular sensors operating in heterogeneous environments [2, 3].

Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) increasingly rely on machine learning to enable vision-based perception in intelligent transportation systems. In real-world deployments, perception models are broadly employed to support training of image-based tasks within diverse automotive scenarios. These models are typically trained on large datasets, allowing them to predict class labels for provided images [1]. Applications such as cooperative perception, driver monitoring, object detection and tracking, and traffic sign recognition contribute to Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), and depend on large-scale visual data collected from distributed vehicular sensors operating in heterogeneous environments [2, 3].

In our work, we focus on one representative image-based perception task, Traffic Sign Classification (TSC), to demonstrate the applicability of our framework, while emphasizing that the proposed approach can be compatible with other vision-based automotive perception tasks. TSC enhances driving safety by categorizing road signs and is broadly integrated into ADAS and autonomous driving systems [4, 5]. It requires reliable classification under varying lighting conditions, weather changes, and viewing angles. As traffic signs serve as key map features for navigation, accurate sign classification also supports localization and motion planning [6]. However, the scale of vehicular data raises communication overhead and data protection challenges. Traffic sign distributions might reveal the vehicle’s driving profile, exposing recurring routes or location-based behavior patterns. Several works [7, 8, 9] propose Federated Learning (FL) to address these concerns by enabling collaborative training without sharing raw data and supporting data protection regulations such as the GDPR [10].

Despite its promise, FL is affected by challenges associated with data heterogeneity, as clients’ data are often Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (Non-IID) due to imbalances and perturbations [11]. In TSC, non-IID effects arise since vehicles operate across diverse regions and experience different sign distributions and environmental conditions. For example, some cars travel on highways, trucks often drive through mountains or rural areas, and buses usually operate on city roads [12]. Traditional server-side aggregation, FedAvg [13], can be ineffective under heterogeneity, since multiple local updates can diverge from the global objective and reduce generalization across clients [14]. To tackle the limitations of standard averaging in these non-IID settings, researchers have adopted knowledge transfer techniques [15] to harmonize learning across diverse client distributions.

Federated Loss Exploration (FedLEx) [16] is one such method that integrates guided transfer learning into FL by analyzing gradient behavior to guide the learning process. Unlike conventional FL approaches, FedLEx does not rely on weight-sharing alone. Instead, it focuses on aggregating the gradient information from the different loss surfaces of each client. This approach is designed to address the challenges of non-IID data, where class distribution differences between clients can create biases that hinder learning performance.

A further concern is privacy: although FL provides a layer of protection, it remains vulnerable to inference attacks, where adversaries reconstruct private training data from intermediate model updates [17, 18, 19]. Such attacks, including gradient and model inversion, can expose sensitive client information, undermining FL’s privacy guarantees [20]. To address these concerns, several privacy-preserving technologies have been proposed. Homomorphic Encryption (HE) [21] allows computations on encrypted data; however, it introduces high computational overhead. Differential Privacy (DP) [22] adds noise to protect privacy, though this may degrade model performance. Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) [23] allows a group of untrusted parties to process their data jointly without revealing individual information and is emerging as a promising solution for multi-party settings. However, existing MPC-based secure aggregation protocols are mainly focused on traditional FL averaging and do not focus on providing privacy for sharing additional knowledge that can be used to optimize performance in non-IID settings. On the other hand, while FedLEx enhances traditional FL training by leveraging gradient analysis, it lacks privacy guarantees, as gradient deviations can still reveal sensitive information such as local label distributions, similar to traditional FL vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Can AI Agents Help Robotic Engineers? Lessons from Two Focus Days in Industry
papers.abstract: Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own. However, it is unclear if and how this transfers to robotic engineering, where engineers program industrial robots in niche, vendor-specific languages and rely on visual feedback from simulation tools. Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots. Our results show that the agent did not make the engineers more productive, with the exception of a task that required the generation of highly repetitive code. However, the results with the agent improved over time, as the engineers learned how to use it and the agent was adapted to the domain. Moreover, the experience with AI mattered more for the success with the agent than the experience with robotic engineering. This shows that AI agents are not a plug-and-play solution. Instead, companies must train their engineers on the usage of agents, plan time for a learning curve, and ensure that agent configurations match the domain and developer requirements. The strong learning curve we observed further implies that studies on productivity gains with AI should be longitudinal, as they otherwise miss how engineers adopt agents in practice.

Programming of industrial robots is a specialized sub-domain at the intersection of software development and industrial engineering: engineers write code in vendor-specific languages like ABB RAPID and check the movements of the robot visually in simulation tools like RobotStudio [1]. Projects often differ from typical software development in multiple aspects, e.g., due to the use of visual programming and because solutions are typically adapted from previous programs rather than re-written from scratch. Thus, repetitive and error-prone tasks like renaming, shifting positions, or reversing paths are common [10].

At the same time, software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step tasks on their own, instead of only completing code or answering questions in a chat [13]. However, the evidence on the productivity effects of such tools is inconclusive [12, 19, 8] and comes from mainstream software development. It is unclear if and how it transfers to robotic engineering. Work on Large Language Models (LLMs) for industrial automation evaluates the AI solutions in isolation, i.e., without engineers in the loop [9, 10]. To the best of our knowledge, there is no empirical evidence on whether agents help robotic engineers in industry with the range of their daily tasks, i.e., beyond isolated code changes. Similarly, we do not know how these engineers use agents and which problems they face when adopting them.

papers.title: Melody Guidance for Audio Diffusion Models Without Retraining
papers.abstract: Controlling melody in audio generation normally requires training a conditional generative model on audio paired with pitch curves or MIDI notes. We instead guide an existing unconditional diffusion model, originally trained without melody inputs, to follow a target melody without retraining or modifying it. During inference, a differentiable pitch detector steers the sampled audio toward the desired pitches, while the diffusion model keeps it close to the distribution of realistic audio learned during training. Our main contribution is a sampling method that balances these two directions, providing melody control while preserving audio quality. To improve stability, we initialize sampling with a simple synthesized version of the target melody rather than pure noise. Experiments on piano, guitar, and singing voice show melody accuracy comparable to conditional models trained specifically for melody control. Our method therefore adds melody control to existing audio diffusion models without requiring paired melody data or task-specific retraining.

papers.title: Non-Expansive Fuzzy Modal Logic Has Uniform Interpolation
papers.abstract: Fuzzy logics with truth values in the unit interval vary in their choice of propositional connectives and their semantics, ranging from just minimum and maximum as in Zadeh logics to truncated addition and subtraction as in Łukasiewicz logics or their extensions with truth constants, known as Pavelka logics. In the more specific world of fuzzy modal logics, non-expansive fuzzy modal logic has recently been proposed as a sweet spot between Łukasiewicz (more precisely, Pavelka) and Zadeh fuzzy modal logic; it restricts Łukasiewicz propositional connectives to have one argument constant, equivalently extends the Zadeh propositional base with constant shift operators. It retains reasonable expressiveness both in practical terms and abstractly; in particular, it characterizes the standard notion of behavioural distance on fuzzy Kripke frames. At the same time, it allows for satisfiability checking in the same complexity as for its two-valued correspondent (the modal logic K, or the description logic ALC), in contrast to the notorious computational hardness of Łukasiewicz modal logic. In the present work, we show that non-expansive fuzzy modal logic admits uniform interpolation, a key property in modularization, information hiding, summarization, and other applications that fails for both Łukasiewicz (or Pavelka) and Zadeh modal logic.
papers.intro:
Fuzzy description logics (see [26] for an overview) serve the specification of vague knowledge, expressing both vague properties of individuals such as tallness and vague relations such as fandom. Fuzzy description logics are equivalent to the more neutrally termed fuzzy modal logics, which may more generally be seen as logics for weighted transition systems, and as such have found application, for instance, in software model checking [6, 25]. The semantics of fuzzy modal logics varies widely even when truth values are fixed to the unit interval, in particular regarding the interpretation of propositional connectives [26], with substantial impact on logical properties and the complexity of reasoning. At one end of the spectrum, Zadeh semantics, which essentially features only minimum, maximum, and fuzzy negation, ensures tractability even of very expressive description logics [36, 34, 35] but on the other hand is semantically almost indistinguishable from its classical counterpart (e.g. for c≥0.5c\geq 0.5, a concept in Zadeh fuzzy 𝒜​ℒ​𝒞\mathcal{ALC} is satisfiable with degree at least cc iff the same concept is satisfiable in classical 𝒜​ℒ​𝒞\mathcal{ALC}) [5, 19, 36]. At the other end, Łukasiewicz semantics, which additionally makes use of the additive structure of the unit interval, is characterized by desirable logical properties [24] but causes high complexity of the main reasoning problems. For instance, the best known upper bound for satisfiability checking in Łukasiewicz fuzzy 𝒜​ℒ​𝒞\mathcal{ALC} is NExpTime [37, 23], and in the presence of global assumptions (i.e. general TBoxes, in description logic terminology), satisfiability checking in fact becomes undecidable [2].

Here, the term non-expansive refers to the fact that formula evaluation is non-expansive w.r.t. the natural behavioural distance on fuzzy transition systems. In fact, non-expansive fuzzy modal logic is expressive for this distance in two senses: It satisfies both a Hennessy-Milner-type theorem saying that logical distance coincides with behavioural distance on finitely-branching systems, and a van-Benthem-type theorem saying that, up to approximation in bounded rank, fuzzy modal logic is precisely the non-expansive fragment of its natural fuzzy first-order correspondence language [45]. Syntactically, the logic lies between Zadeh fuzzy modal logic and the extension of Łukasiewicz fuzzy modal logic with (rational) truth constants, a logic known as (rational) Pavelka logic [15, 30]. Specifically, what is termed the non-expansive propositional base restricts Łukasiewicz connectives to have a truth constant as one argument or, equivalently, extends the Zadeh base with constant shift operators (this propositional base was first used in quantitative modal logics for probabilistic transition systems [41]). For instance, this allows expressing dampening effects in the inheritance of properties, e.g. in axioms saying that friends of football fanatics are also football fanatics, maybe to a slightly lesser degree [10]. Generally, a uniform (post-)interpolant of a formula w.r.t. a propositional atom pp is, roughly speaking, a strongest pp-free consequence of the original formula, i.e. captures the content of the original formula in the reduced vocabulary obtained by removing pp. Existence of uniform interpolants implies Craig interpolation, which says that every valid implication is mediated by a formula mentioning only the shared vocabulary of the two formulae. While interpolation is generally a subtle issue and not stable under extension or restriction of logics, it is known that the basic two-valued modal logic 𝐊\mathbf{K} has uniform interpolation [43]. Applications of Craig interpolation and uniform interpolation in classical modal and description logics include summarization, analysis, modularization, and reuse of knowledge bases [21, 27, 22], information hiding [13], knowledge exchange between agents (e.g. [40]), the computation of separating formulae in supervised concept learning [18], and the computation of explicit definitions [28].

papers.title: EMG Tokenization Preserves Movement Information at a Fraction of the Bitrate
papers.abstract: Wireless electromyography (EMG) interfaces must balance electrode coverage against transmission bandwidth. Here, we show that compact EMG tokens substantially reduce payload while retaining information for three-dimensional hand-pose decoding. We evaluate two causal tokenizers fitted without pose labels: an encoder pretrained to reconstruct EMG spectra and one based on SPAR, an engineered spectral-spatial representation of neighbouring electrodes. In personalized, within-session experiments with 320-channel EMG from nine participants, we compare tokenized and continuous features using matched decoder architectures and training procedures. Averaged across decoders, tokenization changed mean error by +0.01 mm for SPAR (95% confidence interval: -0.12 to 0.14) and +0.45 mm for the learned representation (0.10 to 0.82). Both increases met a 1 mm non-inferiority criterion. Stored token arrays reduced payloads 41-fold relative to raw EMG and 36-fold relative to continuous SPAR features. On sampled windows of the public emg2pose benchmark's test partition, absolute differences in mean error between learned tokens and continuous features were below 0.05 mm across 176 participants and in the subset of 20 participants unseen during training. Electrode coverage, calibration, and unseen recordings affected SPAR decoding more than quantization did. In a computational benchmark, optimized SPAR generated tokens for 63 channels within 20 ms on a Cortex-M55 microcontroller. These findings support tokenization as a compact interface between wearable sensing and movement decoding, allowing decoders to be updated while the wearable encoder and transmitted representation remain fixed.

Electromyography (EMG) interfaces typically transmit either raw signals or continuous feature representations [7, 6, 2, 13, 3]. An alternative is to encode EMG signals as discrete tokens that index vectors in a learned codebook. At the receiver, these vectors are retrieved and passed to the pose decoder. Vector quantization (VQ) has previously been explored for EMG signal reconstruction [14], while more recent approaches have introduced learned token representations for general time series [15] and biosignals [8, 17]. In the context of hand-pose decoding, VQ-MyoPose uses vector quantization to encode ground-truth joint-angle trajectories and trains an EMG model to predict the resulting pose tokens [18]. EMG tokenization separates wearable encoding from receiver-side task decoding.

papers.title: Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells
papers.abstract: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware and thus trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QPPI), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information, and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. QPPI enables all-optical and label-free studies of contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes. It provides both structural and functional readouts at sufficient frame rates to resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. Conventional fluorescent labels bleach over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring. Instead, QPPI enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast and provides structural readouts similar to those provided by established fluorescent labels, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length. It also offers previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, which provides a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity.

papers.intro:
Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is a widely used, fast and inexpensive label-free technique, that provides quantitative phase maps. Typically, computational phase retrieval is achieved by capturing several images at different conditions (e.g., different phase masks or illumination angles). For instance, QPI has been realized by acquiring four separate images with different phase masks as an add-on to conventional phase contrast microscopes [1], or with different analyzer angles as add-on to conventional differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopes [2]. Fourier Ptychography microscopy (FPM) can also generate QPI maps using LED arrays for sequential angle-dependent illumination scanning [3, 4]. More recently, polarization-dependent measurements and computational modeling of anisotropic phase properties have been implemented for FPM [5, 6, 7].

Typically, computational phase retrieval is achieved by capturing several images at different conditions (e.g., different phase masks or illumination angles). For instance, QPI has been realized by acquiring four separate images with different phase masks as an add-on to conventional phase contrast microscopes [1], or with different analyzer angles as add-on to conventional differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopes [2]. Fourier Ptychography microscopy (FPM) can also generate QPI maps using LED arrays for sequential angle-dependent illumination scanning [3, 4]. More recently, polarization-dependent measurements and computational modeling of anisotropic phase properties have been implemented for FPM [5, 6, 7].

With the development of polarization sensitive cameras, single-shot, DIC-based QPI became possible by acquiring four different analyzer angles simultaneously, and computing quantitative phase gradient images [8]. These can then be integrated in a phase map either via Hilbert-based methods [9] or via line-artifact removal (LAR) after axis-aligned shear acquisition [10]. While effective for axis-aligned configurations, these line-by-line reconstructions remain susceptible to streak artifacts perpendicular to the DIC shear direction, which can corrupt the quantitative phase signal in regions of small gradient.

Cardiomyocyte contractility is central to drug screening, disease modeling, and fundamental studies of muscle mechanics [12, 13, 14]. In particular, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes are now widely used as a platform for hypertrophic, dilated, and channelopathy-related disease models [15, 16]. Functional imaging typically relies on fluorescent reporters, as calcium indicators, voltage-sensitive dyes, or fluorescently tagged sarcomere proteins. However, all fluorescent reporters eventually photobleach, while the high-power illumination in the UV or blue range exerts phototoxic stress, both of which severely limit long-term monitoring [17]. Thus, there is a need for label-free, bio-compatible alternatives, capable of resolving contraction dynamics over long durations, at microscopic resolution, and at high frame rates.

However, all fluorescent reporters eventually photobleach, while the high-power illumination in the UV or blue range exerts phototoxic stress, both of which severely limit long-term monitoring [17]. Thus, there is a need for label-free, bio-compatible alternatives, capable of resolving contraction dynamics over long durations, at microscopic resolution, and at high frame rates.

Repeatedly capturing functional biological features during fast muscle contractions requires quantitative, time-resolved measurement of isotropic and anisotropic phase in single living cells, a measurement that has not been accessible at video rate. Existing approaches either lack quantitative polarimetric calibration [18, 19], operate too slowly to capture the contraction cycle [5, 6], measure entire cell colonies instead of single cells [13, 14] or rely on fluorescent labels that bleach and thus prevent extended recordings. Alternative label-free routes face different trade-offs. Electro-physiological impedance measurements do not offer single cell resolution and require expensive gold-coated well plates [13, 14]. Tomographic and Fourier-ptychographic methods provide rich anisotropic and three-dimensional contrast [5, 6, 20], but rely on tens to hundreds of illumination conditions, which precludes the investigation of fast cellular dynamics on the milisecond time scale. Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) microscopy [21] is particularly well-suited for 3D muscle tissue imaging [22, 23, 24, 25]; however, its point-by-point scanning approach typically prevents imaging at sufficient frame rates to resolve muscle contractions. Snapshot refractive-index tomography reaches video rate but at the cost of a strongly restricted field of view, since the camera sensor must be partitioned across many angular sub-images [26]. Earlier multi-frame DIC approaches have combined phase and birefringence contrast [27], but require multiple sequential acquisitions at different specimen orientations and bias settings, again limiting their applicability to dynamic samples.

Repeatedly capturing functional biological features during fast muscle contractions requires quantitative, time-resolved measurement of isotropic and anisotropic phase in single living cells, a measurement that has not been accessible at video rate. Existing approaches either lack quantitative polarimetric calibration [18, 19], operate too slowly to capture the contraction cycle [5, 6], measure entire cell colonies instead of single cells [13, 14] or rely on fluorescent labels that bleach and thus prevent extended recordings. Alternative label-free routes face different trade-offs. Electro-physiological impedance measurements do not offer single cell resolution and require expensive gold-coated well plates [13, 14]. Snapshot refractive-index tomography reaches video rate but at the cost of a strongly restricted field of view, since the camera sensor must be partitioned across many angular sub-images [26]. Earlier multi-frame DIC approaches have combined phase and birefringence contrast [27], but require multiple sequential acquisitions at different specimen orientations and bias settings, again limiting their applicability to dynamic samples.

Here we present quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP²I), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard DIC microscope equipped with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast functional imaging platform. QP²I is based on two complementary reconstructions that share the same instrument. To obtain quantitative phase contrast, we introduce a new single-stage global solver: a finite-difference operator matched to the DIC shear direction, combined with total-variation regularization, which recovers the phase map in one pass and inherently avoids the streak artifacts that have constrained earlier approaches. The reconstruction handles axis-aligned and diagonal shear configurations alike and requires only a single tunable parameter. Removing the Nomarski prisms converts the same instrument to a polarization microscope, enabling a per-pixel Stokes analysis that yields quantitative data on retardance and molecular orientation. Together, the two modes provide complementary contrast on the same biological structures and across co-aligned fields-of-view. The isotropic phase is linked to local mass density and isotropic optical path length, while polarimetry isolates anisotropic, optically ordered components such as the contractile apparatus of muscle cells. We validate QP²I across simulations, static reference targets, and biological samples. Finally, we demonstrate sustained, label-free frame-by-frame readouts of sarcomere length, and quantitative time-resolved retardance during the contraction of individual myofibrils in cardiomyocytes, providing a direct optical window into the photoelastic response of the heart.

papers.title: Real-to-Sim Calibration of Bosch Etching Simulators with Few-Shot XSEM Data and Hybrid Search
papers.abstract: The Bosch process is widely used in MEMS and TSV fabrication, but accurate prediction of etching outcomes remains difficult without calibration against real measurements, which are sparse and costly to obtain. This work presents a few-shot real-to-sim calibration framework that decouples simulator parameters from direct process variables to infer a recipe-specific simulator parameter vector from sparse measurements, enabling reliable prediction of etch depth and sidewall angle under held-out process conditions. We first formulate Bosch profile prediction as a few-shot real-to-sim calibration problem, where a small set of real XSEM measurements is used to identify a recipe-specific ViennaPS parameter vector $z_r^*$ that minimizes the discrepancy between simulated and measured etch depth and sidewall angle. To search this parameter space efficiently, the framework combines local exploration, LLM-guided candidate generation, and XGBoost-based surrogate screening, while retaining ViennaPS simulation as the final verification step for each selected candidate. Experiments on two Bosch etching recipes show that the proposed framework accurately predicts held-out etching results, achieving normalized global errors of 0.340 and 0.249 for the 2 recipes respectively.

papers.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
papers.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

This process is called context compaction.

papers.title: A Robust Control Architecture for Multirate Systems and their Interconnections
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework for analyzing and designing linear multirate control systems and their interconnections through the lens of robust control. The proposed approach models multirate systems as impulsive systems with multiple independent jump maps and corresponding jump-time sequences. We tackle analysis and design problems with stability, dissipativity, and robustness objectives, relying on a multi-clock-dependent Lyapunov function parameterization. Further, we develop a compositional approach for analyzing interconnections of multirate systems based on individual dissipativity properties. The theoretical conditions can be verified via linear matrix inequalities and they require weak assumptions on the sampling rates, allowing for asynchronous and time-varying sampling rates with or without separated time scales. The practicality of the framework is demonstrated with numerical examples.

papers.intro:
The increasing complexity of dynamical systems poses challenges for traditional control paradigms, especially due to the interplay of different layers and time scales. In recent years, the control architecture viewpoint has been put forward to find a common language for describing and tackling these challenges [1]. Tailored control architectures were found for specific domains, e.g., robotic systems with high-layer planning (e.g., temporal logic specifications), middle-layer trajectory generation (e.g., model predictive control, MPC), and low-layer real-time control (e.g., control barrier functions) [2]. However, identifying common features across different domains is challenging and the development of unifying components towards a control architecture theory is an active field of research [1, 3]. In the present paper, we tackle one important component of control architectures through the lens of robust control theory: The presence of multiple time scales.

However, identifying common features across different domains is challenging and the development of unifying components towards a control architecture theory is an active field of research [1, 3]. In the present paper, we tackle one important component of control architectures through the lens of robust control theory: The presence of multiple time scales.

Multirate systems can arise, e.g., due to the presence of sensors and actuators with different time scales, due to network effects, or due to a deliberate design of the control architecture [2, 4, 5]. Beyond common engineering applications, multiple rates also occur in neuromorphic systems [6, 7], in which interconnected neurons admitting different firing times interact, potentially with other dynamical systems. Classical multirate control approaches rely on the lifting approach which reformulates the multirate system as a single-rate system in the slowest time scale. This approach was pioneered by [4] and extended into many directions, e.g., tackling more advanced problems such as ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty}-control [8, 9], gain-scheduling [10], network effects [11], or linear fractional transformations [12]. The main limitation of lifting is a potentially large increase of the input dimension, especially when the sampling intervals differ substantially. Further, it requires periodic and a priori known sampling times, which is in conflict with increasing trends in aperiodic [5, 13] and event-based [14] control. An alternative stabilization approach using Lyapunov-Krasovskii functionals was developed in [15, 16], extending previous results on single-rate sampled-data control [17, 18, 19]. Further, the paper [20] provides an operator-based treatment of asynchronous multirate control, however, yielding infinite-dimensional conditions which are only tractable in the periodic special case. Another recent work [21] develops a multirate control method subject to input saturation, modeling the multirate system as a hybrid system [22]. However, the resulting controller design conditions are not fully convex and only a stability objective is addressed. We compare our framework to these existing works on a more detailed, technical level in Section III-D below. Further, [23, 24] address a conceptually related problem, using singular perturbation theory for sampled-data stabilization of systems with two time scales that are sufficiently far apart. Closely related to the architectural viewpoint mentioned above, the recent work [25] introduces the concept of multiclock logic to study stability, using compositional properties and assume-guarantee contracts. Problems of multirate control were also tackled using MPC, see [26] and the references therein. Further, multirate phenomena were studied in interconnections of networked control systems, e.g., via small-gain [27, 28] or time-delay [29] arguments.

In the present paper, we develop a flexible analysis and control architecture for linear multirate systems based on robust control theory. We model multirate systems via impulsive systems with multiple jump maps, i.e., systems undergoing continuous flow evolution according to a differential equation as well as discrete jumps at multiple independent time sequences and with different jump dynamics. We derive analysis and state-feedback design conditions for such multirate systems using Lyapunov functions depending on multiple clocks, tackling stability, dissipativity, and robustness against uncertainties. Our framework allows for time-varying sampling rates, only requiring them to satisfy a range dwell-time condition (RDTC) and without explicit requirements on the time-scale differences. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of the framework with various numerical examples, including a microgrid with six different and time-varying sampling rates.

papers.title: From Hollow Waveguides to Mie Voids: Low-Index Light Confinement
papers.abstract: The confinement of light within optically thin media challenges the conventional view that optical localization requires high-index dielectric materials and total internal reflection. Over the past decades, a broad range of photonic phenomena has demonstrated that electromagnetic energy can also be guided and localized inside low-index regions or nanoscale void cavities. What first appears to be a curiosity is, in fact, highly relevant: The interaction between light and matter lies at the heart of much in optics and photonics. It enables sensing, nonlinear optical phenomena, and optical manipulation, yet it also inevitably introduces absorption, dissipation, and loss. Pushing localized, enhanced, or guided energy into a lower-index space thus offers entirely new possibilities for light-matter interaction and dispersion control. In this review, we discuss some of these counterintuitive structures, starting with light guidance within optically thin media, such as hollow-core photonic crystal fibers or antiresonant reflecting optical waveguides. We then discuss the optics of bubbles, that is, low-index inclusions in a higher-index surrounding, and ultimately arrive at the so-called Mie void resonators, optical resonators that support localized electromagnetic modes confined within a region of lower refractive index. All these systems demonstrate that there are (resonant) optics beyond simple total internal reflection. Absence can itself become a functional photonic degree of freedom, opening opportunities across sensing, quantum nanophotonics, metasurfaces, and programmable optical matter.

papers.intro:
The ability to guide and confine optical energy within low-index regions has attracted growing interest as it offers a fundamentally different way of controlling electromagnetic fields. Unlike a familiar Fabry-Pérot resonator geometry where light is bounded by mirrors, in most conventional optical systems light resides inside optically dense materials, where confinement emerges through refractive-index contrast and total internal reflection. Confining unbounded light in air appears counterintuitive. Yet this inversion gives rise to optical behaviors and functionalities that are not readily accessible in conventional dielectric structures. Many of these opportunities arise from the direct spatial accessibility of the confined optical fields. If optical fields can be localized directly within air-filled or otherwise accessible regions, surrounding matter can naturally overlap with the electromagnetic hot spots. Gases, liquids, nanoparticles, molecules, and quantum emitters can then interact directly with strongly localized optical fields without requiring penetration into dense dielectric materials. At the same time, reducing the overlap between light and absorbing matter can suppress losses, nonlinear absorption, heating, and material damage. Systems capable of guiding or localizing light in low-index environments therefore promise unusual combinations of many properties such as accessibility, robustness, and flexible optical control. Beyond these considerations, the confinement of light in optically thin media is also intrinsically interesting from a fundamental perspective. Electromagnetic localization has traditionally been associated with “dielectric accumulation”, where optical energy remains trapped inside regions of high refractive index. Structures that confine light in air challenge this intuition by demonstrating that localization can also emerge from interference, resonance formation, inhibited coupling, and inverse dielectric geometries. We formalize this intuition as a variational principle and show where it fails. The ability to localize light within carefully engineered “voids” therefore reflects a broader expansion in how photonics approaches the control of electromagnetic fields. Here we review a range of approaches for guiding and localizing light within optically thin media. We begin with waveguiding concepts based on interference, inhibited coupling, and structured electromagnetic environments before turning to inverse dielectric scattering systems and resonators. Particular emphasis is placed on dielectric Mie voids as a platform for studying inverse dielectric resonances and their applications in sensing, light-matter interaction, and nanophotonics. Finally, we discuss the broader implications and future opportunities arising from optical confinement in low-index environments.

We begin with waveguiding concepts based on interference, inhibited coupling, and structured electromagnetic environments before turning to inverse dielectric scattering systems and resonators. Particular emphasis is placed on dielectric Mie voids as a platform for studying inverse dielectric resonances and their applications in sensing, light-matter interaction, and nanophotonics. Finally, we discuss the broader implications and future opportunities arising from optical confinement in low-index environments.

papers.title: On the Role of Atomic Mobility in the Polyamorphism of Metallic Glasses
papers.abstract: Understanding the microscopic mechanisms underlying polyamorphic transitions requires simultaneous knowledge of thermodynamic and structural evolution, which has remained experimentally inaccessible. Here, we combine chip-based fast differential scanning calorimetry with high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction to simultaneously probe the thermodynamic and structural evolution during the polyamorphic transition of a Pd-Ni-P metallic glass. Correlating heat-flow signals with the corresponding structural evolution during both heating and cooling reveals a direct relationship between thermodynamic evolution and medium-range structural ordering. Based on this relationship, we identify two distinct transition mechanisms. In the glassy state, the transition proceeds continuously through progressive medium-range ordering, accompanied by enhanced thermal stability and strongly temperature-dependent kinetics. In contrast, in the equilibrium supercooled liquid, the transition proceeds through the coexistence of distinct amorphous states, with only a weak temperature dependence of the kinetics. These findings show that atomic mobility governs the transformation pathway by coupling thermodynamic evolution to structural ordering, providing new insights into polyamorphic transitions in nonequilibrium amorphous systems.

papers.intro:
Polyamorphism refers to transitions between distinct amorphous states of the same chemical composition, by analogy with phase transformations in crystalline materials. Liquid–liquid transitions (LLTs) are a typical manifestation of polyamorphism and have been widely reported in molecular [48, 6], atomic [17, 52], and ionic liquids [53, 59]. In the glassy state, the corresponding glass–glass transitions (GGTs) have been observed in amorphous ice [19], silicon [10], chalcogenide glasses [11], and metallic glasses (MGs) [43], which are more commonly induced by changes in pressure and involve transformations between low- and high-density amorphous states. Polyamorphism reveals a rich space for tuning disordered systems: at a fixed chemical composition, the same system can exhibit distinct amorphous states with different structures [17, 52], densities [10], refractive indices [48], enthalpies [7], and mechanical properties [39]. More fundamentally, polyamorphism reflects the intricate interplay between thermodynamics, atomic structure, and kinetics in disordered systems, providing important insights into the nature of amorphous matter and its transformations. Polyamorphism is therefore not only of potential practical relevance but also of central importance in glass and condensed-matter physics.

Metallic glasses are particularly attractive for studies of polyamorphism because (i) in the absence of directional covalent bonding, molecular chains, or ionic interactions, their atomic configurations possess a high degree of freedom [51, 13], and (ii) a rich dynamical pathways that thermally activated atomic rearrangements even in the glassy state [62, 9, 41]. To date, polyamorphic transitions have been reported in Pd–Ni–P [22, 7, 40, 31], La(Ce)–Co–Al [23, 39, 38, 58], Zr–Cu–Al–Y [18], Zr–Ti–Cu–Ni–Be and Zr–Cu–Ni–Al–Nb [46], and high-entropy MGs [25, 3, 57, 61]. These transitions typically manifest as an anomalous exothermic peak or an anomalous change in specific heat near the glass-transition temperature (TgT_{\mathrm{g}}) in calorimetric heating curves. Exceptions include Au–Cu–Si–Ag–Pd [12, 50, 16] and Pd–Ni–P [42, 5] MGs, in which GGTs require prolonged annealing at sub-TgT_{\mathrm{g}} temperatures, while some heating curves show no detectable LLT exotherm. Because such annealing-induced GGTs require active atomic rearrangement within a largely frozen glassy configuration, how polyamorphism proceeds at the microscopic level remains an intriguing yet open question.

Fast differential scanning calorimetry (FDSC) provides access to thermodynamic signatures that are difficult to resolve under conventional heating conditions. By employing sufficiently high heating rates, the FDSC shifts the devitrification temperature far above the fictive temperature, TfT_{\mathrm{f}}, thus improving the glass-transition overshoot endotherm [50, 28, 36, 63] and revealing hidden thermodynamic processes that are inaccessible under conventional heating conditions [56, 14, 37, 1]. In the case of polyamorphism, previous studies have shown that transformed states in both molecular systems and MGs exhibit pronounced glass-transition overshoots during rapid heating, indicating that these overshoots are likely associated with the reverse transition from the transformed amorphous state to the supercooled liquid (SCL) [40, 21]. Further tracking the evolution of the overshoot position and height with annealing time provides insights into the kinetics of polyamorphism and distinguishes between continuous and coexistence transition mechanisms [2, 40, 21]. However, the structural origin of these changes in enthalpy on the atomic scale remains unknown. Moreover, structural aging and polyamorphic transition can occur simultaneously during annealing, making their respective thermodynamic contributions difficult to disentangle solely from calorimetric measurements. A simultaneous investigation of structural and thermodynamic evolution is therefore essential for clarifying their underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Quantifying the effect of heavy-atom only augmented basis sets for the calculation of non-covalent interactions
papers.abstract: Truncating the basis set is a straightforward way of reducing the computational cost of a calculation, often done by augmenting only the non-hydrogen atoms with diffuse functions. Calculations of non-covalent interactions, which require large diffuse basis sets for quantitative results, regularly employ this truncation. Herein, we assess the validity of this basis set truncation across the A24 and S66 datasets and for case study examples at a range of interaction distances. For the majority of non-covalent interactions, we find that the heavy-atom-only augmented basis sets can be safely applied as a method of reducing computational cost. However, for aliphatic-aliphatic and $π$-aliphatic type dispersion interactions, we find that lower cardinal number basis sets with full augmentation for all atoms, including hydrogen, can provide similar or even more accurate results than higher cardinal number basis sets with partial augmentation. These results emphasize that increasing basis set size and computational cost does not necessarily improve accuracy; rather, the composition of a basis set is critical to achieving highly accurate and efficient computations.

papers.intro:
Highly accurate quantum chemical methods are essential for quantitative descriptions of physical and chemical phenomena across materials science, biochemistry, catalysis and beyond. However, precise calculations quickly become computationally prohibitive due to the interplay of system size, basis set and electronic structure method. Balancing these factors is essential for achieving the desired accuracy at reasonable computational cost. Many methods have been developed to improve computational efficiency including local correlation,[10, 31, 33] tailored cluster expansions,[6, 7, 5, 27, 43, 3, 44] rank-reduction[29, 42, 25, 45] and density fitting.[23, 2] Nonetheless, basis set incompleteness errors remain one of the key limitations in modern electronic structure calculations and understanding the relationship between basis set and accuracy is imperative.

The Dunning correlation consistent basis sets are widely used in the quantum chemistry community because they systematically converge to the complete basis set (CBS) limit, allowing for extrapolation. The size of the basis set required to obtain quantitatively meaningful results is highly dependent on the property of interest. Basis set convergence can be accelerated to the CBS through extrapolation[1, 41] or explicit correlation.[11, 39] Within explicitly correlated F12 approaches, basis set convergence is typically accelerated by an additional two cardinal numbers compared to the canonical basis set.[4] However, the explicit correlation does not extend to the perturbative triples contribution, (T), in coupled cluster calculations with singles, doubles and perturbative triples, CCSD(T),[22] meaning an empirical scaling factor is typically applied to this term.[21] Most recently, transcorrelation has been shown to outperform F12 approaches for non-covalent interactions in the aug-cc-pVTZ basis set.[15]

An analogue solution to reducing computational cost is basis set truncation whereby basis functions that have minimal effect on the calculation of the desired quantity are systematically trimmed. Unlike convergence acceleration methods, such as F12 or transcorrelation, this approach reduces computational cost through the use of more efficient basis sets for similar accuracy. Practically, this is commonly done by omitting the diffuse functions from the hydrogen, while including diffuse functions for all other element types. By removing augmentation functions from a fully augmented basis set, we arrive at the cc-pVXZ basis set, where X is the cardinal number, which is also a correlation-consistent basis set itself. In this way, this particular basis set truncation retains systematic convergence to the CBS limit with increasing zeta level.[8, 9] This particular basis set truncation, whereby augmentation functions are removed from the hydrogen atoms, was popularized by Papajak and Truhlar as the so-called ‘jul’-basis set.[8, 9] However, the very same basis set has been presented with a variety of nomenclatures in the literature over the years with aug’[14] and heavy atom-only augmented basis sets[18] being the most commonly used naming alternatives. We find that the ‘heavy atom augmentation’ nomenclature provides the clearest delineation of the basis set being employed. The accurate description of intermolecular non-covalent interactions is particularly sensitive to the choice of basis set.

Electron correlation is known to be slowly convergent with respect to basis set size[30, 35, 41, 37, 24] and, therefore, non-covalent interactions exhibit similarly slow convergence. An accurate description of the inter-monomer space through the use of large, augmented basis sets is required to accurately capture non-covalent interactions.[26]

papers.title: CoupleFlow: Null-Calibrated Auditory Attention Decoding With Time-Locked Brain-Speech Coupling and Flow-Matching Likelihood Ratios
papers.abstract: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) seeks to identify the attended talker from brief noninvasive brain recordings by comparing neural responses with competing speech streams. Recent electroencephalography (EEG) decoders report nearly perfect accuracy from one second of data, yet we show that this performance fails to generalize to unseen speech because models exploit trial leakage, eye gaze, and acoustic cues instead of speech evoked neural activity. We introduce CoupleFlow, which decodes attention through temporal coupling between neural and acoustic embeddings. Its predictions remain at chance when the brain signal contains no informative coupling, preventing shortcuts based on speech content or talker identity. A conditional flow matching head implements a likelihood ratio decision rule based on pointwise mutual information between brain and speech. This rule is Bayes optimal when the recording depends only on the attended talker and removes preferences for speech that is likely a priori. We evaluate CoupleFlow with content disjoint splits recovered from the audio and null tests that distinguish genuine temporal coupling from trial recognition. Across nine EEG and magnetoencephalography (MEG) datasets processed through a common pipeline, spanning four languages, high density EEG recordings, listeners with hearing impairment, and a room with multiple talkers, CoupleFlow outperforms linear and deep baselines while all null tests remain at chance. Finally, we derive an evidence accumulation law that predicts accuracy across window lengths from a single parameter per dataset and predicts that parameter from the strength of neural speech tracking. This law identifies recording signal to noise ratio as a limit on decoding speed and reliability and estimates the window length required to reach a target accuracy.

papers.intro:
When several people talk at once, a listener naturally isolates one voice. The auditory cortex reflects this selection: low-frequency cortical activity tracks the attended talker’s speech envelope far more strongly than ignored speech. (Ding and Simon,, 2012; Mesgarani and Chang,, 2012; O’Sullivan et al.,, 2015). Auditory attention decoding (AAD) asks whether the attended talker can be identified from this activity recorded non-invasively, with electroencephalography (EEG) or magnetoencephalography (MEG). EEG is promising because it offers millisecond time scale resolution and works with a few electrodes near the ear (Mirkovic et al.,, 2015; Fiedler et al.,, 2017). This makes AAD a candidate for neuro-steered hearing devices that amplify the attended talker (Geirnaert et al.,, 2021), since hearing-impaired listeners track the attended talker more strongly than the competing one, as normal-hearing listeners do (Petersen et al.,, 2017; Decruy et al.,, 2020; Fuglsang et al.,, 2020). Building such a device is beyond the scope of this paper, but we study the decoding problem in terms of its ability to generalize to unheard speech using limited data from unseen subjects, solely from brain activity.

Using a few seconds of multichannel neural data and the speech of KK candidate talkers, the decoder identifies the attended voice. The problem is difficult because the neural response to speech is weak (a linear decoder’s reconstruction correlates with the attended envelope at only r=0.07r=0.07–0.170.17 on our two-talker EEG datasets), differs across listeners, and is mixed with activity unrelated to the audio stimulus, while the candidates often differ in ways a decoder can exploit without reading the brain: loudness, voice, or the identity of the recording session.

AAD decoders follow two strategies: Stimulus reconstruction and Direct classification. Stimulus reconstruction uses the EEG to estimate of the attended speech envelope, and it selects the candidate talker that correlates best with this envelope. Direct classification maps EEG to a label, usually the side of the attended talker. In both cases, however, performance usually fails short of expectations (details in App. A). With stimulus reconstruction, linear backward models and canonical correlation analysis (O’Sullivan et al.,, 2015; Crosse et al.,, 2016; de Cheveigné et al.,, 2018) are robust, but they require long signal durations (i.e., tens of seconds) for high accuracy, which is not practical. Deep nonlinear reconstructions have not changed this picture. The best of them still reconstruct the envelope weakly (r≈0.19r\approx 0.19 for VLAAI; Accou et al.,, 2023), nonlinear decoders did not consistently outperform linear ones in an independent comparison on two public datasets (Geirnaert et al.,, 2021), and many reported gains come from evaluations in which training and test data overlap (Puffay et al.,, 2023). Conversely, direct classifiers (Vandecappelle et al.,, 2021; Yan et al.,, 2024; Ni et al.,, 2024; Fan et al.,, 2025) report 95–97% at 1 s, but their accuracy rests largely on shortcuts: training and test windows come from the same trial, so the classifier can recognise the trial rather than decode attention (leakage), and it can read eye gaze toward the attended talker. When training and test data come from different trials, their accuracy drops to near chance (Rotaru et al.,, 2024). Furthermore, datasets replay the same stories to every listener, and test windows are often cut from training trials (Puffay et al.,, 2023). It is also not inherently clear that decoders are not overfitting to audio cues, such as loudness, spectral differences, or trial identity, indicating that the decoder is ignoring the brain signal.Most studies report accuracy at only one or two window lengths, so the window needed for a given accuracy cannot be predicted. Each study also preprocesses each dataset its own way, so numbers cannot be compared across studies or datasets. Finally, in one widely used dataset (NJU) we find that the EEG is not time-aligned with the audio at any offset, so results on it cannot reflect speech tracking (App. C).

Differences in loudness, voice or trial identity cannot raise its accuracy. A generative head adds a new decision rule for AAD, which is optimal under a standard assumption.

It shows that fast, reliable decoding is limited by the quality of the recording, and it gives the window needed for any target accuracy.

papers.title: A probabilistic approach to separate mergers and jellyfish galaxies: Application of morphological non-parametric indexes to the DESI Legacy Survey
papers.abstract: Galaxy morphology traces the physical processes that shape galaxy evolution, but non-parametric diagnostic boundaries depend on image quality and preprocessing. We investigate the classification of regular spirals, regular ellipticals, mergers, and jellyfish (ram-pressure-stripping candidate) galaxies in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Using galmex measurements of ten non-parametric morphological indices, we evaluate two-dimensional diagnostic planes with a cross-validated Bayesian kernel-density classifier and combine all indices using probability-calibrated LightGBM models. For separating regular spirals, regular ellipticals, and perturbed systems, the most informative planes combine Shannon entropy with $M_{20}$ or asymmetry indices, reaching balanced accuracies of 0.76-0.77. We provide survey-specific probabilistic boundaries in the entropy-$M_{20}$ and entropy-shape-asymmetry planes. Separating mergers from jellyfish candidates is more challenging; the best two-dimensional combinations, all involving concentration, reach balanced accuracies of approximately 0.73. The calibrated three-class LightGBM model achieves a balanced accuracy and macro-F1 score of 0.89, while the four-class model achieves 0.75 and 0.76, respectively. We provide class probabilities and preferred classifications for 1,744,454 galaxies. Our results show that non-parametric morphology identifies broad structural disturbance reliably, but distinguishing its physical origin is harder: jellyfish candidates occupy a relatively coherent region of parameter space, whereas mergers span diverse and overlapping morphologies.

papers.title: Aligning Large Language Models with Human Feedback: Mathematical Foundations and Algorithm Design
papers.abstract: This article provides an introduction to the mathematical foundations and algorithmic frameworks used to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intentions, preferences, and values. We discuss standard alignment techniques, such as fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). We also explore the theoretical underpinnings of learning from human preferences, drawing connections to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and discrete choice models. We present state-of-the-art algorithms in a tutorial style, discuss their advantages and limitations, and offer insights into practical implementation. Our exposition is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners, providing both a foundational understanding of alignment methodologies and a framework for developing more robust and scalable alignment techniques.

Background. As large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm, it is clear that generative AI systems will soon become ubiquitous in our lives. More technically, the LLM alignment problem involves fine-tuning or adjusting a base model that was originally trained on extensive, diverse datasets. While such a base model is trained to learn core behaviors and general knowledge, it often falls short when applied to specific tasks or to meeting the nuanced preferences of a human user. To better align the model, additional feedback is gathered from human experts who evaluate and/or rank the model’s performance within a specific task context. As demonstrated in [38, 19], reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant promise for LLM alignment by leveraging additional feedback to enhance their performance. This feedback embodies expert judgments regarding both the accuracy of the model’s responses and any particular preferences they may have. The goal is to refine the model to better meet these specific requirements, ultimately enhancing its task relevance and user satisfaction. Generally, it is observed that after the alignment process, LLMs can follow human instructions well, and can avoid providing toxic and non-preferable responses. Despite extensive study of the alignment problem in recent literature, this research area remains young, and it is still evolving rapidly with many unresolved theoretical challenges. A primary contribution of this article is to introduce the signal processing community to the fundamentals of alignment, highlight state-of-the-art algorithms and approaches, and clarify the intersection

We believe that our article will foster interdisciplinary contributions and expand the role of SP in LLM alignment research. By understanding the alignment problem, SP researchers can leverage their expertise in mathematical modeling, noise handling, inverse problem-solving, and optimization to address a number of key challenges. papers.title: Detection and Validation of Hidden Subgroup Disparities in Clinical AI
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models used in clinical workflows often perform systematically differently across patient groups, raising concerns about equity and patient safety. Traditional subgroup analyses can expose such disparities only when rich metadata (e.g., patient demographics) is available and captures the sources of performance variation, conditions rarely met in practice. Algorithmic subgroup discovery methods offer a solution by identifying coherent groups from learned feature representations, but because true underlying stratifications are unknown, these methods are hard to evaluate. As a result, subgroup discovery has not been systematically applied or assessed for performance monitoring. Our main objective is to evaluate algorithmic subgroup discovery for performance monitoring, assessing the discovered subgroups' performance gaps and semantic coherence. Investigating cardiomegaly classification in a dataset of 223,228 chest X-rays, we showed that the discovered subgroups exhibited larger performance gaps (accuracies of 0.61-0.90) than traditional metadata-based analysis (0.80-0.94) and were frequently interpretable using patient, acquisition, and model metadata. As a proof of concept, we also showed that annotations from learned subgroups can be used to mitigate the biases they expose. We conclude that subgroup discovery is a practical and effective tool to enhance the performance validation and monitoring of ML systems in healthcare.

In the US, for example, the FDA had approved 1,247 AI-assisted medical devices by May 2025, with 523 of these approvals occurring within the last 24 months [30]. However, research shows that even the most capable AI models can reinforce societal biases and fail unpredictably in clinical settings [33]. Consequently, regulatory agencies worldwide are tightening policies governing the development and deployment of medical AI to enhance its fairness and robustness.

A critical concern is that ML models may perform systematically differently across patient subgroups [27, 6, 14, 20]. This has hampered past attempts at safely deploying medical AI, particularly in underserved populations [27, 6]. Model performance can depend on many factors [10], including patient attributes (e.g., sex, age, ethnicity) and image characteristics (e.g., image quality, artifacts, device manufacturer). Chest X-rays model’s performances, for example, were shown to depend on biological sex [15, 31], support devices such as tracheotomy tubes and chest drains [13, 21], artifacts (e.g., laterality markers, highlight arrows) [8], and projection views [8] (anterior-posterior (AP) and posterior-anterior (PA)). Not understanding when and why an ML model systematically fails poses an avoidable danger to patients and delays the development of more robust models. Furthermore, systematic hidden model failures may violate regulators’ demands for safety and effectiveness for all intended use populations of a medical device.

These challenges are central to ensuring the safe and equitable application of AI in healthcare. In response, current frameworks call on AI developers and dataset curators to explicitly identify and annotate potential sources of bias throughout the model development pipeline. Together with clinical metadata, such as patient attributes and data-specific characteristics, the annotation can then be used to define patient subgroups to assess group fairness and evaluate model robustness. In general, the richer the available annotations, the more precisely relevant subgroups can be defined, increasing the chance of uncovering meaningful performance gaps.

In practice, this can lead to severe reporting gaps, as exposed by a recent scoping review of FDA-approved medical AI devices [18]. According to their analysis, less than 4% of approved devices provide information on race or ethnicity, less than 1% report on socioeconomic factors, and less than 19% report on age subgroups [18].

Even under ideal conditions, where multiple metadata attributes are available for a large, heterogeneous population, metadata may only partially align with the major hidden factors of variation that affect ML model performance. As a result, traditional metadata-defined subgroups may fail to reveal relevant performance gaps. Metadata annotations often reflect concepts that are meaningful for human interpretation and categorization, yet may be irrelevant to how machine learning models stratify data to make predictions. For example, stratifying a chest X-ray dataset by patient sex may be of limited value for auditing performance, since observed differences are often driven by correlated factors such as the presence of support devices (e.g., tubes and lines) rather than sex itself [31, 21]. In contrast, stratifying by projection (AP vs PA) is crucial. Standard radiology interpretation emphasizes that the PA view is preferred for assessing cardiomegaly because the AP view magnifies the cardiac silhouette [23]. Accordingly, deep learning models perform better on PA studies than on AP studies for cardiomegaly-related labels (see Table 2). Unrecognized subsets of data are referred to as hidden stratifications. As we will demonstrate in this study, even in one of the most comprehensively annotated large-scale datasets available, CheXpertPlus [5], which contains over 80 annotated factors including patient socio-demographics, comorbidities, and image characteristics for more than 200,000 samples, hidden stratifications remain prevalent. While manual inspection of model errors can sometimes reveal these issues, it is generally infeasible at scale and particularly challenging in medical imaging, where relevant differences across samples are often subtle.

Algorithmic subgroup discovery [9, 28] appears as a potential solution for this problem, as it can learn data stratifications that are relevant to a specific ML prediction model and dataset. The subgroup divisions are found by training unsupervised clustering methods (e.g., mixture models, k-means) on learned feature representations of the data. Aside from the predictions from the investigated model, subgroup discovery methods also leverage complementary knowledge from models trained with different objectives (e.g., multi-modal, generative) or with more data. These models have been used so far only on toy datasets with predefined biases for easier evaluation. We believe they might also be useful for performance evaluation and model surveillance, but they have yet to be proven effective in real-world medical contexts. The main challenge of using subgroup discovery techniques is how to validate the discovered subgroups, as hidden stratifications by definition lack ground-truth labels for evaluation.

papers.title: A Highly Efficient Depth-Averaged Material Point Method for Geophysical Mass Flows
papers.abstract: Probabilistic hazard assessment of geophysical mass flows requires large simulation ensembles and thus fast and robust numerical models. We present an open-source depth-averaged material point method formulated in global Cartesian coordinates, using Lagrangian particles to track the flow margin. A separate basal friction step based on the Coulomb, Voellmy, or $μ(I)$-rheology brings the flow to rest without artificial stopping criteria. Our model reproduces analytical solutions for a sliding block and dam-break problems and matches the deposit of a laboratory granular column collapse. A back-calculation of the 2023 Brienz/Brinzauls rockslide (Switzerland) at 1m resolution (190'000 particles) runs faster than real time on a single CPU core. Calibrated to the observed runout, the three friction laws yield very similar results, but Coulomb friction shows a slightly wider affected area than Voellmy and $μ(I)$. A probabilistic 1632-simulation ensemble at 5m resolution was computed in 76s. The model is one to two orders of magnitude faster than established depth-averaged models used in engineering practice, making catchment-style ensemble simulations feasible on a desktop computer.
