papers.intro:
Gravity-driven geophysical mass flows, such as rockslides, debris flows, and snow avalanches, threaten mountain communities worldwide. These events frequently result in fatalities, cause damage to critical infrastructure, and incur economic costs related to hazard zoning, mitigation, and reconstruction (Dowling and Santi, 2014; Froude and Petley, 2018). Furthermore, climate change is altering the probability, intensity, and nature of these events, for example through permafrost degradation and changing precipitation patterns (Gariano and Guzzetti, 2016; Jacquemart et al., 2024). To address future climate uncertainty, reliable probabilistic hazard mapping requires running simulation ensembles across wide parameter ranges (Bühler et al., 2022; Ortner et al., 2025), necessitating computationally efficient models.

Gravity-driven geophysical mass flows, such as rockslides, debris flows, and snow avalanches, threaten mountain communities worldwide. These events frequently result in fatalities, cause damage to critical infrastructure, and incur economic costs related to hazard zoning, mitigation, and reconstruction (Dowling and Santi, 2014; Froude and Petley, 2018). Furthermore, climate change is altering the probability, intensity, and nature of these events, for example through permafrost degradation and changing precipitation patterns (Gariano and Guzzetti, 2016; Jacquemart et al., 2024). To address future climate uncertainty, reliable probabilistic hazard mapping requires running simulation ensembles across wide parameter ranges (Bühler et al., 2022; Ortner et al., 2025), necessitating computationally efficient models.

The modeling of geophysical mass flows has evolved significantly over the past decades. Early efforts relied on empirical methods based on topographic parameters (Lied and Bakkehøi, 1980) and analytical calculations (Salm et al., 1990) that have since been refined into modern Geographic Information Systems (GIS)-based tools (Horton et al., 2013; Berti and Simoni, 2014). However, while practical and widely used for preliminary assessments, these approaches lack a dynamic representation of the flow physics. The foundational basis for modern continuum models was established when Savage and Hutter (1989) extended the Saint–Venant shallow-water equations to dry granular flows. The Saint–Venant equations, which are derived by integrating the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations over the flow depth, are written in Cartesian coordinates and only valid for small slope angles (almost flat topography), rendering them inapplicable to geophysical mass flows. The Savage–Hutter model overcomes this limitation by integrating the balance laws in coordinates aligned with the bed, thereby only requiring small slope variations (Savage and Hutter, 1991, small curvature,). While strictly one-dimensional, this foundational model combines a Coulomb basal friction law with an earth-pressure closure for internal stresses. Earlier and independently, similar depth-averaged avalanche models were pioneered in the Soviet Union (Grigorian et al., 1967; Eglit et al., 2020). At the time, solving these equations numerically in two dimensions was challenging. Although first two-dimensional formulations existed (Kulikovskii and Eglit, 1973; Hutter et al., 1993; Gray et al., 1999), the first operational numerical tools were restricted to one-dimensional depth-averaged models, such as DAN (Hungr, 1995) and AVAL-1D (Bartelt et al., 1999), which provided insights into flow velocities and flow heights along predefined one-dimensional profiles. As the theoretical framework, numerical schemes, and computational power advanced, a wide variety of two-dimensional depth-averaged models were developed. They can be clustered by their numerical schemes: Eulerian models based on finite volume methods (FVM) or finite difference methods (FDM), e.g., SHALTOP (Mangeney-Castelnau et al., 2003; Bouchut and Westdickenberg, 2004), TITAN2D (Patra et al., 2005), RAMMS (Christen et al., 2010), D-Claw (Iverson and George, 2014; George and Iverson, 2014), and r.avaflow (Pudasaini, 2012; Mergili et al., 2017), and Lagrangian models based on smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH), e.g., DAN3D (McDougall and Hungr, 2004; Hungr and McDougall, 2009), GeoFlow-SPH (Pastor et al., 2009; Pastor et al., 2014), and SAMOS-AT (Sampl and Granig, 2009), which served as the basis of the AvaFrame com1DFA module (Tonnel et al., 2023).

Despite these advancements, significant limitations remain in the current landscape of mass flow modeling. Eulerian models struggle to sharply track the exact flow margin, and suffer from numerical diffusion (LeVeque, 2002). Furthermore, they typically require complex shock-capturing numerical techniques to resolve discontinuities (Nessyahu and Tadmor, 1990), and flow height cut-off thresholds or height-positivity preserving schemes (Mangeney-Castelnau et al., 2003). Additionally, some models require artificial stopping criteria to handle material deposition (Christen et al., 2010; Rauter et al., 2016; Goodwin et al., 2024). Conversely, while Lagrangian SPH models naturally track the flow margin, they often rely on artificial viscosity or smoothing to stabilize shocks and suppress oscillations, and require complex neighbor search algorithms (Monaghan, 2005). Three-dimensional depth-resolved models, such as 3D MPM (Cicoira et al., 2022; Blatny and Gaume, 2025), 3D SPH (Nikooei and Manzari, 2020), or 3D FVM (von Boetticher et al., 2016), are powerful tools for fundamental process understanding, detailed hazard assessment, and mitigation structure design. Due to their high computational cost, however, these models are generally applied to individual slopes or selected high-risk flow paths rather than catchment-scale probabilistic hazard mapping requiring large ensembles of simulations. Finally, several established models (2D depth-averaged and 3D depth-resolved) remain commercial or closed-source.

papers.title: Divalent Yb in the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ Structure Type: Crystal Growth and Physical Properties of Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$
papers.abstract: We report on the single-crystal growth, crystal structure, and physical properties of Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$. Single crystal x-ray diffraction shows that the material crystallizes in the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ structure-type at ambient conditions, described by orthorhombic symmetry $Pbam$. Magnetization measurements reveal a nearly isotropic diamagnetic response, indicating that Yb is stabilized in a non-magnetic divalent configuration. Electrical resistivity measurements show a metallic behavior. First-principles calculations including spin--orbit coupling describe a metal whose states at the Fermi level are dominated by Bi $6p$ orbitals, with a density of states within 1% of that of the isoelectronic compound Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$, consistent with a filled and chemically inert $4f$ shell. They further show that the nonsymmorphic symmetry of the crystal enforces fourfold-degenerate nodal lines on the Brillouin-zone boundary, four of which cross the Fermi level and give symmetry-enforced Dirac points with a linear transverse dispersion. Despite strong metallic and covalent bonding within the Pd-Bi network, Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ is realized as a rare-earth analog of the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ structure type with divalent Yb ions. This result offers a potential avenue to discover other rare-earth analogs within this structural family.

papers.title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

papers.title: Toward Open ISA Supercomputing: A Comparative Study of RISC-V, Arm, and x86 Architectures on HPC Workloads
papers.abstract: RISC-V is emerging as a candidate architecture for high-performance computing (HPC), but its competitiveness against established x86 and Arm processors remains difficult to assess because existing studies use different platforms, workloads, and methodologies, and rarely consider energy efficiency. Our work provides an evaluation of contemporary HPC RISC-V, Arm, and x86 processors using a common software stack and methodology. We characterize the Sophgo SG2044 and compare it with the NVIDIA Grace CPU Superchip and Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ across four HPC benchmarks (STREAM, HPL, HPL-MxP, and HPCG) and four representative applications (iPIC3D, PLUTO, OpenFOAM, and llama$.$cpp). The version of HPL-MxP linked to OpenBLAS built and used for this work is made available as open-source software. The SG2044 reaches 8.02 GFLOP/s of FP64 performance and 7.8 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core, increasing to 294 GFLOP/s and 107 GB/s at 64 cores. L2-cache-aware process placement enables near-linear scaling up to 16 cores, beyond which memory-bandwidth saturation limits further gains. Across generations of RISC-V hardware, in the context of the Monte Cimone (MC) project, the SG2044-based MCv3 doubles both single-core performance and peak memory bandwidth relative to MCv2, while improving memory bandwidth, node-level FP64 performance, and energy efficiency by approximately 100x, 158x, and 10x, over MCv1. Against the Arm and x86 systems, the SG2044 shows 8-15x less absolute performance, reflecting its narrower vector resources and less advanced technology node, but delivers competitive scaling and energy efficiency on several workloads. Its most notable result is LLM decode, where 64-core execution provides the highest relative scaling and energy efficiency among the evaluated platforms while exceeding Intel in throughput. Our results show that RISC-V processors are closing the gap with the competition.

papers.intro:
The open-source instruction set architecture (ISA) RISC-V has seen remarkable growth in recent years, evolving from a research-oriented initiative into a promising alternative to established proprietary ISAs [1, 2]. Its open and modular specification has attracted contributors from academia, startups, and established semiconductor vendors, accelerating the pace of hardware innovation and software ecosystem maturation [1]. As implementations have become more capable and toolchain support has improved, RISC-V platforms have progressed well beyond microcontroller-class devices, giving rise to Linux-capable processors, multi-core system-on-chip (SoC), and accelerators targeting vector processing [3, 4], artificial intelligence (AI) [5], and scientific computing workloads. Compiler and runtime support have advanced substantially, with mainstream toolchains such as GCC and LLVM providing full RISC-V backends and vectorization support, while HPC libraries and programming models such as OpenMP, MPI and BLAS are increasingly being ported and optimized for the architecture [2, 1]. This convergence of open hardware and software ecosystems made it feasible to consider RISC-V as an emerging target platform within the context of high-performance computing (HPC) [2, 6, 1, 7, 8], a field traditionally dominated by Intel’s x86 and, more recently, Arm architectures [9].

papers.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
papers.abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

papers.title: UAE GovTrust Scope Filtering Gains and Routing Failures in Bilingual Public Service Retrieval
papers.abstract: Public-service queries can mention several locations while only one controls the requested service. We study this distinction in UAE GovTrust, a controlled English-Arabic retrieval diagnostic comprising 22 authored service summaries and 50 scenarios with 110 query variants. Twelve methods separate lexical and dense ranking, rank fusion, scope filtering, a multilingual cross-encoder, and direct service lookup. On 72 matched answerable queries with bilingual evidence, role-filtered reciprocal rank fusion retrieves a relevant first result for 69 queries (95.8%), versus 47 (65.3%) for unfiltered fusion; filtered dense retrieval and direct lookup each achieve 68 (94.4%). With English-only evidence, excluding zero-score lexical candidates raises filtered fusion from 52 to 64 correct first hits. However, the unchanged router selects the correct action and scope for only 2 of 168 post-audit perturbations covering paraphrases, irrelevant facts, negation, and corrections. These perturbations are deliberately authored diagnostics, not held-out evaluation. Fresh-environment execution reproduces all 1,320 original ranking orders and actions. The results show that correct scope metadata can improve ranking while brittle scope inference can remove the evidence needed to answer. The study evaluates retrieval and routing, not generated answers or legal correctness; independent Arabic and domain validation remains necessary.

A public-service question may mention where a person lives, where a vehicle is registered, where a property is located, and which authority issued a document. These are different relations. Retrieving a passage about a city named in the question is therefore insufficient: the system must determine which relation controls the requested service. For example, in the catalogue studied here, a question about a toll gate in Abu Dhabi should retrieve the Abu Dhabi toll-system card even when the vehicle is registered in Dubai. Reversing those two locations changes the relevant card without changing the set of location names.

For example, in the catalogue studied here, a question about a toll gate in Abu Dhabi should retrieve the Abu Dhabi toll-system card even when the vehicle is registered in Dubai. Reversing those two locations changes the relevant card without changing the set of location names.

This problem matters to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) because a generator cannot reliably ground an answer in evidence that an upstream filter has discarded. It is also relevant to enterprise service catalogues, policy portals, and operational assistants in which organizational units or service territories overlap. Those applications motivate the study; they are not deployment settings evaluated in the experiments. The present work isolates the retrieval and routing stages so their errors can be observed without a generator or an automated answer judge obscuring the source of failure.

UAE GovTrust is presented as a controlled diagnostic, not as an expert-validated benchmark of UAE law. Its corpus consists of short, authored service summaries, its questions are synthetic, and its labels describe relevance within that catalogue. An initial development experiment suggested a large benefit from scope filtering. A subsequent technical audit reproduced the original arithmetic but exposed failures in the rule-based router. This report incorporates that criticism through stronger comparisons, an explicit post-audit stress set, and a separation of routing errors from errors in ranking eligible evidence.

The contribution has three parts. First, it provides a reproducible bilingual diagnostic in which the service-controlling location differs from an incidental location. Second, it disentangles scope selection, ranking, sparse-branch eligibility, and service lookup through twelve comparison methods. Third, it documents how the benefit of a correct hard filter can coexist with severe failures of the mechanism that chooses that filter. The resulting evidence supports a limited engineering conclusion: scope inference must be evaluated independently of the retrieval gains obtained when the scope is correct. No claim is made to the first UAE regulatory RAG system, a new general filtering algorithm, or production readiness.

papers.title: Rationalizing charge transfer: a single-molecule case study across three distinct surfaces
papers.abstract: Organic molecules are versatile building blocks for the formation of complex low-dimensional nanostructures on surfaces. Recently, interest has grown in translating on-surface synthetic protocols from noble metal surfaces to insulating surfaces, which offer technological relevance, and to magnetic or superconducting surfaces, which offer new routes to correlated phases. It is important, therefore, to understand how these alternative surfaces may alter the properties of adsorbates through processes like charge transfer and screening. Evidence for charge transfer is often obtained experimentally via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), and theoretically via density functional theory (DFT). In this work, we systematically compare the properties of isolated macrocyclic emeraldine (Me$_6$) molecules on three different surfaces: metallic Au(111), a semiconducting ferromagnetic monolayer of FeCl$_2$, and a cleaved superconducting surface of bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$. We show that STS and DFT alone are insufficient to quantify charge transfer for these cases. Instead, we complement these methods with Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) measurements and model Hamiltonian calculations to demonstrate that on Au(111) and FeCl$_2$, Me$_6$ molecules donate a single electron to the substrate, whereas on NbSe$_2$ two electrons are transferred from molecule to substrate. Our work provides insight into the interplay of charge transfer, screening, and molecule-substrate coupling, and develops experimental and theoretical methods for comparing the properties of adsorbates across different surfaces for future studies.

papers.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
papers.abstract: To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure-from-Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse-to-dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non-matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub-pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/flexglue .
papers.intro:
Image matching estimates correspondences across images and is a fundamental building block of 3D vision, from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to visual localization. Most geometric applications only require correspondences for a sparse set of distinctive interest points (Lowe, 2004; Yi et al., 2016; DeTone et al., 2018), which both simplifies the problem and reduces its cost. These points are detected independently in each image and matched by a nearest-neighbor search of their descriptors or by deep networks that learn priors on motion and scene structure (Sarlin et al., 2020; Lindenberger et al., 2023; Nordström et al., 2026). Matching is thus fundamentally bounded by the detector: a 3D point can only be matched if it is detected in both views, and any localization noise of the detections propagates directly into the correspondences.

Dense matchers (Edstedt et al., 2023; Edstedt et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Edstedt et al., 2026) lift this bound by matching all pixels directly, and are remarkably robust to large viewpoint and appearance changes while achieving subpixel accuracy. This comes at a high cost: they estimate and refine a correspondence for every pixel, which restricts them to low resolutions and makes training expensive, even though downstream applications typically use only a sparse subset. Multi-view applications such as SfM further require discrete tracks, forcing pipelines to snap dense correspondences to detected keypoints with additional heuristics (Sun et al., 2021; He et al., 2024). Semi-dense matchers (Sun et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025) reduce the cost by matching on a coarse grid, but anchor correspondences to grid cells and refine all of them, even when only a sparse subset is needed. Existing matchers thus face a clear trade-off between the robustness of dense and the efficiency of sparse matching.

A lightweight Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) aggregates context over a dense token grid of both images, and a cheap readout and refinement head extracts correspondences only at the queries (Fig. 2). Correspondences can thus land on any pixel, removing the dependence on repeatable detections while retaining the efficiency of sparse matching. papers.title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
papers.abstract: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

papers.intro:
Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations (Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009; Deng et al., 2013; Gunn & Anderson, 2015). Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays (Liu et al., 2019; Kuutti et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2025; Bodmer et al., 2026), while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016; Shi et al., 2016). These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety (Shin & Cui, 1995; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004; Ma et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2023; Nan et al., 2026).

Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD (Ma et al., 2026a) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection11 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity (Okanovic et al., 2025), N:MN\!:\!M sparsity (Zhao et al., 2024), and row-/column-wise sparsity (Wen et al., 2016), are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining, allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

papers.title: Phronix: The Capability-Centric Learning Paradigm for Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.

papers.intro:
Scientific computing has begun to delegate its routine engineering to LLM (LLM) agents, which auto-tune HPC code on production supercomputers [13], diagnose parallel I/O performance [11], and work on the repositories and pipelines behind published results [10, 5]. The work delegated there is repetitive rather than novel, such as instrumenting an application, characterizing where a run spends its time, and repeating that for the next application, input scale, and system. An agent, however, is more than a model which operates withing a harness [34], where the LLM proposes each step and observes its result [35], tools exposed through interfaces such as the MCP (MCP) [29, 3] let it touch the world, skills accumulate how a class of task is done [33, 1], memory carries what earlier sessions learned past the context window [24], and the harness orchestrates them into the loop the agent runs. An agent that is good at such a task once should be good at it every time, and it is the harness, not the model, that determines whether it is, because the harness governs how much human steering a task requires and how many tokens and retries it consumes. Improving agent effectiveness is consequently as much a harness problem as it is a model problem.

As these interfaces matured, developers built more complex and capable command-line harnesses such as Codex [22] and OpenCode [23], which let users plug in different skills and agents for each task. All of them are driven primarily by human, who writes the skill or rulebook that a complex task needs before it is assigned.

papers.title: Mimicking Volatilities under Marginal Constraints via $q_x$-Bass Martingales: A Parallel Computing Approach
papers.abstract: We study the calibration of continuous-time martingale models to observed derivative prices via a dynamic martingale optimal transport problem that penalizes deviations from the volatility of a prescribed reference model. Using $q_x$-Bass martingales, we approximate this problem through a sequence of discrete-time problems and prove that the continuous-time interpolations of their optimizers are asymptotically optimal. Building on the theory of $q_x$-Bass martingales, we develop numerical methods for the discrete-time problems that do not require full marginal distributions at calibration maturities.

papers.intro:
Constructing a pricing model consistent with observed market prices of financial derivatives is a central problem in mathematical finance. Classical approaches usually require selecting a class of stochastic models and then calibrating the associated parameters or coefficients to market data. Prominent examples include parametric stochastic volatility models, such as the Heston model [20], local volatility models, such as Dupire’s local volatility model [13], and local-stochastic volatility models [19, 21], which combine the calibration flexibility of local volatility with the richer dynamics of stochastic volatility. While these approaches are widely used, they impose specific structural assumptions on the underlying price dynamics.

While these approaches are widely used, they impose specific structural assumptions on the underlying price dynamics.

An alternative approach is provided by semimartingale optimal transport, where one selects, among all models consistent with market prices, the one closest to a prescribed reference model according to a suitable cost functional. Developed by Guo–Loeper–Wang for the calibration of local-stochastic volatility models [16], this methodology has been extended to joint SPX/VIX calibration [15] and stochastic interest-rate models [22]. These approaches rely on PDE formulations and duality arguments involving Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations.

Moreover, its calibration can be implemented through a simple fixed-point iteration, without solving PDEs, for which rigorous convergence results have been proved [4, 18].

papers.title: IFC-SSL-Bench: Benchmarking Self-Supervised Learning for Annotation-Efficient Multispectral Imaging Flow Cytometry
papers.abstract: Imaging Flow Cytometry (IFC) generates large multispectral datasets, yet the need for expert annotations bottlenecks the development of supervised deep learning models. While Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) offers a solution, its application to IFC remains fragmented and lacks systematic benchmarking. To address this, we present IFC-SSL-Bench, a modular framework for evaluating SSL in IFC. We benchmark six SSL approaches across four backbones on two heterogeneous datasets. By assessing downstream classification performance across annotation regimes of the training sets (1%-100%), we quantify annotation efficiency and identify optimal configurations for high-dimensional biological imaging. SSL matches the performance of fully supervised baselines trained on 100% of annotated data while using as little as 5% of annotations for morphological classification, with advantages in low-data regimes below 5%. Across both datasets, the contrastive approach MoCo-v2 paired with ConvNeXt backbones emerged as the top-performing configuration, with ConvNeXtV1-T best for immunological synapse classification and ConvNeXtV2-T for morphological classification. We identify a clear pattern in transfer dynamics: ImageNet initialization benefits morphological classification, consistent with its visual similarity to natural images, whereas random initialization better captures the more domain-specific immunological synapse classification. SSL elevates class-specific F1-scores by over 35 percentage points for structurally complex classes at 1% of annotated data. We synthesize these insights into a unified set of guidelines for deploying self-supervised workflows in high-throughput IFC, and release the benchmark as a resource for future work.

papers.intro:
Imaging Flow Cytometry (IFC) is a modern technology that combines the quantitative, high-throughput capabilities of Flow Cytometry (FC) with the spatial and morphological detail provided by microscopy [6]. In practice, this is achieved by hydrodynamically focusing cells into a single-file stream that passes through a laser-illuminated imaging zone. High-speed detectors, synchronized with the cell flow, capture multispectral images using combinations of brightfield, darkfield, phase-contrast, and fluorescence channels, to achieve sharp subcellular resolution at high velocities [54, 61]. By capturing multiple images of each cell as it passes through the imaging region, IFC produces high-dimensional image datasets that provide unprecedented single-cell depth [61]. This hybrid technique has advanced research in immunology, oncology, cell biology, and environmental science by allowing detailed examination of heterogeneous cell populations and subtle phenotypic variations with robust statistical confidence [54, 24, 23, 62].

This hybrid technique has advanced research in immunology, oncology, cell biology, and environmental science by allowing detailed examination of heterogeneous cell populations and subtle phenotypic variations with robust statistical confidence [54, 24, 23, 62].

Despite its powerful capabilities, IFC faces significant challenges that stem not only from the inherent biological heterogeneity of cell populations [31], but also from the technical constraints, and therefore hinders effective data analysis. The primary technical hurdle in IFC is the fundamental trade-off to set between throughput and image resolution. While increasing magnification or exposure time gradually improves spatial resolution and fine morphological detail, it inherently reduces acquisition speed. Conversely, high-throughput demands shorter exposure times, which results in reduced image quality with lower magnification and/or low Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) [32]. In multichannel acquisitions, fluorescence signals are additionally subject to background and to spectral crosstalk between detectors, which can obscure weak markers and distort the measured intensity distributions [46]. The appearance of a given cell type therefore depends not only on its biology but also on how it was acquired, so that the morphological differences of interest are superimposed on variation of purely technical origin.

Beyond these acquisition challenges, the analysis of IFC data also faces various bottlenecks. Traditionally, IFC data analysis has relied on manual gating or software-assisted pipelines using handcrafted feature extraction. Tools such as CellProfiler [12] improved throughput by automating cell feature extraction of hundreds of morphological and intensity-based descriptors. However, these classical approaches still require extensive domain expertise to select and tune relevant features for specific biological assays, making the analysis labor-intensive and susceptible to operator subjectivity [59, 35]. This reliance on predefined features introduces variability and limits scalability, as manual or semi-automated gating is not only time-consuming but also prone to inconsistencies across different operators [54, 50].

DL models can automatically learn complex features from raw data, reducing the dependence on manual feature engineering. Several specialized pipelines have emerged to facilitate this transition, including PXPermute [8] for feature importance analysis, Deepometry [19] for multi-channel phenotyping, Deep Cytometry [41] for real-time sorting applications, and Small U-Net [36] for high-throughput segmentation.

Despite these successes, the models still require large amounts of accurately annotated data for supervised training [30, 64]. Given the high cost and expertise required to annotate images, obtaining sufficiently large and diverse annotated datasets remains a significant bottleneck, leading to scarce datasets, limiting generalization performance, and creating a need for annotation-efficient strategies [30]. To address this, Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) methods have emerged as a promising alternative [70, 53]. SSL leverages unannotated data to learn useful representations, reducing the need for costly manual annotations. SSL is a paradigm well suited to IFC, which naturally generates vast amounts of unannotated cellular images at high-throughput scales. The robust performance of SSL in processing high-dimensional data, most notably in natural language [47] and video analysis [56], has provided a strong impetus for its application to other fields such as transcriptomics [51, 55] and visual geo-localization [66]. In medical imaging, SSL has reached a high level of maturity: in digital histopathology, for example, the SSL method Barlow Twins (BT) was used to pretrain a model on whole slide images and demonstrated remarkable robustness to cohorts variations and tissue types [42]. Similarly, on widely used benchmarks like MedMNIST [67], SSL has been investigated to provide clear domain guidelines. Bundele et al. Boukdir similarly reports transferable SSL representations across diagnostic domains [7]. More recently in radiology with nnFoundation, self-supervised pretraining at scale has produced general purpose encoders that transfer across more than a hundred downstream tasks [27].

papers.title: The Minimum Number of Samples in the Labeled Coupon Collector Problem
papers.abstract: The Labeled Coupon Collector Problem (LCCP) is an extension of the classical Coupon Collector Problem (CCP) in which one must deduce an unknown mapping between coupons and labels by collecting unordered subsets of k coupons and their associated labels, where deduction relies on analyzing the intersections and differences of the unordered subsets. In this work, we establish a fundamental connection between the LCCP and the combinatorial theory of separating systems. Using this framework, we completely characterize the minimum required number of samples to deduce all labels in two settings: Type-I, where the label set is known in advance, and Type-II, where it is unknown. We provide deterministic constructions of minimal separating and covering systems, yielding explicit bounds that are tighter than those found in existing literature. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the partial recovery problem, characterizing the minimum number of samples required to identify a specified number of target coupons.

The Coupon Collector Problem (CCP) [10],[11] is a classical combinatorial problem dating back to De Moivre, Euler, and Laplace, which can be described as follows. Consider a promotional contest in which a prize is won by collecting at least one of each type of coupon distributed in packages of a certain product. Assuming the number of coupon types is a finite number nn and that each package contains exactly one coupon, opening a package can be viewed as sampling one coupon independently and uniformly at random with replacement from the set of possible coupon types. The CCP investigates the number of samples, NN, needed to collect all nn coupon types. Specific problems of interest include finding the minimum, expectation, and other properties of the distribution of NN. The minimum is trivially seen to be nn. The sample counts between collecting distinct coupon types are independent geometric random variables; thus, the expectation is found to be 𝔼⁡[N]=n​Hn\mathbb{E}[N]=nH_{n}, where Hn=∑j=1n1jH_{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{j} denotes the nn-th harmonic number [10]. Formulas for higher moments of NN can be computed [14], and limit theorems for the asymptotic distribution of NN have also been studied [9], [3].

papers.title: Acoustic and Lexical Signals for Native Language Identification of Language Learners
papers.abstract: Spoken native language (L1) identification for second language learners has traditionally relied on acoustic attributes of speech. Comparatively little attention has been paid to analysing speech transcripts for L1 traces. In this paper, we present a study of L1 identification using both speech and corresponding transcripts from a spoken learner English corpus. We compare a WavLM-based audio L1 classifier with a zero-shot GPT-4o classifier operating on transcripts and analyse their predictions across proficiency levels using a CEFR-balanced evaluation set. Our experiments show that the audio classifier outperforms the transcript-based approach overall when full transcripts are available, although their relative strengths vary with learner proficiency. Audio performs better at A1, whereas text performs better from A2 to C1 with full transcripts. Transcript-based accuracy generally increases with proficiency, while acoustic performance remains comparatively stable. Restricting transcript length substantially reduces text-based accuracy, whereas audio is less sensitive to input length and performs relatively well with limited input. These findings provide insights into L1 identification from acoustic and textual representations of learner speech and how performance varies with proficiency and the amount of available language material.

papers.intro:
Native language identification (NLI) aims to infer a language user’s first language (L1) from their production in a second language (L2). Much of the existing work has focused on learner writing, using lexical choices, grammatical patterns, and spelling errors as evidence of L1 background (malmasi2017report). In spoken language, cross-linguistic influence may also appear in pronunciation, rhythm, and intonation (piske2001factors). Learner speech therefore offers potentially complementary sources of evidence for NLI: audio retains phonetic and prosodic information, while transcripts provide more direct access to lexical and grammatical patterns.

Learner speech therefore offers potentially complementary sources of evidence for NLI: audio retains phonetic and prosodic information, while transcripts provide more direct access to lexical and grammatical patterns.

The usefulness of these sources of evidence may vary with learner proficiency. Some grammatical errors become less frequent at higher proficiency levels, although developmental patterns differ across error types (thewissen2013capturing). L1-related pronunciation patterns may also change with L2 learning and experience (derwing2013development). More proficient learners may additionally produce longer and more varied responses (alzahrani2024utility), providing different opportunities for identifying their L1. These changes make it unclear whether L1 identification from audio and transcripts follows similar patterns across proficiency levels.

papers.title: Effect of oxygen plasma treatment on the structural and superconducting properties of atomic-layer-deposited NbN thin films
papers.abstract: Surface oxidation is a common concern for ultrathin NbN superconducting devices, yet which superconducting properties it affects has not been established for films grown by plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition. We expose NbN films about 11.4 nm thick to an O$_2$ plasma for 0 to 60 s, which oxidizes the surface without etching the film, and characterize the same sample series by X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and transport measurements on 500 nm wide nanowires. XPS of the surface and the underlying layer shows that the plasma converts the surface to Nb$_2$O$_5$, whereas the bulk of the treated film is chemically identical to that of the untreated film. Crystalline $δ$-NbN remains intact. During exposure, the total film thickness rises and saturates between 40 and 60 s, indicating self-limiting surface oxide growth. The normal-state resistivity rises by 21% (dc) and 25% (optical) with the plasma dose, while the critical temperature and transition width are unchanged. The switching current densities of 4.9-6.2 MA/cm$^2$ at 4.2 K show no systematic dependence on the plasma dose. Their temperature dependence follows the dirty-limit depairing current of Kupriyanov and Lukichev, and the extrapolated switching currents reach 39-46% of the depairing current calculated from the optical resistivity and diffusion coefficient, in agreement with the width dependence reported for nanowires from the same process. The oxygen signature is confined to temperatures near $T_c$, where the supercurrent of the treated wires vanishes at least 0.5 K earlier than that of the untreated wire, consistent with a partially oxidized surface layer that acts on the film by the proximity effect. At these doses, oxygen narrows the temperature range of the supercurrent from above but does not systematically reduce the low-temperature current-carrying capacity of the wires.

papers.title: The MIRI/MRS Library. III. Detector-based optimal spectral extraction and high-contrast imaging applications
papers.abstract: (Abridged) JWST has now been operational for five years, and the associated data reduction pipelines have reached maturity. For MIRI/MRS, one can generally get a good-quality spectrum by simply running the standard pipeline, especially for unresolved sources. However, users are starting to look deeper into the data, trying to detect the smallest features in the faintest objects, and find close companions. Following the corrections derived in Papers I and II in this series, we now introduce a novel way to extract MIRI/MRS spectra: from the detectors directly. Currently the most common way to analyse data from integral field spectrometers is to reconstruct a spectral cube from the detector images. Theoretically, detector-extracted spectra could reach higher S/N, and better handle bad pixels. We generate stable and well-sampled PSF models using the sub-pixel scan of calibration star 10 Lac observed in PID 3779. These PSFs were used in a detector-based optimal extraction algorithm building on past approaches, where the contributions per pixel were weighted by their noise properties and contribution to the total illumination. The PSF models were used to subtract the PSF of a bright central source from the detector, both by direct subtraction, and a PCA approach. We find that our optimal setup allows us to get a $>$1.5 times higher S/N compared to the standard pipeline cube extraction. However, we approximately matched more involved cube processing. We were able to subtract the PSF to sub-percent levels, allowing us to extract spectra from faint companions. The novel approach greatly improves on the current standard pipeline reduction. We have not yet reached the fundamental noise limits. There are clear points of improvement that can be addressed using additional data. We demonstrate that detector-based processing of MIRI/MRS data has great potential.

papers.intro:
The Medium Resolution Spectrometer (MRS, Argyriou et al. 2023a) of the Mid-InfraRed Instrument (MIRI, Wright et al. 2023) on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST, Rigby et al. 2023) is plagued by a variety of effects that limit its performance. One of the most well-known and impactful of these effects is detector fringing, where interference due to the reflectivity of the detector coatings creates a sinusoid pattern in the spectrum (Argyriou et al., 2020, e.g.). A second lesser known, yet equally impactful, effect is charge migration, during which contrast between pixels causes photo-electrons to leak from a bright pixel to a less bright pixel (Argyriou et al., 2023b). The correction of the latter was addressed in Gasman et al. (2024), hereafter Paper I, whereas the former was addressed in Gasman et al. (2025), hereafter Paper II. The results from these two works in this series largely mitigate the aforementioned effects, which we subsequently show here to be essential to make detector-based spectral extraction and point-spread function (PSF) subtraction for the MRS possible. For more details regarding the specific mitigation methods, we refer the reader to these previous works.

Currently, the analysis of MRS data relies on building spectral cubes. As discussed in detail in Law et al. (2023), this involves a complex averaging of multiple pixels to create an evenly sampled datacube. While averaging multiple pixels should reduce spurious features, it does introduce correlated noise. Furthermore, while single bad pixels can be patched quite well by the current outlier detection algorithm, larger clusters of bad pixels still pose a significant problem and result in significant artefacts in the spectrum extracted from an aperture. Cubes do have the advantage of being straightforward to examine when a user is not well acquainted with the detector layout. However, when the data consist of a single unresolved source, or even a bright central source and a close companion, converting to an on-sky image is less important.

Instead of extracting spectra from a reconstructed cube, we aimed to extract spectra from the detector directly. Similar algorithms have been shown to result in an up to 30% increase in signal-to-noise S/N in charge-coupled devices (Horne, 1986; Marsh, 1989; Valdes, 1992, e.g.), and detector-based high-contrast imaging shows great promise for JWST’s Near Infrared Spectrograph (Ruffio et al., 2024; Madurowicz et al., 2025; Ruffio et al., 2026, NIRSpec;). As a result of Papers I and II, the MRS PSF is now much more consistent between observations, and the raster scan of 10 Lac from the calibration programme 3779 (PI: D. Gasman) provides the optimal dataset to generate PSF models for each nominal dither position. Furthermore, by working with the PSF on the detector, we can include scattered light into the model rather than removing it, recovering up to 20% of lost light (Argyriou et al., 2023a). As a result, these models can not only be used to optimally extract spectra from the detector, but also to subtract a central bright source to uncover and extract the spectrum of a faint companion. We note that, as discussed in Papers I and II, the calibration star only provides a sufficient S/N in the shorter wavelength range of the MRS (channels 1 and 2). We therefore set up the framework in the short wavelengths in this work, which is to be supplemented by suitable data in the future.

papers.title: Modification of optical properties in ultrathin ALD-grown NbN layers using oxygen plasma treatment
papers.abstract: NbN thin films with a nominal thickness of 10 nm were grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) on Al$_2$O$_3$-buffered Si substrates and treated with oxygen plasma for 0 s (untreated), 20 s, 40 s, and 60 s to investigate oxygen-induced changes in their optical properties. Spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) measurements were performed before and after oxygen plasma treatment over the ultraviolet-visible-near-infrared (1.24-6.20 eV) and infrared (0.041-0.827 eV) spectral ranges. Film thickness determined by X-ray reflectivity (XRR) was used as a fixed parameter in the optical modeling to extract the dielectric function, optical constants, and effective free-carrier concentration. We observed the emergence of a distinct absorption feature near 4.9 eV following oxygen plasma treatment, consistent with the oxidation of the NbN surface and the resulting change in its optical properties. Increasing the treatment time from 0 to 60 s reduced the effective carrier concentration from $1.20 \times 10^{22}$ to $1.03 \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$ and the effective carrier mobility from 2.44 to 2.27 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. The obtained results provide a basis for understanding the effects of oxygen plasma treatment on NbN thin films.

papers.intro:
Niobium nitride (NbN) is a transition-metal nitride distinguished by its electrical, optical, and superconducting properties [44], which make it attractive for superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) [52, 23], hot-electron bolometer mixers [61, 67], and superconducting microwave resonators [19, 1]. High-quality NbN films exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (TcT_{\mathrm{c}}) around 16 K [43, 66, 27], critical current densities (JcJ_{\mathrm{c}}) exceeding 10710^{7} A/cm2 [4, 35, 9], low microwave surface resistance [53], and strong optical absorption from the visible to the infrared spectral range [32]. Since these properties are highly sensitive to film thickness, microstructure, and composition [27, 46, 38], precise control over the deposition process is particularly important for ultrathin NbN films. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) offers atomic-scale thickness control through self-limiting surface reactions, together with high thickness uniformity and conformal coverage [58, 21]. These characteristics make ALD particularly suitable for the controlled growth of ultrathin NbN films, where small variations in thickness or composition can substantially affect their superconducting and optical properties [47, 65].

In ultrathin NbN films, surface oxidation can reduce the effective thickness of the superconducting NbN layer and alter the composition of the near-surface region [46, 14, 26]. Ermolieff et al. reported the formation of Nb2O5 as the predominant surface oxide, together with NbO and NbO2 species at the surface of NbN [14]. Further XPS measurements showed that oxygen initially diffuses into the NbN film and and the progressive formation of Nb–O bonds with increasing oxidation [13, 48]. Such oxidation-induced modifications may alter the population of delocalized carriers in NbN and, consequently, its effective free-carrier concentration. This behavior is supported by experimental observations of a progressive decrease in carrier concentration with increasing oxidation in transparent conducting oxides (TCOs) films [75, 31, 3]. The reflectance of conducting films increases with increasing free-carrier concentration [22, 60, 62]; consequently, oxidation-induced carrier depletion is expected to lower the reflectance of NbN. The resulting reduction in reflectance allows a larger fraction of the incident light to enter the NbN layer, thereby enhancing its optical absorption. Such enhanced absorption is particularly advantageous for NbN-based superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), where efficient absorption of incident photons is essential for the detection process [24].

In this work, we investigate oxygen-plasma-induced modifications in the optical and electronic response of ALD-grown NbN thin films using SE. papers.title: Combinatorial Minimum Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time on Dense Graphs
papers.abstract: We give a combinatorial algorithm that computes an exact minimum-cost flow in $n^{2+o(1)}$ time. This is the first combinatorial improvement since Goldberg-Tarjan [GT87], and is almost optimal in dense graphs. All previous faster algorithms, including the almost-linear-time algorithm of Chen et al. [CKL+22], rely on interior-point methods. Our main conceptual contribution is a black-box reduction from exact minimum-cost flow on general graphs to its approximation on DAGs, with only an $n^{o(1)}$ loss on the running time. This reduction allows future work on combinatorial minimum-cost flow to focus on DAGs, typically much easier to handle than general graphs. Our $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm follows by combining this reduction with a simple augmenting-path-based approximation algorithm on DAGs. The reduction is based on a new structural result, called a flow-cost-preserving DAG projection. Given an arbitrary directed graph, this construction produces a DAG that approximately preserves both the congestion of flows and their cost up to a small loss.

papers.title: Risk Adequacy and Anti-Discrimination in Insurance Pricing: Classification, Aggregation, and Transfers
papers.abstract: Insurance tariffs must reconcile risk-based pricing, portfolio coverage, and anti-discrimination requirements. We introduce a framework in which tariffs are constructed through classification, aggregation of benchmark risk prices within classes, and balanced transfers, and are evaluated by several distinct criteria. This yields a multi-objective tariff-design problem whose attainable objective set and Pareto frontier describe the resulting trade-offs. Risk adequacy is measured by the discrepancy between charged premiums and individual benchmark risk prices. Portfolio coverage is assessed through the capital required to make aggregate claims net of premium income acceptable. Anti-discrimination is examined through differences in protected-group composition across tariff classes and through premium effects experienced by protected groups. We analyze the trade-offs among these criteria and prove mathematical results characterizing their relationships: (i) the inferential threshold for perfect risk adequacy with finitely many benchmark-price levels; (ii) lower bounds on risk inadequacy under stricter inferential constraints; (iii) exact changes in risk inadequacy and inferential disparity when classes are merged, and dynamic programming for scalarized optimization over consecutive benchmark-price classes; (iv) attainable protected-group total premium effects and their minimum risk inadequacy costs under balanced transfers; (v) a sharp lower bound linking inferential disparity to the risk inadequacy required under a bound on protected-group premium-effect dispersion; and (vi) conditions for portfolio-coverage improvement and its additional risk inadequacy cost at fixed protected-group total premium effects. A numerical motor-insurance study illustrates the results.

Insurance pricing combines two features that do not naturally collapse into a single objective. Policyholders differ in the risks they bring to an insurance portfolio, while insurance operates by pooling risks and financing losses collectively. A risk model and a premium principle can therefore associate an individual benchmark risk price with each policyholder type, but an insurance tariff does not generally charge these benchmark risk prices individually. Instead, policyholders are assigned to tariff classes, benchmark risk prices are aggregated within those classes, and the resulting class premiums may be modified by transfers between classes.

Instead, policyholders are assigned to tariff classes, benchmark risk prices are aggregated within those classes, and the resulting class premiums may be modified by transfers between classes.

Anti-discrimination requirements introduce further constraints on insurance pricing. Protected groups are groups defined by one or more characteristics designated for protection against discrimination, such as sex or ethnic origin. Insurance pools risks and therefore treats policyholders collectively, but this collective treatment can interact with protected-group membership in different ways. Tariff classes may differ in their protected-group composition, so one may make the classification coarser in order to reduce these differences. Doing so, however, can require pooling policyholders with different benchmark risk prices and thereby move charged premiums away from individual benchmark risk prices. Pooling within tariff classes can also generate different average premium effects across protected groups. Transfers between tariff classes can be used to modify these protected-group-level effects, but doing so can move individual premiums still further away from their benchmark risk prices. The resulting tariff-design problem therefore involves trade-offs between protected-group requirements and risk adequacy.

papers.title: When is more search useful? An Empirical Study of Search Utility in Quality-Aware Decoding for Machine Translation
papers.abstract: Quality-Aware Decoding (QAD) improves machine translation through test-time scaling, generating multiple candidate translations and selecting the final output with a quality-aware decoder. Usually the same candidate budget N is spent on every source sentence, assuming that all inputs require the same amount of search. We show that this assumption does not hold and that the quality gain obtained from additional candidates varies across sentences. We study search utility through three quantities: total scaling gain, how much quality a sentence can gain from a much larger candidate pool; marginal scaling gain, the expected gain from generating one additional batch of candidates; and the sampling saturation point, the candidate budget required to realize most of the total scaling gain. We investigate two sources of information for predicting these quantities: signals available before candidate-set expansion, and statistics computed from the candidate pool accumulated during search. We find that sentence-level signals correlate with total scaling gain but are less informative about the sampling saturation point. In contrast, properties of the current candidate pool provide useful signals of marginal scaling gain. Finally, we show that these signals can identify sentences that obtain larger gains when additional search is selectively applied.

papers.title: Optimal Random Taxation
papers.abstract: We consider the Ramsey problem of optimal government policy and give examples where lotteries are essential for the optimal solution. When markets are complete and the representative agent's coefficient of relative prudence is bounded, lotteries are typically not optimal. For the incomplete markets case, we prove analytically that lotteries improve welfare for some calibrations with CRRA utility, and we give a simple numerical example for this claim. When the agent's coefficient of relative risk aversion is unbounded for small consumption, lotteries typically improve welfare and can be used to approximate the first-best solution arbitrarily well in both the complete and the incomplete markets cases. However, in the complete markets case, when debt constraints are not too tight and the representative agent is sufficiently patient, lotteries can be purified in the sense that there is a deterministic solution that gives the same value.

We consider the models from Lucas Jr and Stokey (1983) and from Aiyagari et al. Crucially, they assume the government can issue a complete set of state-contingent claims. Aiyagari et al. (2002) relax the complete-markets assumption, restricting the government to a single non-contingent bond. but allow for randomized tax policies. In these models, the constraints that capture the optimal intertemporal behavior of households need not be concave, implying that the government faces a non-convex optimization problem. papers.title: Agent-Based Transport Model Calibration via Online Stochastic Batch Optimization
papers.abstract: Calibrating agent-based models (ABMs) is computationally demanding, as traditional black-box optimization typically requires hundreds or thousands of independent simulation runs. To reduce this burden, we introduce an online calibration framework that estimates parameters within a single simulation run. The approach combines black-box optimization with stochastic batch optimization, a method widely applied in machine learning but not yet explored in ABM calibration. Using MATSim as a case study, we treat each simulation iteration as a stochastic batch, enabling incremental parameter updates as agents make decisions. This online calibration paradigm allows model parameters and agent behaviors to co-evolve, achieving convergence without restarting the simulation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by calibrating utility function parameters in MATSim for a large-scale transportation scenario of Switzerland. Results show that mode shares align closely with observed data within a typical simulation timeframe, confirming the feasibility and efficiency of the approach. By embedding calibration directly into the simulation loop, our method opens new possibilities for real-time, scalable, and efficient calibration of complex ABMs.

papers.intro:
Agent-based modeling (ABM) has become a key tool in transportation planning for simulating the unique characteristics and complex behaviors of individual travelers and their interactions (Bonabeau, 2002; Bastarianto et al., 2023). By representing each traveler as an agent with detailed attributes, plans, and decision rules, ABMs can capture heterogeneous responses to policy interventions, network changes, and emerging mobility solutions (Hörl et al., 2019a; Becker et al., 2020).

A major challenge for the practical deployment of ABMs is calibration (Robertson et al., 2025a; Bastarianto et al., 2023; Windrum et al., 2007), the process of adjusting model parameters so that simulated outputs align with real-world observations. Calibration involves running the model with varying parameters and evaluating performance by comparing outputs against observed data, with the goal of finding parameter sets that minimize discrepancies between simulation and reality (Windrum et al., 2007).

Calibration involves running the model with varying parameters and evaluating performance by comparing outputs against observed data, with the goal of finding parameter sets that minimize discrepancies between simulation and reality (Windrum et al., 2007).

For instance, in MATSim (Multi-Agent Transport Simulation (Horni et al., 2016)), an open-source, agent- and activity-based modeling framework that simulates individual travel behavior within transportation networks, mode choice models rely on utility functions with multiple parameters such as alternative-specific constants or marginal utilities. While these parameters can be initially estimated from survey data, they often require adjustment to align simulated mode shares with observed values. Such adjustments compensate for (i) model discrepancy, as models inevitably simplify real-world systems and cannot perfectly reproduce them (McCulloch et al., 2022), and (ii) potential biases or limitations in survey data, which may be incomplete or unrepresentative, necessitating the inclusion of additional data sources. Furthermore, unmeasured factors not explicitly modeled in MATSim (Rakow et al., 2025), such as comfort, public transport crowding, or perceived safety, can strongly influence travel behavior and vary across different regions. Consequently, when extracting a regional model from a larger model, calibration is necessary to account for these regional differences.

The standard calibration workflow for large-scale ABMs such as MATSim is computationally intensive. Each candidate parameter set requires a full simulation run to generate output metrics (e.g., mode shares, traffic counts) for comparison with observed data. A new parameter set is then proposed, and the iterative process continues until the output metrics fall within an acceptable range. Calibration methods typically rely either on manual parameter tuning by domain experts (Hörl and Balac, 2021a; Ziemke et al., 2019; Dib et al., 2025; Tiwari et al., 2024) or on “black-box” optimization algorithms that explore the parameter space without explicit knowledge of the model structure (Hörl, 2022; Liang, 2018). Although these methods can be effective, they often require hundreds or thousands of full simulation runs. For large-scale applications, where simulations may involve millions of agents and complex networks, with a single run lasting several hours or more, this approach becomes impractical.

papers.title: Cross-Scenario Controller Parameter Transformation from Real-World Driving Data through Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems have become increasingly widespread, aiming to support drivers, reduce workload, and improve traffic safety. However, many systems are rarely used because their behavior feels unnatural and does not match individual driving behavior. The growing availability of large-scale, real-world human driving data enables more human-like and driver-individual assistance functions. This paper formulates the adaptation of Adaptive Cruise Control parameters as a driver-individual scenario-to-scenario transport problem, transforming controller parameters from one driving context to another. Using flow matching, we train a generative model to predict the target-scenario behavior of previously unseen drivers from only a few demonstrations in a source scenario. We compare the approach with a linear parameter-shift baseline and evaluate flow-matching variants incorporating driver-consistent coupling, driver embeddings, and classifier-free guidance based on driving profiles extracted from trajectory data using a variational autoencoder.

papers.title: Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication
papers.abstract: Hazard maps are essential tools for public risk communication, preparedness, and evacuation planning, yet effective cartographic design is not always ensured due to limited access to cartographic expertise across local governments and communities. We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that automates hazard-map production by emulating professional cartographic workflows and iterative design trade-offs while adapting design decisions to different data, locations, and hazard contexts. We conducted a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, followed by a user study and interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners. The generated maps improved participants' spatial understanding and evacuation-planning performance, reduced perceived workload and task completion time, and were generally preferred over corresponding municipal maps. We further discuss human oversight, adaptation across users and communication contexts, and opportunities to extend agentic support across broader stages of hazard-map production and risk communication.

papers.title: Sounding Surgical Instrument Localisation through Audio-Visual Correspondence
papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is a prerequisite for context-aware and intelligent systems in the operating room. Current methods rely mostly on visual data, although sound carries complementary information on surgical activity. This work investigates whether the active instrument can be localised from a single microphone and a camera by learning the correspondence between the appearance and sound of surgical instruments. We adapt weakly supervised audio-visual localisation, which learns from the co-occurrence of image and sound, to the surgical setting. Trained without any spatial annotation, the model predicts a heatmap over the sounding instrument. We extend its training objective by silence and area terms, which suppress the output for silence and background noise, and a composite term, which trains the model to select the sounding one of two visible instruments. For training, we record a new corpus of simulated surgical sawing, drilling, and chiselling. On an independent corpus recorded with a different camera and microphone and with optically tracked instrument positions, the model localises the active instrument, separates instrument activity from silence and background noise, and attributes sound correctly when two instruments are present. Ablations show that the silence and area terms are required for detecting activity, and the composite term for selecting between instruments. Audio-visual correspondence learned from in-domain recordings connects the sound of a surgical action to the instrument that produces it. This proof of concept introduces a novel paradigm that enables the detection and localisation of surgical activity without annotating instrument positions.

papers.intro:
Over the past decades, Computer Assisted Surgery (CAS) has evolved from the first image-guided navigation systems into a broad technological spectrum that aims at improving the accuracy, safety, and reproducibility of surgical procedures Mezger et al. (2013). A central building block towards the next generation of intelligent systems in the operating room (OR) is a fine-grained understanding of the surgical scene, its workflow, and the actions performed within it Maier-Hein et al. (2017). The community has addressed this need, e.g., through automated surgical phase recognition from video Twinanda et al. (2017) and semantic scene graphs that model the interactions between staff, patient, and objects Özsoy et al. (2022). More recently, surgical digital twins have been proposed as interpretable, geometry-aware representations of the surgical scene that can serve as an internal model for robots and agentic systems Ding et al. (2024).

More recently, surgical digital twins have been proposed as interpretable, geometry-aware representations of the surgical scene that can serve as an internal model for robots and agentic systems Ding et al. (2024).

Current approaches for surgical scene understanding, however, rely almost exclusively on the visual modality. Vision-based pipelines require free line-of-sight and are therefore sensitive to occlusions by staff, drapes, and equipment, and they cannot directly capture the physical signature of instrument-tissue interaction, e.g., whether a power tool is running and in contact with the anatomy, which is straightforward to perceive in the acoustic domain. Acoustic sensing has consequently been shown to complement vision in a variety of interventional applications, such as tissue characterisation during needle insertion Illanes et al. (2018), error prevention in orthopaedic drilling Seibold et al. (2021b), implant insertion monitoring Seibold et al. (2021a), and event detection in the OR Fuchtmann et al. (2024). While these works demonstrate that surgical sound carries rich semantic information about what is happening and when, they do not reveal where in the surgical field an action is taking place.

To bridge this gap, sound source localisation (SSL) based on acoustic beamforming with a phased microphone array has recently been introduced to surgery to localise active surgical tools and to fuse acoustic activity maps into dynamic 3D representations of the surgical scene Seibold et al. (2024); Hein et al. (2026). Although these works demonstrated the potential of spatial acoustic information for surgical scene understanding, beamforming-based SSL has considerable limitations that hinder its clinical translation: microphone arrays are bulky and expensive and the computation of acoustic heatmaps is demanding and limits real-time capabilities. Moreover, as beamforming localises the physical sound source, only a part of the instrument is detected (e.g., the engine of a power drill or the point of hammer impact during chiselling), and the resulting maps are frequently corrupted by artefacts such as acoustic reflections. Finally, detection and localisation are solved in separate stages Hein et al. (2026), rather than jointly.
