Moreover, as beamforming localises the physical sound source, only a part of the instrument is detected (e.g., the engine of a power drill or the point of hammer impact during chiselling), and the resulting maps are frequently corrupted by artefacts such as acoustic reflections. Finally, detection and localisation are solved in separate stages Hein et al. (2026), rather than jointly.

A promising alternative is to exploit the natural co-occurrence of sound and vision. Audio-visual sound source localisation (AV-SSL) methods learn to associate sounds with the visual objects that produce them. Since audio-visual correspondence arises naturally in video, these methods can be trained in a self- or weakly supervised manner without costly spatial annotations. In the general computer vision domain, large-scale benchmarks such as VGG-SS Chen et al. (2021) have driven the development of a variety of approaches based on contrastive learning Chen et al. (2021); Mo and Morgado (2022); Park et al. (2026). For surgery, this paradigm has the potential to overcome the limitations of beamforming-based SSL: the hardware is reduced to a single consumer-grade camera with a microphone, inference requires only a single forward pass of a neural network, and the full sounding object rather than only its physical emission point is localised, while detection and localisation are addressed jointly. To date, however, AV-SSL has not been investigated in the surgical domain. In addition, the surgical setting introduces challenges for general-purpose AV-SSL methods: instruments are frequently visible but silent and multiple similar-looking tools are present in the scene at the same time.

In this work, we present the first investigation of learned audio-visual correspondence for the localisation of surgical activity. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We provide the first proof-of-concept for AV-SSL in surgery, demonstrating that audio-visual correspondence can be leveraged to detect and localise active surgical instruments without microphone arrays. 2. papers.title: Traces of Green's functions on $\mathbb{H}^q$ over point-hypersurface pairs
papers.abstract: The famous algebraicity conjecture of Gross and Zagier for the values at CM points of higher Green's functions was recently proven by Bruinier, Li and Yang. Motivated by this the values of the automorphic Green's function at pairs of special points in hyperbolic $3$-space $\mathbb{H}^3$ were studied by Herrero, Imamoglu, von Pippich and Schwagenscheidt, and an analogous algebraicity result for traces of Green's functions was established. In this paper, we consider higher automorphic Green's functions $G_{s}(P,Q)$ on hyperbolic $q$-space $\mathbb{H}^q$ for $q\geq 2$ when the spectral parameter $s$ is a positive even integer, and prove an explicit finite formula for their traces over geodesic hypersurfaces in one of the variables. This formula provides a geometric interpretation of the traces of Green's functions for every choice of a point in $\mathbb{H}^q$ for the second variable. As an application, we obtain rationality results when the second variable is evaluated at a special point providing further evidence that such results for traces of Green's functions do not depend on any underlying complex structure.

papers.title: On the continuity of conditional distributions and stratification for derivative pricing
papers.abstract: Stratification can reduce the estimator variance in Monte Carlo simulations by partitioning the sample space according to a low-dimensional factor and sampling separately within the resulting strata, making it well suited to the valuation of path-dependent claims in high-dimensional financial models. Its performance, however, depends critically on the choice of the stratification factor, and effective low-dimensional factors are generally difficult to identify in complex continuous-time models. Neural networks provide a flexible approximation class for this purpose and have proved useful in related variance-reduction problems in quantitative finance. In this paper, we study the construction of neural stratification factors for derivative pricing under proportional allocation in continuous-time models. Since the numerical construction of a stratification factor typically involves approximation, we establish continuity results for the associated conditional expectations and, more generally, conditional distributions, and provide several counterexamples showing the limits of this continuity theory. Combined with density results for neural networks, our findings yield a universal approximation theorem for admissible stratification factors. We conclude with numerical experiments involving a constant-maturity-swap range accrual in a two-factor Gaussian short-rate model and a worst-of autocallable in a Wishart stochastic covariance model, where the learned factors outperform all considered benchmarks.

papers.intro:
Many valuation and risk measurement problems in quantitative finance involve expectations that are not available in closed form. This often occurs when a model contains several risk factors or a payoff depends on the path of the underlying process. Let XX be a possibly multivariate stochastic process under a probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P}, interpreted where appropriate as a pricing measure, and let H⁡(X)H(X) be an integrable, possibly path-dependent discounted payoff. The quantity of interest is then V=𝔼⁡[H⁡(X)].V=\mathbb{E}[H(X)]. Monte Carlo methods estimate VV by averaging H⁡(X)H(X) over simulated realisations of XX. This approach extends naturally to models with intricate dependence structures and high-dimensional state spaces, provided that XX can be simulated and H⁡(X)H(X) evaluated pathwise. Continuing advances in computing power further expand the scale and complexity of the financial problems that can be treated in this way.

The use of random sampling as a numerical method predates its application in finance. An early systematic account was given by Metropolis and Ulam (1949), who presented Monte Carlo as a statistical approach to problems in mathematical physics. Boyle (1977) subsequently developed a simulation method for option valuation under risk-neutral pricing. The scope of financial simulation was extended by Kemna and Vorst (1990) to options on average asset values and by Longstaff and Schwartz (2001) to American options in path-dependent and multifactor settings. Broadie and Kaya (2006) later developed exact simulation methods for stochastic-volatility and affine jump-diffusion models. Together, these contributions established Monte Carlo simulation as a general framework for valuing financial claims with increasingly complex contractual and model features.

This variance problem has led to several methods for improving simulation accuracy without increasing NN, including antithetic variates, control variates, importance sampling, stratified sampling, and quasi-Monte Carlo; see, e.g., Glasserman (2003, Chapters 4–5). Control variates use correlated quantities with known expectations, while importance sampling changes the sampling measure to place more weight on regions that materially affect the target expectation (e.g., by increasing the probability of the event {H(X)≠0}\{H(X)\neq 0\}). (1999) derive asymptotically optimal changes of measure for path-dependent options, while Guasoni and Robertson (2008) obtain explicit continuous-time drift changes in the Black–Scholes model, and Lemaire and Pagès (2010) develop recursive schemes with convergence guarantees. The deep importance sampling approach of Arandjelović et al. (2025) uses neural networks to learn changes of measure for complex path-dependent models.

papers.title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
papers.abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

papers.title: Learning Nonlinear Waveform Fusion Across Scales for Integrated Sensing and Communication
papers.abstract: Fixed source superposition and frequency partitioning constrain how communication content interacts with a probing reference in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). We learn nonlinear waveform fusion across scales for image transmission and localization of multiple targets in range and angle. Reception uses the information available at each end. Adaptive temporal feature weighting and spectral updates combine image features and a deterministic linearly frequency-modulated reference in a shared complex state, generating a waveform with fixed total energy over the array frame. At the user equipment (UE), the reference and channel state information condition a neural demixer for image reconstruction. At the base station, the realized transmit pulse defines a coherent dictionary for sequential localization with learned local correction, physical refinement, and residual updates. We compare the proposed waveforms with superposition in the time domain and learned spectral linear fusion on 512 independent test images, using a shared fixed UE receiver and a baseline sensing receiver using coherent peak search. Averaged across eleven task weights, the proposed waveforms reduce normalized localization error by 29.0\% and 27.0\%, respectively, while increasing mean peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.40 and 0.82~dB. With the proposed waveforms fixed, learned local correction reduces mean normalized localization error by 12.2\% relative to the same sequential receiver without learned correction.

Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) uses a shared radio platform for information delivery and environmental sensing [1, 2]. A shared waveform must deliver recoverable information to a communication terminal and illuminate targets for parameter estimation [3, 4]. For image transmission and target localization, we optimize the shared waveform directly in terms of image reconstruction error and errors in range and angle.

Designs centered on communication reuse the structure of communication signals for sensing. Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) supports radar processing through known symbols and subcarriers [5]; adaptive designs adjust their allocation to communication and sensing requirements [6]. Designs centered on sensing instead embed information into signals designed for radar. Sidelobe control and waveform diversity preserve selected probing properties while carrying data [7], and chirp modulation provides another mechanism for embedding information [8]. Tunable filter design controls sidelobe levels, range sidelobe modulation, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) loss for waveforms integrating radar and communication [9]. In these approaches, prescribed signal structures guide information embedding and radar processing.

Joint optimization adjusts waveform and spatial degrees of freedom. Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar and MIMO communication designs serving multiple users optimize transmission and beamforming for both functions [10, 11]. Criteria based on beampatterns and estimation bounds connect sensing quality to communication constraints [12, 13]. Analyses of the Cramér–Rao bound (CRB) and communication rate characterize the attainable tradeoffs for specified Gaussian and MIMO models [14, 15], while symbol-level precoding also uses instantaneous data symbols in waveform design [16]. These formulations provide flexible waveform parameterizations, but their objectives at the signal level need not coincide with reconstruction and localization error.

papers.title: ViT-H: Generative Video-To-Humanoid Control with Motion Tracking Feedback
papers.abstract: Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.

papers.intro:
Monocular human videos record whole-body behaviors at a scale and diversity that motion capture datasets (Mahmood et al., 2019) cannot match, making them an attractive source of skills for humanoid robots. Recent works have leveraged human videos to learn expressive whole-body skills (He et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Sleiman et al., 2026), environment-aware behaviors that interact with surrounding geometry (Allshire et al., 2025), and interactive skills involving objects and humans (Wang et al., 2026b). Most existing systems realize this capability through a reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipeline, which first reconstructs human motion from video, then retargets it to the humanoid embodiment, and finally tracks the resulting reference motion. This modular separation is increasingly practical as recent advances in general whole-body tracking enable a shared tracker to execute diverse reference motions (Luo et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). However, the upstream reconstruction-and-retargeting stages remain an indirect route from video to humanoid motion, where errors can accumulate to produce inconsistent, distorted, or dynamically infeasible references, making downstream tracking more difficult.

Prior work has sought to improve reference motion quality by strengthening individual stages of this pipeline, either by enforcing physical plausibility in reconstructed human motions (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025) or by improving motion retargeting (Araujo et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a; Cao et al., 2026). However, such stage-local remedies expose two structural limitations of the pipeline. First, its system-level scalability remains bounded by the remaining stages. Human motion reconstruction is not optimized for the morphology and dynamics of the target humanoid, while retargeting can only operate on reconstructed motions after upstream errors have propagated and discarded visual evidence can no longer be revisited. Second, executability is difficult to optimize end-to-end. Tracking results are observed only after reconstruction and retargeting, making it difficult to use execution outcomes to directly improve the complete video-to-humanoid mapping. Consequently, plausible reference motions at intermediate stages may still be difficult for the control policy to track.

At the core of ViT-H are (i) a motion generator that maps monocular videos directly into the target humanoid motion space, eliminating the intermediate bottleneck of human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and (ii) whole-body control policies that not only track the generated reference motions but also evaluate their executability, providing motion-tracking feedback for post-training the reference motion generator, thereby closing the loop between generation and control (Figure 2).

At the core of ViT-H are (i) a motion generator that maps monocular videos directly into the target humanoid motion space, eliminating the intermediate bottleneck of human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and (ii) whole-body control policies that not only track the generated reference motions but also evaluate their executability, providing motion-tracking feedback for post-training the reference motion generator, thereby closing the loop between generation and control (Figure 2).

Concretely, our motion generator is a video-conditioned humanoid motion diffusion model (Ho et al., 2020) first pre-trained on video-motion pairs and motion-only data. The whole-body control policies are fine-tuned from a pre-existing general motion tracker, yielding a deployable tracking policy and a privileged variant with additional global observations. We evaluate motions sampled from the generator with both tracking policies and use the resulting tracking outcomes to construct preference pairs for dpo (dpo) (Rafailov et al., 2023; Wallace et al., 2024), explicitly incorporating executability into the humanoid motion generator. Because preference pair construction needs no ground-truth motion, post-training extends to unannotated internet videos. Additionally, we further extend ViT-H with an autoregressive variant of the motion generator that produces motions in temporal segments, enabling online control from streaming video and real-time video teleoperation of a physical Unitree G1 from a single RGB camera (Figure 1).

papers.title: OGLE-2015-BLG-1395Lb: A Cold Sub-Saturn Mass Planet Orbiting an M Dwarf
papers.abstract: We present an analysis of the high-magnification microlensing event OGLE-2015-BLG-1395 and report the discovery of a sub-Saturn mass companion to the lens. Photometric coverage of the planetary anomaly in the light curve was obtained from the University of Tasmania's Harlingten 1.27m telescope. Additional data were obtained following the peak from several other observatories, allowing photometric calibration and color measurement of the source. Fits to the light curve reveal a companion with mass ratio of q = 0.00062 +/- 0.00007 and two degenerate solutions for the projected separation, s = 1.7 +/-0.1 or 0.59 +/-0.04 Einstein ring radii. Source and lens parameters are further constrained by Subaru and Keck adaptive optics (AO) imaging in 2016. Finite source effects and AO flux constraints allow us to determine the planet and host star parameters to better than a factor of 2. The system is an ~0.2 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting an ~0.25 solar mass (early-mid M-dwarf) main-sequence star in the Galactic disk, at a distance of ~2 kpc. The two degenerate solutions from the light curve both place the planet beyond the snow line. As a cold sub-Saturn around an M dwarf, OGLE-2015-BLG-1395Lb is in possible conflict with core accretion theory. Spitzer photometry from the time of the event is consistent with this conclusion, although highly uncertain due to faintness and crowding. The inferred relative proper motion of 9.4 mas/yr is consistent with a source star in the bulge and a lens in the disk, and predicts that the source and lens could be resolved a decade after the event.

papers.intro:
The occurrence of gas giant planets around low-mass stars (≲\lesssim0.5 M⊙M_{\odot}) is a matter of high significance for testing theories of planet formation [58, 25, 59, e.g.,]. Because the host stars are very low-luminosity and are also likely to be chromospherically active [92, 48, e.g.,], this is an observationally challenging area to investigate. By comparison to studies of FGK stars, the sample of known planets around M dwarfs is far smaller [46, and references therein], presenting difficulties for any tests of model predictions based on statistics of planet masses and orbital distances as functions of stellar host mass or metallicity. While the broad expectations from core accretion theory are that giant planets should be rare around stars below 0.5 M⊙M_{\odot} [4, 32], multiple examples are known from gravitational microlensing observations [40, 71, e.g.,], with some additional examples from radial velocity and transit studies [e.g., 63, 30, and references therein].

Gravitational microlensing is a sensitive probe of planets around low-mass stars, simply because the sample of gravitational lenses is drawn from the general Galactic disk and bulge stellar population. Owing to stellar lifetime and initial mass function effects, this sample is heavily weighted toward low-mass stars. The Einstein ring radius of a lensing mass depends only weakly on the lens mass [θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} ∝ML1/2\propto M_{\mathrm{L}}^{1/2}; 41, and references therein], giving an advantage compared to techniques that depend on detecting light from the host star directly [47, 14, L∗∝MαL_{*}\propto M^{\alpha}, with α≈2.5\alpha\approx 2.5 for low-mass stars;]. Similarly, the time variation of flux during a microlensing event depends primarily on the Einstein ring crossing time, controlled by the relative proper motion of the distant source and foreground planetary system. For a planet orbiting a low-mass star with semimajor axis of a few astronomical units (au) or more, this timescale is expected to be ∼\sim1–2 orders of magnitude shorter than the orbital period of the planet, promoting quick detections.

In the vast majority of binary microlensing events, the mass ratio and instantaneous projected separation (in units of the Einstein ring radius) between the lens components are usually well-measured, but the physical parameters of the system are not. This is because the Einstein radius crossing time (tEt_{\mathrm{E}}) depends on the lens mass but also on the source and lens distances, and their relative proper motion (μrel\mu_{\mathrm{rel}}). Physical parameters such as the planet mass and host stellar type must be inferred statistically using additional information, for example an estimate of the source distance based on Galactic structure models, and the colors of the source.

An independent measure of the Einstein ring radius can be made when the finite angular diameter source transits a caustic of the lens [11, e.g.,]. On its own, this does not determine the lens mass and distance, but a mass-distance relation. There are two further possible mass-distance relations, whose intersection allows measurement of physical parameters to 5% or better under favorable conditions. High angular resolution observations after the source has returned to its baseline magnitude allow the inference or direct measurement of the lens apparent magnitude, which can constrain the lens mass and distance if a mass-luminosity relationship is known, e.g., from theoretical isochrones [12, 24, 95, 96]. A third mass-distance relation can be derived if observers at widely-separated locations are able to simultaneously observe the event. The difference in magnification due to the parallax effect can provide a completely independent measure of the source and lens relative distance11 1 Parallax effects may also be observed due to the Earth’s orbital motion, but this is typically only possible when tEt_{E} is a significant fraction of a year. [43]. The separation of ∼\sim106 km or more between ground-based observers and space telescopes at L2 or in Earth-trailing orbits has proven to be a useful tool in this context [e.g., 100, 89, 13, for the Spitzer Space Telescope].

papers.title: Differential and integral scaling laws of the mass density of molecular clouds
papers.abstract: In this work we investigate the mass density - size scaling law in molecular clouds (MCs). This relation reflects the fractal nature of MCs and plays a key role for understanding the physics, structure and evolution of these objects. We make use of the notion "ensemble of MCs", introduced in our previous work (Donkov, Veltchev \& Klessen, 2017), in which all MCs with the same probability density function (PDF) of mass density and effective size are represented by an abstract spherical cloud with the same PDF and size. In this spirit, the model is built on the base of abstract scales of the clouds' substructures (which are simply the radii of the spherical object). We consider two forms of the mass density - size scaling law: differential and integral, which in turn reveal the local and the global fractal clouds' structure. Both scaling functions are characterized by their scaling exponents, which can be explicitly expressed by the PDF of mass density, in the general case. Moreover, we derive a first order linear differential equation connecting the two scaling exponents and obtain its exact solution. As examples we apply this abstract construction to two PDFs: the so called power-law tail and the log-normal. Both have great importance for MC structure and evolution, as the latter corresponds to the earlier stages of clouds' evolution, when supersonic turbulence dominates the physical processes, while the former describes the latest stages of evolution, when star-formation takes place. The obtained results for the scaling exponents in both examples are qualitatively and numerically consistent with respective observations and simulations of MCs.

papers.intro:
Molecular clouds (MCs) are places of star-formation (e.g. Semkov, 2023). This is valid not only for our Galaxy, but also for a large number of nearby and distant galaxies in the Universe, whose star-formation processes have been studied. So the great importance of MCs, for galaxy structure and evolution, is undoubted (Hennebelle & Falgarone, 2012; Klessen & Glover, 2016; Ballesteros-Paredes et al., 2020). MCs are gaseous structures containing mostly molecular hydrogen and, in our Galaxy, a few percent of heavier species and one percent of dust particles (Hennebelle & Falgarone, 2012; Klessen & Glover, 2016). Their temperatures reside in a narrow range T∼10−30​KT\sim 10-30~{\rm K} (Ferriere, 2001). Their physics is governed by gravity, (supersonic) turbulence, accretion of gas from the surrounding medium and from larger to smaller substructures in the cloud, nearly isothermal equation of thermodynamic state and magnetic fields (Hennebelle & Falgarone, 2012; Klessen & Glover, 2016; Vázquez-Semadeni et al., 2019; Ballesteros-Paredes et al., 2020). The feedback of new-born stars and supernovae, which eventually disrupt the parental cloud, complete the picture.

Molecular clouds display fractal structure (see e.g. Elmegreen & Scalo, 2004; Federrath et al., 2010; Hennebelle & Falgarone, 2012; Klessen & Glover, 2016) on spatial scales spanning several orders of magnitude: 0.001 pc ≤l≤\leq l\leq 100 pc. This interval is thought to be the inertial range of turbulence (Elmegreen, 1997; Elmegreen & Scalo, 2004; Hennebelle & Falgarone, 2012; Klessen & Glover, 2016), too. Additionally, the density contrast between large and small substructures spans several orders of magnitude. At scales l∼l\sim 100 pc the number density nn is about 10210^{2} cm-3, while at scales approaching those of pre-stellar cores (l≤l\leq 0.1 pc), nn is of order 10510^{5} cm-3 and more. If we look at denser gas, we arrive at scales of pre- and proto-stellar cores, and densities greater than 10510^{5} cm-3.

As a natural outcome of the fractal structure, the study of MCs, during the last four decades has revealed several scaling laws. First Larson (1981) discovered that the number density nn scales as l−1.1l^{-1.1}, where ll is the effective size of the cloud or cloud’s substructures. This leads to a scaling law for the mass: M∼l1.9M\sim l^{1.9}. He also found that turbulent velocity fluctuations δ​v\delta v scale as l0.39l^{0.39}, which was interpreted as the non-thermal velocities in the MCs caused by turbulence. These first findings for the clouds’ fractality were deepened and extended in later works, including many observational (e.g. Solomon et al., 1987; Myers & Goodman, 1988; Heyer et al., 2009), numerical (e.g. Vazquez-Semadeni, Ballesteros-Paredes & Rodriguez, 1997; Ballesteros-Paredes & Mac Low, 2002; Dib, Burkert & Hujeirat, 2004; Padoan et al., 2006; Kritsuk et al., 2007; Federrath, Klessen & Schmidt, 2008; Federrath et al., 2010) and theoretical papers (e.g. Padoan et al., 2006; Ballesteros-Paredes, 2006; Kritsuk et al., 2007; Federrath, Klessen & Schmidt, 2008; Federrath et al., 2010). In these works scaling exponents for density, mass and non-thermal velocity are also specified. The listed scaling laws not only reveal the fractal cloud structure, but are also tools of theoretical modelling the cloud’s physics and evolution, and hence, of the process of star-formation (e.g. Padoan & Nordlund, 2002; Veltchev, Klessen & Clark, 2011; Donkov, Veltchev & Klessen, 2011; Donkov, Veltchev & Klessen, 2012; Donkov, Stanchev & Veltchev, 2012; Veltchev, Donkov & Klessen, 2013; Veltchev, Donkov & Klessen, 2016).

To our knowledge, the scaling exponents in scaling laws (i.e. mass-size or density-size), revealing the fractal structure of MCs, are defined in two different ways. They can be generalized as integral (or global), when the exponent does not depend on the scale and the respective scaling law holds for a range of spatial scales (e.g. Larson, 1981; Kritsuk et al., 2007; Federrath et al., 2010; Lombardi et al., 2010; Kauffmann et al., 2010a,b) and differential (or tangential), when the exponent is defined locally, at a given scale, as a slope of the tangent to the respective (e.g. mass-size or density-size) curve (Kauffmann et al., 2010a,b). The above two forms of scaling laws reflect the fractal nature of MCs from different points of view. The integral (global) form reveal the fractality of a cloud in a averaged sense over the range of spatial scales, in which it holds, while the differential (tangential) form uncover the local (at a given scale) properties of the fractal. Both forms complement each other in attempts to describe the MCs’ structure, which is a key ingredient of any theory of star formation. Hence a good understanding of scaling laws, and their different forms, is crucial in attempts to develop our knowledge. In this study our aim is to generalize and deepen the definitions for integral and differential scaling laws, and also to find a relation (if such exists) between them. According to our definition, which is more general, the integral (or global) scaling exponent may depend on the scale, unlike some previous paper.

The present paper is dedicated on study of the mass density scaling laws in a given MC’s class of equivalence (or ensemble of MCs) (both notions are introduced in Donkov, Veltchev & Klessen, 2017 and are used as synonyms). In section 1 we present the cloud’s model, which is an abstract model of the probability density function of mass density (so called PDF). In this section we remind the notion of MC’s class of equivalence in terms of abstract scales. Also, we express mass, volume and mean density of cloud’s substructures through the PDF, and the normalized relation between them (Donkov, Veltchev & Klessen, 2017). In section 2 we consider two forms of the mass density scaling law: differential (local in regard to the PDF) and integral (for a whole substructure), and shortly justify the importance of these two relations. In section 3 we establish the relationship between differential and integral scaling exponents through a linear ordinary first-order differential equation. We solve the latter and its general solution, namely, the integral scaling exponent is presented through the PDF ( before, in section 2, the differential scaling exponent is, also, presented through the PDF). Then, in section 4, we demonstrate our abstract approach by use of two examples of PDFs: power-law tail and log-normal (both are very important for cloud structure and star-formation). Finally, we present a short discussion and our conclusions in section 5.

papers.title: Forward model of the Gaia DR3 selection function
papers.abstract: The completeness of an astronomical catalogue depends on its selection function, which is a combination of the observing strategy, instrumental characteristics, and intrinsic properties of the sources being observed. This is particularly complex for Gaia, whose non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas make its selection function vary strongly with celestial position and source brightness. We estimate the Gaia DR3 source catalogue selection function across the whole sky and over the full magnitude range, using only data from the Gaia catalogue and knowledge of the nominal scanning law as provided by the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the number of times Gaia scanned each celestial position jointly with the source detection efficiency, and fit it via Markov chain Monte Carlo to the 1 806 196 447 sources in Gaia DR3 with reported celestial positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts. Gaia DR3 is essentially complete for G in (5, 19.5) in the on-sky median. After that, the completeness decreases with magnitude according to the scanning law pattern combined with the imprint of crowded regions. The completeness is also lower at the very bright end of the survey, consistent with the known limitations on Gaia observations of bright stars. We find an unexpected completeness increase beyond G ~ 21, which we conclude is an artefact caused by extended sources, as confirmed by cross-matching against Euclid's Q1 catalogue. Treating the scanning law as part of the inference process, and anchoring it to all Gaia DR3 sources of all magnitudes on a fine-grained grid on the sky, removes the need for an explicit crowding correction. The resulting selection function, valid everywhere where Gaia data are available, is released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package. [abridged]

papers.intro:
The scientific conclusions drawn from an astronomical catalogue come from an inference process carried out on the catalogue data, not directly on sources in the sky. A catalogue will likely never contain every source with the properties of interest, but only those sources that satisfy some combination of observing strategy, detection limits, and quality cuts. The probability that a source with given properties enters the catalogue, the selection function, is therefore not a nuisance to be minimised by discarding data until the sample looks complete, but a quantity to be modelled and included in the inference process (Rix et al. 2021).

A catalogue will likely never contain every source with the properties of interest, but only those sources that satisfy some combination of observing strategy, detection limits, and quality cuts. The probability that a source with given properties enters the catalogue, the selection function, is therefore not a nuisance to be minimised by discarding data until the sample looks complete, but a quantity to be modelled and included in the inference process (Rix et al. 2021).

Selection effects have been a concern in astronomy since Malmquist (1922), who showed that a sample limited in apparent magnitude preferentially includes intrinsically luminous objects, biasing the inferred mean absolute magnitude of the population. Modern surveys face a substantially harder version of the same problem. This is particularly true for the Gaia survey (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016), whose selection function is determined by a complex, non-uniform scanning law and by an onboard source-prioritisation strategy that favours bright sources in crowded fields (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016). The boundary between detected and undetected sources varies non-trivially with both celestial position and magnitude, in a way that no analytical correction can capture.

Modern surveys face a substantially harder version of the same problem. This is particularly true for the Gaia survey (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016), whose selection function is determined by a complex, non-uniform scanning law and by an onboard source-prioritisation strategy that favours bright sources in crowded fields (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016). The boundary between detected and undetected sources varies non-trivially with both celestial position and magnitude, in a way that no analytical correction can capture.

Efforts to estimate this selection function have concentrated on two strategies. The first calibrates Gaia’s completeness empirically, comparing the Gaia DR3 catalogue (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2023) directly against a deeper external survey acting as ground truth (Cantat-Gaudin et al. 2023, hereafter 5). Gaia, however, is the largest all-sky survey of the Milky Way at an angular resolution of ∼0.2\sim 0.2 arcsec, and no comparable deep all-sky survey exists to calibrate against. The calibration in 5 is anchored to the sky regions and magnitude range where an overlap exists with the Dark Energy Camera Plane Survey (Schlafly et al. 2018; Saydjari et al. 2022). The second strategy uses only Gaia data, and forward-models the catalogue generation process with a Bayesian model (Boubert and Everall 2020; Everall and Boubert 2022), applied respectively to Gaia DR2 and Gaia EDR3 (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2018; Gaia Collaboration et al. 2021). To keep the model tractable, Boubert and Everall (2020, hereafter B&E20 ) reconstructed Gaia’s scanning law from the data, and held it fixed while the selection process is estimated. Because the reconstructed scanning law is tied to the same detections it is meant to explain, the resulting estimated completeness tends to be overestimated (see Sect. 5.2 for further explanation).

The second strategy uses only Gaia data, and forward-models the catalogue generation process with a Bayesian model (Boubert and Everall 2020; Everall and Boubert 2022), applied respectively to Gaia DR2 and Gaia EDR3 (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2018; Gaia Collaboration et al. 2021). To keep the model tractable, Boubert and Everall (2020, hereafter B&E20 ) reconstructed Gaia’s scanning law from the data, and held it fixed while the selection process is estimated. Because the reconstructed scanning law is tied to the same detections it is meant to explain, the resulting estimated completeness tends to be overestimated (see Sect. 5.2 for further explanation).

In this paper we extend the Bayesian forward modelling approach described in 4, by treating the scanning law as unknown and estimating it jointly with the selection process. This joint inference, anchored to all Gaia sources, results in completeness estimates across the full sky and the full Gaia magnitude range. The inference is done over a fine grid on the sky which implicitly accounts for crowding effects. This work is part of the GaiaUnlimited project, which aims to determine selection functions for different Gaia data products, and make them available to the astronomical community through Python tools11 1 https://gaia-unlimited.org.

papers.title: Random nodes with positive weights: Richter-Tchakaloff rules and optimal positive quadrature
papers.abstract: We show that independent random points support exact quadrature rules with positive weights. For any $n$-dimensional space $V$ of integrable functions a constant multiple of $n\log n$ points sampled from a suitable density yields, with high probability, positive weights which integrate the functions in the space exactly. The weights stay close to the natural importance sampling weights according to the Lewis density with respect to $V$. They are the result of a weight adaptation procedure which requires an explicit $L_1$-norm discretization result that is proved on the way. As an application, we study numerical integration in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Combining the random rules with a subsampling step, we show that positive quadrature rules with constantly oversampled nodes achieve the best possible worst-case error bound in terms of the singular numbers of the embedding into $L_2$.

papers.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in a graph $G$ in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries that take as input variables the vertices $a$ and $b$ and are of the form ''are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between $a$ and $b$?''. All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. When starting from a biconnected graph, all updates take worst-case $O(\log n)$ time, and all queries are answered in $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get a deterministic algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case update and query time of $O(\log^2 n)$. Both algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.

papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
papers.abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.

papers.intro:
Multimodal embeddings map heterogeneous inputs such as text, images, and videos into a shared dense representation space, supporting applications from cross-modal retrieval to clustering and recommendation (Zhai et al., 2022; Frome et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022). Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) (Singh et al., 2025; Comanici et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) have shifted the field beyond the dual-encoder vision–language models (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021) toward instruction-aware universal multimodal embeddings (UME) models, which follow nuanced instructions across tasks such as visual question answering and video moment retrieval (Meng et al., 2026), and generalize better in zero-shot settings (Jiang et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2025). Yet most UME models still use the MLLM purely as an encoder, leaving its generative reasoning capacity untapped.

Yet most UME models still use the MLLM purely as an encoder, leaving its generative reasoning capacity untapped.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves MLLMs performance across diverse multimodal tasks by enabling a deeper understanding of complex inputs (Zhang et al., 2024b). Several works extend this idea to UME by augmenting each query or candidate with a self-generated reasoning trace and encoding the input together with its trace into a single embedding (Cui et al., 2026; Lan et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026a). Despite their effectiveness, existing approaches face a fundamental mismatch between reasoning generation and retrieval supervision. During training, queries are paired with relevant candidates with other candidates serving as negatives. These positive–negative relations identify relevant matches but leave the reasoning needed to distinguish them unspecified. Consequently, multiple reasoning traces may be relevant to the same input yet differ substantially in their ability to distinguish positive candidates from negative ones. Existing methods sample reasoning from the individual inputs alone, with relational supervision applied only through post-hoc rewards. This creates a fundamental exploration bottleneck. Without access to relational evidence, the model is unlikely to discover the discriminative reasoning needed to distinguish relevant candidates from distractors, and post-hoc rewards can only reinforce already sampled sub-optimal trajectories.

We address this bottleneck with PILOT (Privileged-Information-guided Latent Reasoning Optimization and Transfer), a framework that models reasoning traces as latent variables. This formulation naturally distinguishes an inference-time prior conditioned only on the target input from a training-time privileged posterior that additionally uses relational evidence to infer retrieval-relevant reasoning. We instantiate both distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a single MLLM. Explicitly identifying the positive and negative counterparts allows the model to explain a given relevance relation without first determining which counterpart better matches the target. To encourage more fine-grained, discriminative reasoning, we construct a blind contrastive posterior that observes the target alongside a randomly ordered positive–negative pair with relevance labels withheld. The model must compare both candidates against the target and predict which is positive, encouraging it to identify subtle semantic distinctions that determine relevance. Using mode-specific prompt templates, a stronger annotation MLLM synthesizes reasoning traces for both distributions. Posterior traces are retained only when the annotator correctly identifies the positive counterpart. The prior traces and verified posterior traces jointly initialize the two modes in the shared embedding MLLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

papers.title: Numerical approximation of probabilistically strong solutions to the stochastic harmonic map heat flow
papers.abstract: We study the stochastic harmonic map heat flow into the sphere driven by a Stratonovich noise term that formally preserves the spherical constraint by construction. Starting from a fully discrete, implementable numerical scheme, we prove its convergence to the novel solution concept of probabilistically strong, analytically energy-variational solutions. This yields the first existence result for probabilistically strong solutions in the three-dimensional setting on the prescribed stochastic basis. In addition, we establish weak-strong uniqueness and illustrate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

In this article, we investigate the convergence of a fully discrete implementable structure inheriting scheme, similar to the one in [7]. We will prove convergence of solutions to that scheme to a stochastically strong analytically energy-variational solution. This direction contrasts the usual way results for stochastic evolution equations are shown. Typically, after establishing finite moment bounds through appropriate a priori estimates, the Skorokhod–Jakubowski representation theorem [28] is invoked in order to deduce almost sure convergence of the approximations to a limit. The downside of this procedure is the required change of the underlying probability space. Therefore, such a procedure leads to probabilistically weak solutions, so-called martingale solutions. Often, the only way to infer the existence of probabilistically strong solutions on the original probability space is via pathwise uniqueness and an application of the Yamada–Watanabe theory (see e.g. [42, 37, 41] and the references therein). This can be done in a constructive way by employing the Gyöngy–Krylov characterization of convergence in probability (cf. [24, 10]).

papers.title: Embodied Emissions of 2.5D and 3D Scaling in Chipletized GPUs for Low-Carbon AI
papers.abstract: GPU compute resources are scaling to support growing AI workloads, leading to further rises in the climate change impact of hyperscale data centers that rely on high-performance GPUs. To model how packaging decisions impact the carbon footprint we have estimated the embodied emissions (EE) of a chiplet-based GPU that has been scaled in 2.5D and 3D using the imec.netzero modelling platform. We doubled the number of compute units and high bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity in the 2.5D and 3D scaled systems and found that 3D scaling results in an 89% increase in EE, as compared to an increase of 141% for 2.5D scaling, positioning 3D scaling as an attractive solution to limit the embodied emissions due to GPU scaling.

papers.title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Replay-based Continual Learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting by keeping a buffer of past samples, making buffer composition critical under a fixed memory budget. Recent coreset-based replay methods improve buffer quality using model-derived gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization, but incur substantial computational overhead as memory is repeatedly updated. We propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach for buffer construction that instead exploits the geometry of a frozen pretrained feature space using class-aware, density-weighted coverage. We evaluate CARES across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings. On Tiny-ImageNet, CARES is 2.3 to 8.8 times faster than existing coreset-based selectors. Although CARES achieves this speedup using no training signal from the continual learner, it ranks among the state of the art across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance while also attaining higher average accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet. Code will be released upon publication

papers.intro:
Continual learning (CL) studies how a model can acquire knowledge while being trained on a sequence of tasks without losing performance on previously learned tasks. This setting reflects realistic learning scenarios, where data does not arrive all at once but instead appears as a stream over time (Wang et al., 2024). However, deep neural networks trained under this constraint suffer from catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989; Robins, 1995), in which updates on newer tasks overwrite representations useful for older ones. This problem is particularly challenging in class-incremental learning, where the model must distinguish among all classes observed so far without receiving the task identity at inference time.

Methods for mitigating catastrophic forgetting are commonly grouped into regularization-, architecture-, and rehearsal-based approaches. Regularization methods constrain model updates to preserve previously acquired knowledge (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2018; Chaudhry et al., 2018; Ritter et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2018). Architecture-based approaches modify the network architecture through expansion or parameter isolation (Rusu et al., 2022; Schwarz et al., 2018; Mallya and Lazebnik, 2018; Xu and Zhu, 2018; Yoon et al., 2020; Hung et al., 2019; Sokar et al., 2021). Finally, replay-based methods maintain a buffer of samples from past tasks, which are replayed during training to address forgetting (Chaudhry et al., 2019a; Chaudhry et al., 2019b; Buzzega et al., 2020; Aljundi et al., 2019b; Aljundi et al., 2019a; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2022).

Under a fixed memory budget, the effectiveness of rehearsal depends not only on the number of samples stored but also on which samples are retained in the buffer (Rebuffi et al., 2017; Yoon et al., 2022; Aljundi et al., 2019b). Methods such as experience replay (Chaudhry et al., 2019b) provide inexpensive buffer updates but do not select samples that accurately represent the previously seen data. Other works employ distillation losses or constrain updates in addition to replaying past samples (Buzzega et al., 2020; Chaudhry et al., 2018; Chaudhry et al., 2019a). Consequently, recent work has formulated buffer construction in rehearsal as a coreset selection problem (Yoon et al., 2022; Tiwari et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023).

Consequently, recent work has formulated buffer construction in rehearsal as a coreset selection problem (Yoon et al., 2022; Tiwari et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023).

In a continual learning stream, buffer updates happen repeatedly and must keep pace with incoming data; selection is not a one-time cost, but one incurred at every task boundary or even every incoming batch (Wang et al., 2024). Gradient- and loss-based criteria (Aljundi et al., 2019b; Aljundi et al., 2019a; Tiwari et al., 2022; Yoon et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023) produce effective buffers, particularly under extreme memory limits, but they rely on additional computationally heavy optimization steps. Because this cost recurs at every update rather than once, it accumulates over the lifetime of the stream and can become a substantial fraction of total training time. This computational burden creates a practical tension: the very methods designed to make rehearsal more sample-efficient often introduce overhead that undermines the efficiency gains they seek to provide, particularly when buffer updates must keep pace with a continuous data stream (Tiwari et al., 2022; Aljundi et al., 2019a).

These limitations raise a more fundamental question: must a continually updated model also provide the signal that determines what it should remember? We investigate a complementary hypothesis: a replay buffer can instead be constructed by preserving the representative structure of the observed data in a stable feature space. Features from a frozen encoder provide a continual model-independent representation space in which examples can be compared throughout the stream. Within this space, geometric coverage encourages the buffer to represent distinct regions of the data distribution. However, pure coverage may overemphasize isolated candidates, whereas prioritizing only dense regions risks selecting redundant examples from dominant modes. Density-aware coverage provides a natural compromise between these two objectives.

SubZeroCore (Moser et al., 2025) addresses this coverage-density tension in static coreset selection through a density-aware coverage objective. We build on this rather than classical geometric selectors such as herding (Welling, 2009; Rebuffi et al., 2017), or k-Center Greedy (Sener and Savarese, 2018), which primarily emphasize representativeness or coverage (Moser et al., 2026), because SubZeroCore incorporates density without requiring model-derived training signals. This makes it well suited to the repeated memory updates of online continual learning. However, it assumes simultaneous access to a fixed candidate pool, whereas continual learning requires a bounded buffer that must be updated as new task data arrives and the distribution of available candidates may become strongly imbalanced across classes. Directly applying a global geometric selector can therefore allocate disproportionate memory to classes with more candidates.

To address these challenges, we propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach to replay-buffer construction for online continual learning. At each memory-update step, CARES combines the existing replay memory with a staging pool of newly observed examples and embeds the resulting candidate set using a frozen pretrained encoder. It then allocates the fixed replay budget across observed classes and applies density-aware coverage independently within each class before reconstructing the memory. In this way, CARES adapts training-free geometric coreset selection to a continually evolving replay buffer of fixed capacity.

papers.title: PASTA: Prompt-Aware Annealed Diffusion Sampling
papers.abstract: While Diffusion models produce high-quality images, real-world visual design requires intentionally preserving clean regions for headlines, logos, or UI elements. Existing layout-aware text-to-image methods struggle to strictly preserve reserved regions, often introducing unwanted content that complicates downstream editing. Existing approaches either manipulate attention to displace content or suppress conditioning via noise-level interventions. However, these methods sacrifice visual coherence, producing flat regions or noticeable style inconsistencies between reserved and non-reserved areas. To address this limitation, we propose a Prompt-Aware Shared-Latent Training-Free Annealed Diffusion Sampling (PASTA), a training-free framework that enforces reserved-region constraints by selectively applying semantic guidance to object-allowed regions during sampling. PASTA operates on a shared latent trajectory, where full-prompt and context-prompt guidance are fused through mask-guided sampling. An annealed schedule suppresses semantic leakage during early denoising stages while gradually restoring visual consistency in later stages. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PASTA improves reserved-region fidelity while preserving overall image realism and perceptual consistency.

papers.intro:
Diffusion models [26, 23] have enabled high-fidelity text-to-image generation from text prompts, reshaping visual content creation in art [13, 11], design [27, 7], and media [17, 16]. In real-world design, however, creators often need not only to place objects but also to reserve clean regions for text, logos, or interface elements, such as headlines, UI components, or subtitles. These reserved regions should remain free of salient content while visually matching the surrounding background. Existing layout-aware text-to-image methods do not treat reserved regions as first-class constraints, leading to unwanted objects or distracting textures that complicate downstream editing.

These reserved regions should remain free of salient content while visually matching the surrounding background. Existing layout-aware text-to-image methods do not treat reserved regions as first-class constraints, leading to unwanted objects or distracting textures that complicate downstream editing.

Several recent works have explored space-aware text-to-image generation to address this need. TextCenGen [14] manipulates cross-attention to push object evidence away from a target region and free space for text placement. While effective when only mild repositioning is needed, attention relocation may have difficulty satisfying large, strictly reserved regions. SAWNA [20] injects non-reactive noise into reserved regions, ensuring that no objects are generated from the start. Although this strategy reliably enforces empty space, suppression produces monotone regions, leading to noticeable visual inconsistencies between reserved and non-reserved areas. papers.title: Dual companions and improved regularity of Lagrange multipliers in optimal control
papers.abstract: We investigate optimal control problems whose state equation takes the form $\mathcal{A}x-\mathcal{B}u=b$, where $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{P}'$ is an isomorphism from a Banach state space $\mathcal{X}$ onto the dual of a reflexive Banach space $\mathcal{P}$. The adjoint equation involves the Banach space adjoint $\mathcal{A}':\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{X}'$, so that, in general, state and multiplier are of different regularity. For particular classes of partial differential equations, the typically weaker regularity of the multiplier is improved a posteriori by bootstrapping. In this work, we provide an abstract foundation for this methodology on the operator level. More precisely, we show that whenever the state cost extends to a differentiable function on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ in which $\mathcal{X}$ is densely embedded, as for $L^2$-tracking costs on Sobolev-type state spaces, the multiplier automatically lies in a subspace of $\mathcal{P}$, the dual companion, on which $\mathcal{A}'$ restricts to an isomorphism onto $\mathcal{H}'$. This yields an optimality system with balanced regularity, where state and multiplier solve equations of the same type. In applications, the dual companion can be identified by integration by parts in time or space. We illustrate the framework by linear elliptic and parabolic equations, Cauchy problems governed by general $C_0$-semigroups, and a wave equation with accumulated-state observation.

papers.intro:

papers.title: DIGOM: Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare
papers.abstract: Multimodal healthcare data contain relational information that extends beyond individual patient observations. Effective clinical outcome prediction therefore requires not only integrating information from multiple modalities, but also modeling the relationships between them. Standard fusion approaches do not explicitly capture these interactions, while existing graph-based approaches typically model only a subset of them. We propose DIGOM (Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare), a graph-based framework that jointly models three complementary interaction types: Intra-patient cross-modal, Cross-patient same-modal, and Cross-patient cross-modal interactions. DIGOM learns a sparse multiplex graph with disentangled views, each encoding interactions between pairs of modalities across patients. Discrete adjacency matrices with patient-adaptive connectivity are sampled via a differentiable mechanism, enabling end-to-end learning and allowing the model to select informative relationships without imposing a fixed number of neighbors. A regularization objective maintains overall graph sparsity, while message passing integrates this relational context into patient representations for outcome prediction. We evaluate DIGOM on two multimodal healthcare datasets, MIMIC-IV and NIH-TB, across five clinical prediction tasks. DIGOM achieves the highest AUROC on all five tasks while using fewer connections than existing multi-interaction approaches. Ablation studies reveal that each interaction type's contribution varies across tasks, highlighting the need to adapt relational structures per task. DIGOM also demonstrates greater robustness to missing modalities, suggesting learned relationships provide complementary information when modalities are unavailable. Post-hoc analyses further reveal task- and outcome-specific connectivity patterns in the learned graphs.

papers.intro:
The growing availability of digital healthcare data creates new opportunities for artificial intelligence to improve patient care [1]. Depending on a patient’s condition and the available hospital resources, different types of information may be collected during their hospital stay, including demographic information, clinical notes, vital signs, laboratory test results, medical imaging, and genomic profiles. These sources of information, referred to as modalities, each provide a partial description of a patient’s condition, while together, they offer a more complete view of their health status [2]. This naturally reflects the way clinicians reason in practice, where they integrate complementary sources of information before making diagnostic or prognostic decisions. Consequently, multimodal learning has become an active area of research in medical artificial intelligence, frequently demonstrating improved predictive performance compared with unimodal approaches across a wide range of clinical applications [3, 4].

Consequently, multimodal learning has become an active area of research in medical artificial intelligence, frequently demonstrating improved predictive performance compared with unimodal approaches across a wide range of clinical applications [3, 4].

Despite this promise, effectively integrating multimodal healthcare data remains a major challenge. Standard multimodal fusion approaches are typically classified into three categories: early fusion, which concatenates modalities before learning; joint fusion, which combines latent representations learned from each modality; and late fusion, which aggregates predictions generated independently by each modality [5]. Although effective in many settings, these approaches ultimately aggregate modality-specific information into a single representation or prediction without modeling relationships between individual observations across modalities. Consequently, they may fail to capture how observations from different modalities complement or reinforce each other, limiting their ability to leverage fine-grained relationships in multimodal healthcare data.

Consequently, they may fail to capture how observations from different modalities complement or reinforce each other, limiting their ability to leverage fine-grained relationships in multimodal healthcare data.

However, medical decision-making rarely consists of simply aggregating independent observations. Instead, clinicians interpret each finding in relation to other clinical findings, as the significance of one observation often depends on the context provided by others [6]. For example, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging become suggestive of severe pneumonia when accompanied by elevated temperature and inflammatory markers. Likewise, physicians routinely compare current patients with previously encountered similar cases. A patient presenting with a chest radiograph or laboratory profile similar to previously observed cases with poor outcomes may provide valuable prognostic information [7]. Once similar patients are identified, their remaining clinical profiles, including laboratory measurements, vital signs, procedures, and treatments, can provide additional information for understanding the current patient and anticipating their clinical course [8]. As such, beyond comparing the same modality across patients, clinicians also leverage knowledge acquired from previous cases to relate findings across modalities, anticipating which abnormalities are likely to emerge next or which interventions may become necessary. Importantly, some decisions may rely primarily on complementary findings within a patient, while others may benefit more from information provided by similar patients or from other modalities.

Graph-based methods provide a natural mechanism for modeling such relational reasoning by representing patients or their modalities as nodes and their relationships as edges, through which Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [9] propagate information for prediction. For fusion, existing approaches generally follow one of two paradigms. The first constructs patient graphs, where different modalities belonging to the same patient are connected to capture Intra-patient cross-modal interactions [10, 11]. The second builds population graphs, connecting patient modalities according to feature similarity or shared clinical characteristics to leverage Cross-patient same-modal interactions [12, 13, 14]. Although both paradigms have demonstrated promising results, they have largely evolved independently. Patient graphs ignore potentially informative cohort-level relationships, whereas population graphs overlook the rich interactions that exist between modalities within an individual patient. Consequently, neither paradigm captures the full range of relationships described above.

More recently, [15] proposed jointly modeling the three intra-patient and cross-patient interactions defined in Figure 1, bringing graph-based fusion closer to the clinical reasoning described above and demonstrating promising results. However, although a sparsity mechanism was introduced to control the graph connectivity, the resulting graphs remain relatively dense because the method does not explicitly control the number of retained edges. Such a large number of relationships increases computational cost, limits scalability to larger cohorts [16], may promote over-smoothing [17], and reduces the interpretability of the learned graph. Furthermore, this sparsity mechanism is uniform across all patients, where a single threshold determines which relationships are retained, regardless of the nodes involved. A natural extension is to make graph connectivity patient-adaptive, because clinically less complex cases may require only a few informative relationships, whereas more complex cases may benefit from integrating evidence from a larger number of related patients.

papers.title: OWLS: Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields for Zero-Shot Rover Navigation
papers.abstract: Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set. We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM. Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory. OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera. We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery. Project page: https://chahyon-ku.github.io/owls/

papers.intro:
Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Whether a robot can cross a stretch of terrain depends on information such as the size of obstacles relative to its footprint and clearance, load bearing, and slip, which a camera cannot measure directly. Planetary rovers must reason about these physical properties under severe conditions. Rovers drive without GPS, and communication delays force long stretches of onboard autonomy [1].

Whether a robot can cross a stretch of terrain depends on information such as the size of obstacles relative to its footprint and clearance, load bearing, and slip, which a camera cannot measure directly. Planetary rovers must reason about these physical properties under severe conditions. Rovers drive without GPS, and communication delays force long stretches of onboard autonomy [1].

Existing systems model physical traversability in several ways. Hand-designed geometric heuristics, such as step-height or slope limits, require substantial per-platform engineering [2]. Learned terrain models [3, 4, 5] predict a fixed set of classes from annotated data, and each class still needs a hand-assigned planning cost, so neither the classes nor the costs cover terrain the dataset did not anticipate. Self-supervised estimators learn traversability from the robot’s own driving [6, 7], which presumes experience on the target terrain. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) remove the fixed label set, but navigation systems built on them take free space from depth or LiDAR and use the VLM to select a goal, rank candidate paths, or annotate that geometric map [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. None of these existing approaches plan over the VLM’s dense output itself, although that output already scores every pixel against a description of drivable terrain.

We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), a local navigation method that plans directly over the dense feature map of an open-vocabulary VLM (Fig. 1). Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores each pixel of the camera image, and OWLS turns this score map into a trajectory in three steps. Ground projection places each score at a metric position in the robot frame. Two morphological operations then encode the platform, since a semantic score does not say whether a particular robot can drive over a rock or how far it must keep from one: a dilation removes low-scoring regions small enough to drive over, and an erosion surrounds the rest with a clearance buffer scaled to the vehicle. Finally, rather than thresholding the result into occupancy, OWLS uses it as the speed at which the robot moves through each cell and plans the minimum-time trajectory to the goal, which a waypoint controller tracks. Obstacle clearance and the VLM’s judgment of the terrain thus enter a single optimization. OWLS uses the VLM without fine-tuning and needs no terrain annotation, and adapting to a new rover needs at most two radii set from the rover’s dimensions. It keeps no persistent map, replanning from each new image with a single camera and wheel odometry.

papers.title: Beyond What to Say: Proactive Utterance Timing with Inner Thoughts for Werewolf Agents
papers.abstract: Participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also whether to speak at all. This judgment carries even greater significance in environments like the Werewolf game, where participants' interests conflict, because both utterances and silence are subject to interpretation and assessment by others. Therefore, determining when to speak, as well as what to say, is crucial for an LLM agent playing the Werewolf game. In this study, we introduce a Werewolf AI agent developed for the Anytime Utterance Track of the AIWolfDial shared task. Our system builds on the existing Inner Thoughts framework, which determines utterance timing during conversations by generating internal thoughts and evaluating the value of each thought for expression at that moment. Since existing methods were designed for general dialogue, we have redesigned the system specifically for the competitive environment and incomplete information setting of Werewolf games. We call our adapted method Adversarial Inner Thoughts. Through experiments involving analysis of self-play logs and human evaluations, we analyze and discuss the effectiveness of our approach.

papers.intro:
Recent large language models (LLMs) OpenAI (2026); Anthropic (2026) have demonstrated advanced conversational capabilities and are increasingly used as assistants that respond to user inputs. However, in human communication, participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also choosing whether to speak at all. This choice is governed by conversational context and social norms, and carries even greater significance in competitive dialogue environments.

However, in human communication, participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also choosing whether to speak at all. This choice is governed by conversational context and social norms, and carries even greater significance in competitive dialogue environments.

The importance of choosing between speaking and remaining silent extends beyond everyday conversation to games that involve communication. A prominent example is the Werewolf game. The Werewolf game is an incomplete information game in which players are divided into a villager team and a werewolf team, each aiming to eliminate the opposing side without their roles being revealed. In this game, utterances containing contradictions may provide clues that allow others to infer one’s true identity. Thus, utterances are constantly monitored and evaluated by other players, serving as evidence that influences suspicion and trust. At the same time, silence is also subject to interpretation. Refraining from speaking may be perceived as non-cooperation in the discussion and invite suspicion, while revealing too much information may make one a target of the werewolf team. In other words, the Werewolf game constitutes a dialogue environment in which both utterances and silence carry strategic significance.
