papers.title: G-ORACLE: A Fast Geometric Method To Explore All Near-Optimal Designs for Energy Systems
papers.abstract: Modeling to Generate Alternatives (MGA) methods explore the near-optimal solutions of energy system optimization models (ESOMs), i.e., alternative planning pathways whose cost lies within a small predefined slack of the optimum but which can differ substantially in technology composition, regional distribution, and environmental impacts. Among MGA methods, ORACLE uniquely guarantees convergence to the near-optimal set within a targeted tolerance by iteratively refining inner and outer polytope approximations. At each iteration, given a trial point, it solves a problem as hard as the ESOM to find the nearest near-optimal solution to it. However, the trial point is obtained by solving a bilevel problem whose solution time grows rapidly with the number of iterations and eventually dominates the computational cost of the method. To eliminate this bottleneck, we present G-ORACLE, which exploits the fact that an optimal solution of the bilevel problem is always attained at a vertex of the outer approximation. G-ORACLE therefore replaces the bilevel problem with incremental vertex enumeration by the double description method and one convex projection per vertex, while retaining the convergence guarantee of ORACLE. A supporting-hyperplane check further avoids unnecessary recomputation of these projections as the inner approximation grows. We evaluate G-ORACLE on an electricity-only PyPSA-Eur model, exploring the near-optimal space of the installed capacities of six generation and two storage technologies. While ORACLE's bilevel problem exceeds 20 minutes at iteration 64, G-ORACLE performs the trial-point search in at most 14 seconds throughout 240 iterations, leaving the ESOM solves as the only significant computational cost.

papers.intro:
Energy system optimization models (ESOMs) determine the optimal capacity, technology mix, and operation of energy infrastructure by minimizing total system costs subject to technical, environmental, and regulatory constraints. They serve as key decision-support tools for long-term planning, ranging from macro-level decarbonization pathways to the granular sizing and siting of generation, storage, and transmission assets.

Energy system optimization models (ESOMs) determine the optimal capacity, technology mix, and operation of energy infrastructure by minimizing total system costs subject to technical, environmental, and regulatory constraints. They serve as key decision-support tools for long-term planning, ranging from macro-level decarbonization pathways to the granular sizing and siting of generation, storage, and transmission assets.

However, cost-optimality is strictly bounded by the assumptions and constraints built into the optimization formulation. Qualitative or hard-to-quantify considerations, such as political feasibility, social acceptance, and localized environmental impacts, are rarely fully represented in the objective function or constraints. Consequently, a mathematically optimal solution may prove undesirable or infeasible in real-world decision-making. This divergence stems from two distinct sources of uncertainty: parametric uncertainty in inputs such as demand, renewable availability, and fuel prices, and structural uncertainty arising from model abstractions and idealized system assumptions. Modeling to Generate Alternatives (MGA) addresses these limitations by shifting focus to the near-optimal set, i.e., all feasible solutions whose cost lies within a predefined slack of the optimal cost. This enables decision-makers to systematically evaluate alternative planning pathways against unmodeled criteria [10].

This capability has made MGA a widely used tool in energy system studies. Trutnevyte [36] demonstrated that the historical development of the Swiss electricity system diverged substantially from cost-optimal trajectories, arguing against reliance on a single optimum. Applying MGA to the global TIAM-UCL model, Price and Keppo [28] identified technologically distinct decarbonization pathways with nearly the same total cost under climate policy constraints. Using the open PyPSA-Eur model, Neumann and Brown [24], Neumann and Brown [25] showed that the near-optimal set contains a technologically diverse range of renewable power system designs, leaving policymakers considerable freedom in planning, and that a subset of these designs remains robust to uncertain technology costs. Building on this work, Grochowicz et al. [13] intersected near-optimal sets across historical weather years to identify system configurations that are robust to weather variability. Other studies used MGA to examine the spatial distribution of infrastructure. Sasse and Trutnevyte [30] exposed trade-offs between cost-efficiency and regional equity in the near-optimal set, and Lombardi et al. [20] introduced a spatially explicit MGA variant to identify alternative locations for renewable deployment. Finally, Schwaeppe et al. [32] derived near-optimal shadow prices to reveal cost-effective flexibility options. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the value of exploring near-optimal sets and highlight the need for algorithms capable of doing so reliably.

ESOMs contain far more variables than are of direct interest to decision-makers, so MGA studies typically focus on a few aggregated properties of interest (PoIs), such as the total installed capacity of a technology. Since the near-optimal set cannot be derived analytically, most MGA methods approximate it by repeatedly solving the ESOM with an additional constraint that bounds its cost, each time finding the near-optimal solution furthest in a given search direction in the space of PoIs (Section 2.1). Each of these problems is as hard to solve as the original ESOM, so the number of solves required for an adequate exploration largely determines the computational effort of MGA, a trade-off examined by Lombardi et al. [21]. Heuristic MGA methods select the search directions by ad-hoc rules: Variable Min/Max (VMM) [35, 23, 24, 25] maximizes and minimizes each PoI; Random Vector (RV) variations [7, 36, 3, 30, 31] draw the objective weights at random and converge to the near-optimal set with probability one as the number of iterations tends to infinity; Hop-Skip-Jump (HSJ) [5, 8, 10] minimizes the sum of the variables that were nonzero in previously found solutions, pushing the next solution away from them; and Manhattan MGA (MMGA) [28] maximizes the Manhattan distance to previously found solutions. However, these methods provide no stopping criterion, leaving the number of iterations to be set by the user, and no measure of how much of the near-optimal set has been explored. Modeling All Alternatives (MAA) [26, 13] instead uses the Quickhull algorithm [1] to compute the facets and the volume of the convex hull of the points found so far. The facet normals serve as new search directions; since the near-optimal set has finitely many vertices, this procedure recovers it in a finite number of iterations [26]. In practice, the method can be stopped once the volume increase per iteration falls below a given threshold, which suggests that little of the set remains undiscovered. Since MAA maintains only an inner approximation, this criterion does not bound the unexplored part of the set; moreover, the computational cost of the convex hull grows exponentially with the number of PoIs, which in practice limits MAA to at most about 10 PoIs [26]. A detailed review of these methods is given by Lau et al. [19].

Linear bilevel programs are strongly NP-hard in general [15], and the number of binary variables in this MILP grows with the number of points in the inner approximation, that is, with every iteration. As shown in Section 4, the solution time of this bilevel problem grows rapidly with the number of iterations, whereas that of the ESOM does not, so the bilevel problem eventually dominates the computational cost of the method.

papers.title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
papers.abstract: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $μ$s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

papers.title: Combining Simulations and Spectroscopy to Design Protective Coatings on Sulfide Solid Electrolytes
papers.abstract: Sulfide solid electrolytes are attractive for all-solid-state batteries because of their high Li-ion conductivity and favorable processability, but their practical use is limited by electrochemical instability and moisture-induced degradation. Molecular surface coatings offer a scalable strategy to improve humidity tolerance and interfacial stability, yet there is limited understanding of the molecular-level factors governing surface interactions. By combining large-scale atomistic simulations enabled by a machine-learning potential with targeted experiments, we present a comprehensive framework for designing molecular coatings on Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl (LPSCl). Using a PET-MAD interatomic potential fine-tuned on an r$^2$SCAN reference dataset covering LPSCl surfaces, molecular adsorbates, and their interactions, we model surface adsorption of carboxylic (CA), sulfonic (SA), and phosphonic (PA) acids with alkyl chains of varying lengths and the interaction of these coated surfaces with water at finite temperature. The simulations show that lithiated head groups generally exhibit more favorable adsorption energies. Impedance spectroscopy shows that the lithiated coatings maintain 40--55\% of the initial ionic conductivity after powder processing. While adsorption strength is largely controlled by head-group chemistry and lithiation state, coating morphology depends primarily on alkyl-chain length and surface coverage. In particular, long-chain lithiated carboxylates form dense, brush-like hydrophobic layers that reduce water access to reactive Li surface sites, with protection setting in at a coating thickness of approximately 0.8 nm. Consistent with these predictions, longer carboxylate chains suppress H$_2$S evolution more effectively. Because thicker coatings also hinder Li-ion transport, intermediate chain lengths offer the best balance between moisture protection and ionic conductivity.

papers.intro:
All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) have attracted significant interest owing to their potential to deliver higher energy density and improved safety compared with state-of-the-art Li-ion batteries. [7, 43, 68, 32, 70] In contrast to conventional Li-ion batteries, which rely on flammable liquid electrolytes, ASSBs employ solid electrolytes (SEs), thereby reducing safety risks associated with electrolyte leakage and flammability. Beyond safety, SEs can enable operation over wider temperature ranges, [34, 7] support faster charging by mitigating concentration polarization in the electrolyte, [32] and have the potential to enable higher energy and power densities through the use of Li-metal anodes and bipolar cell architectures. [33] Over the past decades, several classes of SEs with high ionic conductivities have been developed, including oxide, polymer, halide, and sulfide solid electrolytes. [11, 46, 72] Among these, sulfide solid electrolytes (SSEs) are considered particularly promising because of their high room-temperature ionic conductivity and their good processability. Within this family, argyrodite-based SSEs with the general formula of Li6​PS5​X\mathrm{Li_{6}PS_{5}X} (X = Cl, Br, I) have received considerable attention due to their ionic conductivities of up to 5 mS cm-1 at room temperature. Despite these advantages, their adoption in industrially relevant applications remains limited. [23] Besides the low intrinsic electrochemical stability of SSEs, commercialization is also hindered by the pronounced moisture sensitivity of SSEs, which leads to the release of toxic H2S gas and degradation of the active material, even in dry rooms with low levels of water. This reactivity stems from the P–S framework, where the hard acid P readily reacts with the hard base O from atmospheric H2O, replacing the softer sulfur atom. Various strategies have been explored to improve the moisture stability of SSEs, including the incorporation of softer acids to replace phosphorus and reduce susceptibility to attack by hard bases, as well as partial substitution of sulfur by oxygen. Recently, several groups have focused on coating SSEs with moisture-repellent layers, [81, 35, 45, 40, 37, 22, 59] in particular, octadecylphosphonic acid coatings proved to significantly improve the retention of ionic conductivity during dry-room exposure, while simultaneously improving electrochemical stability with both the anode and the cathode. [21]

Such detailed insight, however, is difficult to obtain experimentally owing to the limited number of characterization tools and remains challenging to achieve using conventional simulation methods. Recent experimental studies have demonstrated that molecular coatings can substantially improve the stability of sulfide electrolytes. In these studies, [59, 64, 51, 85] static DFT calculations provide valuable atomistic insight into coating adsorption and interfacial interactions. However, the computational cost of DFT limits simulations to small systems and short timescales, preventing the study of collective finite-temperature phenomena such as surface reconstruction, molecular self-assembly at realistic coverages, and water penetration. These processes require large-scale simulations extending over nanoseconds and involving thousands of atoms.

MLIPs, once trained on accurate quantum-mechanical reference data, reproduce DFT accuracy at a cost only marginally higher than empirical force fields. More recently, foundation MLIPs [52, 5, 44, 82] appeared, such as PET-MAD, [52] which is built on the Point Edge Transformer architecture (PET) [58] and trained on the chemically diverse Massive Atomic Diversity (MAD) dataset. [53] PET-MAD proved to be sufficiently accurate to allow direct application to a variety of different systems, including SSE. [52, 16, 75, 21] Here we fine-tune PET-MAD to LPSCl surfaces and organic coating adsorbates using an r2SCAN reference dataset (Sec. II.1). Starting from a foundation potential pretrained across chemically diverse atomic environments provides a transferable representation that can subsequently be adapted to the specific LPSCl–organic interfaces considered here. This strategy enables the large-scale, finite-temperature simulations of coated surfaces and water interfaces that underpin this study. In this work, we present an integrated design study of molecular coatings for SSEs, combining targeted experiments with large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to reveal how coating molecules dynamically behave and interact with water at realistic interfaces. Fig. 1 shows an overview of the studied systems. Based on our previous work showing promising performance of phosphonic acid (PA) head groups with long alkyl chains, [21] we expanded the head group selection to include also carboxylic acid (CA) and sulfonic acid (SA) to study how head group chemistry affects surface binding. Additionally, we selected alkyl chains with different lengths to investigate the effect on surface morphology. The molecules are denoted according to the alkyl chain length and head group, where Cn indicates the total number of carbon atoms in the alkyl chain and the suffix specifies the head group. Machine-learning-driven atomistic simulations establish the design rules step by step: we first identify the relevant LPSCl surface, investigate how different head groups interact with the surface, analyze how the adsorbed chains organize as a function of alkyl-chain length and surface coverage, and finally quantify how the resulting molecular layer protects the surface from water penetration and affects ionic conductivity. At every step, theoretical predictions are complemented with relevant experimental trends, such as conductivity measurements of the coated SSE, interfacial adhesion (FTIR and TGA), and the chain-length dependence of moisture protection (H2S evolution), for carboxylic, sulfonic, and phosphonic acids of varying chain lengths.

papers.title: KiRoSe: Using Kinematic Data for Efficient Segmentation of Robot Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis. Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error prone process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi camera video streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows. In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of robot kinematic data. Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events. SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with temporal segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features. We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences. Evaluation against human labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion, while preserving the language models open vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed.(website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)

papers.intro:
Large-scale robot demonstration datasets, such as Open X-Embodiment (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2023), can grow to terabyte or even petabyte scale and span diverse robot embodiments and manipulation tasks. Beyond directly training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, understanding the structure within these trajectories is important for effectively using them. Robot demonstrations of “put the cup in the cabinet” and “put the book on the shelf,” for example, share stages such as reaching, grasping, transporting, and placing, potentially mixed with pauses or corrective motions. We refer to recurring, temporally localized motion patterns underlying these stages as kinematic events (Figure 1). Identifying meaningful kinematic events supports demonstration generation through subtask reuse (Mandlekar et al., 2023), learning and sequencing reusable skills (Garrett et al., 2024), and retrieving relevant behaviors for policy adaptation (Memmel et al., 2024). Such intervals also provide useful units for inspecting demonstration quality, complementing approaches that improve policy learning through data filtering (Chen et al., 2025) or progress-based weighting (Chen et al., 2026b).

papers.title: Low-energy collective electronic excitations in a gold monolayer
papers.abstract: The low-energy plasmonic properties of a free-standing Au(111) monolayer, frequently referred to as goldene, are investigated by time-dependent density functional theory in the random phase approximation. In the evaluation of dielectric and loss functions the first-principle band structure characterized by a single $s-p$ energy band at the Fermi level is taken into account. In this system with apparently simple band structure around the Fermi surface the calculations show the presence, besides the standard two-dimensional (2D) plasmon mode, at even lower energies of three anomalous branches in the momentum-energy region usually assigned to incoherent electron-hole pairs. This is an unexpected result since the electronic system of the gold monolayer is characterized by a single energy band crossing the Fermi level. The dispersion of these anomalous plasmonic branches is strongly anisotropic in-plane and gapless. A general feature is that at small in-plane momentum transfers the modes have a sound-like dispersion in certain momentum directions. We rely the appearance of these anomalous modes to a notable deviation of the Fermi surface of a gold monolayer from a circular shape. As a result of its almost perfect hexagon shape, there is possibility to realize in a {\it single} electronic energy band a scenario of a multi-component electron system with the carrier groups moving with different Fermi velocities in certain momentum directions. The found modes correspond to the out-of-phase charge oscillations of the carriers at different sides of the hexagonal Fermi surface. Hence our work presents evidence how in a metal system with apparently simple band structure around the Fermi level its shape can result in conversion of single-particle charge excitations into collective charge excitations.

papers.intro:
Since the discovery of graphene about two decades ago,[1] two-dimensional materials have attracted great interest in many research fields. One of the topics extensively studied by solid state community has been the plasmons in two-dimensional (2D) systems. Which kinds of charge excitations, namely incoherent electron-hole (e-h) pairs and a collective mode (plasmon) can be generated in the low-energy domain in 2D was known since the work on the electronic excitations in a 2D free-electron gas.[2] In contrast to three-dimensional bulk systems a 2D plasmon has a gapless excitation spectrum with a characteristic square-root dispersion at small momentum transfers. This picture describes well the plasmons in dilute electronic systems.[3] Moreover, it can still be appropriate for metallic systems. A first experimental observation of a 2D plasmon in metallic systems was realized using a Ag monolayer adsorbed on silicon surface.[4] In doped graphene, in addition to two high-energy plasmons, may appear in the low-energy range, a 2D plasmon.[6, 5] Its dispersion is essentially similar to that of a conventional 2D plasmon.[2, 5, 7] Last years the similar collective electronic excitations have been studied in other 2D systems based on the layered materials.[8] This is facilitated by its relatively easily synthesis.[9, 10, 11]

papers.title: Heterogeneous superconductivity emerging from a charge-stripe state in kagome lattices
papers.abstract: Charge density wave (CDW) and superconductivity have long been recognized as competing orders. However, recent achievements establish that the interplay between these two collective electronic phenomena can be more perplexing, with emergent phenomena arising from their cooperation. Here we report a distinctive case of the kagome superconductors CsV3Sb5-xSnx, in which the characteristics of superconductivity evolve in accordance with the form of CDW order. As the triple-Q CDW in CsV3Sb5 transforms to a short-range stripelike CDW at xc = 0.07, a sudden change in superconducting properties occurs concomitantly. A combination of thermodynamic, electrical transport and scanning tunneling microscopy experiments reveals a heterogeneous superconducting state beyond xc: the superconducting gap exhibits pronounced spatial variation, in conformity with a distribution of critical temperature and the resulted superconducting precursor effects. Moreover, abundant normal fluid persists deep into the superconducting state, as evidenced by remnants of electronic specific heat and zero-energy quasiparticle interference. These observations are unrelated to the chemical inhomogeneity and residual strain effect introduced by Sn substitution. Instead, they emulate the phenomenology that a sign-changing superconducting order parameter is subject to strong pair-breaking scattering with the short-range charge stripes and hence reflect the unconventional nature of superconductivity developing inside the charge-stripe state.

papers.title: Bilinear Strichartz estimates on the hyperbolic space and the cubic NLS
papers.abstract: We prove bilinear Strichartz estimates for the Schrödinger equation on the hyperbolic space. These bilinear estimates are then applied, as part of an I-method argument, to establish global well-posedness for the cubic defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the hyperbolic plane for regularities above 4/7. The I-method is implemented in physical space using a heat-based modified energy.

papers.title: Interpolation in the Inquisitive Hierarchy
papers.abstract: We show that each of the infinitely many extensions of the basic inquisitive logic has the Craig interpolation property, and deduce from this that each of these extensions also has the Beth definability property. These results stand in contrast to existing characterizations of interpolation within lattices of extensions, in which the distribution of logics with interpolation is sparse.

authors.institution: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Computer Science

papers.intro:
Our understanding of interpolation phenomena in non-classical logics has progressed rapidly in the last several years. New methods have led to the resolution of many old, stubborn questions in the field, with notable successes including characterizations of logics with interpolation among extensions of Hájek’s basic logic [15] and the normal modal logic 𝖲𝟦\mathsf{S4} [28]. We now have a detailed picture of interpolation phenomena in some broad classes of logics, such as substructural logics characterized by totally ordered models [16], as well as a repertoire of techniques from algebra, model theory, and proof theory for addressing questions about interpolation [3]. The accumulated insights from these advancements invite us to turn to more global questions about interpolation across varying logical environments. This paper concerns an extended case study—namely, the question of how interpolation presents in the lattice of extensions of the basic inquisitive logic 𝐈𝐧𝐪𝐁\mathbf{InqB}—that turns out to contribute much to our global understanding of interpolation. In our main result (Theorem C), we show that all of the infinitely many extensions of 𝐈𝐧𝐪𝐁\mathbf{InqB} have the Craig interpolation property.

To overcome this difficulty, we use the non-standard algebraic semantics for 𝐈𝐧𝐪𝐁\mathbf{InqB} given in [5, 6]. From this fact, one may derive that extensions of 𝐈𝐧𝐪𝐁\mathbf{InqB} are in order-reversing bijection with certain varieties of Heyting algebras, called inquisitive varieties. papers.title: Binary Dynamics and Mergers in a Stellar Disk and the Formation of Dusty Objects in the Galactic Center
papers.abstract: For more than a decade, observers have been tracking a population of enigmatic dusty objects orbiting the central supermassive black hole of the Milky Way, Sagittarius A$^\star$ (SgrA$^\star$). In one interpretation, these objects are products of stellar mergers enshrouded in gaseous-dusty envelopes, which account for their infrared excess, emission lines, and stability against the tidal forces of SgrA$^\star$. Recent near-infrared observations of D9, one of the dusty objects, revealed that it embeds a spectroscopic stellar binary. In this work, we present full-fledged N-body simulations of an eccentric disk of binary stars similar to the young stellar disk observed around SgrA$^\star$. We find that some of the binaries in the disk are naturally drawn towards SgrA$^\star$ and merge there due to Kozai-Lidov (KL) oscillations in their orbits. Together with the observed nature of D9, these findings represent a self-consistent picture of how the population of the observed dusty objects could have been brought into existence. The binary fraction in our N-body model evolves to increase with distance from SgrA$^\star$, which is also in agreement with the observational constraints. Our simulations also suggest that beside the dusty objects, stellar mergers are present within the young stellar disk, which could be identified as chemically peculiar or fast-rotating stars. Our results show that dynamical evolution of binary stars in the young stellar disk plays a crucial role in shaping the stellar content in the Galactic Center.

The center of our Galaxy harbors a supermassive black hole (SMBH) associated with the compact and variable radio source SgrA∗with a mass of about 4.3×106​M⊙4.3\times 10^{6}M_{\odot} [40, 23]; see also Eckart et al. [21], Genzel [31], and Ciurlo and Morris [17] for recent reviews. It is embedded in an old (nuclear) star cluster whose total mass is about six times higher than that of the SMBH and a characteristic (half-light) radius of roughly 4 pc [85]. The presence of such an old and massive cluster around SgrA∗has always been expected [106, 30, 66], but what came as a surprise was the discovery of very young stars closer than 0.5 pc from SgrA∗[19, 33, 3, 16, 74, 73]. Moreover, it turned out that a significant fraction [104, 20-50%;] of these stars are orbiting SgrA∗coherently in multiple well-defined disc-like structure, with the most prominent one spanning between 40​mpc≲r≲400​mpc40\ \mathrm{mpc}\lesssim r\lesssim 400\ \mathrm{mpc} and known as the clockwise disk [56, 71, 100]. Quite in contrast, closer than 40 mpc from SgrA∗(within the so-called S-cluster), the orbits of the young stars are more or less isotropically oriented [32, 22]; however, see Ali et al. [3] who suggests that the young stars form various disk like structures as well. The origin of the young stars in the innermost half-parsec of our Galaxy and the configuration of their orbits around SgrA∗is still debated.

Interestingly, this hypothesis immediately raises another puzzling question: How can individual stars form so close to SgrA∗[32, 67]?

Another interpretation of the dusty objects is that they could result from stellar binary mergers which eject material that condenses into dusty envelopes. Notably, these various formation scenarios are not mutually exclusive. The recent discovery of a stellar binary behind the dusty curtain of the object D9 provides an example of stellar cores in dusty objects, while also demonstrating that dusty envelopes can develop in binary systems before merging [76].

A necessary prerequisite for the stellar binary merger formation scenario is a source of stellar binaries. A natural source for these stellar binaries can be the clockwise disk [14, 27]. Šubr and Haas [93] studied the evolution of binary systems made up of point masses in a disk-like system, where the binaries undergo KL oscillations due to the disk. KL oscillations lead to an increase in eccentricity of the outer orbits (the orbits of the binary system’s center of mass around SgrA∗), resulting in close passages near SgrA∗ and the production of hyper-velocity stars (HVS) and S-stars through the Hills mechanism [46]. At the same time, the inner orbit (orbit of the binary system around their own center of mass) of the binaries can undergo KL oscillations due to the influence of SgrA∗. The KL oscillations increase the eccentricity of the inner orbit, resulting in close passages of the two stars that can drive the individual binaries towards mergers [70, 91, 90, 16].

papers.title: On the homeomorphism group of the Cantor set: monotone and measure preserving maps
papers.abstract: Let $E$ be the Cantor set, $G=\operatorname{Homeo}(E)$, let $P\le G$ be the group of order preserving homeomorphisms and $L\le G$ the group of homeomorphisms preserving the Cantor--Lebesgue measure $λ$. We study how $G$ is built from these two subgroups. In 2003, Glasner and Weiss stated that $G=LP=PL$. We show that this is not the case, in fact $PL$ and $LP$ are two different proper subsets of $G$. On the other hand, $PL$ is a dense $G_δ$ subset of $G$, the multiplication map $P\times L\to PL$ is a homeomorphism, and $G=PLP=LPL$. In particular, every homeomorphism of $E$ is conjugate to an element of $PL$. We classify the double cosets $PgL$ using special clopen values set. There are continuum many of them, and $PL$ is the only one which is not meager. We prove that $G$ is topologically generated by one element of $P$ and one element of $L$ and these two generators produce the Thompson's group $V$. We also show that the generic homeomorphism of $E$ is the product of a generic element of $P$ and a generic element of $L$. The equality $G=PL$ fails also if $λ$ is replaced by any other full nonatomic measure.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Link Prediction on Dark Web Hyperlink Graphs
papers.abstract: We analyze HTML content and hyperlinks from an offline Tor crawl containing 383 onion hosts and 2,067 directed cross-host links. The study combines semantic analysis with degree-controlled quantum--classical link prediction. Two directory groups emit 94.8\% of the observed host links. Directed preferential attachment reaches ROC-AUC 0.976 with random non-edges, but falls to $0.550\pm0.014$ under source-conditioned target-degree matching. With disjoint training and test pairs, multimodal logistic regression reaches $0.672\pm0.021$, GAE $0.899\pm0.016$, and VGAE $0.906\pm0.016$. A four-qubit variational quantum classifier (VQC) comparison tests two encodings across 20 disjoint-pair graph splits under exact and 1,024-shot simulation, with classical controls using the same inputs and training examples. Its best exact mean ROC-AUC is $0.549\pm0.023$, compared with $0.551\pm0.016$ for RBF SVC and $0.573\pm0.029$ for a 16-parameter MLP on the same inputs and training examples. These results support predictive signal in combined graph/content features and show why degree control, feature compression, and optimization conditions matter in quantum--classical comparisons.

Tor onion services form a web ecosystem that is difficult to observe completely. Services appear and disappear, discovery depends on crawl seeds and traversal rules, and directories can have a large influence on the observed hyperlink graph. Previous studies have examined Tor connectivity, content categories, community structure, redirects, and page/site relationships Sánchez-Rola et al. (2017); Avarikioti et al. (2018); Bernaschi et al. Earlier crawls show large differences between the linking patterns of Tor services. Griffith et al. found that most sites in their sample had no outgoing links to other sites Griffith et al. (2017). Bernaschi et al. described a small strongly connected core in which directories link to many peripheral services Bernaschi et al. (2022). Zabihimayvan et al. studied page topics together with hyperlink structure to characterize service categories and their connections Zabihimayvan et al. (2019). Al-Nabki et al. proposed ToRank to identify influential onion domains from hyperlink connectivity and compared it with PageRank, HITS, and Katz Al-Nabki et al. (2019). Node embeddings and graph auto-encoders also provide methods for learning features used in link prediction Grover and Leskovec (2016); Kipf and Welling (2016). We study whether graph and content features predict withheld hyperlinks when the evaluation reduces the advantage of using endpoint degree alone.

Common heuristics and learned models can exploit endpoint degree when positive and negative examples have different degree distributions Wu et al. (2022); Li et al. (2023); Aiyappa et al. (2025). This is especially relevant in crawled web graphs with hubs and directories. We therefore measure this bias directly and use degree-matched negatives for the main comparison.

Quantum machine learning (QML) models can use quantum feature maps to introduce nonlinear interactions between numerical inputs Havlíček et al. (2019). Parameterized circuits are trained with classical optimizers, allowing shallow models to be studied with limited qubit counts Cerezo et al. (2021). Schuld et al. showed how data-encoding gates determine the Fourier frequencies available to a broad class of circuit models Schuld et al. (2021). In our setting, graph and content features must be compressed to fit a small qubit register. Link prediction therefore gives a task on which to test how much useful signal a compact circuit retains after compression. Huang et al. showed that training data can make classical learners competitive on quantum-motivated tasks Huang et al. (2021), and Bowles et al. found that standard classical models generally performed better than the quantum classifiers in their small-task benchmarks Bowles et al. (2024). Studies of variational energy minimization also report changes in optimizer performance under finite-shot noise Novák et al. (2025); Novák et al. (2026c). We compare variational quantum classifiers (VQCs) with classical models using the same inputs and training examples, and examine the effects of encoding, optimization, and finite-shot measurement.

papers.title: Comprehensive Visible and Near-infrared Keck and Gemini Monitoring and Characterization of Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS during its Encounter with the Solar System
papers.abstract: We present 14 optical imaging and eight optical spectroscopic epochs of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS from Keck/LRIS and Gemini/GMOS, two near-infrared (NIR) imaging epochs from Keck/MOSFIRE, and four NIR spectroscopic epochs from Gemini/Flamingos-2 and GNIRS, obtained between 2025 July and 2026 May. Mean GMOS colors of $g-r=0.732\pm0.029$, $r-i=0.237\pm0.025$, and $i-z=0.109\pm0.022$ mag show no significant change across perihelion. Phase-corrected red-band activity follows $Afρ\propto r_h^{-2.10\pm0.14}$ inbound and $r_h^{-3.34\pm0.43}$ outbound. Transverse-width and sunward-plume speeds imply dust losses of $2.7\times10^9$ and $1.0\times10^{10}$ kg over 2025 July 3--2026 May 15 for 1-$μ$m--1-mm grains, equivalent to global layers of 0.26 and 0.99 m under the adopted grain and nucleus assumptions. The concentrated coma, compact sunward feature, and antisolar tail seen on 2025 August 27 broadened by 2025 November 26; extended dust persisted through 2026 February 17. C$_2$/CN nearly doubled from $0.257\pm0.014$ on 2025 September 14--15 to $0.481\pm0.080$ on 2025 November 26, while C$_3$/CN fell from $0.327\pm0.024$ on 2025 August 28 to $0.214\pm0.009$ on 2025 September 14--15. MOSFIRE NIR imaging on 2025 July 11 gives $Y-J=0.466\pm0.143$, $J-H=0.239\pm0.052$, $H-K_s=0.454\pm0.150$, and $J-K_s=0.693\pm0.202$ mag. Spectra give $J-H=0.24$ mag on 2025 September 5--6 and $J-H=0.27$--0.28 and $J-K_s=0.21$--0.22 mag on 2025 December 1--2 over the retained passband intervals. Model-calibrated imaging on 2026 February 6 gives near-solar $J-K_s=0.303\pm0.051$ mag. No water-ice absorption is robust to the tested continuum and calibration choices in the NIR spectra. These observations provide a lasting record of the comet's evolution through the Solar System and a benchmark for studying and monitoring future interstellar objects.

papers.intro:
Interstellar objects (ISOs) carry material formed in other planetary systems into the Solar System [40]. Their ejection links this population to planetary scattering and the solid inventory of their parent systems [99, 86, 101, 73]. Radial drift, migrating ice lines, and volatile redistribution affect the material available for ejection [124]; white-dwarf pollution provides independent evidence for volatile-rich extrasolar planetesimals [102]. Irradiation modifies ISO surfaces, while solar heating releases gas and dust that can obscure the nucleus [41, 46]. Observations across an encounter help separate this evolution from compositional differences, although size, activity, and survey sensitivity bias the small detected sample.

1I/‘Oumuamua showed a red continuum and a large-amplitude, irregular lightcurve consistent with a strongly nonspherical body in non-principal-axis rotation [80, 21, 38]. Its featureless optical/NIR spectrum resembled primitive Solar System surfaces [41], and its nongravitational acceleration occurred without a resolved dust coma [81]. 2I/Borisov had a coma and tail with comet-like optical colors [66, 46, 19]. Although the coma complicated nucleus and rotation measurements [20], HST profiles constrained its radius to <0.5<0.5 km for geometric albedo 0.04 [64]. Ultraviolet and millimeter spectra revealed high CO/H2O abundance [10, 34]. Optical–millimeter observations favored compact grains exceeding approximately 1 mm and found evolution in CO/H2O across perihelion [120]. Ni I was also detected in its cold coma [47]. Comparing the surface-dominated spectrum of 1I with 2I’s coma requires accounting for grain size, phase angle, and activity.

Denneau et al. [37] announced the ATLAS discovery of 3I/ATLAS, followed by early characterization by Bolin et al. [14] and Seligman et al. [110]. The comet showed a red continuum and resolved coma, with weak or undetected canonical gas bands near discovery [89, 96, 2, 35]. Rubin observations cover 2025 June 21–July 20 [32]; ATLAS resolves changes in the inbound growth law [115], and TESS, HATPI, and smaller telescopes extend the inbound baseline [76, 53, 117]. Optical monitoring tracks the changing continuum, morphology, and gas emission [5, 97, 9, 106, 1], including the CN and Ni coma observed with UH88/SNIFS and Keck/KCWI [55, 56, 57]. JCMT constrains parent molecules [54], while infrared observations probe ice, volatiles, and dust mineralogy [121, 6, 7]. The red visible continuum flattens in the NIR [79, 121], becoming neutral or slightly blue in IRTF spectra [70]. Polarimetry reveals an unusually deep, narrow negative branch [44].

We use Keck and Gemini imaging and spectroscopy before and after perihelion to measure 3I/ATLAS’s morphology, colors, dust activity, and gas production and constrain water ice. Comparisons use a common physical aperture, phase correction, and orbital-plane geometry, following the 2I/Borisov and P/2019 LD2 studies [19, 16]. Prediscovery observations of 2I demonstrate the value of extending the baseline beyond efficient water sublimation [122]. We compare our measurements with preliminary reports [13, 26, 24, 23, 22, 25]; the December 22 GMOS spectra also appear in Appendix A of Belyakov et al. [7].

papers.title: Single-Machine Guarantees on Unrelated Machines and Beyond: Proportional Fairness for Nonclairvoyant Polytope Scheduling
papers.abstract: The Polytope Scheduling Problem (PSP) is a general framework for preemptive scheduling in which feasible instantaneous job allocations form a packing polytope. In the nonclairvoyant online setting, Proportional Fairness (PF), a practical allocation rule rooted in market theory, is the leading general-purpose algorithm. On a single machine, PF coincides with weighted Round-Robin, which is $2$-competitive for weighted completion time with uniform release dates (optimal for nonclairvoyant algorithms) and $(2+\varepsilon)$-speed $O(1/\varepsilon)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Known guarantees beyond a single machine are weaker. This raises a central question: Are these heterogeneous environments intrinsically harder than a single machine under nonclairvoyance? We show that they are not: PF retains both single-machine guarantees on the novel class of support-submodular polytopes, which includes unrelated machines and polymatroids. On unrelated machines, this refutes a belief (JACM'18, SODA'25) that PF is not $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Our main technical contribution is an equivalent characterization: a polytope is support submodular if and only if, for all job weights, the optimal weighted completion time is concave in the processing requirements. This structural insight underlies both guarantees. For general PSP, the picture changes: we give the first lower bound above $2$, showing that every randomized nonclairvoyant algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least $2+10^{-5}$ for weighted completion time, even with uniform release dates. On the positive side, we substantially improve the best known guarantee for weighted completion time from $27$ (SICOMP'26) to $4$ via a new dual-fitting analysis of PF. For weighted flow time, we show that PF achieves the first $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive nonclairvoyant guarantee for graph scheduling.

papers.title: The GAPS Programme at TNG LXXXI. The puzzle of the HeI absorption signal in the atmosphere of V1298 Tau b with GIARPS@TNG
papers.abstract: Atmospheric escape shapes close-in planets mostly in their first tens of Myr. The young V1298Tau system (10-30Myr) is a benchmark for investigating photoevaporation and planetary evolution at early stages. The metastable HeI near-infrared triplet is a key proxy for atmospheric escape. We aim to detect and characterise HeI in the extended atmosphere of V1298Taub. We analysed four transits over a 4-year baseline using GIARPS (GIANO-B + HARPS-N) at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo. We re-derived the projected spin-orbit angle by modelling the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect. Using simultaneous optical and near-infrared high-resolution transmission spectroscopy of V1298Taub, we monitored the HeI triplet alongside key chromospheric indicators ($\log R'_{HK}$, H$α$, and NaI) to disentangle stellar activity from planetary evaporation. While the stellar spectra show significant night-to-night variability, transmission spectroscopy reveals persistent HeI absorption across all four epochs. This contrasts with H$α$ and NaI, observed over two nights with simultaneous HARPS-N monitoring, which fluctuate between emission and absorption due to stellar activity. The consistent presence of HeI over 4 years may suggest a planetary origin, despite stellar-driven depth modulation. ATES hydrodynamic simulations show that stellar XUV flux variations modulate the HeI absorption depth and equivalent width. Furthermore, stellar wind fluctuations likely drive the observed night-to-night variability of the exospheric structure. The detection of HeI across all epochs may support planetary evaporation, despite modulation by stellar activity. Our results underscore that disentangling a planetary signal from stellar contamination remains challenging for highly active hosts; securing the planetary nature of the HeI signature requires activity monitoring and full transit coverage to establish a robust baseline.

papers.intro:
Understanding exoplanet evolution is crucial to explaining system architectures and atmospheric stability. A key feature is the “radius gap” (or “evaporation valley”) around ∼\sim1.8 R⊕R_{\oplus}, separating dense, rocky super-Earths from larger, volatile-rich mini-Neptunes (Fulton et al. 2017; Fulton and Petigura 2018, e.g.,). Its origin likely involves both formation and evolutionary processes: migration may shape the sub-Neptune peak, while photoevaporation can produce the super-Earth population (Burn et al. 2024). Alternatively, mechanisms such as core-powered mass loss could produce the observed bimodal distribution on their own (e.g., Gupta and Schlichting 2019; Loyd et al. 2020). Studying atmospheric escape in planets near the radius gap therefore lets us test whether evaporation drives these demographics to understand the transition from gas-rich planets to stripped cores, especially in young systems where escape is most efficient (Sanz-Forcada et al. 2011 and references therein). The primary driver of atmospheric erosion is stellar X-ray and extreme ultraviolet (XUV) irradiation (Lammer et al. 2003; Lecavelier des Etangs et al. 2004, e.g.,). As a star ages and spins down, its magnetic activity and XUV output decrease significantly (Owen 2019, e.g.,). Consequently, for most exoplanets orbiting mature stars, the atmospheric evaporation responsible for the radius gap has largely concluded. Planets around young stars (≲100\lesssim 100 Myr) therefore offer a unique opportunity to observe atmospheric escape in action during its most transformative epoch. In this context, the metastable helium triplet at 10832.06 Å, 10833.22 Å, and 10833.31 Å (vacuum wavelength He I, e.g., Seager and Sasselov 2000; Oklopčić and Hirata 2018; Spake et al. 2018) has emerged as a premier diagnostic of escaping atmospheres. The He I λ\lambda10833 Åtriplet is an important astrophysical diagnostic, tracing neutral helium in its triplet state. It forms mainly through photoionisation by ultraviolet radiation (λ\lambda <504 Å), followed by recombination into the metastable orthohelium 23S state. Once in this state, He atoms can absorb incoming photospheric near-infrared photons, producing the He I 10833 Å absorption feature. Unlike traditional tracers such as Lyα\alpha, the He I triplet is less sensitive to interstellar medium absorption and geocoronal contamination, and its accessibility from the ground enables high-resolution instruments to probe the dynamics of planetary outflows in detail (Nortmann et al. 2018; Allart et al. 2018, e.g.,).

The V1298 Tau planetary system is a key laboratory for studying atmospheric photoevaporation in the early stages of planetary evolution. The host star is a young (∼\sim10–30 Myr, David et al. 2019a; Suárez Mascareño et al. 2021), rapidly rotating (Prot≈P_{\mathrm{rot}}\approx2.91 days, Finociety et al. 2023) K-type dwarf. Hubble Space Telescope (Barat et al. 2024) and James Webb Space Telescope (Barat et al. 2025) observations revealed an H/He-dominated atmosphere, detecting CO2\text{CO}_{2}, H2​O\text{H}_{2}\text{O}, CO, CH4\text{CH}_{4}, SO2\text{SO}_{2}, and OCS, alongside a high “internal temperature" TintT_{\mathrm{int}} of ∼\sim500 K (TintT_{\mathrm{int}} is a parameter of the temperature–pressure profile model from Parmentier and Guillot 2014, as adopted by Barat et al. 2025, that accounts for the intrinsic internal heat flux). These studies imply a low planetary mass of 12–15 M⊕M_{\oplus}, independently confirmed by Livingston et al. (2026), whose dynamical estimate of ∼\sim13.1 M⊕M_{\oplus} was derived by modelling the transit timing variations (TTVs). Previous campaigns yielded either non-detections from partial transits (Vissapragada et al. 2021) or ambiguous absorption signals blended with stellar variability or the transit of planet d (Gaidos et al. 2022). papers.title: Visualization of Single Spin-chain Propagation using Bragg Coherent Diffraction Imaging
papers.abstract: Domain wall dynamics and their manipulation in finite-size systems serve as a promising platform for beyond Moore's law applications. Yet, the imaging techniques to track their motion in real-space and time are limited. Here, we use magnetic domain walls formed in permalloy artificial square lattice to demonstrate that single-shot Bragg coherent diffraction imaging (BCDI) is a powerful approach for this purpose. Our BCDI reconstructed images revealed milliseconds time-scale dynamics of the antiphase magnetic domain walls traveling through an antiferromagnetically ordered sample.

papers.title: From archive to resource: bringing legacy data back to life at scale with large language models
papers.abstract: Pharmaceutical companies maintain vast archives of legacy preclinical study reports that contain study-context details, such as fasting, anesthesia, and laboratory instrumentation, that are rarely captured in structured data formats, yet they can correlate with clinical pathology parameters values and limit the reuse of historical data. This work demonstrates practical, scalable solutions to recover such descriptors from heterogeneous report texts using large language model (LLM)-based extraction pipelines developed independently by two industry teams. The pipelines identify and normalize metadata fields and return verbatim evidence with page and section reference, hasting human verification and iterative refinement. Evaluation of over 400 documents against expert-curated reference values showed high agreement across a broad set of metadata fields. Performance was strongest for consistently reported items and lower for descriptors subject to linguistic or report structure variability. Extraction time has shrunk from 25 minutes in the manual benchmark to 1.6 minutes. As a concrete biological demonstration, we show that fasting status extracted from report text was associated with species- and analyte-specific shifts in clinical chemistry parameters, illustrating how recovered metadata can improve selection of historical controls. Key strengths of the approach are scalability, traceability, and the ability to recover information missing from current industry standards. Main limitations are dependence on source-report quality and initial expert effort to define and refine schemas. These results establish how LLMs can convert heterogeneous, unstructured legacy reports into evidence-grounded, reusable and structured metadata, leading to better experimental comparability, and thus enabling reliable data pooling or informed virtual control selection.

papers.title: Single-molecule cold chemistry: Isotopic branching ratios of the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction at cryogenic temperatures
papers.abstract: Isotopic branching in ion-molecule reactions influences interstellar deuterium fractionation, yet its dynamics remain poorly understood for many important systems at astrophysically relevant temperatures. Here, we investigate H- and D-atom transfer in the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction using single sympathetically cooled water ions in a cryogenic radiofrequency trap. Nondestructive identification of the products from 441 individual reaction events at a mean collision energy of 7 K reveals an $\mathrm{H_3O^+/H_2DO^+}$ product branching ratio of $1.50 \pm 0.15$ demonstrating a preferential H-atom transfer. The experiments are rationalized using quasi-classical-trajectory calculations which indicate a transition from direct dynamics at higher energies to a complex-mediated reaction under the present experimental conditions and point to an important role of intramolecular vibrational redistribution affecting the isotopic branching in this regime. The present results extend measurements into an astrochemically relevant energy regime and establish cryogenic single-ion chemistry as a new platform for resolving competing reaction pathways.

papers.title: Finite element approximation on piecewise smooth domains
papers.abstract: The approximation theory by finite elements is usually described on the simplified geometry of polygonal or polyhedral domains. While avoiding the question of boundary approximation makes the analysis simpler, real applications may involve piecewise smooth domains and in some cases the extension of classical results to general boundaries may be tricky. In this paper we discuss in a systematic way the approximation properties and the error analysis of standard non-isoparametric finite element spaces on piecewise curvilinear domains in two and three dimensions. We show in detail how the geometric error introduces a barrier for the $H^1$ and $L^2$ error of the solution of both Dirichlet and Neumann elliptic problems independently of the regularity of the problem and of the degree of the finite element spaces used.

papers.title: SyncPro: Synchronous Reasoning and Responding for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires assistants to track unfolding events and respond when a user's requested condition is met. To make these decisions, assistants must accumulate relevant evidence and reassess response conditions as new observations arrive. Existing work offers complementary capabilities for this process: proactive video assistants learn when to respond, while streaming video reasoning methods generate scheduled intermediate text to organize observations and support subsequent answers. Together, these capabilities provide a foundation for proactive reasoning, but how to coordinate ongoing reasoning with timely responses remains underexplored. In a direct adaptation, fixed reasoning intervals can trigger updates when nothing relevant has changed or postpone useful updates until the next scheduled step. Sharing one generation path also couples two distinct requirements: preserving evidence for future decisions and producing only the response requested by the user. Moreover, responses generated after reasoning must wait for it to finish, even when sufficient evidence is already available. To address these challenges, we introduce SyncPro, a synchronous dual-stream framework with specialized generation paths for evidence tracking and user-facing responses. Its Inner and Response branches share causal history and activate independently, allowing relevant evidence changes to trigger internal updates and responses to proceed concurrently with ongoing reasoning. We construct 189K dual-stream examples and train SyncPro through supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. Experiments across three proactive benchmarks show improved response timing and more accurate answers to user requests.

papers.title: Learning Fine-Grained Visual Classification with Text as Privileged Information via Multimodal Distillation
papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual classification (FGVC) requires distinguishing between highly similar categories by focusing on subtle, localized visual differences. Recent multimodal methods have demonstrated that textual attribute descriptions can provide valuable semantic supervision by explicitly describing discriminative object characteristics. However, these descriptions are typically unavailable at test time, limiting their direct use in deployment. We propose FG-LUPI, a Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI)-based framework that leverages attribute descriptions during training. We train a multimodal teacher that integrates image patches and textual attributes via gated cross-attention, allowing semantic attributes to condition visual representations. We distill this knowledge into an image-only student using multi-level distillation at the prediction, patch, and attention levels, aligning global predictions, patch representations, and attention patterns with the teacher. This encourages the student to inherit attention structure learned from multimodal supervision while maintaining image-only inference. Experiments on multiple FGVC benchmarks show consistent improvements in classification accuracy over strong ViT-based baselines. Furthermore, evaluation using Expected Calibration Error (ECE) shows that FG-LUPI also produces better-calibrated predictions across all six benchmarks. These results suggest that textual attribute supervision can benefit not only fine-grained recognition performance but also the reliability of model confidence, while preserving the efficiency and practicality of image-only inference.

This task is challenging due to strong inter-class similarity and intra-class variations [58, 56]. As a result, FGVC models must effectively localize and exploit discriminative visual features.

To address this challenge, prior work has explored part-based modeling [16, 26, 27], attention mechanisms [17, 63], and language-guided supervision for fine-grained recognition [1, 23, 64, 59]. Natural language provides complementary semantic information that explicitly describes discriminative attributes. Such descriptions often highlight fine-grained features, including color patterns, beak shape, wing structure, or other category-specific characteristics. Moreover, language-based supervision aligns well with real-world recognition settings, where domain experts frequently rely on textual resources such as field guides, species descriptions, or taxonomic annotations to distinguish visually similar categories.

This is especially relevant when several categories share similar visual characteristics: a model may assign high confidence to an incorrect fine-grained prediction, making it difficult to identify ambiguous or uncertain cases [57]. Classification accuracy alone does not capture this aspect of model behavior. Calibration provides a complementary perspective by measuring the agreement between predicted confidence and empirical prediction accuracy. Thus, improving fine-grained recognition also raises an important question: Can the supervision used to learn discriminative visual features improve the reliability of the resulting confidence estimates?

Motivated by these questions, we study textual attributes under the Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm [55, 54], where textual information is available only during training and is not used at inference time. Prior LUPI work uses privileged information to supervise attention [41] or improve detection [3]. In this work, we formulate deep FGVC as a LUPI problem in which textual attribute descriptions provide training-time privileged semantic supervision. Unlike classical LUPI, where privileged information may provide additional information unavailable from the primary modality, our textual descriptions provide semantic guidance about the visual content during training. The text supervises a multimodal teacher toward fine-grained visual distinctions, whose knowledge is subsequently transferred to an image-only student through distillation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to investigate such semantic textual supervision for deep FGVC under the LUPI setting.

We propose Fine-Grained Learning Using Privileged Information (FG-LUPI), a teacher-student framework built upon Vision Transformers (ViTs) [9]. The teacher is extended into a multimodal model that learns from both images and textual descriptions, while the student operates only on visual inputs. By integrating textual attributes with visual representations via gated cross-attention, the teacher learns richer semantic representations that capture fine-grained discriminative features. This knowledge is then distilled into the image-only student, allowing it to inherit the teacher’s language-guided attention patterns without requiring textual input at inference time. We design a multi-level distillation framework that transfers the knowledge acquired by the multimodal teacher to the image-only student across multiple representation levels. Using this framework, the student is trained to inherit: (i) global predictive behavior through prediction distillation, (ii) localized feature representations through patch-level distillation, and (iii) spatial relationships through attention distillation. Together, these objectives encourage the student to reproduce both the discriminative patch representations and the attention patterns learned by the multimodal teacher.

Together, these objectives encourage the student to reproduce both the discriminative patch representations and the attention patterns learned by the multimodal teacher.

Experiments on multiple fine-grained recognition benchmarks, including CUB-200-2011 [59], NABirds [53], Stanford Dogs [25], FGVCAircraft [35], Stanford Cars [28], and iNaturalist 2021 [22], demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves performance over strong ViT-based baselines and competitive fine-grained classification methods. In addition to classification accuracy, we evaluate Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to examine the confidence calibration of the resulting image-only classifier. FG-LUPI achieves lower ECE than the vanilla ViT baseline across all six benchmarks, suggesting that the benefits of privileged textual supervision extend beyond predictive accuracy. Qualitative analyses of attention maps further show that the student focuses on meaningful and discriminative image regions (see Fig. 1), suggesting that text-guided attention patterns learned by the multimodal teacher are retained through distillation.

papers.title: BAARC: Uncertainty-Driven Adaptive Partial Spectral Measurement to Full Reconstruction for Material Classification
papers.abstract: Spectroscopic instruments with limited wavenumber coverage require accurate scan positioning or multiple measurements to complete the material analysis. This often requires prerequisite knowledge about the material under diagnosis to measure the spectral regions with distinguishing peaks. In our study, we simulate a Bayesian Adaptive Acquisition with Reconstruction-driven Classification (BAARC) framework for Raman spectral measurements, using masked training to learn spectral features that dynamically drive laser channel selection until the material is identified. We present a jointly trained two-level framework that takes progressive partial measurements of small wavenumber patches across the complete spectral range and, at each step, first attempts to reconstruct the full spectra until the model uncertainty is low. Secondly, material classification is performed at each reconstruction step until stoppage. Uncertainty quantification during reconstruction steps helps determine the measurement position of our next patch, while combining it with classification uncertainty determines measurement termination. By closing the loop between hardware acquisition and deep probabilistic modeling, the proposed system minimizes physical measurement steps while maintaining both spectral fidelity and diagnostic accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves high-accuracy sample identification using only a fraction of full-spectrum channels, offering a scalable solution for real-time, high-throughput spectroscopic instruments.

papers.intro:
Raman spectroscopy is a powerful analytical technique for characterizing materials through their intrinsic molecular vibrational signatures (Raman, 1928b; Raman, 1928a). When coupled with microscopy, it enables non-destructive, label-free chemical imaging of spatially inhomogeneous specimens. However, spontaneous Raman scattering suffers from inherently weak signal intensity, requiring long integration times that severely limit its applicability to dynamic biological processes (Krafft et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2011). Coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy was developed to overcome this bottleneck by enhancing signal intensity through coherent nonlinear excitation (Cheng and Xie, 2003; Müller and Zumbusch, 2007; Maker and Terhune, 1965). However, CARS suffers from non-resonant background contributions that distort its spectral shape compared to spontaneous Raman (Polli et al., 2018). Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy resolves this limitation by delivering background-free, quantitative spectra identical to spontaneous Raman (Shen, 1975; Mohn et al., 2025; Ranjan and Sirleto, 2024).

Raman spectroscopy is a powerful analytical technique for characterizing materials through their intrinsic molecular vibrational signatures (Raman, 1928b; Raman, 1928a). When coupled with microscopy, it enables non-destructive, label-free chemical imaging of spatially inhomogeneous specimens. However, spontaneous Raman scattering suffers from inherently weak signal intensity, requiring long integration times that severely limit its applicability to dynamic biological processes (Krafft et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2011). Coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy was developed to overcome this bottleneck by enhancing signal intensity through coherent nonlinear excitation (Cheng and Xie, 2003; Müller and Zumbusch, 2007; Maker and Terhune, 1965). However, CARS suffers from non-resonant background contributions that distort its spectral shape compared to spontaneous Raman (Polli et al., 2018). Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy resolves this limitation by delivering background-free, quantitative spectra identical to spontaneous Raman (Shen, 1975; Mohn et al., 2025; Ranjan and Sirleto, 2024).

Despite these advancements, SRS microscopy faces a fundamental trade-off between spectral coverage, acquisition speed, and sample viability. Acquiring a full spectrum across a wide wavenumber range requires continuous laser tuning, prolonging total measurement times, increasing hardware complexity, and elevating the risk of phototoxicity in biological samples (Yu et al., 2024; Pence et al., 2021; Mohn et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2017). As a result, practical constraints often force experimentalists to acquire only partial or sparse spectral bands. Similar limitations arise across many spectroscopic modalities, such as hyperspectral imaging (Gao and Smith, 2014), near-infrared spectroscopy, and diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (Andries and Martin, 2013), where only a fraction of the available spectral information can be acquired within a given measurement budget.

While real-time uncertainty propagation and active sensing have been successfully applied in dynamic tracking and active vision tasks (Trummer et al., 2010; Trummer et al., 2009), existing Raman spectroscopy methods predominantly rely on static acquisition grids. We call this the Bayesian Adaptive Acquisition with Reconstruction-driven Classification (BAARC) framework. From partial scans of a spectrum, a completely reconstructed spectrum with its prediction uncertainty is obtained. It has been shown previously that sensing in a high-uncertainty region optimally increases information gain (Krause et al., 2008; Houlsby et al., 2011). Our autonomous measurement control follows this by measuring the next high uncertainty region at each measurement step, as shown in Figure 1. The reconstruction of each step is used for classification along with its uncertainty. Both uncertainties are used as stoppage conditions in our framework, automatically halting physical measurement the moment confidence in sample identification stabilizes. Bayesian uncertainty quantification offers a principled criterion for both guiding laser selection toward ambiguous spectral regions and determining when measurement can be safely halted.

papers.title: Integrated elliptical III-V nanopillar arrays on silicon for dual photodetection and light emission
papers.abstract: Next-generation on-chip photonic devices require compact, energy-efficient components integrating photodetection and light emission on silicon platforms. Achieving broadband photodetection combined with efficient emission in a single nanoscale device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate elliptical nanopillar arrays monolithically integrated as III-V-on-Si templates, exhibiting broadband photoresponse across visible to near-infrared wavelengths, dynamic neuron-like graded responses under modulated light, and pronounced electroluminescence at around 865 nm under forward bias. The nanostructured elliptical geometry approach enhances optical absorption and carrier dynamics within an active area significantly smaller than commercial detectors, enabling responsivities up to 0.55 A/W at 830 nm in compact nanoarrays. This work advances the development of miniaturized active nanophotonic devices suitable for integrated sensing, emitting and communication circuits, and neuromorphic processing on silicon substrates.

papers.title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
papers.abstract: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.

papers.intro:
The efficiency of ultrafast laser processing of bandgap materials (i.e., non-metallic materials) is directly related to energy deposition. The latter is determined by linear and nonlinear mechanisms which in turn depend on how concentrated is the delivered photon packet in space and time. Most common ways to vary energy deposition experimentally consist of tuning independently the pulse energy, as well as the spatial and temporal pulse properties. As the overwhelming majority of mechanisms dictating laser–matter interaction are wavelength-dependent, another method to optimize the irradiation and achieve the desired material transformations is to adjust the wavelength. When aiming for ultrafast laser processing applications, it is therefore paramount to understand how laser–matter interaction scales with the wavelength so that the most appropriate laser system can be selected with respect to the expected outcomes.

In this Chapter, we first recall how experimental conditions vary with the wavelength, including the refractive index of the irradiated materials, the three-dimensional (3D) focus characteristics of the laser beams used for processing, and the driving light absorption mechanisms. From these considerations, we introduce the compromises existing between the minimum focal spot size and the ideally needed nonlinearities for high processing resolution on the surface and in the bulk of transparent bandgap materials. Then, the impact of the wavelength on laser–dielectric interaction is detailed. This includes recent and non-intuitive results indicating a modest wavelength dependence of the performance of ultrafast laser ablation in dielectrics from the ultraviolet to the mid-infrared domain. However, the wavelength is a unique control parameter on the period of surface and in-volume nanostructures, as well as on the performance of laser-written waveguides. Combining ultrashort pulses at different wavelengths can also represent a smart approach to individually control different mechanisms and improve the process efficiency as investigated in recent works on machining and drilling applications. Finally, we make a special emphasis on emerging near- and mid-infrared laser technologies which hold promises to transfer ultrafast laser 3D writing from wide- to narrow-gap materials, i.e., semiconductors. This is strongly supported by the advent of a new generation of stable and powerful ultrashort pulse sources which emit in the transparency range of semiconductors. In contrast to dielectrics, enhanced nonlinearities are found when focusing intense infrared laser pulses in semiconductors. In practice, this strongly limits the space-time energy localization, and thus, the energy deposition in these materials. We review the different strategies which have been recently developed to solve these limitations. This has led to experimental demonstrations of new laser processing capabilities and 3D solutions to meet important challenges in the semiconductor industry.

papers.title: Automated Multi-Line Bug Repair Using Model Checker Aided LLMs: A Case Study on RISC-V Processors
papers.abstract: Functional verification of Register-Transfer Level(RTL) designs has become a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor development, often consuming the majority of project resources. Debugging, in particular, remains an especially time-consuming task, requiring careful analysis of simulation traces or counterexamples. Recent work has explored applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to RTL debug and repair with great promise. However, the existing approaches typically are for single-line bugs, operate in open-loop, rely heavily on prompts or retrieval, lack scalability, and often produce incorrect fixes. In this paper, we propose a novel automated RTL bug repair methodology that combines LLMs, assertions, and a model checker to provide scalable, trustworthy semantic grounding and formal guarantees. Concretely, the methodology leverages failing assertions to guide the LLM in generating patches for multi-line bugs. Each candidate patch is formally verified using a model checker (JasperGold), ensuring only valid repairs are accepted. We evaluate the efficacy and scalability of our methodology on the BRISC-V RISC-V core using mutation testing, introducing several mutation types, and demonstrate that our methodology can repair up to 98% of single-line RTL bugs and 93% of the multi-line bugs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show automated, LLM-assisted RTL multi-line bug repair results on a complex RISC-V processor design in a scalable manner.

papers.intro:
Functional verification of Register-Transfer Level (RTL) designs has emerged as a principal bottleneck in the semiconductor development process, often consuming up to 70% of overall project resources [1, 2]. This growing burden is largely driven by the increasing complexity and functional richness of modern digital systems, which incorporate deep pipelines, multiple interacting sub-systems, and a variety of protocols and timing constraints. As designs scale in size and sophistication, the verification effort required to ensure correctness and safety has grown disproportionately. Among the various verification tasks, debugging, i.e., identifying and correcting functional errors in Hardware Description Language (HDL) code remains particularly time-consuming. It often requires manual analysis of simulation traces or counterexamples, and demands a detailed understanding of both the design intent and implementation [3, 4].

papers.title: PersonaScienceBench: Evaluating Scientific Agents with Diverse Simulated Researchers
papers.abstract: Scientific agents collaborate with researchers whose expertise and preferences differ, but benchmarks usually hold the collaborator fixed. We introduce PersonaScienceBench: 200 tasks from five benchmarks across four scientific domains. Simulated researchers provide context and feedback according to persona profiles, while task objectives and grading remain fixed. Agents encounter researcher preferences only through conversation. Across eighteen modelconfigurations, task performance, fact recovery, and self-repetition reveal different strengths. Detailed GPT 6 Astra analyses show distinct agent responses across researcher profiles; interaction traces illustrate targeted clar ification and workflow revision. These behaviors can differ even when final scores match. PersonaScienceBench therefore evaluates how agents collaborate with diverse researchers alongside whether they complete the task.
