papers.intro:
Language-model agents now perform substantial parts of the scientific workflow. They search literature, propose hypotheses, write and execute analysis code, and assemble results into reports Lu et al. (2024); Yamada et al. (2025); Gottweis et al. (2026); Mitchener et al. (2025b). The benchmarks used to measure this progress have followed the same trajectory, moving from recall and reasoning questions toward executable analysis tasks drawn from real studies Majumder et al. (2025); Mitchener et al. (2025a); Kon et al. (2026); Ye et al. (2025). These capabilities do not remove the need for human collaboration, and recent work questions their suitability for unsupervised discovery Bisht et al. (2026). Researchers often hold context that determines whether an analysis is valid: why samples were excluded, whether a covariate is confounded with batch, or which normalization a laboratory uses. Such information may be absent from the data directory. An agent’s scientific output can therefore depend on how it consults a researcher who may explain readily, answer only the literal question, or misremember a detail.

papers.title: Finitely many solutions for the prescribed scalar curvature problem at the critical flatness order
papers.abstract: We study the following prescribed scalar curvature problem $$ -Δu=K(y)u^{2^*-1},\ \ u>0 \,\ \ \text{in}\ \ \mathbb{R}^N, $$ where $2^*=\frac{2N}{N-2}$. For $N\geq4$, we construct a positive $K(y)$ with maximum set $\{|y|=1\}$ and critical order of flatness $m=N-2$ at $|y|=1$, such that the equation admits only finitely many positive solutions in $D^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. To this end, we prove the compactness of the solution set for this equation by blow-up analysis and then apply Sard's theorem to choose $K$ for which each solution is non-degenerate and hence isolated, so that the solution set is finite. Our results also give a definite answer to Wei--Yan's conjecture in [J. Wei and S. Yan, JFA, 2010].

papers.title: EDWARD-NMT: Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for Neural Machine Translation
papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful paradigm for scaling Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and managing language heterogeneity. However, practical limitations hinder its deployment on resource-constrained devices: the entire expert pool must remain in memory, and the per-token compute budget is statically fixed during training by rigid top-k routing. We introduce EDWARD-NMT (Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for NMT), a novel MoE encoder-decoder architecture designed for a train once, deploy anywhere paradigm that exposes a family of deployable sub-networks at inference time. EDWARD-NMT integrates three key innovations: (i) Matryoshka-style elastic dimensions to flexibly reduce the memory footprint; (ii) an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned, task-conditioned threshold, allowing each token to dynamically determine its active expert count; and (iii) a dual-consistency objective to maximize the performance of the extracted sub-networks. Extensive experiments on PhoMT (En-Vi), WMT-14 (En-De), multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain De-En benchmark validate our approach. The full-capacity architecture matches or exceeds strong MoE baselines with improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, the sub-networks seamlessly extracted from a single checkpoint consistently outperform comparably sized dense Transformers without any retraining.
papers.intro:
Managing language and domain heterogeneity is a fundamental challenge in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) Britz et al. (2017); Koehn and Knowles (2017); Pham et al. (2021), as training corpora routinely mix diverse lexical and stylistic distributions Stahlberg (2020); Gain et al. (2026). The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm addresses this by routing tokens to conditionally activated experts, scaling capacity to specialize in distinct patterns while keeping per-token computation tractable Shazeer et al. (2017); Fedus et al. (2022); Dai et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2024); Liang et al. (2025).

Despite state-of-the-art performance, MoEs face deployment bottlenecks in resource-constrained environments. First, the entire expert pool must reside in memory Hoffmann et al. (2022); Xu et al. (2023). While lightweight adapters reduce this overhead Zhang et al. (2024), they still yield static, hardware-specific models. Second, standard MoEs rely on rigid top-kk routing, applying an identical compute budget regardless of token complexity Jawahar et al. (2023); Guo et al. (2025). Although Neural Architecture Search can design heterogeneous sub-networks Jawahar et al. (2023), it requires complex offline phases. Consequently, NMT practitioners lack a unified framework to dynamically adjust memory and compute footprints on the fly.

To overcome memory bottlenecks, we apply Matryoshka representation learning Kusupati et al. (2022) to expert dimensions, allowing the MoE to be deterministically sliced into weight-sharing sub-networks at inference. To eliminate rigid compute constraints, we replace top-kk selection with an adaptive sigmoid router using a learned, task-conditioned threshold, empowering tokens to dynamically dictate their active expert count. Finally, to ensure aggressively truncated sub-networks maintain translation quality without post-hoc fine-tuning, we introduce a novel in-place dual-consistency objective that explicitly aligns predictive distributions across nested structural scales.

papers.title: The Calabi-Yau and Sullivan conjectures for minimal surfaces with symmetries
papers.abstract: Let \(G\) be a finite group acting on a connected open Riemann surface \(X\) by holomorphic automorphisms and acting on a Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^n\), \(n\ge 3\), by orthogonal transformations. In a previous paper, the second author gave a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a \(G\)-equivariant conformal minimal immersion \(F:X\to\mathbb R^n\), and he asked whether such \(F\) can be chosen to be a proper map. Assuming that this condition holds, we give an affirmative answer when \(X\) is a bordered Riemann surface and \(G\) acts freely on the boundary of \(X\). This contributes to the Sullivan conjecture concerning the existence of proper hyperbolic minimal surfaces in \(\mathbb R^3\) of finite topology. Under the same conditions, we also construct a \(G\)-equivariant proper conformal minimal immersion of \(X\) to the unit ball of \(\mathbb R^n\) which is complete in the induced metric, thereby opening a new direction in the Calabi--Yau theory regarding the study of complete bounded minimal surfaces. Analogous results hold for null curves in \(\mathbb C^n\).

The classical Calabi-Yau and Sullivan conjectures concern the existence of complete bounded minimal surfaces in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, and of proper hyperbolic minimal surfaces in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} of finite topology, respectively. Since the pioneering positive results of Jorge-Xavier [19] and Nadirashvili [24] concerning the former, and of Morales [23] regarding the latter, a primary topic of interest has been to understand the topological, geometric, and conformal properties of such surfaces; we refer to [7, Sec. 3.10 and Ch. 7] for surveys on these questions. Concerning possible conformal restrictions, Alarcón and López proved that every open Riemann surface is the underlying complex structure of a proper minimal surface in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} [8], while the authors showed that every bordered Riemann surface is the complex structure of a complete bounded minimal surface in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} [5].

papers.title: Honest Inference for Synthetic Controls with Imperfect Fit: Time-Split Validity and the Choice of Anchor
papers.abstract: Synthetic controls are used for one treated unit that lies outside its donors' range, with a pre-treatment window too short for residual-based standard errors to be trusted. We propose inference that separates the periods used to fit the synthetic control from the periods used to assess its error. Weights are fitted on an early block of pre-treatment periods, and the gap on a later block calibrates the bias and the noise. The resulting interval has finite-sample coverage under an explicit restriction on how far the counterfactual may depart from the extrapolated pre-treatment gap, for any fitting rule that uses only the early block. The leading restriction bounds the curvature of the gap and leaves its slope free, and the breakdown curvature at which the interval first includes zero states how much extrapolation a conclusion needs. We show when drift bounds calibrated from donor placebos are valid and how to allow for serial dependence. In simulations, conventional intervals undercover when the treated unit drifts from its donors, while the proposed interval covers whenever its restriction holds and the noise is serially independent. Re-analyses of three classic applications show that some well-known conclusions rest on far stronger extrapolation than others.

papers.intro:
Synthetic controls estimate the effect of an intervention on one unit by comparing it with a weighted combination of untreated units (Abadie and Gardeazabal, 2003; Abadie et al., 2010). In a short panel the pre-treatment outcomes must select the weights, assess the fit and inform the uncertainty, and these tasks place conflicting demands on the same observations. When the treated unit lies outside the donors’ range, exact fit is infeasible and imperfect fit can carry bias that does not vanish with more periods (Ferman and Pinto, 2021). The synthetic unit then drifts away from the treated unit as soon as it is evaluated on periods it was not fitted to, and the question is how far that drift may be extrapolated into the post-treatment period.

This paper answers with a time split and an explicit sensitivity class. Donor weights and a temporal anchor are chosen on a training block of pre-treatment periods. The estimator subtracts the anchored gap on a later validation block from the average post-treatment gap. Conditional on training, its error is a bounded bias plus a Gaussian disturbance, and an orthogonal projection of the validation residuals gives a scale estimate independent of that disturbance. Adding the worst-case bias to a Student critical radius then gives an interval with coverage at least its nominal level in finite samples, uniformly over the class, for any fitting rule that uses the training block, including the weights of Abadie et al. (2010), Doudchenko and Imbens (2016), Ben-Michael et al. (2021) and Hollingsworth and Wing (2020), and with as few as three validation periods, although with so few the Student critical value is too large to be useful.

papers.title: Optimality of finite field dimension expanders
papers.abstract: We show that random tuples of matrices over a finite field are uniform dimension expanders for every expansion coefficient below the optimal one, using elementary counting arguments. The same holds for the optimal coefficient along a set of dimensions of density 1. By contrast, along Fibonacci dimensions random pairs of matrices fail to be optimal dimension expanders with probability bounded away from zero.

papers.title: Zero photoemission from icosahedral superatoms
papers.abstract: Photoemission is expected to occur when the photon energy exceeds the binding energy of an electron, with the photoemission yield generally remaining non-zero above this threshold. Yet, it can be suppressed at specific photon energies, a phenomenon known as the Cooper minimum. Although complete suppression represents an extreme limit of this phenomenon, such zero photoemission has previously been reported only for atoms with an outermost s-type orbital and has never been observed in non-atomic systems. Here, we demonstrate the deliberate realization of zero photoemission from Ag12W-, an artificial icosahedral superatom, by observing a vanishing photoemission cross section 0.85 eV above the detachment threshold and reproducing this behavior in theoretical simulations. These simulations predict that zero photoemission can be common in nearly spherical nanoclusters, a prediction we experimentally confirm using Ag12Mo-, an isoelectronic counterpart of Ag12W-. Because superatoms offer systematic control over both size and elemental composition using the periodic table, our findings establish a route toward active control of photoemission in finite-size quantum systems and stimulate further investigations of underexplored physical phenomena such as nondipole effects.

papers.title: RVG-Bench: A Benchmark for Reasoning-Driven Audio-Visual Temporal Grounding
papers.abstract: Existing temporal video grounding (TVG) benchmarks primarily focus on localizing target video segments according to descriptive text queries of the visual content. However, real-world queries are more diverse and often require the model to first understand the user's intent before localization, such as finding visual evidence, identifying the cause of an event, or recalling a remembered moment, yet such queries remain largely overlooked. To mitigate this gap, we introduce RVG-Bench, a benchmark for reasoning-driven audio-visual temporal grounding, where every query is constructed such that the target segment can only be identified through reasoning about the query's underlying intent. We carefully construct the benchmark and rigorously verify its data quality to ensure models truly comprehend the audio-visual content. RVG-Bench comprises 1,255 videos and 1,890 query-interval pairs across eight reasoning types. We evaluate 22 models and find that the strongest, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, achieves only 49.6 mIoU. Through a series of controlled analyses, including oracle-grounding probes and test-time scaling experiments, we systematically examine where and why current models struggle, providing insights for future model development.

Temporal Video Grounding aims to localize a temporal segment in an untrimmed video given a natural language query. In existing benchmarks, the query explicitly describes the visual content of the target segment, such as “A boy pouring water on the stairs,” shown on the left of Fig. 1. Temporal Video Grounding aims to localize a temporal segment in an untrimmed video given a natural language query. In existing benchmarks, the query explicitly describes the visual content of the target segment, such as “A boy pouring water on the stairs,” shown on the left of Fig. 1. This formulation effectively reduces grounding to description-to-segment matching, where the model aligns textual descriptions with video frames through cross-modal semantic similarity.

However, real-world video grounding rarely follows this pattern. Users typically do not describe what a segment looks like; instead, they express an intent: locating evidence for a question, identifying the cause of an observed outcome, or recalling a moment from a vague memory. Such queries are inherently indirect. For example, “Locate the action that caused the burglar to fall” in Fig. 1 requires tracing the fall back to the boy pouring water on the stairs, then localizing that earlier action. This reasoning-driven grounding is a core capability required by many downstream video understanding tasks, yet it remains unevaluated by existing benchmarks.

To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce RVG-Bench, a benchmark designed around a key principle: the target segment cannot be identified through surface-level semantic matching and must instead be inferred through reasoning. Every query is intentionally indirect, requiring the model to interpret the underlying intent before localization becomes possible. To comprehensively cover the different dimensions of reasoning ability, we organize the benchmark using a structured reasoning taxonomy with three major categories: relational, intrinsic-attribute, and relative-attribute. These categories are further divided into eight subcategories. In addition, we incorporate the audio modality, since narration, dialogue, and environmental sounds frequently provide critical cues that are absent from the visual stream. More than half of the queries therefore require audio evidence, either alone or jointly with vision. To ensure dataset reliability, we implement strict information-leakage prevention and multi-stage verification so that each query corresponds to a unique and unambiguous target segment. RVG-Bench contains 1,255 videos and 1,890 query–interval pairs constructed through a four-stage pipeline with full human validation.

papers.title: First- and Second-Order Electron Position Correlators Reveal Topological Phase Transitions
papers.abstract: The theory of conventional critical phenomena is built around the concepts of fluctuations and correlators of local observables. Here, we show that topological phase transitions can also be characterized through spatial and temporal two-point correlation functions associated with fluctuations of the electronic position operator. The key object is the antisymmetric part of the position-position correlation function, which yields the Chern number in the equal-time and equal-space limit. When the system is translationally invariant in space or time (the latter case corresponding to an equilibrium condition), these two-point correlators reduce to one-variable functions of the remaining variable. Remarkably, these functions are both reminiscent of critical behaviour, including divergent correlation times and lengths signalling the phase transitions. Away from these conditions, namely in non-periodic systems or genuinely dynamical processes, criticality is instead better captured by higher-order Chern-Chern correlators constructed from local or dynamical markers obtained as coincident-point limits of the position correlators. These higher-order Chern-Chern correlators can be seen as double Levi-Civita contractions of second-order position correlators, selecting the antisymmetric sector in each index pair. We substantiate this framework through numerical simulations and analytic calculations. Our results establish a general correlator-based description of topological phase transitions, applicable to crystalline, noncrystalline, equilibrium, and dynamical systems.

Topological phase transitions are often regarded as lying outside the conventional paradigm of critical phenomena, as distinct topological phases cannot, in general, be understood in terms of spontaneous symmetry breaking. However, the absence of a conventional Landau framework does not exclude an underlying description in terms of fluctuations and correlations [12, 16]. Here we show that such a description emerges naturally from the fundamental objects of quantum geometry and topology.

papers.title: Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson classes of symmetric powers and applications
papers.abstract: The Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson class $c_{SM}(X)$ is defined in the Chow group $A_*(X)$ of a scheme $X$, and generalizes $c(T_X)\cap [X]$ if $X$ is smooth. In this paper we independently compute $c_{SM}(S^nX)\in A_*(S^nX)$ modulo $n!$ torsion; we use this result to compute the pushforward to $S^nX$ of $c_{SM}(Quot^n_X(E))$ (and in particular $c_{SM}(Hilb^n X)$) when $X$ is smooth and $E$ is a vector bundle on $X$. Finally, when $X$ is smooth and complete of dimension $3$ we propose a refined version of the the MNOP conjecture that computes the image of the pushforward of $[Hilb^n X]^{vir}$ to $A_0(S^nX)$ and prove it modulo $n!$ torsion when $X$ is Calabi-Yau.

papers.title: Energies with values in networks and geometric quasiconvexity
papers.abstract:
We study the asymptotic behaviour, as $\varepsilon	o 0^+$, of the $p$-Dirichlet energy of maps $u\colonΩ\subset\mathbb{R}^2 	o \mathbb{R}^2$ constrained to take values in the rescaled periodic network $\varepsilon\mathcal Z$, where $\mathcal Z$ is a standard square network in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The oscillations are carried by the constraint in the target, not by the energy density, and their effect depends on $p$. For $1<p<2$ the constraint disappears in the limit: the $Γ$-limit is an integral functional on the whole of $m{W}^{1,p}(Ω, \mathbb{R}^2 )$, whose density is given by an asymptotic cell formula on tilted cells. This density is equal to $(|a_1|+|a_2|)^p$ on rank-one matrices $a\otimesν$, $|ν|=1$, and exceeds its convex envelope by a quantity comparable to $|\det A|\,|A|^{p-2}$, with constants of order $(2-p)^{-1}$. Consequently, although the original energy density is convex, the limit density is quasiconvex but neither convex nor polyconvex: quasiconvexity is generated by the geometry of the constraint. For $p\ge2$ the constraint survives in the limit as $\det
abla u=0$, and the $Γ$-limit is the degenerate energy $\int_Ω(|
abla u_1|+|
abla u_2|)^p\, m{d} x$, that is, the $p$-energy of $u$ considered as a map into the normed plane $(\mathbb{R}^2,|\cdot|_1)$, the metric limit of the networks.

papers.title: Fast and Scalable Influence Estimation in the Independent Cascade Model: a unified framework
papers.abstract: Computing diffusion processes on networks is fundamental to applications including influence maximization, epidemic modeling, information propagation, and diffusion inference. The Independent Cascade (IC) model is one of the most widely used models of progressive diffusion, yet exact computation of its activation probabilities is #P-hard, while Monte Carlo simulation becomes costly when accurate estimates are required repeatedly. Despite its central role, analytical approximation of the IC diffusion function has received comparatively little systematic attention relative to the extensive literature on influence-maximization algorithms. We present a comprehensive study of analytical approximations for the IC model. We review a wide range of existing approaches and unify them through a common framework based on temporal representation, retained propagation information, and aggregation rule. This perspective exposes connections between previously distinct approximation families and motivates several new methods. We further conduct, to our knowledge, the first large-scale cross-family comparison of analytical IC approximations for node-level marginal activation probabilities. Our benchmark spans real-world and synthetic networks with systematically varied topology, seed-set size, edge-probability model, and diffusion strength. The proposed second-order dynamic message-passing method achieves the lowest pooled median error and the lowest dataset- or graph-family-level median error on every network considered. The results reveal systematic differences between approximation families, identify regimes in which higher-order corrections are most beneficial, and establish analytical IC approximation as a rich accuracy-efficiency design space rather than a collection of isolated methods.

papers.title: Best Bulk Bennu (B3): Elemental compositions of aggregate samples from asteroid Bennu
papers.abstract: Ivuna-type (CI) carbonaceous chondrites have long served as proxies for the bulk Solar System composition due to their close agreement with solar photospheric abundances and enrichment in volatile elements relative to other chondrite classes. However, CI chondrites have been subject to terrestrial alteration, which may have modified their original mineralogies and redistributed aqueously mobile elements. NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission delivered pristine material from the carbonaceous asteroid Bennu, and initial analyses revealed close compositional similarities with CI chondrites. This provides a valuable opportunity to refine estimates of the bulk Solar System composition. We report concentrations of 63 elements in aggregate (bulk, unsorted) Bennu material (representing a combined mass of ~8 g) analyzed across four laboratories. Within analytical uncertainties, we find no statistically significant differences among aliquots of two aggregate samples that were homogenized into powders, or among subsamples (including two previously reported) of a non-homogenized aggregate sample. Nor do we find measurable variations among sample masses ranging from tens of milligrams to several grams. These findings indicate that the material returned from Bennu is well mixed at the aggregate scale. Combining all of the data, we derive an average bulk elemental composition that we term Best Bulk Bennu (B3). Comparison of B3 with an average CI chondrite composition shows excellent agreement within analytical uncertainties, confirming that terrestrial alteration of CI chondrites is effectively isochemical for non-highly volatile elements. B3 and the CI chondrite average composition compare similarly to solar photospheric composition. Thus, CI meteorites and returned samples of carbonaceous asteroids are the best available materials for estimating the bulk Solar System composition of non-highly volatile elements.

papers.title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites
papers.abstract: Perovskites have been studied for a wide range of applications, from oxide-based ferroelectrics to halide-perovskite photovoltaics. Despite their diverse functionalities, these materials share strong lattice anharmonicity arising from structural instabilities such as polar off-centering and octahedral tilting. These anharmonic distortions strongly influence the low-frequency vibrational response and can be observed in infrared (IR) and Raman spectra. However, low-frequency IR and Raman signatures are typically investigated separately, hindering the development of a unified understanding of vibrational spectroscopy across perovskite classes. In this work, we use machine-learning-based molecular dynamics to simulate the IR and Raman spectra of oxide perovskites (SrTiO$_3$ and BaTiO$_3$), halide perovskites (CsPbBr$_3$, CsSnBr$_3$, and CsGeBr$_3$) and double halide perovskites (Cs$_2$AgAlBr$_6$ and Cs$_2$AgBiBr$_6$). By comparing materials exhibiting polar, tilt-driven and mixed instabilities, we find that polar off-centering leads to enhanced low-frequency IR and dielectric responses, whereas nonpolar modes, particularly octahedral tilting, are associated with Raman central peaks. The strength of the low-frequency features also depends on how strongly the underlying modes couple to polarization or dielectric susceptibility. Finally, we show that the dynamics of these instabilities play an important role, with slow polar reorientations shifting the dielectric response to very low frequencies and overdamped tilting modes producing persistent Raman central peaks. These results establish a unified framework connecting low-frequency IR and Raman spectra to the symmetry, coupling and dynamics of their underlying anharmonic lattice instabilities.

papers.intro:
Perovskite materials with stoichiometry ABX3\text{ABX}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} constitute one of the largest and most versatile families of functional materials. Their exceptional chemical flexibility has enabled the development of various fields, from oxide ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics [57, 29, 4, 24, 3, 41] to the more recent applications of halide perovskites in solar cells and optoelectronic devices [23, 62, 34, 42, 7, 74, 68]. Beyond conventional oxide and halide compounds, the perovskite family also encompasses double perovskites [30, 10, 37, 17], chalcogenide perovskites [61, 65, 59, 52, 31], and low-dimensional perovskites [78, 2, 45, 32], further expanding the range of accessible functionalities. Alloying and doping offer additional avenues for tuning the properties of existing perovskite materials [82, 54, 38, 79, 21, 80]. This structural and chemical versatility provides an exceptionally broad playground for tailoring physical properties through composition and crystal chemistry. In addition to this remarkable diversity, perovskites generally possess highly anharmonic lattices that give rise to unusual behaviors at finite temperatures and rich phase diagrams [51, 55, 81, 26]. In most perovskites, this anharmonicity originates from a small number of lattice instabilities, primarily tilting of the BX6\text{BX}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}} octahedra and polar off-centering of the B site [75, 76, 22, 81]. These distortions govern structural phase transitions and strongly influence dielectric, ferroelectric, optical, and thermal properties. Establishing general relationships between these structural instabilities and experimentally accessible observables is therefore essential for understanding and designing functional perovskite materials.

These distortions govern structural phase transitions and strongly influence dielectric, ferroelectric, optical, and thermal properties. Establishing general relationships between these structural instabilities and experimentally accessible observables is therefore essential for understanding and designing functional perovskite materials.

Among these lattice instabilities, polar off-centering in oxide perovskites is well known to give rise to soft phonon modes. Near the phase transition, the frequency of these modes vanishes, leading to a substantial enhancement of the dielectric response. This enhancement is central to the design of high-performance piezoelectric materials, where alloying is commonly employed to tune structural instabilities and maximize the dielectric response. A more modest dielectric enhancement has also been observed in hybrid halide perovskites and attributed to a combined motion between the organic molecules and the inorganic octahedra [9, 28, 1]. Another prominent low-frequency feature is the central peak observed in Raman spectra of oxide perovskites near structural phase transitions [44, 18]. Although two-phonon processes can produce a central Raman contribution in crystals [43], the pronounced intensity and strong temperature dependence of central peaks in perovskites have raised debate over their origin [48, 58]. In the ideal cubic phase (Pm3¯\bar{3}m), such peaks cannot be explained by first-order Raman scattering, which is forbidden by symmetry. Raman central peaks have also been observed in hybrid and inorganic halide perovskites, indicating that they cannot originate solely from the rotation of the organic molecules [73]. Machine-learning-based molecular dynamics simulations further linked the central peak to dynamic octahedral tilting [8]. However, recent work compared the Raman spectra of CsPbBr3\text{CsPbBr}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} and Cs2​AgBiBr6\text{Cs}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{AgBiBr}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}, and showed that the latter exhibit no persistent central peak at high temperatures, despite the presence of anharmonic tilting modes [11]. More recently, a study compared the low-frequency Raman spectra of various halide perovskites, arguing that the central peak cannot originate from octahedral tilting, but instead from broad Raman-active modes amplified by Bose-Einstein statistics at low frequencies [39]. While the relationship between polar soft modes and dielectric enhancement is well established, the microscopic origin of Raman central peaks remains debated. Moreover, the low-frequency IR and Raman signatures are generally interpreted independently and often within separate material communities. Consequently, a unified understanding of vibrational spectra and their connection to the underlying lattice instabilities across different perovskite classes remains lacking.

papers.title: On the closure under barycenters of location-scatter families with a normalized generator
papers.abstract: We provide an example of a normalized absolutely continuous probability whose location-scatter family (LSF) does not contain all the 2-Wassertein geodesics passing through its elements. In particular, we find a counterexample for Corollary 4.5 in [2]. Finally, we prove that LSFs with a (possibly singular) radially symmetric generator are closed under 2-Wasserstein barycenters.

The quadratic Wasserstein space (𝒫2​(𝐑n),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}({{\mathbf{R}}^{n}}),W_{2}) is a geodesic metric space, and its geodesics are described by displacement interpolation along optimal transport plans [4, 12, 14]. A subset 𝒦⊆𝒫2​(𝐑n)\mathcal{K}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{2}({{\mathbf{R}}^{n}}) is said to be geodesically convex if for any two of its elements μ1,μ2∈𝒦\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\in\mathcal{K} all the W2W_{2}-geodesic joining μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} are contained in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. papers.title: Intermittency in firm bankruptcies from register data
papers.abstract: By analysing the clustering of bankruptcy activity from administrative register data in the Netherlands over time, the intermittency of this process is investigated. Using methodology from survival analysis a statistical characterization of bursts is obtained: short active periods alternating with quieter periods. Using Statistics Netherlands microdata on Dutch business bankruptcies declared on court hearing-days from 2009 to 2024, combined with input-output tables from the Dutch national accounts, it is studied whether this clustering can be explained by differences between sectors, years, and inter-sectoral exposure. Sector differences explain most of the heterogeneity in the data, while year effects matter to a lesser extent and the inter-sectoral exposure variables constructed from the input-output tables further improve model fit.

papers.intro:
Modern economies are highly interconnected sociotechnical systems in which firms, institutions, and technical infrastructures are linked through supply chains and financial linkages. Financial stress in one part of the economy can propagate through supply chains, financial relations and other forms of interdependence, potentially resulting in firm failures, bankruptcies, elsewhere.

Modern economies are highly interconnected sociotechnical systems in which firms, institutions, and technical infrastructures are linked through supply chains and financial linkages. Financial stress in one part of the economy can propagate through supply chains, financial relations and other forms of interdependence, potentially resulting in firm failures, bankruptcies, elsewhere.

The Dutch national statistical institute, Statistics Netherlands (SN, also known under the Dutch abbreviation: CBS), publishes tables concerning bankruptcies as part of its regular output on economic indicators. The underlying dataset, which is used for this research, consists of information on bankruptcies declared by Dutch courts, including the date of the court decision and the sector classification, from which bankruptcy counts are constructed indexed by economic sectors and hearing-days. This administrative dataset has the properties of individual firms that were declared bankrupt, and is combined with publicly available input-output tables from the Dutch national accounts. These tables are used to construct exposure measures in order to study inter-sectoral dependencies at different timescales.

These tables are used to construct exposure measures in order to study inter-sectoral dependencies at different timescales.

One feature of bankruptcy data is that bankruptcies are not evenly distributed over time: even within a given sector, calm periods may be followed by short episodes in which multiple bankruptcies occur on several consecutive hearing-days, a property known as intermittency.

Earlier work at SN shows that the aggregate bankruptcy process over 1981-2023 exhibits features of intermittency. Specifically, Lopes Cardozo (2024) show that a Weibull model fitted to the residual component of the aggregate bankruptcy time series yields a shape parameter below one, which suggests clustering of bankruptcies rather than a memoryless arrival process. Building upon this result, this thesis develops a framework that decomposes intermittency into burst onset and burst size components that can both be related to observed covariates.

Building upon this result, this thesis develops a framework that decomposes intermittency into burst onset and burst size components that can both be related to observed covariates.

The analysis is divided into two parts. First, the burst onset analysis (BOA) studies the probability that a new burst starts after inactivity. This probability is formulated as a discrete-time hazard in a proportional hazards model and estimated using a Bernoulli generalised linear model with a complementary log-log link and a Weibull baseline. Second, the burst size analysis (BSA) studies the size of bankruptcy counts on active hearing-days. Because the data contain many zero-count days and the positive-count days are overdispersed, this component is modelled using a zero-truncated negative binomial structure. These two analyses allow us to distinguish between when bursts start after a period of inactivity and the size of activity once a sector is active, yielding a more informative description of bankruptcy dynamics than a single count model would provide.

Intermittency is a property of a dynamical system in which a process alternates between phases of relatively low activity and active episodes at seemingly irregular times. Within dynamical systems theory, intermittency been studied extensively and has been formalised in several ways (Ott and Sommerer, 1994; Pomeau and Manneville, 1980). This concept is not restricted to purely theoretical systems, however. In fact, many economic and social processes exhibit similar alternations of quiet and active periods, and can therefore be studied from the same perspective.

Intermittency is a property of a dynamical system in which a process alternates between phases of relatively low activity and active episodes at seemingly irregular times. Within dynamical systems theory, intermittency been studied extensively and has been formalised in several ways (Ott and Sommerer, 1994; Pomeau and Manneville, 1980). This concept is not restricted to purely theoretical systems, however. In fact, many economic and social processes exhibit similar alternations of quiet and active periods, and can therefore be studied from the same perspective.

A related notion is self-organised criticality (SOC). In SOC, a system evolves towards a critical state in which relatively small events can trigger large cascades of events, often referred to as avalanches. In economic networks, avalanches are often discussed in relation to financial structures such as supply chains, where limited buffers may increase local stress and amplify shocks. Recent work on timeliness criticality and critical fragility formalises how efficiency pressures can move sociotechnical systems closer to a critical state (Moran et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2025). The SOC perspective offers one interpretation under which firm failures may increase financial stress on economically connected firms through supply chains. Intermittency and SOC are distinct concepts, but they share a common feature: both involve extended periods of calm followed by bursts of activity associated with the slow build-up of pressure and the depletion of buffers. It has been shown that Dutch bankruptcies occur in bursts of activity (Lopes Cardozo, 2024), and related work shows that bankruptcy cascades tend to exhibit SOC-like behaviour (Hong et al., 2007). Hong, Lee & Lee specifically analyse Korean firm bankruptcies, but argue that the mechanisms are not intrinsically Korea-specific. These findings support the idea that bankruptcies should not be treated as time-independent events, but rather as a process in which clustering in time is present.

papers.title: Smoothing splines with some discontinuities
papers.abstract: We generalize cubic smoothing splines to signals with a finite number of discontinuities at unknown positions. Rather than changing the roughness penalty, we deform the domain over which it is computed: every interval between consecutive observations can be stretched by a non-negative warp, subject to a total budget, and the optimizer spends the budget only where a jump makes stretching cheaper than bending. The estimator inherits the state-space form of smoothing splines, so it can be fitted by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, and it also admits a fast alternating algorithm that solves a banded linear system and takes a projected-gradient step on the warps. The budget is selected by an extended Bayesian information criterion whose constant is calibrated by simulation. In a Monte Carlo comparison the new estimators reconstruct a piecewise-smooth signal more accurately than the cubic smoothing spline with discontinuities of Storath and Weinmann, at the cost of more false alarms. Two energy applications illustrate the method: the temperature response of electricity demand in Northern Italy, and retail fuel prices, whose discontinuities, changes in excise duties, are dated by public record. The three supplements follow the references.

papers.intro:
Data recorded over an ordered index often behave smoothly for long stretches punctuated by a handful of sharp, isolated changes: a policy shock in a price series, a phase transition in a physical process, a saturation threshold in a demand curve. Cubic smoothing splines (Wahba, 1978; Wecker and Ansley, 1983), and their equivalent state-space signal-extraction formulation (Harvey and Koopman, 2000), recover the smooth part of such signals well, but they are twice continuously differentiable by construction: the roughness penalty that makes them smooth also prevents them from reproducing a discontinuity, which is either washed out over several observations or, if the penalty is relaxed everywhere, accommodated at the price of overfitting the noise elsewhere. What is needed is an estimator that is smooth almost everywhere and sharp exactly where the data demand it, without the analyst having to specify in advance where.

Data recorded over an ordered index often behave smoothly for long stretches punctuated by a handful of sharp, isolated changes: a policy shock in a price series, a phase transition in a physical process, a saturation threshold in a demand curve. Cubic smoothing splines (Wahba, 1978; Wecker and Ansley, 1983), and their equivalent state-space signal-extraction formulation (Harvey and Koopman, 2000), recover the smooth part of such signals well, but they are twice continuously differentiable by construction: the roughness penalty that makes them smooth also prevents them from reproducing a discontinuity, which is either washed out over several observations or, if the penalty is relaxed everywhere, accommodated at the price of overfitting the noise elsewhere. What is needed is an estimator that is smooth almost everywhere and sharp exactly where the data demand it, without the analyst having to specify in advance where.

This paper proposes such an estimator. The idea is to leave the classical roughness penalty unchanged and to deform the domain over which it is computed. Every pair of consecutive observations is allowed a non-negative domain warp γi≥0\gamma_{i}\geq 0, an amount of fictitious domain length inserted between them, subject to a total budget MM, and the roughness of the spline is penalized on the warped domain. Where the signal is smooth, warping buys nothing, the optimal γi\gamma_{i} is zero and the fit coincides with an ordinary smoothing spline. Where the signal jumps, the same vertical change can be spread over a longer warped interval at a much lower curvature cost, so the optimizer concentrates the budget on the few intervals where a jump is present. Strictly speaking, the fitted function remains continuous: it approximates a discontinuity much as a steep sigmoid approximates a step function. Because the mechanism is a reparameterization of the domain, the estimator inherits the state-space representation of smoothing splines, which we use for maximum likelihood estimation via the Kalman filter, and it also admits a fast alternating algorithm that avoids numerical likelihood maximization altogether.

The idea of penalizing discontinuities directly, rather than smoothing through them, goes back to the weak rod and weak plate models of Blake and Zisserman (1987) and to the Mumford–Shah functional (Mumford and Shah, 1989), which penalize the roughness of a piecewise-smooth function together with the number of its discontinuities and lead to a combinatorial search over candidate discontinuity sets. The estimator closest to ours, and our benchmark throughout, is the cubic smoothing spline with discontinuities (CSSD) of Storath and Weinmann (2024), which specializes the weak-rod functional to cubic splines and non-equidistant data and solves it exactly by dynamic programming. Wavelet shrinkage (Donoho and Johnstone, 1994) denoises jumpy signals by thresholding multiresolution coefficients, but it targets equidistant designs and does not produce a piecewise-smooth curve. The fused lasso (Tibshirani et al., 2005) and trend filtering (Kim et al., 2009; Tibshirani, 2014) penalize the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm of successive differences of the fitted values or of their derivatives, a convex problem with automatic knot placement, but the knots are a by-product of a coefficient-level penalty rather than of an explicit, interpretable deformation. Free-knot splines (Koo, 1997) and two-stage procedures, which first locate breaks with a changepoint detector such as PELT (Killick et al., 2012) and then smooth between them, decouple detection from estimation. Our formulation keeps the roughness penalty unchanged and reparameterizes the metric in which it is computed, so that detection and estimation are solved jointly, through a single continuous, non-negative vector 𝜸\bm{\gamma}.

Free-knot splines (Koo, 1997) and two-stage procedures, which first locate breaks with a changepoint detector such as PELT (Killick et al., 2012) and then smooth between them, decouple detection from estimation. Our formulation keeps the roughness penalty unchanged and reparameterizes the metric in which it is computed, so that detection and estimation are solved jointly, through a single continuous, non-negative vector 𝜸\bm{\gamma}.

Section 2 introduces the domain-warping formulation, its state-space form, the alternating algorithm and the tuning of the method. Section 3 compares the estimators with CSSD and with a classical smoothing spline by Monte Carlo simulation, and Section 4 applies them to two energy-related data sets, chosen to cover the two kinds of data the method is meant for. The first application investigates the temperature response of electricity demand, a cross-sectional relation estimated on hourly observations ordered by temperature rather than by time, irregularly spaced and with many ties, whose discontinuities are thresholds of the physical system and are not known in advance. The second uses weekly time series of retail fuel prices, serially dependent and close to a stochastic trend, in which changes in the excise duty shift the level of the prices at dates that are a matter of public record, so that the estimated discontinuities can be checked against a ground truth that real data rarely offer. Section 5 concludes. Three supplements accompany the paper: the Computational Supplement collects derivations and implementation details, the Calibration Supplement the tuning of the method, and the Application Supplement additional results for the two applications.

papers.title: On the Propeller Conjecture
papers.abstract: We simplify and improve OpenAI's proof of the propeller conjecture of Khot and Naor from 2008: the sum of the squared lengths of the Gaussian moments of any partition of Euclidean space is at most $9/(8π)$. We show equality only occurs for three 120 degree sectors in the plane (up to symmetries, measure zero changes, and taking orthogonal cross products with Euclidean space). We also remove computer assistance from the three-dimensional case of the conjecture, which previously used an epsilon net traversal.

papers.title: The Fundamental Semigroup and Associative Lifts of Topological Semigroups
papers.abstract: We introduce the fundamental semigroup $Λ(S)$ of a nonempty path-connected topological semigroup $S$, defined using right translations and change-of-basepoint isomorphisms on its fundamental group. We prove that this construction is closed under composition and independent of the chosen basepoint up to isomorphism. It is also invariant under homotopy equivalences that preserve multiplication up to homotopy. We characterize exactly when the fundamental semigroup is a group and identify that group with an inner automorphism group. For a connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected topological semigroup, we show that multiplication admits a continuous associative lift to the universal cover if and only if $Λ(S)$ contains an idempotent. Every such idempotent can be realized by an associative lift, and any two associative lifts are isomorphic over $S$ through a deck transformation. We obtain existence results when the fundamental group has finite inner automorphism group or contains no subgroup isomorphic to Thompson's group $F$, and when the underlying space is a finite-dimensional CW complex. In contrast, we construct a path-connected countable CW topological semigroup with cells in arbitrarily high dimensions whose multiplication admits no continuous associative lift to its universal cover.

papers.title: The Effects of Generative AI on Collaboration and Social Networks Among Knowledge Workers
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. We test these competing predictions using passively collected behavioral data from more than 12,000 knowledge workers observed over 13 months during the staged organizational rollout of an AI-powered assistant (Microsoft Copilot). Using two complementary quasi-experimental designs -- a staggered difference-in-differences model and a fixed-effects instrumental-variable approach -- we estimate the effects of generative AI on workers' collaboration behavior and social network structure. We estimate that generative AI increased collaboration time across communication channels and reshaped individual networks. Those using generative AI interacted with more colleagues and their networks became less clustered, indicating broadening in collaboration structures. At the same time, they also concentrated more of their collaboration on ties with stronger prior histories, deepening reliance on already trusted colleagues. Together, these findings suggest that, while generative AI changes how people work, it may not displace human-to-human interactions.

papers.title: The scintillating fibre beam monitor for the CHNet-MAXI experiment at ISIS: characterisation of the light collection and detection system
papers.abstract: The CHNet-MAXI experiment at ISIS aims at a non-destructive isotopic characterisation of lead samples, based on muonic atom formation. A custom scintillation-based detector is used for the reconstruction of the time and space distributions of the low-energy muon beam employed in the experiment. The beam monitor consists of two orthogonal planes of 10 cm-long, 3 mm $\times$ 3 mm square scintillating fibres, totalling 64 fibres, read out by four arrays of 16 Hamamatsu S14160-3015PS SiPMs each. The optical performance of the detector has been characterised, focusing on the SiPM behaviour, and also checking and correcting the uniformity of the light response across channels with a $^{60}$ Co source. A first detector test with protons at the CNAO-XPR has been carried out. The results of the Geant4 simulation of the detector, fundamental for the detector operation and data analysis, are also presented. All these activities are preliminary to the final detector operation in the CHNet-MAXI experiment at the RIKEN-RAL Port4 decay muon beamline at ISIS.

The CHNet-MAXI (Cultural Heritage Network - Muonic Atom X-ray spectroscopy for Isotopic analysis) experiment aims to develop a non-invasive technique (Muonic Atom X-ray Emission Spectrometry, μ\upmu-XES) to determine the Pb isotopic ratios in ancient artefacts [8]. The stable isotopes of lead are 204Pb, 206Pb, 207Pb, and 208Pb. Since 204Pb is primordial, and 206Pb, 207Pb, 208Pb are at the end of radioactive chains, their ratio provides important information about the provenance of lead-containing artefacts. This experiment is funded by the INFN CSN5 as part of the INFN Cultural Heritage Network (CHNet)[6].

This design follows the experience gained with the FAMU[9, 1] experiment beam monitor development[3, 12]. papers.title: Distributed Swarm Morphogenesis with Neural Cellular Automata
papers.abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site assignment and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.

papers.intro:
Swarm morphogenesis aims to generate large-scale physical structures through local interactions among robots. Applications include coordinated aerial displays, distributed inspection, search, surveillance, and defence, where formations may need to scale or adapt across environments. Reliance on GPS, motion capture, or centralized estimation can limit applicability where signals or infrastructure are unavailable, including GNSS-denied environments; relative-sensing approaches instead use onboard vision [1], ranging and odometry [2], or distance-only measurements [3, 4]. In this paper, we consider local-relative sensing without globally referenced robot poses.

Distributed task-allocation methods assign tasks to robots [5], while assignment-based shape-formation methods allocate or dynamically select robot goals [6, 7]. Assignment-free methods guide robots to fill specified shapes without explicit robot-to-site assignments [8, 9]. These approaches differ in how robots occupy the shape, but both assume its geometry is supplied beforehand. We instead consider distributed attachment-site discovery. Essentially, we determine which physical attachment sites should exist as the morphology develops, so that a global structure can emerge from a local developmental rule trained offline, rather than an explicitly stored goal list. Existing assignment and control methods then coordinate robots to occupy these sites.

papers.title: POS-Signature Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Dependency Parsing
papers.abstract: Demonstrations for in-context learning are often retrieved by semantic similarity, which may be a poor proxy for relevance in structured prediction. We study demonstration selection for Universal Dependencies parsing with a POS-signature policy that represents sentences with weighted part-of-speech statistics and retrieves three length-compatible, gold-parsed examples from the labeled training split. We evaluate two open-weight language models without fine-tuning on all 2,077 sentences of the UD English Web Treebank test set, comparing the policy with shot- and format-matched fixed and semantic three-shot baselines, as well as zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and critique-refinement systems. POS-signature retrieval yields the highest labeled attachment score among the tested prompting systems for both models (72.4 and 73.2), outperforming semantic retrieval by 1.9 and 2.7 points; paired-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals exclude zero for both contrasts. Chain-of-thought and refinement comparisons vary across models. These exploratory results favor the tested POS-signature retrieval approach on English-EWT. We release the prompts, archived outputs, and evaluation code.

papers.title: WADE: An LSTM-Based Anomaly Detection Engine for WebAssembly Applications
papers.abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) enables near-native performance for web applications through a portable and sandboxed execution model. However, its limited runtime protection mechanisms (e.g., the lack of stack canaries and address space layout randomization (ASLR)) leave Wasm applications vulnerable to traditional attacks. We present WADE (WebAssembly Anomaly Detection Engine), a system that detects anomalous runtime behaviors in browser-executed WebAssembly applications. WADE monitors function-level execution traces collected under benign conditions and trains a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn the normal execution behavior of each application. At runtime, the model flags deviations from these learned patterns as potential attacks. Unlike signature-based approaches, WADE builds application-specific behavioral models, enabling detection of both known and previously unseen attacks without per-vulnerability signatures. We evaluate WADE on a dataset of 67 WebAssembly applications spanning ten vulnerability classes, achieving zero false negatives and a 0.42% false positive rate.

WebAssembly (Wasm) has rapidly evolved into a key technology for high-performance web applications. It provides a portable, low-level binary format that enables near-native execution speeds in the browser, supporting a wide range of use cases (e.g., from 3D rendering and gaming to cryptographic computations and machine learning inference) directly on the client side. Its efficiency, combined with language-agnostic compilation support, has made WebAssembly an integral component of modern web platforms.

Although Wasm was designed with security in mind, it still exposes a non-negligible attack surface. Its sandboxing model enforces isolation between the executing module and the host environment, and its type-safe interface prevents certain classes of memory violations. However, several critical runtime protection mechanisms commonly available in native environments are absent. As a result, traditional memory-corruption attacks, including buffer overflows and format-string vulnerabilities, can still subvert a WebAssembly module’s control flow and compromise its intended execution logic within the sandbox.

papers.title: An explicit bound on $|ζ_K(1+it)|$
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $n$ and discriminant $Δ$. The estimate $|ζ_K(1+it)|\le C_K\log{t}$, where $C_K$ is an unspecified constant depending on $K$, is a well--known result in the literature. We obtain an explicit upper bound for $|ζ_K(1+it)|$, depending only on $n$ and $Δ$. We also show how improvements on the bound depend on improvements on estimates of the ideal counting function $I_K$ and the residue of $ζ_K$ at $s=1$.

papers.title: Fuglede's theorem in the Heisenberg group
papers.abstract: We prove a Fuglede-type quantitative isoperimetric inequality for the Pansu sphere, the conjectured isoperimetric set in the sub-Riemannian Heisenberg group $\mathbb{H}^1$. We show that, among suitable volume-preserving normal perturbations of the Pansu sphere that are small in a weighted $C^2$-norm, the difference between the sub-Riemannian perimeters of the perturbed and unperturbed regions is bounded below by a positive constant times the square of their $L^1$-distance. The proof is based on a Riemannian approximation argument with uniform estimates.

papers.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning with Time-Varying Movement Costs
papers.abstract: We study strongly adaptive regret for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) with time-varying movement costs, a setting that evaluates a learner's performance over arbitrary sub-intervals. This framework captures complex sequential decision-making problems where both the environment and the cost of switching decisions fluctuate over time. We propose a novel algorithm which, for any interval $[a,b] \subseteq [T]$, achieves a data-dependent regret bound of $ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \sqrt{(D^2+DP_{[a,b]})\sum_{t \in [a,b]}(\|g_t\|^2+λ_t\|g_t\|)} \right) $, where $D$ is the diameter of the decision domain, $P_{[a,b]}$ is the path length of the comparator sequence over $[a,b]$, $g_t$ is the gradient of the loss, and $λ_t$ is the movement-cost coefficient at round $t$. Key to our approach is a novel reduction to sleeping experts with movement costs, a previously unexplored variant that is of independent interest. As a result of this development, we further establish the first strongly-adaptive guarantees under delayed feedback. Our approach also naturally extends to OCO with time-varying memory, where we obtain strongly-adaptive guarantees which improve the best-known bounds.

Online convex optimization (OCO) (Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006; Hazan, 2016; Orabona, 2019) is a fundamental framework for sequential decision making under uncertainty. At each round, a learner selects a decision wtw_{t} in a convex decision set 𝒲\mathcal{W} before observing the current loss function ft:𝒲→ℝf_{t}:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{R}, and then incurring the corresponding loss ft​(wt)f_{t}(w_{t}). The objective is to design algorithms whose cumulative loss is close to that of a benchmark comparator sequence chosen in hindsight. Classic (static) regret guarantees compare the learner’s performance against a single fixed comparator over the entire time horizon, and are therefore most appropriate in stationary environments. However, many modern applications are inherently non-stationary: the best decision may evolve over time, the environment may undergo abrupt shifts, and the performance on short or intermediate time intervals can be just as important as performance over the full horizon.

papers.title: Sparse Bayesian Neural Networks via Sticky Piecewise Deterministic Markov Processes
papers.abstract: There is growing evidence that the performance of a neural network depends largely on a small subset of its weights, which are typically identified by training a dense network and pruning it afterwards. Within a Bayesian framework, pruning can be directly incorporated through a spike-and-slab prior, providing a proper treatment of the uncertainties involved, both with respect to pruning and to parameter uncertainty. In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), sampling by MCMC is notoriously hard. We demonstrate that modern Monte Carlo methods based on piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) can be used to sample posteriors of BNNs asymptotically exact whenever numerically constructed rate bounds hold. Spike-and-slab priors can be incorporated through sticky versions of the PDMPs, setting weights exactly to zero during sampling. We examine the predictive performance and convergence of the samplers, and show that sparse BNNs sampled this way can be more robust to input noise than dense ones.

papers.intro:
Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) quantify uncertainty for models that are otherwise prone to overconfidence, but characterizing their posterior over the network weights is difficult. Variational inference (Graves, 2011) replaces the posterior with a tractable distribution, whereas stochastic gradient samplers (Welling and Teh, 2011; Chen et al., 2014) use minibatches, which scales well but introduces bias. Asymptotically exact samplers target the posterior without bias and have been shown feasible for larger networks (Izmailov et al., 2021b; Sommer et al., 2024), but remain too costly to be practical.

Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) quantify uncertainty for models that are otherwise prone to overconfidence, but characterizing their posterior over the network weights is difficult. Variational inference (Graves, 2011) replaces the posterior with a tractable distribution, whereas stochastic gradient samplers (Welling and Teh, 2011; Chen et al., 2014) use minibatches, which scales well but introduces bias. Asymptotically exact samplers target the posterior without bias and have been shown feasible for larger networks (Izmailov et al., 2021b; Sommer et al., 2024), but remain too costly to be practical.

Computational cost is not the only problem in BNNs. The networks are highly over-parametrized, which makes Bayesian inference difficult as the parameters are not identifiable due to symmetries (Papamarkou et al., 2022). Furthermore, weights that do not affect the data fit, such as those connected to inputs that are zero across the training set, retain their prior variance in the posterior, which can make BNNs less robust to covariate shift than networks trained by SGD (Izmailov et al., 2021b; Izmailov et al., 2021a). Setting such weights to zero removes this source of variance, and BNNs can indeed be pruned substantially with little loss of predictive performance (Molchanov et al., 2017; Hubin and Storvik, 2024), suggesting that a subset of the parameters suffices to characterize the posterior predictive. The canonical method for sparsifying a Bayesian model is the spike-and-slab prior (Mitchell and Beauchamp, 1988), which places positive prior probability on parameters being exactly zero, so that parameters the data do not inform are exactly zero in most draws. Traditionally, it has been hard to make use of spike-and-slab priors in Bayesian deep learning, as the efficient gradient-based samplers require a differentiable density, which a prior with point masses at zero does not have. Thus, such priors have been applied only approximately (Hubin and Storvik, 2024).

Piecewise deterministic Markov process samplers (Fearnhead et al., 2018, PDMPs,) are a class of non-reversible, continuous-time Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers. A trajectory is simulated over a time horizon TT from a process that evolves deterministically between random event times, constructed so that the target distribution is the position marginal of its stationary distribution. Once the trajectory is long enough, samples are obtained by evaluating the position at time points along the path. Such methods have received great interest recently (Bierkens et al., 2019; Corbella et al., 2022; Fearnhead et al., 2024; Chevallier et al., 2025), as exact subsampling can keep their cost per effective sample constant in the dataset size (super-efficiency). Furthermore, the PDMP samplers can be made sticky (Bierkens et al., 2023b), so that they target the posterior under a spike-and-slab prior directly, and sparsity arises during sampling without any post-processing or thresholding.

papers.title: Ginzburg-Landau Theory with Elastic Incompatibility Describes the Liquid-G-phase-Crystal State Diagram
papers.abstract: We derive a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory for the metastable heterogeneous G state reported in deeply undercooled metallic liquids. The central result is that type-II-like mixed-state physics can emerge structurally with the random internal stress field playing the role of the magnetic field. Frozen eigenstrain due to elastic incompatibility between ordered cores and the amorphous matrix generates incompatible stress, while the non-affine internal strain in the liquid-like matrix in between the ordered cores relaxes that stress over a finite screening length $λ_σ$ (analogous to the London length in the superconducting problem). Structural order heals over a distinct mechanically-dressed length $ξ_G$; their ratio $κ_G=λ_σ/ξ_G$ provides the structural counterpart of the Ginzburg-Landau parameter. Because the matrix is transiently rigid yet locally relaxational only over an intermediate time window, the same mechanism selects crystal for slow protocols, a heterogeneous G state at intermediate rates, and a homogeneous L-like glass under rapid arrest. Residual incompatibility frustrates coarsening, allowing finite ordered cores and screened, orientation-dependent core interactions. The resulting texture is an inverted Abrikosov analogue: structural order resides in the cores, whereas incompatible-stress screening is carried by the surrounding disordered matrix. The theory yields direct simulation and experimental tests through stress-decay, structural-healing, non-affine-susceptibility, and kinetic measurements.

papers.intro:
Mixed states provide some of the clearest examples of how competing length scales can reorganize a phase transition. In a type-II superconductor, the competition between the coherence length and the magnetic penetration depth permits an intermediate vortex state rather than a direct transition between spatially homogeneous phases. A natural question is whether an analogous mechanism can arise in structural condensed matter problems, where the competing field is mechanical rather than electromagnetic and where elastic compatibility and nonaffine displacements produce the screening mechanism.

Mixed states provide some of the clearest examples of how competing length scales can reorganize a phase transition. In a type-II superconductor, the competition between the coherence length and the magnetic penetration depth permits an intermediate vortex state rather than a direct transition between spatially homogeneous phases. A natural question is whether an analogous mechanism can arise in structural condensed matter problems, where the competing field is mechanical rather than electromagnetic and where elastic compatibility and nonaffine displacements produce the screening mechanism.

Deeply undercooled metallic liquids offer a concrete setting in which to ask this question. Molecular-dynamics studies of Ag, Cu–Ag, and Cu–Zr report a first-order transformation from a homogeneous liquid state (L) to a metastable, mechanically rigid and spatially heterogeneous glassy state (G), in competition with crystallization into the equilibrium crystal (X) [3, 4, 5, 6]. The G state is not a homogeneous “partly crystalline” phase. It consists of defective, crystal-like ordered cores embedded in and separated by a continuous disordered liquid-like matrix, while long-range translational order remains absent. papers.title: Low-Complexity Wideband Channel Estimation for ISAC in Analog Millimeter-Wave Systems
papers.abstract: Accurate wideband channel estimation is a key enabler for millimeter-wave (mmWave) integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems. In the narrowband scenario, the Transformed Spatial Domain Channel Estimation (TSDCE) method was previously shown to provide fast and accurate angle estimation with substantially lower complexity than conventional compressed-sensing approaches based on orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP). However, wideband ISAC scenarios additionally require delay estimation, making joint angle-delay sparse recovery computationally expensive due to the multidimensional dictionary search. In this paper, we propose a wideband extension of TSDCE, namely TSDCE-TD, which incorporates time-domain support and decouples angle and delay estimation. Two variations are proposed for delay estimation: TSDCE-TD (Dict), which uses a one-dimensional delay dictionary, and TSDCE-TD (FFT), which applies Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) zero-padding interpolation. Path estimates are iteratively refined through successive interference cancellation and alternating angle-delay updates. Simulation results show that the proposed methods outperform OMP-based baselines under practical dictionary sizes, while achieving comparable performance at high-resolution settings with substantially lower computational complexity. Moreover, the angle-delay estimates obtained using the proposed approach enable accurate single-anchor indoor localization in a ray-traced environment, achieving sub-20 cm positioning errors and satisfying practical indoor positioning requirements.

papers.intro:
Millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication is fundamental to fifth-generation (5G) and sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, leveraging the abundant spectrum in the 30–300 GHz band [1]. The short wavelengths enable compact antenna arrays with highly directional beamforming to overcome severe path loss propagation. Building on these capabilities, mmWave is increasingly explored for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) [2], where large bandwidths and directional beams provide fine spatial resolution, accurate target detection, and enhanced data rates [3]. A fundamental characteristic of mmWave propagation channels is their inherent sparsity, where only a few dominant propagation paths typically contribute to the received signal. This sparse structure has been widely exploited in channel estimation through compressed sensing and sparse recovery techniques, with orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) and its variants being among the most commonly adopted approaches. More recently, sparse recovery methods have also been extended to ISAC applications, including user localization [4], target detection [5], classification [6], and environment sensing [7]. Despite their effectiveness, OMP-based approaches often suffer from relatively high computational complexity due to their iterative dictionary atom selection and signal reconstruction procedures, particularly in wideband large-scale mmWave systems. This motivates the development of lower-complexity sparse recovery techniques that can maintain accurate sensing and estimation performance while enabling faster processing for practical ISAC deployments [4].

In this work, we present a low-complexity algorithm for sparse recovery in mmWave ISAC systems, referred to as TSDCE with Time-Domain support (TSDCE-TD), which extends the Transformed Spatial Domain Channel Estimation (TSDCE) algorithm [8] to include delay estimation. Two variants are analyzed. First, TSDCE-TD (Dict) utilizes a one-dimensional delay dictionary, following an approach analogous to OMP-based methods but restricted solely to the delay dimension, where the computational cost scales only linearly with the grid size. Second, TSDCE-TD (FFT) leverages Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) zero-padding interpolation, thereby yielding the lowest computational complexity. The proposed approaches are evaluated against OMP-based baselines in terms of channel estimation accuracy, computational complexity, and user positioning performance within a ray-traced indoor scenario. Simulation results show that TSDCE-TD achieves channel estimation accuracy comparable to or better than OMP-based methods, while reducing complexity by several orders of magnitude, and that the recovered parameters are sufficient for accurate indoor localization.

papers.title: Foliations on abelian surfaces in positive characteristic
papers.abstract: This paper studies foliations on abelian surfaces in positive characteristic. We provide an explicit description of all smooth foliations, linear and turbulent, and establish criteria for being $p$-closed. We explicitly determine the moduli spaces of such foliations. We give an application to the construction of $p$-closed foliations, with mild singularities, on Kummer $K3$-surfaces in positive characteristics.
papers.intro:
The study of foliations is an important theme in topology and differential equations and is an active and vast area of research. Foliations on real manifolds can be thought of as a decomposition of a manifold into a disjoint union of leaves, where locally the leaves have the structure of the collection of dd-dimensional planes parallel to ℝd×{0n−d}\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\{0^{n-d}\} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. From a different perspective, foliations can be thought of as a geometric incarnation of the study of differential equations, where the connection is made through Frobenius’ theorem, which gives necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of a maximal set of independent solutions to an overdetermined system of first-order homogeneous linear partial differential equations.

papers.title: A Stationary Mean-Field Model for Carbon Market Stability Reserve
papers.abstract: We formulate the design of a market stability reserve as a stationary mean-field singular control problem. The allowance balance follows a regime-switching diffusion, while the regulator injects or withdraws allowances through bounded-variation controls. The objective trades off the average allowance balance, its stationary dispersion, deviations from a long-run target, and intervention costs. The optimal policy is a regime-dependent band rule characterized by four reflecting thresholds. Its computation reduces to a scalar fixed-point problem combining a coupled variational inequality with the invariant distribution of the reflected process. A calibration to the EU ETS yields thresholds of the same order of magnitude as the existing Market Stability Reserve rule. Comparative statics show that volatility is the main determinant of the intervention band, whereas the frequency and duration of crisis regimes have limited effects. A simpler two-threshold policy based on average regime dynamics closely reproduces the optimal regime-dependent policy in terms of liquidity and intervention volumes.

papers.intro:
To decarbonize its economy, the European Union has developed a broad set of transition instruments, combining direct support for low-carbon technologies, renewable energy subsidies, regulatory standards, and carbon pricing. Among these instruments, the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is one of the central pillars of the EU decarbonization strategy. Launched in 2005, the EU ETS is the world’s first international carbon market and is currently in its fourth trading phase. It covers greenhouse gas emissions from around 15,000 installations in the energy sector and manufacturing industry, as well as aviation within its scope; since 2024, it also covers maritime transport. Overall, the system accounts for roughly 35–40 percent of the EU’s greenhouse gas emissions. This achievement is a spectacular application of the seminal work of Montgomery (1972).
