For this reason and to align the needs of the firms covered by the ETS together with the objectives of emissions reduction, the EU designed and adopted in 2015 a stabilising system named the Market Stability Reserve (MSR). The MSR is a rule-based mechanism that adjusts auction volumes in response to the total number of allowances in circulation (TNAC). In the 2014 Commission proposal (European Commission, 2014, sec. 6.2.3), allowances are added to the reserve whenever the TNAC exceeds 833833 million allowances and released whenever it falls below 400400 million. The use of the TNAC to determine the increase and decrease of allowances to be auctionned is explicitly justified as a direct measure of the supply–demand imbalance in the EU ETS, compared to more indirect indicators such as GDP, fuel prices, or weather conditions. The proposal further explains that the upper and lower thresholds were determined following consultations with stakeholders and were meant to define a range in which, according to market experience, the system could operate in an orderly manner. An associated release volume of 100100 million allowances per year was chosen to ensure predictability and gradual adjustment, and was justified as being roughly 5%5\% of current annual EU ETS emissions, which historical experience suggested would be sufficient even in the presence of sudden and strong increases in demand.

This paper provides, to the best of our knowledge, a first attempt to model an optimal Market Stability Reserve directly. The objective is to describe how a regulator should define the lower and upper boundaries of an MSR in order to provide firms with the flow of permits needed to cover their emissions, while remaining consistent with long-run decarbonization objectives. In our model, the total number of allowances in circulation is represented by a controlled consumption process: allowances are depleted by emissions, while the regulator can adjust their supply through cumulative injections and withdrawals. The regulator’s objective combines three components. The first one penalizes the aggregate volume of allowances, reflecting the will to operate a market under a minimal amount of allowances. The second penalizes fluctuations in the stock of allowances in circulation, capturing the idea that excessive volatility in allowance availability may lead to an excess in price volatility and destabilize the market. The third penalizes deviations from a target level, interpreted as the amount of allowances needed for the market to operate normally over a yearly horizon and also, the long-term target of emissions rate the regulator wishes to set.

In our model, the total number of allowances in circulation is represented by a controlled consumption process: allowances are depleted by emissions, while the regulator can adjust their supply through cumulative injections and withdrawals. The regulator’s objective combines three components. The first one penalizes the aggregate volume of allowances, reflecting the will to operate a market under a minimal amount of allowances. The second penalizes fluctuations in the stock of allowances in circulation, capturing the idea that excessive volatility in allowance availability may lead to an excess in price volatility and destabilize the market. The third penalizes deviations from a target level, interpreted as the amount of allowances needed for the market to operate normally over a yearly horizon and also, the long-term target of emissions rate the regulator wishes to set.

To account for unexpected macroeconomic or energy-market shocks, the emissions rate is allowed to switch between two regimes according to a continuous-time Markov chain. This specification captures the fact that emissions needs may differ substantially between normal periods and crisis periods, while the regulator observes the current regime and adjusts allowance injections accordingly. The resulting problem is a singular stochastic control problem with regime switching, in which the regulator chooses when and how much to inject into or withdraw from the market so as to stabilize the allowance stock while taking into account the long-run allowance level generated by its own intervention policy.

papers.title: Quantitative nodal domain count for Maass forms
papers.abstract: We consider a real even Hecke-Maass cusp form $φ$ on the modular surface, with Laplace eigenvalue $1/4+T^2$. We prove that its restriction to any fixed compact segment $β$ of the vertical geodesic above $i$ has $\gg_{β,\varepsilon} T^{1/6-\varepsilon}$ sign changes, yielding the same lower bound for the number of distinct inert nodal domains meeting the segment. Building on ideas of Jang-Jung and Jung-Young, we study correlations between values at points on the vertical geodesic separated by distances of order $T^{-1}$. Using arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity and Dirichlet-polynomial estimates, we show that the correlation is negative for a suitable choice of separation. An elementary counting argument and the Iwaniec-Sarnak supremum bound then give the claimed lower bound.

papers.title: A generalization of Gordon's Theorem to arbitrary winding number
papers.abstract: We study minimizers of the Keplerian action functional with homogeneous potential of type $1/|u|^α$ on periodic loops with fixed winding number $k \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$. This extends the classical theorems of Gordon and Venturelli, closing the previously open case $α\in (1,2)$, $|k|\geq 2$. We show that the $k$-circular solution loses local minimality below the threshold $α= 2-1/|k|^2$, and that minimizers are collision-free above $α= 2-1/|k|$. Combining these results with the existence of precessing periodic orbits in between, we obtain a full classification of the minimizer in terms of $α$ and $k$, which we also verify numerically for $k=2$.

papers.title: Beyond 3SUM-Hardness for Geometric Problems
papers.abstract: Since the early days of fine-grained complexity, many geometric problems have been shown to require quadratic time under the 3SUM Hypothesis. But as the 3SUM Hypothesis was recently refuted, these lower bounds have lost their foundation. In this note we point out that many of them can be recovered under an alternative hardness assumption, the $k$-AP Hypothesis. The required changes to the proofs are trivial, so the lower bounds remain just as easy to teach.

papers.intro:
Even before “fine-grained complexity” became a field with a name, Gajentaan and Overmars [19] established some of its very first conditional lower bounds. Their starting point was the 3SUM Hypothesis, which postulated that no algorithm can decide in time O⁡(n2−ϵ)O(n^{2-\epsilon}) (for any constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0) whether a given set of nn numbers contains a solution to a+b=ca+b=c. From this assumption, they derived quadratic-time lower bounds for a diverse set of geometric problems: detecting three collinear points, finding separating lines, covering, visibility and motion planning problems, and many more. Follow-up work kept adding to this list [15, 6, 10, 18, 1, 8, 26, 5, 17, 13, 7, 12, 11, 23, 21, 20, 2, 9, 24]. Part of the appeal of these lower bounds is their simplicity: most of the reductions are elementary and can be explained with a single picture. Unsurprisingly, they have become standard material in courses on fine-grained complexity, where they are often among the very first lower bounds that students encounter.

Part of the appeal of these lower bounds is their simplicity: most of the reductions are elementary and can be explained with a single picture. Unsurprisingly, they have become standard material in courses on fine-grained complexity, where they are often among the very first lower bounds that students encounter.

But recently, fine-grained complexity witnessed a spectacular breakthrough: Alman and Vassilevska Williams [3] gave a truly subquadratic algorithm for 3SUM, thereby refuting the 3SUM Hypothesis. At the same time and based on the same new technique, the APSP Hypothesis was refuted as well.11 1 The APSP Hypothesis postulates that no algorithm can compute all pairs of distances in a given nn-vertex directed edge-weighted graph in time O⁡(n3−ϵ)O(n^{3-\epsilon}) (for any constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0). As a consequence, a large body of conditional lower bounds based on these two hypotheses has become vacuous. The reductions themselves of course remain correct, but a reduction from 3SUM or APSP no longer constitutes evidence that a problem is hard. For algorithm design, this is good news: the complexity of the many 3SUM- or APSP-hard problems is now open, and for each of them we may hope for a polynomially faster algorithm. But at the same time, many of these problems will likely remain hard for other reasons. Sorting out which is which, either by designing faster algorithms or by restoring hardness results under other credible hypotheses, will be an important task for the fine-grained complexity community now.

The observation is simple, and we make no claim of technical depth. The reason for writing this note is more practical: several colleagues I talked to are teaching courses on fine-grained complexity this semester, and many of the lower bounds they had planned to cover have disappeared overnight. A kk-term arithmetic progression (or kk-AP for short) is a sequence of numbers of the form a,a+d,a+2​d,…,a+(k−1)​da,a+d,a+2d,\dots,a+(k-1)d; we call it nontrivial if d≠0d\neq 0. In the kk-AP Detection problem the task is to decide whether a given set A⊆{1,…,N}A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\} contains a nontrivial kk-AP. (Note that NN bounds the universe, and not just the size of AA.) The trivial algorithm enumerates the first two terms a,a+d∈Aa,a+d\in A and tests whether the remaining k−2k-2 terms are present in AA, in total time O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}). For k=3k=3 there is a much faster O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N)-time algorithm based on the Fast Fourier Transform. For k≥4k\geq 4, however, no polynomial improvement over the trivial algorithm is known, which motivated the following hypothesis for all constants k≥4k\geq 4 [16].

As argued before, the smallest interesting case is k=4k=4. Moreover, it is known that the kk-AP Hypothesis implies the (k+1)(k+1)-AP Hypothesis [16], and so the 44-AP Hypothesis is the strongest member of this family. The lower bounds in this note hold even under the weakest one: it suffices that the kk-AP Hypothesis holds for some constant k≥4k\geq 4.

Why should we believe in the kk-AP Hypothesis, especially now that 3SUM has been refuted? First, let us take a step back. Fine-grained complexity has never been about hardness for its own sake. Its ultimate goal is to find the fastest possible algorithm for every problem, and its hypotheses serve as signposts that tell us where not to look: as long as a problem is hard under some hypothesis, any faster algorithm for it would refute the hypothesis, so there is little point in attacking the problem directly while the hypothesis stands. In this view, whether a hypothesis is ultimately true is less important than whether it faithfully marks the limits of our current algorithmic techniques. Read in this way, this note puts many of the signposts for geometric problems back in place: whoever hopes to solve one of these problems faster should first find a faster algorithm for detecting arithmetic progressions. Second, there is good reason to trust this particular signpost: despite the problem’s natural appeal and its close connection to additive combinatorics, the fastest known algorithms for kk-AP Detection improve upon the trivial running time by merely subpolynomial factors [16, Section 5].22 2 The fastest known algorithm has in fact improved since [16]. OpenAI recently announced quasipolynomial bounds for Szemerédi’s theorem [25]: for every k≥3k\geq 3, every set A⊆{1,…,N}A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\} without a nontrivial kk-AP has size |A|≤N/2Ω⁡((log⁡N)c)|A|\leq N/2^{\Omega((\log N)^{c})}, for some constant c=c⁡(k)>0c=c(k)>0. This immediately yields a simple algorithm: if AA is larger than this bound, the answer is yes; otherwise, the brute-force algorithm runs in time O⁡(N+|A|2)=N2/2Ω⁡((log⁡N)c)O(N+|A|^{2})=N^{2}/2^{\Omega((\log N)^{c})}. Third, the recent breakthrough [3] does not seem to extend to 44-APs easily. At its core, their algorithm is still a Strassen-like algebraic algorithm. Algorithms of this type are tailored to trilinear problems, such as matrix multiplication or 33-AP Detection. In contrast, 44-AP Detection is inherently a 44-linear problem, and to the best of our knowledge Strassen-like techniques have so far never been extended to 44-linear problems in a nontrivial way. See [16, Section 5] for a more detailed discussion of the kk-AP Hypothesis.

papers.title: Selection under partial information
papers.abstract: The selection problem asks to find the $k$-th smallest element in a given set $X$. Its complexity is well-known to be $Θ(|X|)$ for every fixed $k$. We consider the poset selection problem where a partial order $P$ on $X$ is given, and the underlying order of $X$ is guaranteed to be a linear extension of $P$. This generalizes several variants of the selection problem studied before. Our main result is an algorithm that performs $O( k + \operatorname{OPT}(P,k) )$ comparisons, where $\operatorname{OPT}(P,k)$ is the minimum number of comparisons required for the input $(P,k)$. If $P$ is a rooted tree, we obtain an $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log (k / \operatorname{OPT}) )$ algorithm, which can be further improved to $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log \log (k/\operatorname{OPT}) )$ or $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log \operatorname{OPT})$ under mild assumptions about $P$. Our algorithms are based on the work of Kaplan, Kozma, Zamir, and Zwick [SOSA 2019], who used Chazelle's soft heaps [J. ACM 2000] to simplify several older results. We introduce a new soft heap variant, the weighted soft heap, which allows greater control over which elements get corrupted.

papers.title: Research profiles and the mathematical landscape: A grassroots proposal for mathematics with AI
papers.abstract: Repeated mathematical work with AI leaves behind corrections, failed arguments, and sometimes useful ways of asking questions. I propose keeping these in a research profile that the mathematician develops and controls. The profile marks parts of the mathematical landscape according to the researcher's understanding and makes those markings available to later work with AI. This suggests experiments with individual profiles, shared readings of papers, and graduate education. It also raises mathematical questions about the landscape itself: its connections, distances, and changes under discovery. I describe two examples, searching for branches of mathematics with a common base and recovering useful questions from the history of Floer theory. The aim is to give mathematicians something to try and a part in deciding how mathematical AI develops.

papers.title: RootDown: Deploying and Benchmarking Models for Beet-Root Detection on Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Quality inspection of sugar beets after harvest and storage is critical to preserve sugar content and ensure optimal processing efficiency. The transfer of harvested beets to field clamps or trucks provides an opportunity to visually inspect individual beets automatically on loader conveyors. However, this is a challenging task as the large number of beets causes partial overlap and occlusion, complicating both annotation and detection. In this work, we propose an end-to-end image-based pipeline for detecting partially occluded sugar beets in loading scenarios as a first step toward automated quality inspection. We introduce a dedicated benchmark and present an automatic annotation strategy that leverages the SAM 3 foundation model to generate bounding boxes. We compare models trained on manually annotated and automatically generated labels. Additionally, we investigate deployment considerations by benchmarking multiple inference configurations, including execution on an edge device, under realistic operational constraints regarding precision, inference time and power consumption. Our results show that, despite substantial occlusion and inherent annotation ambiguity, foundation-model-based labels can substitute for a substantial share of manual annotation, trading labeling effort for data volume at a modest accuracy cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Raspberry Pi 5 equipped with a Hailo accelerator enables high-performance, low-power inference, making it a practical solution for mobile outdoor deployment.

papers.intro:
The availability of sugar beets during harvest far exceeds the processing capacity of sugar factories, resulting in most beets being stored in field clamps, which typically consist of several hundred thousand beets. After storage periods of up to 90 days, the clamps are transferred to sugar factories by truck, where a human estimator assesses beet quality by visual inspection, focusing on soil adhesion, topping quality and the presence of mold, rot and vegetation. Detached soil settling at the bottom of truck beds during transfer reduces the effectiveness of visual inspection, which is limited to the top layer of beets. Internal evaluations at sugar factories show that human estimators mostly base quality estimates on overall appearance and generally underestimate total soil tare. Time constraints limit the inspection of individual beets to a small number of samples. The use of an automated image-based visual inspection system during transfer can provide many advantages over manual inspection, as individual beets can be observed directly after rudimentary in-loader cleaning before soil accumulation occurs.

papers.title: ReLEAP: Upcycling Vision Datasets through Cross-Task Unification and Semi-Supervised Annotation
papers.abstract: Developing robust vision models requires large amounts of annotated data, especially for tasks involving fine-grained class distinctions under variable environmental conditions. Even in domains with numerous existing datasets, differences in annotation formats, label definitions and targeted learning tasks hinder data reuse and integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ReLEAP, a scalable Python framework for unifying heterogeneous image datasets through data-source abstraction, systematic reuse of annotations across learning tasks, and mapping of labels to a shared hierarchical taxonomy. We demonstrate its applicability in precision agriculture by integrating fifteen diverse datasets covering a broad range of plant species and annotation types. Beyond unification, ReLEAP enables systematic recycling of existing data and provides a robust foundation for learning-based annotation upcycling. Leveraging this foundation, we conduct extensive cross-dataset and fine-tuning experiments to investigate how domain-specific models trained on unified data and foundation models can be used to automatically generate higher-level annotations under unsupervised, weakly supervised and semi-supervised settings, and how dataset characteristics influence their effectiveness. Our results show that unified data access and annotation upcycling substantially expand the pool of reusable training data and annotations while improving data transparency, enabling more sustainable and resource-efficient use of existing datasets. We release the framework and trained models for academic use to support accessible and collaborative research, particularly in data-scarce and heterogeneous domains.

papers.intro:
Training broadly applicable vision models typically requires large volumes of annotated data tailored to specific domains and learning tasks. Acquiring this data remains time-consuming and resource-intensive, particularly in niche applications that are not sufficiently covered by state-of-the-art foundation models and require distinction between visually similar classes under diverse environmental conditions. Precision agriculture exemplifies this challenge: detecting and localizing specific plant species requires robust differentiation among similar plant types across varying growth stages, weather conditions and seasonal effects, all of which significantly influence visual appearance. Even with efficient recording pipelines and semi-automatic annotation tools, the efforts and required expert knowledge for fine-grained label assignment of rare species remain substantial.

papers.title: Direct Simulation of Poisson and Newton Kernel Distributions
papers.abstract: The Poisson kernel-based (PKB) distribution is a flexible and numerically convenient family on the unit sphere used for model-based clustering, uniformity testing, and directional data analysis. Available random variate generators rely on rejection from a von Mises-Fisher, angular central Gaussian, or projected Saw envelope and therefore require a rejection loop, tuning or root-finding, or a univariate setup phase. We show that none is needed. A uniformly random line through the interior point $ρμ$ meets the sphere in two points; selecting one with probability proportional to the opposite segment length returns exactly the target density. The sampler is exact, rejection- and tuning-free, uses one uniform direction and one Bernoulli draw, and costs $O(d)$ operations. We place the distribution in the power-Saw family of densities proportional to $\|x-ρμ\|^{-ξ}$ and show that, for $d\geq3$, the same construction is exact for one further exponent. This introduces the Newton kernel-based (NKB) distribution, whose normalizing constant is identically one. Across a wide grid of dimensions, concentrations, and sample sizes, the direct sampler is faster than the better of two previously recommended methods in every case, with the largest gains at moderate concentration.

papers.title: Analysing Austrian Parliamentary Speeches by Predicting Party Affiliations
papers.abstract: This paper examines speech characteristics of the Austrian National Council members (CMs). We introduce analysis methodology based on a fine-tuned BERT-Model which assigns to every speech a probability distribution over Austrian parties. These are then aggregated at the speaker and party level. We perform an extensive evaluation to ensure the quality of the generated distributions prior to further analysis. Instead of considering mis-assignments of predicted parties as a performance issue, we leverage them to derive insights about the CMs and political developments. Our findings show that parties that govern together become more similar in their speech characteristics, while, analogously, parties that are in opposition move further away from governing parties. Moreover, CMs who switch party usually adapt their speech characteristics only after the switch occurs. Finally, we publicly release a data set containing party affiliation predictions for the speeches of the Austrian National Council from 1996 to 2018.

papers.intro:
While political scientists have long analyzed party behavior through manual discourse analysis, NLP enables us to systematically quantify speech patterns, where misclassifications reveal how politicians adapt their rhetoric: aligning with coalition partners or distancing themselves in opposition. We are trying to find answers to the following research questions: Q1 :Can party political affiliations be modeled using parliamentary speeches? Q2: How are coalition and opposition relations reflected in speech behaviour? Q3: Does the switching of parties affect CM speeches?

Specifically, we explore the party-political dynamics of Austrian parliamentary speeches from 1996 to 2018. These speeches are public and represent a core part of our democratic society. Because of the vast number of speeches, this dataset represents an ideal test bed for our methodology. Furthermore, enabling analysis of this data can help both researchers and engaged citizens explore and better understand the dynamics in Parliamentary discussions. Thereby, it can help build a bridge from the National Council directly to the public. Moreover, learning more about language use within the Parliament is interesting from the perspective of social sciences as well as linguistics. Finally, our methodology could be applied to similar data from other domains, fostering research in related fields which currently mostly rely on qualitative manual methods.

papers.title: The Galactic rotation curve from the ALS III catalogue of OB Stars
papers.abstract: The Galactic rotation curve reveals the radial mass distribution of the Milky Way, but its determination depends on the tracer population. Young massive stars are the least dynamically evolved tracer, retaining the kinematics of the gas from which they formed, yet previous determinations from OB stars were confined to the solar neighbourhood. We determine the rotation curve and the solar motion from 14017 spectroscopically confirmed OB stars from the ALS III catalogue, using Gaia DR3 five-dimensional astrometry with revised distances and corrected proper motions. The curve is parameterised as a fourth-degree Chebyshev polynomial in Galactocentric radius and fitted to the proper motions by weighted least squares, solving simultaneously for the solar motion. Uncertainties are derived from 1000 bootstrap resamplings. We obtain a circular velocity at the solar radius (8.178 kpc) of 236.3 +/- 1.1 km/s, solar motion components U = 8.06 +/- 0.41, V = 10.91 +/- 0.86 and W = 7.53 +/- 0.14 km/s, and Oort constants A = 16.35 +/- 0.21 and B = -12.54 +/- 0.19 km/s/kpc. The curve rises inside the solar circle and declines gently beyond it, with a local gradient of -3.81 +/- 0.38 km/s/kpc, and is constrained between 5.5 and 11 kpc. Because the tracer is dynamically cold and the proper motions are fitted directly, no asymmetric drift correction or Jeans modelling is required, so the systematics differ from those affecting older tracers. The gentle decline beyond the solar radius agrees with determinations from older tracers where they overlap, making it unlikely to be a methodological artefact. Only the solar radial motion is poorly constrained by tangential data, without affecting the curve. The stars departing most from the curve (1474 to 1662, depending on the selection criterion) form the largest sample of OB runaway candidates to date, to be analysed in a forthcoming paper based on Gaia DR4.

Their main-sequence lifetimes are between ∼\sim3 Ma and ∼\sim30 Ma, so they remain, with few exceptions, close to their birthplaces and have undergone minimal dynamical heating. They therefore retain, to a good approximation, the velocity field of the interstellar medium out of which they formed, and constitute the dynamically coldest tracer available. It is the most complete compilation of Galactic OB stars with reliable spectroscopic identifications available, and it has been cross-matched with Gaia DR3 and provided with distances and proper motions specifically revised for bright stars. Spectroscopic confirmation removes the contamination by evolved or misclassified objects that affects photometrically selected samples. Its span in heliocentric distance is unprecedented for such a sample, reaching well beyond the solar vicinity, so the rotation curve can be mapped as a function of radius over a large fraction of the disc rather than characterised by a local gradient alone. Proper motions and distances suffice to constrain the model, so the measurement can be made from the five-dimensional Gaia astrometry alone, without recourse to spectroscopic radial velocities.

papers.title: New time-periodic solutions to the cubic conformal wave equation on $\mathbb{S}^{3}$: I Spherical symmetry
papers.abstract: We present a rigorous construction of novel time-periodic solutions to the radially symmetric cubic conformal wave equation on the Einstein cylinder $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{3}$. Their existence, hinted by the earlier numerical studies (arXiv:2504.10513), complements prior results on Cantor sets of infinitesimally small solutions. Our proof, based on the contraction principle, requires extensive computations that are performed on a computer by the means of rational arithmetic. We are able to significantly reduce their amount by a thorough analysis of the inverse of the associated linear operator, leading to sharper analytical bounds, as well as introduction of simplified versions of certain relevant operators. We provide examples of three solutions with specific frequency; however, our techniques and tools can be directly adapted to prove the existence of other solutions conjectured in (arXiv:2504.10513).

papers.title: Natural Language Autoencoders Identify Without Explaining
papers.abstract: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) express a model's internal activations in the form of readable text. The verbalizer turns an activation into an English explanation; the reconstructor then converts that explanation back into an activation, and the explanation is considered successful if the round trip brings back the original activation. We claim that this criterion evaluates whether the information is sufficient and does not address descriptive faithfulness. A sentence can contain sufficient information to make it possible to identify an activation even if it wrongly explains what the activation does: in the case of reconstruction, the primary aim is to accurately identify the activations and not to describe them. This issue has the same structure as the chain-of-thought faithfulness problem, in which verbal output that has been trained to go with a process is taken as a report on that process, and it parallels the dissociation between an individual's introspective report and the actual governing process as documented in human psychology. Although proposed as interpretability tools for the purpose of alignment, NLAs reintroduce, through unverified explanations, the epistemic problem that they were intended to resolve.
papers.intro:
More than 250 years ago, Wolfgang von Kempelen built a Mechanical Turk: a device that supposedly played chess. He wanted to impress the empress, Maria Theresa. The Turk toured around Europe, playing against Benjamin Franklin in Paris, and, after Kempelen’s death, even beating Napoleon under its later owner, Johann Maelzel. In reality, there was a chess master hiding inside the machine, while Kempelen, like a magician, would show the audience the inner gears, switches, pipes, and the whole mechanism, causing the man inside to move and hide. The most convincing part of this demonstration was actually the explanation – showing what the inside looks like, and therefore leading people to believe this was actually the best possible explanation of how the machine wins.

In reality, there was a chess master hiding inside the machine, while Kempelen, like a magician, would show the audience the inner gears, switches, pipes, and the whole mechanism, causing the man inside to move and hide. The most convincing part of this demonstration was actually the explanation – showing what the inside looks like, and therefore leading people to believe this was actually the best possible explanation of how the machine wins.

Recently, philosophy and other disciplines have taken a lot of input from interpretability, especially the fields of alignment, AI consciousness, and explainable AI, since it gives us the ability to, like in the Mechanical Turk, look inside. Interpretability investigates what exactly takes place within a model between the input and the output – its objective is to explain what an internal state means in a way that can be verified. Throughout most of the relatively short history of the field, the method of verification has been intervention – that is, going into the network, changing a state, and then seeing whether the output changes in accordance with the explanation (Lindsey et al., 2025; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). The explanation and the test are distinct from one another, and the test does not rely on the explanation.

If we want to talk about natural language autoencoders, it is first necessary to explain what autoencoders and sparse autoencoders are. An autoencoder is a type of network that is trained so that its output becomes identical to its input. It consists of two components: an encoder which converts the input into an internal code and a decoder which transforms the code back into a reconstructed output, while both parts are trained together with the aim of reducing the difference between input and output (Hinton and Salakhutdinov, 2006). Since it would be straightforward to copy the input if the code were as large as the input itself, the code is restricted – traditionally by making it smaller than the input – in order to force the network to find a concise description of the data so as to be able to reproduce it.

An autoencoder is a type of network that is trained so that its output becomes identical to its input. It consists of two components: an encoder which converts the input into an internal code and a decoder which transforms the code back into a reconstructed output, while both parts are trained together with the aim of reducing the difference between input and output (Hinton and Salakhutdinov, 2006). Since it would be straightforward to copy the input if the code were as large as the input itself, the code is restricted – traditionally by making it smaller than the input – in order to force the network to find a concise description of the data so as to be able to reproduce it.

In sparse autoencoders, on the other hand, there is a penalty imposed when too many of the code units are active at the same time, so that each input has to be reconstructed using only a small number of these units (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Ng, 2011). When language model activations are used, the superposition hypothesis holds that there are more features than there are dimensions, so the features overlap, and each neuron takes part in a great many of the features (Elhage et al., 2022). A sparse autoencoder that is trained on these activations discovers a large number of directions such that each activation is a sparse combination of just a few of these. These directions are often interpretable and may correspond to concepts, entities, syntactic patterns, or safety-related behaviors (Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024).

Natural Language Autoencoders (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) have recently been employed in order to give a clear answer to the question of why a frontier model behaved as it did. Let us now look at how they function. Two copies of the target language model are adapted for the task: an activation verbalizer (AV) converts an activation into a textual description, and an activation reconstructor (AR) takes the description and turns it back into an activation. After a supervised warm start, both of these are trained jointly in order to reduce the reconstruction error: the AR is trained by ordinary regression and the AV is trained by reinforcement learning, where the AR’s reconstruction serves as the AV’s reward. The result that engineers or users obtain is fluent English regarding the model’s internal state, generated without the need for human annotations, and regardless of the scale at which the model operates. Although the authors explain the method in detail and list its limitations, such as confabulation and the possibility of a degenerate objective, our focus is on the criterion itself and on the situation that arises when this output is passed on downstream.

Our argument, succinctly put, is that just because a reconstruction works, it only shows that the explanation has enough information to recreate the activation, but it does not prove that the explanation truly describes what the activation does – that is, it does not check whether it is actually a good explanation. Namely, a sentence can identify a state without saying anything about what that state does, and since identification is all that the reconstructor needs, the explanatory content of an NLA output is not constrained by the criterion that verifies it. We will develop this idea further, connect it to earlier examples in machine learning and psychology, and discuss what it means for using these explanations in safety checks.

papers.title: Migration as a Steady-State Execution Primitive: A Runtime for Virtual Stationarity in Low-Earth Orbit
papers.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations enable orbital edge computing for latency-critical geocentric applications, but satellite motion compresses line-of-sight communication windows to mere minutes. To maintain logical geographic proximity, a paradigm termed Virtual Stationarity (VS), applications must continuously migrate across passing satellites in the constellation. Traditional live migration mechanisms optimize individually initiated relocations or replication, but not the continuous handover between successive hosts that orbital motion requires. We reformulate live migration as a steady-state execution model and introduce a novel virtual stationarity runtime paradigm. We formalize the viability of continuous migration through a lightweight model capturing latency and availability service-level objectives (SLOs), continuous migration overhead, and the convergence bound of state replay. To satisfy these constraints, we derive a Virtual Stationarity Runtime (VSR) framework whose Migration Membrane combines Capability Virtualization and Continuous State Projection to rebind host resources and reconstruct evolving execution on a successor. Evaluation on physical heterogeneous hosts shows 95th-percentile downtime below 6 milliseconds across 300 recurrent handovers, migration time effectively invariant to memory-write rate, and no cumulative growth in migration time or continuation state. A 1,600-satellite simulation further confirms completion within orbital handover windows.
papers.intro:
By mid-2026, more than 16,200 active payloads were in orbit, more than twice the number recorded three years earlier (McDowell, 2026). This rapid proliferation is catalyzing a fundamental shift in spaceborne computing (Denby and Lucia, 2020): recent research increasingly envisions satellites not only as passive communication relays but as active compute nodes interconnected via optical ISL and linked to the ground through GSL, forming a unified distributed computing continuum that bridges space and Earth (Bhattacherjee et al., 2020; Denby and Lucia, 2020). At altitudes between 80 km and 2,000 km (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2023), LEO satellites yield single-digit-millisecond propagation delays to ground users (Bhattacherjee et al., 2020). Hosting latency-critical workloads onboard passing spacecraft can therefore exploit this physical proximity to satisfy stringent real-time SLO (Meng et al., 2023; Rong et al., 2024; Pfandzelter and Bermbach, 2024).

To maintain logical proximity, applications must therefore continuously migrate across passing spacecraft at high frequencies, elevating live migration from an exceptional terrestrial operation (Attar-Khorasani et al., 2025; He and Buyya, 2023) to a steady-state LEO execution primitive. As §2 demonstrates, canonical migration strategies fail during high-frequency handovers by causing prolonged downtime, non-convergence under write pressure, or lingering predecessor dependencies. Advanced terrestrial mechanisms rely on assumptions – such as kernel homogeneity, deterministic behavior, or extended predecessor reachability (Scheuer et al., 2026; Nadgowda et al., 2017; Bergan et al., 2010) – that collapse in orbit, where nodes differ in ISA (ISA) and payload capabilities, migration budgets are tightly bounded, and source connectivity terminates abruptly.

papers.title: InferSlice: A Reference Architecture for SLO-driven LLM Inference over a Telco Wide-Area Network
papers.abstract: LLM inference is increasingly deployed as a core service for enterprise and interactive applications, but sovereignty, compliance, latency and resource-locality requirements can limit the suitability of centralised cloud deployments. Telco operators offer geographically distributed compute and network infrastructure for addressing these constraints. However, existing LLM serving frameworks are designed for tightly coupled data centres and provide limited support for coordinating geographically distributed and heterogeneous resources. We present InferSlice, a reference architecture for Service-Level Objective (SLO)-driven LLM inference over a telco infrastructure, integrating network slicing, GPU partitioning, elastic serving and observability. Led by BT in collaboration with the University of Bristol and NVIDIA, and realised on the JOINER UK national-scale wide-area network (WAN), InferSlice is evaluated on service differentiation across tiers, elastic scale-out, client-edge bandwidth as a bottleneck, and the reach of tensor, pipeline, data parallelism, and prefill/decode disaggregation over the WAN. Our results show that, on a general-purpose telco network, tiers yield distinct latency-throughput regimes, and weight streaming shortens scale-out time. Replication is placement-insensitive but memory-bound; pipeline parallelism tolerates near- and mid-cross-site hops, while tensor parallelism and disaggregation fail beyond a single subnet hop. We share practical insights from operating SLO-driven inference on a telco network, lessons learned and open questions, and hope to encourage further research on distributed and heterogeneous LLM inference systems.

papers.title: Solvent: Long-Horizon Reasoning for Multi-Step Retrosynthesis
papers.abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis requires recursively transforming a target molecule through successive reaction steps into purchasable building blocks, and recent work has begun to draw on large language model (LLM) reasoning to tackle the task. In its latest evolution, LLM reasoning has entered the long-horizon regime: models pursue objectives across interdependent steps, interact with environments, and adapt to feedback. This shift has markedly advanced LLM capabilities, as illustrated by breakthroughs in AI-driven mathematical research. At this frontier, we introduce Solvent, an 8B LLM that successfully extends long-horizon reasoning to multi-step retrosynthesis. Through a two-round post-training curriculum, Solvent learns to interleave iterative synthesis planning, external availability verification, and adaptive route revision. Experiments show that, following a $2.1\times$ performance boost from RL, Solvent scores 61.86% across four benchmarks, surpassing mid-scale language models and prior search-based retrosynthesis systems, and rivaling frontier trillion-parameter LLMs.

papers.intro:
Retrosynthetic planning plays a central role in organic synthesis and drug discovery (Corey, 1991; Zheng et al., 2022) by working backward from a complex target molecule to identify simpler, readily accessible precursors from which the target can be synthesized. This task is studied at two levels of granularity. Single-step retrosynthesis predicts the immediate reactants capable of producing a specified product through one chemical transformation (Jiang et al., 2023). Multi-step planning further requires a sequence of interdependent decisions that recursively decomposes the target into commercially available building blocks (Zheng et al., 2022; Segler et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020).

This task is studied at two levels of granularity. Single-step retrosynthesis predicts the immediate reactants capable of producing a specified product through one chemical transformation (Jiang et al., 2023). Multi-step planning further requires a sequence of interdependent decisions that recursively decomposes the target into commercially available building blocks (Zheng et al., 2022; Segler et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020).

Traditional AI-based multi-step retrosynthesis casts route planning as an explicit search built on single-step reaction proposals. Progress has come from improving the local proposal model itself and from learning value functions that prioritize expansions in search algorithms (Segler et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023). This decomposition has made large-scale synthesis planning practical, but it also ties route recovery to the coverage of the single-step model, incurs substantial search costs as routes deepen, and leaves both the global chemical analysis of the target and the rationale behind individual bond disconnections implicit in the search procedure.

Recently, large language models (LLMs) have evolved from single-turn chatbots into long-horizon agents, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in mathematics, coding, and scientific problem solving through persistent iteration across reasoning, verifying, and revising (Dong et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026b; Alpöge & Furman, 2026). However, this paradigm remains underexplored in multi-step retrosynthesis, a task naturally suited to long-horizon reasoning, with route construction involving recursive subproblems, precursor checking, and feedback-guided revision. Existing approaches refine LLM-generated routes through external optimization or search (Wang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026), guide planning over reaction candidates supplied by single-step models (Liu et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026), or generate a complete route directly in one turn (Wang et al., 2026). Across these designs, the LLM’s reasoning capacity remains constrained.

We introduce Solvent, an 8B LLM that frames multi-step retrosynthesis as a long-horizon task, solving it through iterative planning, external verification, and adaptive revision. Solvent jointly reasons over global strategy and stepwise disconnections, checks precursor availability against a building-block inventory, and updates proposed routes accordingly, keeping all retrosynthetic decisions within the model. Achieving this requires retrosynthetic knowledge and the capacity for continual interaction with the environment, which we develop in Solvent through a two-round, multistage post-training curriculum. The first round develops a seed policy that incorporates retrosynthetic knowledge and exhibits a stable pattern of long-horizon reasoning; the second bootstraps a stronger starting policy, preparing the model for final RL that boosts its capabilities. The resulting model shows strategic chemical insight, devising protecting-group schemes and convergent routes where appropriate.

papers.title: The Verra involution on special cubic fourfolds
papers.abstract: We present a detailed study of the Hodge theory, geometry and derived categories of Verra fourfolds, and their relationship with twisted K3 surfaces and cubic fourfolds. We classify Brauer classes of Verra type on K3 surfaces of degree 2, and use this to derive an explicit counting formula for Fourier--Mukai partners of a large class of Verra fourfolds. We develop the basic theory of cohomology of Verra fourfolds and apply it to prove a derived Torelli theorem for a large class of Verra fourfolds. As an application, we prove that L-equivalent Verra fourfolds in this class are Fourier--Mukai partners, and conjecture that this implication holds for all Verra fourfolds. We then give a construction of cubic fourfolds birational to Verra fourfolds. The construction yields examples of cubic and Verra fourfolds whose associated twisted K3 surfaces have non-trivial Brauer classes. Therefore, these fourfolds are expected to be irrational.

papers.title: Decision Timescales in Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control: Theory, Methodology, and Validation
papers.abstract: Max-pressure (MP) control adapts signal phases to prevailing traffic states, but its decision timescale is typically fixed a priori. This paper treats the decision timescale as an explicit dimension of MP control. We first characterize the trade-off between responsiveness and switching efficiency by quantifying how an equivalent switching loss reduces service capacity over a finite decision interval. This yields a load-dependent critical timescale determined by switching loss and normalized traffic load, together with a performance-oriented operating range above the stability boundary. Building on this result, we propose Variable-Timescale Max-Pressure (VT-MP), in which each intersection selects its decision interval according to local operating conditions, allowing the control timescale to vary across time and space. We establish strong stability of the resulting asynchronous heterogeneous controller under uniformly admissible local loads and bounded decision intervals, and introduce a downstream receiving-supply correction for finite-storage implementation. Three experiments provide mechanism validation and network-level evaluation. A single-intersection experiment confirms that the preferred decision interval increases systematically with traffic load and follows the derived characteristic timescales. In a store-and-forward network, heterogeneous VT-MP reduces total queueing time by 31.0% relative to the best fixed-interval benchmark. In a microscopic 5x5 SUMO network, it reduces mean trip delay by 24.3%, from 213.3 s to 161.5 s, and peak network accumulation by 12.3%. These findings show that the MP decision timescale should be treated as a traffic-state-dependent control variable rather than a fixed implementation parameter.

papers.intro:
Urban traffic signal control requires allocating limited intersection capacity in response to traffic conditions that vary across both space and time, a problem that has motivated a broad range of traffic-responsive and network-wide control strategies (Papageorgiou et al. 2003, Diakaki et al. 2002, Aboudolas et al. 2009). Among network-level traffic-responsive control approaches, Max-Pressure (MP) control has attracted sustained interest because it combines a decentralized control structure with rigorous network-level stability properties. Originating from backpressure scheduling for constrained queueing networks (Tassiulas and Ephremides 1992), MP selects signal phases according to pressure differences between upstream and downstream traffic states. Its application to urban traffic networks established that locally computed signal decisions can stabilize network queues for admissible demand under standard store-and-forward assumptions (Wongpiromsarn et al. 2012, Varaiya 2013). Subsequent work further developed decentralized MP formulations and examined their implementation in urban networks (Le et al. 2015). The resulting combination of traffic responsiveness, low computational complexity, decentralized operation, and analytical stability guarantees has made MP an important framework for network traffic signal control (Levin 2023).

The resulting combination of traffic responsiveness, low computational complexity, decentralized operation, and analytical stability guarantees has made MP an important framework for network traffic signal control (Levin 2023).

A major direction in the development of MP has been to enrich the traffic information represented by pressure. The original queue-based formulation, commonly referred to as Q-MP, uses vehicle queues on upstream and downstream movements to characterize local traffic imbalance (Varaiya 2013). Capacity-aware backpressure modifies this representation to account for finite downstream storage and congestion propagation (Gregoire et al. 2015), while position-weighted backpressure (PW-MP) incorporates the spatial distribution of vehicles along links (Li and Jabari 2019). Other studies have explored traffic states that can be obtained without relying exclusively on conventional queue measurements. Travel-time-based pressure uses observed travel times to characterize traffic conditions (Mercader et al. 2020), crowdsourced delay information has been used for pressure-based traffic signal control (Dixit et al. 2020), and Delay-based Max-Pressure (D-MP) formally uses vehicle delay as the pressure metric while retaining the maximum-stability property (Liu and Gayah 2022). More recently, connected-vehicle information has enabled traffic state estimation under incomplete and spatially heterogeneous observations (Tan et al. 2021, Tan et al. 2022, Bin Al Islam et al. 2020, Comert and Cetin 2021, Tan et al. 2026c). CV-MP, for example, constructs pressure from connected-vehicle travel-time information and establishes stability conditions under partial and heterogeneous connectivity (Tan et al. 2026d). Collectively, these developments have progressively expanded the traffic states available to MP, from aggregate queues to spatial, temporal, and connected-vehicle observations.

MP has also been extended to explicitly incorporate pedestrian queues while maintaining decentralized control and network-stability properties (Liu et al. 2024). At a larger spatial scale, MP has been coupled with macroscopic perimeter control (Tsitsokas et al. 2023) and subsequently extended to incorporate regional network states directly into the pressure framework through N-MP (Liu and Gayah 2024). Alongside the choice of traffic state and control application, MP contains another fundamental design dimension: the timescale at which pressure is re-evaluated and a signal decision is reconsidered. In conventional time-step implementations, pressure is evaluated at a prescribed control interval, whereas cycle-based formulations organize MP decisions within a predefined or bounded cycle structure (Anderson et al. 2018, Levin et al. 2020). The selected timescale determines how long a pressure-based decision remains in effect before the controller reacts to newly evolving traffic conditions. Thus, MP control involves not only determining which phase should receive service, but also determining when that decision should be reconsidered. The latter is commonly specified through a control step, decision interval, cycle, or holding period rather than derived directly from the prevailing traffic load. This motivates a basic question for MP control: what is an appropriate decision timescale for a given traffic operating condition?

papers.title: Regret-Based Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control under Uncertain Traffic States
papers.abstract: Max-pressure (MP) traffic signal control selects phases using pressure scores computed from estimated traffic states, but these states are uncertain and their consequences depend on whether they alter phase ranking and how much pressure is lost. This paper develops a decision-oriented Regret-Based Max-Pressure framework that represents uncertainty through phase-selection regret, defined as the pressure loss of a candidate phase relative to the pressure-maximizing phase under each plausible latent state. We propose Stochastic Regret MP, which minimizes expected regret under a calibrated residual distribution, and Distributionally Robust (DR) Regret MP, which minimizes worst-case expected regret over a Wasserstein ambiguity set. Robustifying regret rather than absolute pressure makes the formulation invariant to state-dependent pressure components shared by all candidate phases, thereby focusing robustness on relative phase quality. We further derive an explicit queue-linear pressure-loss bound and establish strong queue stability when the net-service reserve exceeds the resulting loss coefficient. Numerical experiments show that both methods reduce normalized true-state pressure regret by about 70% relative to Point-estimate MP, while DR Regret MP yields lower network queues than direct robustification of absolute pressure. In microscopic SUMO experiments on a 28-intersection real-world network, Stochastic Regret MP and DR Regret MP reduce mean delay by 18.9% and 14.9%, respectively, and retain benefits under detector undercount and failure. The results show that representing uncertainty through its decision consequences can improve reliable traffic control under imperfect state information.

Max-pressure (MP) traffic signal control selects phases by comparing pressure scores constructed from local traffic states. Originating from maximum-throughput scheduling (Tassiulas and Ephremides 1992), MP was adapted to signalized road networks as a decentralized control principle with queue-stability guarantees for demand within the admissible region (Wongpiromsarn et al. 2012, Varaiya 2013). Subsequent studies further extended the decentralized MP framework and its network-level analysis (Le et al. 2015, Levin 2023, Liu and Gayah 2024). The combination of local computation and network-level stability makes MP attractive for large-scale traffic control. At the same time, because MP determines phase actions by ranking state-dependent pressure scores, the resulting decisions depend directly on the traffic-state information used to construct those scores.

Modern MP formulations increasingly rely on richer, and often estimated, traffic information. Beyond conventional queue lengths, existing formulations incorporate vehicle positions (Li and Jabari 2019), travel-time or delay information (Liu and Gayah 2022, Zoabi and Haddad 2025), and connected-vehicle or heterogeneous observations for traffic-state estimation under partial observation (Cao et al. 2020, Tan et al. 2026c, Tan et al. 2026a, Tan et al. 2026b). As a result, the pressures used for phase selection may depend on estimated queues, turning proportions, and effective movement service. Existing MP studies have considered unavailable turning information and noisy or estimated queues (Grégoire et al. 2014, Charalambous et al. 2023, Liaquat et al. 2024), but these treatments largely address individual information components. They do not provide a common representation of how heterogeneous traffic-state errors jointly affect the relative ranking of candidate phases and the pressure loss associated with the resulting phase decision.

Existing MP studies have considered unavailable turning information and noisy or estimated queues (Grégoire et al. 2014, Charalambous et al. 2023, Liaquat et al. 2024), but these treatments largely address individual information components. They do not provide a common representation of how heterogeneous traffic-state errors jointly affect the relative ranking of candidate phases and the pressure loss associated with the resulting phase decision.

The central difficulty is that the magnitude of a traffic-state error does not by itself determine its consequence for MP control. A sizeable perturbation can alter several phase-pressure values without changing their ordering, whereas a smaller perturbation can reverse the preferred phase when competing pressures are close. The relevant consequence of uncertainty is therefore decision-relative: it depends on how the uncertain state changes the relative quality of candidate phases and how much pressure is lost when a nonoptimal phase is selected. More broadly, traffic signal control has addressed uncertainty through stochastic, reliability-based, and robust optimization, including uncertain arrivals and demand (Jia et al. 2025, Pedroso et al. 2024), traffic-flow variation (Yin 2008, Tan et al. 2025a), uncertain turning and network interactions (Fei et al. 2023, Wan et al. 2024), and sensing or estimation errors (Jia et al. 2023, Tan et al. 2025b). These approaches incorporate uncertainty into signal timing, prediction, network flows, or estimated states, but they do not directly characterize uncertainty in pressure-based phase ranking. Regret-based optimization provides a natural decision-relative perspective by measuring the loss of a chosen action relative to the action that would be optimal under the realized uncertain state (Kouvelis and Yu 1997, Aissi et al. 2009). Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) further accounts for ambiguity in the probability distribution of uncertain states (Delage and Ye 2010, Gao and Kleywegt 2023), with Wasserstein ambiguity sets providing a data-driven construction (Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn 2018); recent studies have also combined distributional robustness with regret-based criteria (Al Taha et al. 2023, Cho and Yang 2024, Kargin et al. 2024). For MP control, however, two questions remain unresolved: how to define a decision loss that is consistent with pressure-based phase ranking, and how robustifying this decision-relative loss differs from directly robustifying absolute phase pressure under distributional ambiguity.

papers.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

papers.title: Counting curves with bounded intersection
papers.abstract: This paper counts curves, and multicurves, on hyperbolic surfaces, providing explicit upper bounds that depend polynomially on length and exponentially in terms of an upper bound on self-intersection.
papers.intro:
Curve counting, in its different forms, is a popular sport in geometric topology. In light of how they link geometric and dynamical points of view, counting closed geodesics on hyperbolic surfaces is particularly beloved. Two points of view are notable for their contrasting interpretations. The first is to consider all (primitive) closed geodesics. For closed and geodesically complete finite area surfaces, closed geodesics are dense in the unit tangent bundle, and by a theorem of Huber [21], as LL grows, the number of geodesics of length at most LL is asymptotic to eL/Le^{L}/L. In contrast, Birman and Series [5] showed that restricting to simple closed geodesics, that is those without self-intersection points, paints a completely different picture. They are nowhere dense, form a Hausdorff dimension 11 subset of the surface and only grow polynomially in length. Mirzakhani [24] famously proved that the growth function of simple closed geodesics was in fact asymptotic to a polynomial of degree the dimension of the underlying moduli space, with a leading term that depends on the geometry of the surface. So closed geodesics are everywhere, whereas simple ones are special. Understanding closed geodesics is key to understanding the geodesic flow whereas understanding simple ones is intimately related to growth in the mapping class group, the group of self-homeomorphisms of the surface up to isotopy, a group of great importance.

Here is the rough idea of the proof. We first push all curves to a geometric spine without distorting length too much, using an idea from [3]. When pushed to a spine, when you forget how parts of the curve are pasted together and in which order they appear, a multicurve now looks like a simple multicurve, the number of which can be bounded by a polynomial of the length. Additional data, such as the orientation of pieces of the curve on the spine, can also be bounded by a polynomial function of length. The key to the above inequality is to now encode the rest of the data in a way that the remaining necessary data to recover the original multicurve only depends on the upper bound on the self-intersection number KK. This is done via a type of encoding which associates binary words to the edges of the spine, and the rest of the count of words can be bounded using classical bounds on the number of multi partitions. The idea of using a word encoding for curves dates back to Poincaré and Dehn, but is particularly effective in the work of Birman-Series [5], Cohen-Lustig [11], Chas [9] and Chas-Lalley [10]. The encoding used here is also similar to one used in Torkaman’s bounds [29]. What makes the bound more effective is a clear separation between what data can be bounded by a polynomial, and which absorbs all of the length, and the exponential part, which only depends on the topology and the self-intersection number. This separation of length and intersection is reminiscent of what is called ”fixed parameter tractable” for algorithms.

papers.title: Radiation damage and recovery of SiPMs exposed to low-momentum muon beams for innovative scintillation-based muon beam monitors
papers.abstract: Silicon PhotoMultipliers (SiPMs) are among the standard devices for light detection in scintillator detectors. Some detector designs require these devices to be placed in radioactive areas or directly exposed to particle beams. Specifically, the damage from exposure to low-momentum muons is particularly important, as they have a high energy deposit and they have several applications in material science and particle physics. Eight SiPM models from different manufacturers were exposed to 29 MeV/c positive muons, with an intensity of O(10^6) muons/s for 13 hours, maximising the charge deposited in the depletion region. I-V curves were measured before/after irradiation and annealing; DCR and crosstalk analyses are ongoing, to extract dark count rate and optical crosstalk. Despite showing a measurable increase in dark current, the devices preserved operational stability. Thermal annealing has also been tested by heating the devices at 125°C, showing a recovery of the optimal SiPM features. This work is part of a collaboration between the University of Pavia and ISIS, to develop detectors for low-momentum muons (< 40 MeV/c), based on thin scintillators.

The ISIS Neutron and Muon Source features two different muon facilities[8], with a total of 7 beamlines, as shown in Figure 1. The EC muon facility is capable of delivering surface μ+\mu^{+} beams, coming from the decay of π+\pi^{+} at rest in the production target, with high intensity and fixed momentum around 29 MeV/c. On the other hand, RIKEN-RAL is a decay muon facility: in addition to surface muons, it features a decay solenoid, which transports π+/−\pi^{+/-} and allows them to decay in flight. For this reason, muons of both polarities and in momentum range 17-120 MeV/c can be delivered by RIKEN-RAL. Figure 2 shows the values of beam intensity and momenta available at RIKEN-RAL.

Several groups have developed beam monitors for muon beamlines. The most used design for low-momentum beams is a set of two planes of square scintillating fibres, either in a dense plane geometry[1, 16, 17], or with gaps between fibres[5, 13, 14, 18]. The first geometry allows for the highest spatial resolution, but it can be more difficult to assemble and it can interfere with the beam or block it completely; the second one is less invasive, but it needs thorough calibration to extract useful information, and in general it has worse spatial resolution.

A new geometry for scintillator-based beam monitors is being designed and tested as part of a collaboration between Pavia research institutions (University, INFN and CNAO) and ISIS. It basically involves a single thin scintillator read out by SiPMs in a way to reconstruct the position and shape of the scintillation site, hence the beam spot.

The easiest geometry, presented in this paper, consists of a thin scintillator coupled with a 2D SiPM matrix. However, with this setup the SiPMs are exposed directly to the muons and might go through a radiation damage process[7, 10]. In particular, muons are expected to cause lattice defects (displacements), increasing the number of generation-recombination centres, which eventually yields an increase of the dark count rate, hence an increase of the dark current. Thermal annealing (e.g. 24 hours at 125 ∘C) allows partial recombination of lattice defects, with an expected reduction of the measurable damage in terms of dark current and dark count rate. In addition, muons are not expected to modify the junction effective doping during their interaction with the nuclei, therefore, no variation in the breakdown voltage is expected. Some preliminary evidence of radiation damage of SiPMs exposed to low-momentum muon beams is presented in this work, even though extensive testing is still ongoing.

papers.title: Fiscal Dominance and Global Determinacy
papers.abstract: The existing literature on monetary-fiscal policy interactions emphasizes that an active monetary/passive fiscal policy regime causes global indeterminacy of equilibrium, supporting liquidity traps and self-fulfilling hyperinflations as possible equilibrium outcomes. In a nonlinear New Keynesian model with costly price adjustment, I show that an analogous critique, with different global macroeconomic dynamics, extends to a passive monetary/active fiscal policy regime whenever the fiscal response to government liabilities is below the steady-state real interest rate but positive. In this case, although the equilibrium is locally unique according to the Blanchard-Kahn conditions, there exist multiple inflation paths originating around the saddle path that converge asymptotically to the central bank's target rate while satisfying the private sector's transversality condition. I demonstrate that global determinacy instead requires a pure regime of fiscal dominance, with primary surpluses set independently of the real value of government liabilities. Only then are all nonlinear off-saddle trajectories ruled out as equilibria, for they violate the private sector's transversality condition or its no-Ponzi game condition, or imply an infeasible allocation. The transversality condition coincides with the government debt valuation equation, in which primary surpluses are discounted at the endogenous real interest rate, and pins down a unique initial jump in inflation onto the saddle path, leading to the unique steady state. The results imply that, when globally determinate, inflation is a fiscal phenomenon, shaped by the central bank's interest-rate policy.

One influential strand of the literature on monetary-fiscal policy interactions, initiated by Leeper (1991) and further developed by Woodford (2001, 2003, Ch. 4.4),11 1 See Canzoneri, Cumby and Diba (2010), Leeper and Leith (2016), and Bassetto and Sargent (2020) for comprehensive reviews of the literature on the interactions between monetary and fiscal policy, and Bianchi (2012, 2013) and Cochrane (2022a, 2022b) for empirical interpretations of the monetary-fiscal mix in the United States over the post-World War II period. typically points out the stabilizing properties of two alternative policy regimes. The first one is characterized by an “active monetary policy”, which overreacts to inflationary pressures according to the Taylor principle (Taylor, 1993, 1999),22 2 See also Galí (2015) and Walsh (2017) for textbook treatments, and the references therein. and a “passive fiscal policy”, which per se preserves the stability of public debt, irrespective of the inflation path. The second regime is characterized by an “active fiscal policy”, which disregards debt stabilization for any inflation trajectory, and a “passive monetary policy”, which accommodates the erosion of the real value of government liabilities through inflation to rule out debt escalation.33 3 These results are known in monetary theory as the “active/passive dichotomy”, and prove to hold in Ramsey-type economies with either flexible or sticky prices. Differently from Leeper (1991), Woodford (2001, 2003, Ch. 4.4) labels a “passive (active)” fiscal policy as “locally (non-)Ricardian”.

A common methodological feature of these monetary-fiscal studies—largely relying on the workhorse dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models—is the fact that they restrict attention to local dynamics, or small fluctuations, in the neighborhood around the steady state in which inflation is at the target rate. This simplification, however, has severe consequences for the issue of macroeconomic stability. papers.title: GELLI: A Generator for Experiential Language Learning Interactions
papers.abstract: Learning a second language requires extensive practice across situations personal to each learner, yet the most effective existing approaches --- narrative situations designed around specific learning goals and delivered through media --- demand substantial authoring effort, limiting practice to the scope of what was built. We present GELLI, a system that generates narrative practice worlds from a learner's goals: situated scenes with characters to converse with, support alongside the interaction, and reflection, all produced at runtime with no pre authored content. In a within-subjects study with 40 learners of Japanese, GELLI produced greater vocabulary recall and confidence than expert-authored videos targeting the same goals, with no significant difference in speaking performance. Learners turned remembered or imagined situations into experiences they could shape and learn through. Support made experimentation feel safe, while unexpected narrative developments and language suggestions gave them new possibilities to pursue beyond what they initially intended to practice.

papers.title: Avalanches of the Abelian sandpile on the hierarchical lattice
papers.abstract: We study the Abelian sandpile model on a sequence of finite fractal graphs: the hierarchical, or Migdal--Kadanoff, lattices. Our first main result consists of matching power-law tail bounds for the avalanche and the uniform wave started at certain "pivotal" vertices. We also establish a limiting result for the pivotal reach of the avalanche and, finally, a scaling limit for the size of a uniform wave started at a vertex of high degree.

papers.title: Pseudo-Labels as Rewards, Not Targets: Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Semi-Supervised ASR
papers.abstract: Adapting ASR to a domain with only untranscribed audio typically relies on pseudo-labeling, a strong teacher transcribes the audio and a student is fine-tuned on it. Because supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats every pseudo-label token as a target, the student inherits the teacher's errors. We show that using the same pseudo-labels as a reward reference for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is more robust to label noise. In the banking domain, GRPO yields 29.3% to 56.2% relative WER improvements over SFT on Whisper-generated labels, and the advantage holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains and four languages. While SFT reproduces almost 100% of teacher errors verbatim, GRPO passes through only 27%. Rollout statistics explain why, erroneous pseudo-label words rarely appear in on-policy rollouts, so group-relative advantages stay aligned with the clean transcript, whereas SFT forces them into the policy's support and collapses the reward variance GRPO relies on.

papers.title: Residual Expert Routing for Text-Only Domain Adaptation of Factorized Transducer ASR
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the non-blank predictor of a factorized transducer on target-domain text improves recognition on that domain but degrades performance on the source domain. A single interpolation weight between base and adapted predictors cannot resolve this: the adapted predictor helps at some prefixes and hurts at others, often within one utterance. We propose conservative residual routing: the adapted predictor becomes a residual correction to the base, and a 16k-parameter gate decides at each prefix how much of it to admit. Closing the gate reproduces the base exactly. On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retains essentially all of the text-only gain on two held-out domains (19.89 to 16.74, 20.91 to 16.21 WER) while leaving source-domain WER unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone costs 1.08 WER. Routing needs no per-domain tuning on target-domain audio. Analysis reveals the gate does not behave as a simple domain-level switch: it modulates intervention through the disagreement between the two predictors, suppressing it in-domain and amplifying it out-of-domain.

papers.title: Noisy Target Training Meets Drifting for Weakly-Supervised Speech Enhancement
papers.abstract: In speech enhancement, standard supervised training requires pairs of noisy and clean speech. Such pairs are typically created by artificially degrading clean speech, leading to a domain mismatch between synthetic training data and real recordings. Noisy target training (NyTT) mitigates this limitation by training an enhancement model to predict a noisy recording from a noisier version generated by adding extra noise. However, since the training target is noisy, NyTT might learn to leave residual noise in the enhanced output. In this paper, we address this issue in NyTT by incorporating a Sinkhorn drifting loss that matches the distribution of the enhanced speech to that of unpaired clean speech. The Sinkhorn drifting loss attracts enhanced speech toward high-density regions of the clean-speech distribution while repelling it from the current enhanced-speech distribution in latent space. This loss uses only unpaired clean speech rather than the clean counterpart of each degraded recording, preserving the weakly-supervised nature of NyTT. Experimental results on VoiceBank-DEMAND and CHiME-3 real recordings demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed combination.

papers.title: From Parameter Rebasin to Functional Transfer Across Heterogeneous Transformers
papers.abstract: Adapting pretrained Transformers to downstream tasks produces task-specific updates that are expensive to reproduce for every model variant. Reusing these updates across different depths and widths is challenging because their parameters have incompatible shapes and do not share a canonical coordinate system. We introduce Ariadne, a training-free method that transfers task-specific behavior across heterogeneous Transformers without resizing the source model or transporting its parameters. Rather than treating the source task vector, i.e. the difference in parameter space between the fine-tuned and the base models, as the object to move, Ariadne characterizes fine-tuning by the activation changes it induces at matched blocks. First, it aligns these effects to a target base through local Procrustes maps. Then, it directly synthesizes a native target update by closed-form ridge regression. Across Transformer expansion, reduction and language-model transfer, Ariadne improves target-model performance while substantially reducing the time and memory required to construct an update relative to previous cross-architecture rebasin approaches. These results show that local functional effects provide an efficient alternative to parameter transport.
