papers.title: Lessons Outlive Their Failures: A Case Study of Rules for AI Coding Agents
papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly work inside a harness: rule files such as AGENTS.md, on-demand skills, runtime hooks and automated checks. Most studies of harnesses look at a single point in time or at short benchmark runs. I report a six-week case study of my personal system of record, a plain-markdown repository that three AI agent tools edited daily under one shared rule set. I built a ledger of 118 agent failures, their fixes and whether they came back. I also tested the system's monthly LLM documentation audit against 47 known stale statements and 20 planted errors. Finally, I replayed five past failures in isolated git clones, with and without their fixes. All results come from one repository with three runs per condition, so I report them as exploratory. Stale documentation (drift) was the largest failure class (48 of 118), although 35 of those were found on one audit day. A single audit run found about half of the known drift (Claude Sonnet 5.5 mean: 50%), and at least 93% of its findings were correct. On Sonnet 5.5, the agent finished four of the five replayed tasks. In three of those four, the failure did not happen, with or without its fix. Only the stale-count failure came back without its check, and the check stopped it in every run. On older models, an agent drafted an em-dash once while the em-dash lint check was active, and the check rejected it. A written rule on run-time estimates did not change Sonnet 4.5's overestimates. These results suggest that harness lessons can outlive the failures they were written to fix, while drift persists and still needs mechanical checks. Tools that evolve a harness add lessons faster than they retire them, so they should re-test their rules from time to time and retire the obsolete ones.
papers.intro:
An AI coding agent does not act on its language model alone. It works inside a harness: the instructions it loads at session start, the skills it loads on demand, the hooks that run around its tool calls, and the checks that run before a commit is accepted [12, 43, 46]. Rule files in the repository, such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, have become the standard way to give these instructions [1, 26]. Recent studies describe what these files contain [8, 9, 18], how they grow over time [6, 4], and how they affect task cost and completion [24, 13, 48].

Recent studies describe what these files contain [8, 9, 18], how they grow over time [6, 4], and how they affect task cost and completion [24, 13, 48].

Two gaps remain. First, almost all existing studies are cross-sectional: they mine snapshots of open-source repositories or measure single-turn benchmark runs. Galster et al. call for longitudinal and experimental studies of harnesses in daily use [12]. Second, people who maintain a harness respond to agent failures by adding lessons. A lesson is either a prose rule that the model reads or an executable check that the runtime enforces. Recent frameworks automate this loop: Harness2 keeps a growing library of lessons across tasks [45], and Harness-R1 writes executable harness patches from failure traces [34]. Yet little is known about what happens to a lesson after it enters the harness. Does the failure come back? Is the lesson still needed after the model is upgraded?

The system is my personal system of record: one git repository of plain markdown files and Python scripts that holds my job search, my language learning and my life administration. Three agent runtimes (three different AI agent tools) edit this repository daily under one shared rule set. From the start of the study period, I enforced a logging policy: every repeatable agent failure and its fix had to be recorded with the reason. The commit history and change logs therefore record every harness change made through a commit or a log entry.

The paper makes three contributions. First, a ledger of 118 agent failures, coded in two LLM passes whose disagreements I resolved, with daily measurements of how much rule text the harness holds (Section 4). Second, a test of how much drift an LLM documentation audit finds, against an answer key of 47 real stale statements and 20 planted errors. Third, a replay of five past failures in throwaway git clones, with and without their fixes, on several model versions (a counterfactual replay). The results (Section 5) point to one main conclusion: lessons can outlive their failures. A behavioural failure is a mistake in what the agent does, such as quoting an outdated decision. On the current model, I could replay one behavioural failure with its written rule removed, and it did not recur. Two other failures did not occur even without their fixes. Documentation drift, by contrast, comes from how the repository changes, not from how the agent behaves. It came back again and again as the repository changed, a single LLM audit pass caught only half of it, and code checks were still needed to block it.

papers.title: Deformations of cohomology classes and spectral sequences
papers.abstract: We study spectral sequences as an obstruction theory to deforming cohomology classes via the Rees construction. A filtered complex is interpreted as an equivariant family over the affine line, in which higher spectral sequence differentials arise as obstructions to lifting cohomology classes through infinitesimal neighborhoods of the special fibre. This leads to various geometric and module-theoretic degeneration criteria. We give various applications to $\mathrm{Ext}$ spectral sequences for complex Lagrangians and the formality results of Melani-Rubió amongst others. For double complexes, we revisit the Khovanov-Qi decomposition on the Rees side and introduce a two-parameter Rees construction over the affine plane. The higher differentials of the two associated spectral sequences correspond to torsion modules supported on the thickened coordinate axes. We obtain degeneration criteria in terms of these modules and an intrinsic characterisation of the $\partial\bar\partial$-lemma.

papers.title: The Standard Deviation in VICReg Buys a Safety Margin
papers.abstract: VICReg prevents collapse with a hinge on the standard deviation of each embedding dimension, and its authors argue from the gradient that a hinge on the variance would fail. To our knowledge, this claim has not been tested experimentally. We test it in a controlled setting (ResNet-18, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), changing only the hinge and sweeping its weight $μ$ over five orders of magnitude. At the default weight ($μ= 1$), the two hinges reach the same linear-probe accuracy on CIFAR-10 (about 89.5%). Both collapse below a threshold weight, but the standard-deviation hinge's threshold is 35-130$\times$ lower. CIFAR-100 shows a consistent gap. In training, the variance hinge's gradient fades as the feature variance shrinks, while the standard-deviation hinge's does not until that variance is very small. The standard-deviation hinge therefore buys a safety margin: it keeps training at weights far below the point where the variance hinge collapses.
papers.intro:
VICReg (Bardes et al., 2022) keeps a joint-embedding model from collapsing with three loss terms: an invariance term that pulls the two views of an image together, a covariance term that decorrelates embedding dimensions, and a variance term that keeps every dimension spread out across the batch. The variance term is a hinge on the standard deviation of each dimension. Bardes et al. (2022, Section 4.1) state that using the standard deviation rather than the variance is crucial: with a hinge on the variance, the gradient vanishes as the embeddings shrink, and training collapses. This argument is made from the form of the gradient; to our knowledge it has not been tested directly. The EB-JEPA library (Terver et al., 2026), which we build on, uses the same standard-deviation hinge.

papers.title: Instability of mean curvature flow in expander coordinates
papers.abstract: We study rotationally symmetric graphical solutions to mean curvature flow that are initially close to a homothetic reference expander, in particular near infinity. Based on a computer algebra aided proof, we show that under appropriate conditions, at large times, the solutions are closer to a different expander than to the reference expander.

papers.title: Hot Spots: From Smooth to Nonsmooth Simply Connected Planar Domains
papers.abstract: Assuming the absence of interior local extrema for first positive Neumann eigenfunctions on bounded smooth simply connected planar domains, as reported in \cite{SmoothInput}, we extend the hot spots conclusion to simply connected domains of finite area with compact Sobolev embedding and simple first positive Neumann eigenvalue. The supremum and infimum are approached in arbitrarily thin boundary layers. For bounded domains and eigenfunctions continuous up to the boundary, both extrema are attained on the boundary. We also transfer polynomial Neumann heat-kernel bounds uniformly along a conformal exhaustion and construct explicit bounded and unbounded examples, including domains with cusps and a domain with infinitely many corners and bottlenecks. Some of these examples admit no polynomial Neumann heat-kernel bound.
papers.intro:
The hot spots conjecture of J. Rauch asserts that a first positive Neumann eigenfunction of a planar domain attains its maximum and minimum on the boundary. See [8] for a precise formulation. The conjecture has inspired a vast literature, with connections to probability, analysis, partial differential equations, and geometry. These notes make no attempt to survey this literature, and results closely related to the questions considered here may have been overlooked. These notes take an assertion about smooth domains as an external hypothesis and derive a weaker conclusion for domains with irregular boundary.

Deng, Jiang, and Yang [22] prove that the maximum modulus of every first positive Neumann eigenfunction on a bounded convex planar domain is attained only on the boundary. Their result requires neither boundary smoothness nor simplicity of the eigenvalue. For centrally symmetric convex planar domains, they obtain the strict hot spots conclusion for both extrema. Atar and Burdzy [6] construct a bounded starlike Lipschitz domain in three dimensions with simple first positive Neumann eigenvalue whose corresponding eigenfunction has its unique global maximum at an interior point.

papers.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
papers.abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every incoming message, its type and urgency and whether to draft a reply, create a task or ignore it. In production these decisions are delegated to a generative LLM or to rules, and their error rate is rarely measured. We describe Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, a frozen snapshot of the model input, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, and human labels collected in the agent's own review loop) that produces ground truth before any training. On 231 real emails in Italian and English we compare the production rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, five typed decision models, local and hosted (Tev1, Nimble, Jev), and three hosted generative LLMs. Four results. First, the production rules for message type score 28% against a 58% majority class. Second, with about two hundred labels a logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90) at a latency three orders of magnitude lower; the best zero-shot system reaches 0.74 on type. Third, the sender's relationship to the owner is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy on the 63% of emails whose sender has been seen before. Fourth, per-email accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the baseline ignores 18% of the emails that needed a reply or a task, against 4% for the best generative model; a cost-chosen threshold cuts that rate to 6% and makes the classifier the cheapest system at every price on the unbiased corpus. A third, adversarially sampled round (722 emails in total) with eleven pre-registered hypotheses confirms seven and refutes four. Two blind annotators agree with the reference at kappa = 0.81 and 0.86 on type. We release the protocol, the harness and the pre-registration; the emails stay private.
papers.intro:
A growing share of what personal AI agents do is not generation but decision: which project does this email belong to, is it urgent, does it need a reply, is it noise. Generative LLMs answer these questions by producing text that is then parsed; typed decision models, introduced with TypeSafe’s Jev in September 2026 [1] and followed within weeks by open models (Nimble [2], Tev1, Clef, Strands Decider) and a local endpoint in Ollama [3], answer them directly with a probability distribution over caller-defined options, in one forward pass and without free text.

Whether this new class of models is good enough to replace the generative step in a personal agent is an empirical question, and it cannot be answered with the data such agents typically keep: the stored labels are the model’s own output. Early evidence is mixed. Classical classifiers trained on a few thousand records outperform Jev on network-traffic classification [7]; a community benchmark reports a plain 9B instruct model ahead of every decision model on triage tasks; the vendor’s own benchmark places the open models within three points of Jev [3]. None of it concerns personal, multilingual correspondence.

papers.title: Conformance as a Distribution: Delegation Contracts, Error Budgets, and the Allocation of Evaluation Authority in Use-Based AI Regulation
papers.abstract: Use-based AI regulation assigns obligations by deployment risk but lacks an evidentiary object to carry them. A benchmark score is a property of a model; conformance of a deployment is a failure rate under a declared distribution of contexts, bounded by a scope and subject to expiry. We take the delegation contract of earlier work (frozen configuration, scoped claim, executable revision rule) and study it under strategic play between a deployer, an auditor, and an enforcement point. We ask whether a declared context mixture can be made truthful; whether an audit can be unbiased against a system that detects evaluation traffic; whether a certification error budget can sustain a long-lived deployment; whether an aggregate audit can support a per-subgroup guarantee; and whether an incident metric that counts system failures but not fallback costs ranks arrangements correctly. For each we give a mechanism and a proposition: a proper-scoring penalty on the declared mixture bounds the excess failure of a best-responding deployer by $O(λ^{-1/2})$ in the penalty weight; a commit-reveal audit drawn from live traffic is unbiased by construction and grades the evaluator with the same sample; a halving error budget drives certification coverage below $(1-p)^n$ while $α$-investing sustains it under a marginal false-certification guarantee; a per-subgroup guarantee costs audit size scaling as $1/m$ in subgroup mass; and any failure-only incident metric prefers withdrawal at every fallback cost, even when total loss ranks the arrangements oppositely. Five preregistered synthetic studies test each claim; no language model or production system is evaluated. Enforcement sits at distribution, capability-access, monetization and risk-transfer choke points, expiry of the conformance record is a standard of care, and conformance-as-a-rate is set against the EU AI Act's static conformity assessment.
papers.intro:
A regulatory regime that assigns obligations by the use to which an AI system is put, rather than by the artifact from which it is built, needs an object that can carry an obligation. That object cannot be a benchmark score. A score is a property of a model measured under one protocol; an obligation attaches to a deployment: a model together with its prompts, tools, memory, resource limits, fallback and the rule that decides when the system acts. Prior work has argued that such a deployment should be evaluated through a delegation contract: a frozen configuration, a scoped claim about its failure rate under a declared mixture of contexts, and an executable rule that withdraws the claim when its assumptions no longer hold [1]. That work is single-agent decision theory: an evaluator chooses experiments to minimize decision regret at stated cost.

The present paper studies the same object once a second party enters. A deployer who declares the mixture has an interest in the declaration. A system under audit may recognize audit traffic. A firm that re-enters a deployment many times exhausts any fixed error budget. An aggregate audit says nothing about a small subgroup. An incident regime that counts failures but not the cost of the human fallback rewards the wrong arrangement. None of these is a statistical problem in the ordinary sense; each is a problem of who declares what, who holds which budget, and what the enforcement point can verify. We call the resulting object a regulatory conformance claim and give five mechanisms that make it truthful, verifiable, sustainable, fair and enforceable, each with a proposition and a preregistered synthetic study.

The thesis can be stated in one sentence. Conformance of an AI deployment is a distribution, not a property: a failure rate under a declared mixture, holding at a declared confidence within a declared scope, until a declared expiry. The paper’s contribution is to show what follows institutionally when that definition is taken seriously, and to locate the places where the definition cannot be enforced by statistics alone.

papers.title: Ampe-DB: A Dataset for Human Activity and Interaction Analysis Using the Ghanaian Game Ampe
papers.abstract: Human activity recognition benchmarks underrepresent culturally situated forms of movement and interaction. We introduce Ampe-DB, a multimodal dataset based on Ampe, a traditional Ghanaian game involving coordinated jumping, leg movements, and two-person interaction. It contains 637 canonical clips from 15 participants, with RGB video, two-person pose representations, participant and pair metadata, four-class movement labels, and derived binary movement-relation labels. We evaluate four-class movement recognition and binary movement-relation classification using three protocols: a duplicate-safe fixed benchmark, four-fold pair-held-out evaluation, and participant-held-out diagnostics for participants with complete class coverage. Baselines comprise a frozen Kinetics-400-pretrained R(2+1)D-18 RGB encoder, a two-layer bidirectional GRU for pose sequences, and validation-selected RGB-pose late fusion. For four-class recognition, RGB macro-F1 falls from 0.955 on the fixed benchmark to 0.418 under pair-held-out evaluation and 0.384 under participant-held-out evaluation. Pose is more robust, achieving 0.957, 0.811, and 0.839 across the same protocols. Fusion reaches 0.976 on the fixed benchmark and 0.824 under pair-held-out evaluation, but does not consistently improve on pose under participant shift. Binary movement-relation recognition also becomes substantially harder under held-out evaluation, especially for different-leg configurations. These findings show that strong fixed-benchmark scores can mask failures to generalize across people and pairings. Ampe-DB supports research on fine-grained movement recognition, human-human interaction, multimodal learning, and identity-aware generalization.

papers.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
papers.abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI drafts of the same kind of brief, built from SEC filings made after the models' training data were collected. Told the drafter's true error rate, the reviewer checked more as it rose, but all-or-nothing, switching near where its prompt's costs break even. Told that the drafter erred ten times less often than it did, it checked 7 fewer of 9 figures and let a wrong figure through in 22.5% of briefs instead of none: faster and worse, entirely through reduced effort.
